Tuchel did not have to work hard to persuade him to return to the England fold, he said: “The boss didn’t need to say too much. The effort he made to speak to me and reach out was so nice, and I really appreciated it. I think when you see a manager like that you want to learn from him. It was a huge thing to play for Thomas.”

Dan Burn has been called into the squad after Marc Guéhi withdrew with an injury.

Sports.title: Manchester City’s Kerstin Casparij: ‘I love football – but it takes over your life’
Sports.content:
Kerstin Casparij loves football, especially Champions League nights under the lights, but perspective is important too. “I would say football is my most important secondary thing in life, and I’ve found that such a refreshing way of looking at it,” she says before Manchester City’s trip to Milan to face Inter on Tuesday.

“It is so important to me and I love it so much and if I lose I’m going to have a terrible day, but my family’s healthy, my friends are healthy, I am, and I don’t have to worry about anything; I don’t have to worry about getting the food on the table. Being able to see things from that perspective makes it so much easier to stay the person I’ve always been.”

The 26-year-old Dutch full-back has had a phenomenal year, winning a first league title and FA Cup with Manchester City in her fourth season in England. Casparij was integral, having arguably her best season in the Women’s Super League, scoring three times and providing seven assists – the joint-most assists in the league with Aston Villa’s Lynn Wilms.

Key to her growth last season under Andrée Jeglertz was that “now I’m allowed to really play on almost the whole right side”, she says. “And I’m allowed to and trusted with pushing forward and taking risks in the final third.”

Like all team players, Casparij credits her teammates, but her contribution was recognised with a place on the Ballon d’Or shortlist. She finished in 24th place, the fifth-highest defender.

Being able to share these wins with her team outside the team is important too. They “work tirelessly to help me out”, she says. “Especially my partner, who is so invested in my career and has been such an incredible support and helped me out in more ways than I can count. There are so many incredible people around me and I’m just really happy I can give back to them as well, as much as I’m proud of myself for achieving it.”

Casparij’s authenticity, openness and playfulness have made her a fan favourite, not only at City but across the league. Her pun-loaded Instagram captions are as witty and self-critical after a defeat as they are sharp when City win. She is funny, shows fire on the pitch and is not afraid of banter with rivals, and is also a passionate advocate for the causes that matter to her, including as an LGBT Foundation patron and by sharing her experiences growing up with ADHD. Social media is a key tool for connecting.

View image in fullscreen Kerstin Casparij: ‘I’m allowed to and trusted with pushing forward and taking risks in the final third.’ Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

“I always want to be me and I want people that I knew 10 years ago to now speak to me and be able to be like: ‘Oh you haven’t changed a single bit, you’re still the same person.’ I have a lot of friends outside of football and it gives you such a sense of normality because football, the industry, is not normal and we are not necessarily normal.”

The connection with people matters because it cuts through the abnormality. “We’re in the spotlight every three days at times. We’re getting judged on our performance, we’re getting judged on how we do our work, so I kind of need that sense of normality to make sure I don’t take things too seriously and really keep both my feet on the ground.”

Having a partner who isn’t fazed by what comes with being a professional football player and understands the schedule and lifestyle is a big part of that. “I absolutely love football, I love everything about it, but it takes over your life and it’s definitely taken over ours,” she says. “You need a partner that understands that and loves it and is like: ‘Yeah, let’s do this together.’

“I’m so grateful for her and am so appreciative of her. She’s got weekends off but she doesn’t really have weekends off because they all revolve around me. Life revolves around me a lot and I try to make extra effort to make sure she knows it’s about her, too. We’re definitely a two-person team here, but to have her support and know she’s always there, she’s a massive part of my football journey.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

That journey has taken her a long way from Heerenveen, for whom she made her debut at 15. Almost two years ago, when Casparij signed a new long-term City contract, she told the Guardian she felt she had unfinished business at the club. She wanted to win, so what did securing the Double in May feel like? “Incredible. It was such a long time coming and I’d been dreaming of that for so long.

“There was a big feeling of relief. We were very determined to win the league and I feel like we remained very calm for very, very long, pretty much up until the end. We just knew what we needed to do to get the job done and we made a big point of having a winning language. As a leadership team we started to talk about ‘when’ we win the league rather than ‘if’ to create an environment that believed and where everyone was going to do everything we could to win.”

View image in fullscreen Kerstin Casparij was 24th on this year’s Ballon d’Or rankings and the fifth-highest defender. Photograph: Mike Egerton/PA

Whether City can retain their title is the big question. They did not play in the Champions League last season and there were questions before this campaign over whether they could juggle the workload. After nine games they are top and unbeaten, two points clear of Chelsea, who drew 1-1 with Everton at the weekend, before their meeting on Saturday at Stamford Bridge. City look as formidable as ever in attack but earned only their second clean sheet in their 5-0 defeat of West Ham on Saturday. In the Champions League, they have three draws from three games as they get reacquainted with the demands of European competition.

Were they aware of the doubts some had in pre-season? “Late last season some were still thinking we were going to bottle it,” Casparij says with a smile. “We see it. I’m not going to say we don’t, because we all follow the media, we all have social media, but it’s not something that gets really discussed very heavily. But it definitely adds fuel to our fire …

“It also allows us, as a team, to keep innovating, to keep thinking: ‘OK, what can we change? What can we improve? Where can we get better? Where do we sometimes need to tweak little things? What does the opponent do?’ And that’s the beauty of it and the fun part because it never gets boring.”

Sports.title: Manchester’s soulless content machine football clubs sum up post-imperial Britain | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
In Manchester this weekend it was possible to bookend your Thursday‑to‑Sunday entertainment with two cultural events. First up, a debut screening of the re‑released and uncensored Ken Russell film The Devils at Trafford Odeon. And three days later, three miles down the road, Manchester United versus Aston Villa at Old Trafford.

As expected, one of these events provided a visceral cinematic experience, a deeply disturbing two-hour public meditation on the meaning of faith, blood, fear, power, ritual and the fetishising of objects, climaxing in an orgiastic crowd scene of depraved but undeniably erotic abandon, all acted out on a set in a state of glorious and performative ruin. And the other one was a film with Oliver Reed in it.

By the final whistle that wild 4‑4 draw at Old Trafford felt like a fitting endpoint to the opening quarter of the Premier League season. As we head into a 12‑day international break it is customary at this point to take a set of readings, to anatomise the season to date, to offer up a state of the Premier League address.

Five games since the last time we did this, not a great deal has changed. Brighton have maintained their luminous insurgent energy. The headline chart-breakers are Tottenham, up from second‑bottom to 11th. The official Home Office Spurs In Crisis threat level has been downgraded from Definitely In Crisis to Probably In Crisis A Bit Later On. Roberto De Zerbi no longer looks like a doomed and haunted cartoon caterpillar. Instead he looks like a feisty and fun haunted cartoon caterpillar.

Otherwise there has been only one story in town across that autumn segment. And that story is Manchester, and the extraordinary contortions of two contrasting, but deeply conjoined mega-clubs.

Manchester City’s run from October to November kicked off with the guilty verdict on almost all of their financial charges, followed by an adrenal victory at Anfield, and finally a run of three problematic league defeats. United have basically fallen through the floor in the same period: played eight in all comps, won one, and a point off the bottom of the Premier League table.

At the same time both Manchester clubs have dominated the news cycle, inexhaustible content machines, and the source of football-adjacent stories so strange and so vast they threaten to surge up over the seawall and consume the rest of the league.

It is necessary at this point to talk about Michael Carrick and whether he has been sacked yet (current answer: no). It seems likely that this will happen in the current break, once the designated replacement has been lined up. Another Manchester United paradox: only here, in the realm of the mid-season panic-sacking do we suddenly feel ourselves in the hands of a slick and well-practised machine. Stand aside. We’re old hands at this. Leave it to the experts.

View image in fullscreen Manchester United fans stage a protest before the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday. Photograph: Conor Molloy/ProSports/Shutterstock

But Carrick is of course essentially another bystander to the ongoing reactor core meltdown. He didn’t appoint Michael Carrick. He has done nothing surprising in his role as head coach, simply been the best Michael Carrick he can be, which is a Michael Carrick unqualified for this level of management.

Even the club executives captured by the TV pictures in insinuating close-up every week are essentially bit-part players, useful idiots for the regime: the director of football, Jason Wilcox, who looks every week a bit more like an office clerk trapped inside a hijacked foreign embassy trying to signal desperately with his eyes that he’s close to the edge and can someone in a flak jacket please appear at the fire escape window pretty soon. And the chief executive, Omar Berrada, who personally oversaw the Manchester City commercial sponsorship regime, and surely can’t be allowed to stay in his role at a listed company if the appeal against City’s charges is dismissed.

These are just the visible symptoms, not the cause. This is what happens when you run an institution where it is necessary to appoint people at significant levels who are willing to exist at a compromised level, who feel delighted to have the chance to run this organisation, even badly.

And by now it feels too easy to say the obvious thing. Manchester United have one competent but entirely self-motivated majority owner, for whom this has been a wonderful financial opportunity; and another owner whose only addition to the spectacle is to demonstrate the non‑transferable skills of the average billionaire.

We know this now. United are trapped in a cycle of self‑consumption. It is an ingrained, self-cannibalising decline, like a depressed post‑industrialised city in miniature. All that remains is rust, people and unspent heritage.

But it has also created something extraordinary in the past few weeks. Right now the Old Trafford match‑day atmosphere feels entirely unlike anything else, not just in sport but any other human activity at which you care to point.

View image in fullscreen Roberto De Zerbi no longer looks like a doomed and haunted cartoon caterpillar. Instead he looks like a feisty and fun haunted cartoon caterpillar. Photograph: Scott Heppell/Reuters

The periphery is now enshrined definitively as The Event. Here is a man in sodden navy woollen menswear haunted by strange noises, striding the touchline like King Lear on his way to a golfing weekend. Here is the United crowd clamped together inside a clanky and leaking stadium, gripped by macro‑forces, shouting at the tides of power, a drama of alienation taking place just beyond the white lights around the lip of the stand.

The currents of energy are so mixed and nuanced. Who is cheering what? Where exactly is the love, the fear, the rage directed at this moment? Like all the best human dramas it is both sweeping and bathetic, thousands of human souls in that same shared space, all focused on an abstract idea, the act of faith and memory they identify collectively as Manchester United, while in front of them Harry Maguire trots about like an ageing police horse and Diogo Dalot attempts to play football with his legs on the wrong way round.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

To the unconverted, football can seem like a distraction, a silly thing, the society of the spectacle with the society part aggressively deleted. But there is still something noble about howling into this physical space, about expressing dissent, protest, rage, which is the opposite of so many things that are unsatisfying about the wider world: fakery, remote emotion, remote experience.

Take a look at the world that surrounds the team on the pitch: asset-stripping owners, branding overload, a club that is entirely committed to monetising your emotions. To rage at this thing is not just rational and human but an appropriate act of resistance.

This is where the autumn 2026 version of Manchester City also enters the picture. On the pitch City were muddled and unusually open in midfield during the 3-1 defeat by an excellent Nottingham Forest on Saturday. But something has changed around the club in this period, expressed most powerfully in that travelling support.

The urge to defy the independent tribunal verdict, to lean into being “villains”, has been a little baffling from the outside. It is hard to understand how truth, freedom, sunlight, the little man kicking against the pricks is compatible with swallowing the party line of an autocratic propaganda project.

But the space is more complex than that, the tension less linear. The City fans in Cheetos shirts waving inflatable mnemonic bananas, raising their fists to the world, have also become strangely captivating, persuasive, unexpectedly likeable.

View image in fullscreen The Manchester clubs feel in their separate ways like a version of their own city’s modern form. Photograph: Michael Zemanek/Shutterstock

Because this is also at bottom a protest against a world that feels beyond your reach. Forget the accounting regulation stuff and it isn’t hard to find plenty that is cheerless in the Premier League model, in the complete prostration of elite football at the altar of money. Whatever its source, no matter how muddled the logic, there is a base‑level majesty in this spectacle of defiance and collectivism.

If it feels addictive, moreish, impossible to look away from, then maybe this is because something authentic is happening in a world of fakery and illusions. The Manchester clubs feel in their separate ways like a version of their own city’s modern form, of the way post‑post‑imperial Britain has tried to create energy from inward investment or stripping its parts, selling its soul for some glass and steel high-rises and a tramline. It is a process that also includes turning supporters of a football club into product, a piece of staging, the trees on an architects drawing.

There is no obvious solution to this, no way of reversing that process given the selling off of land, control, intellectual property, just as it can seem like there is no obvious practical route towards the soft, comforting, previously attainable things Andy Burnham conjures up in his speeches about the future.

But it is interesting to see football directly confronting this alienation, expressing, however incoherently, that the only sensible response is a refusal to be silent. The Premier League is in its own way a perfect reflection of the nation, with its ailing but wealthy boomer generation, its lightweight pop-up entities filling the vacant spaces in the high street.

The other key story of the autumn period is of course Arsenal, who are basically London in the form of a football club, economically functional, geographically privileged, ticking along under its carefully curated restrictions. Is this the story of the season from here? Even with 28 games still to play it is hard to see Arsenal’s five‑point lead as anything other than a steady progression towards another league title.

At the same time every metric, from social media spikes to estimated TV figures, suggests that the event of the weekend was by some distance a theatrical but essentially meaningless 4-4 draw in the rain on Sunday night. Drink it in. Raise a fist to the world. Manchester has been the capital of English football for so long. It remains, even in a state of football‑adjacent crisis, its most potent spectacle, still able to provide a sense of something real in a post-real world.

Sports.title: Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’
Sports.content:
In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.”

With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week.

View image in fullscreen Players and staff line up during the tribute in Tenerife to Jesús de Miguel. Photograph: Borja Suárez/Reuters

Two days earlier Tenerife had been in Navahermosa, La Mancha, the tiny village their teammate’s family are from, carrying the coffin of the friend their captain called “our Demigol”. They were supposed to be in Granada on Saturday; instead, they were back on the island, in their home ground, to say goodbye and pay homage. Publicly, this time. Lilies had been laid on the pitch there too, a Tenerife shirt with them, and a stage built at one end. “We’ve seen how fragile life is,” the captain, Enric Gallego, said, offering words he said could never be enough, carrying the burden for all of them. “We think of the journeys, the wins, the losses, and hold on to those moments that seemed normal, but that now … a few days ago we shared that with you. To talk of you in the past tense is unfair. None of us are prepared to live what we’re living through.”

View image in fullscreen Tenerife’s Enric Gallego speaks during his tribute to Jesús de Miguel. Photograph: Borja Suárez/Reuters

No one ever could be. Across Spain this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them. That, Budimir had told his teammates, was something they must think about but not think about too. The players’ union in which De Miguel had a role, a footballer there for others, had asked for the competition to stop. Respect demanded that it did, they said, requesting a judge intervene when the league did not hear them. But it had gone on. The only matches postponed were those involving Tenerife; Andorra, whose goalkeeper Jesús Owono had crashed into De Miguel; and Castellón, who he had taken to the second division, delivering them to segunda for the first time in 16 years and himself for the first time at all, aged 27.

On the eve of the game that opened this weekend’s fixtures, the Sevilla head coach, Luis García, said he thought they should wait. It was too soon, too raw, too theirs. His midfielder Giorgi Kochorashvili had missed training the day before: a former Castellón player, Kochorashvili had asked permission to go to the funeral, leaving early and returning late, his mind elsewhere. Of course he could, García had replied, “we are humans above all else”. And it was not just him. García had worked with Owono – “let’s not make two victims, we have had enough; he is in hell, for sure”, he had pleaded – and now he said: “If there’s a play that’s similar … what do I say to my goalkeeper?

“We need time,” García had said. “We need to reflect.”

Instead, they played. From Seville on Friday night to Madrid on Sunday, via stadiums everywhere. It was, some suggested, the best way to pay homage to De Miguel but no one truly knew. “We can’t ask him what he would have wanted,” José Mourinho said before Madrid went to Valencia and won 3-0, Tenerife’s flag flying at half-mast at Mestalla. He might not have wanted anything at all. “You never wanted any attention,” Gallego said, but this weekend he was on all their minds.

“Forever in our memories,” the league’s line read. At every game in the first and second divisions, the ritual was repeated. Teams came out together wearing the same white shirts bearing his name. Flowers were laid, a little uncomfortably, on the spot inside the centre circle where he had fallen and there was a minute’s silence, players and officials gathered around the wreath. As they stood before Cádiz-Oviedo, tears ran down the cheeks of the Tenerife-based referee Marta Huerta de Aza. On stadium screens, an image of De Miguel appeared. On television screens, a QR code did: a link to a crowdfunding campaign for the young family he left, set up by the former Tenerife player Fran Sol.

View image in fullscreen Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé after a minute’s silence in memory of De Miguel at Mestalla. Photograph: Pablo Morano/Reuters

The games began and then, in the ninth minute or as near as the referee could manage, they paused again: the teams stopped, looking up to the screen, where a video of his best moments played out. It was not always an easy watch, and some preferred not to.

At Sevilla, where fans saw Antonio Puerta collapse on the pitch and pass away, applause still offered in the 16th minute every game, Kochorashvili stood by the bench, eyes lost somewhere his mind was not. At Espanyol, where in the 21st minute they applaud Dani Jarque, the captain who died during a pre-season tour and to whom Andrés Iniesta dedicated the winning goal at the 2010 World Cup final, Álex Calatrava and Álvaro González, teammates at Castellón and Tenerife respectively, looked about to break. In the ninth minute at the Metropolitano, the place was still rocking, the timing out of sync: Giuliano Simeone had just scored, so the referee Javier Alberola Rojas allowed a couple of minutes to pass, choosing his moment, Diego Simeone helping him impose silence on the stands when he finally stopped it. Then they started again, expected to carry on regardless.

In Pamplona, Alejandro Catena, who scored the late equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Athletic, raised an Osasuna shirt with De Miguel’s name and number on the back. Theirs was the game that felt most out of place, attention drawn from where it should have been, where it was. It would not be true to say that it did not matter, the Osasuna head coach, Jagoba Arrasate, admitting he had been carried along with it like everyone else, the calmness he thought they had found in the months out of the game soon abandoned again.

View image in fullscreen The Diocese of Tenerife, Eloy Alberto Santiago, speaks during Jesús de Miguel’s tribute. Photograph: Borja Suárez/Reuters

As they played, grateful for the grand day that they had before them, all the days they did, the tribute continued in Tenerife. The Heliodoro had filled early, access by every gate except eight and nine, engulfed by flowers and candles. De Miguel’s shirt lay on the turf where he had, lilies to one side, a spotlight on it. Another wreath occupied the bench. A giant shirt stretched across one end where the stage was, a lectern awaiting the speakers. A cross presided over it. Staff and players wore No 9 badges on their lapels. Supporters came in Tenerife shirts. And in the yellow shirts of rivals Las Palmas, whose president and captain Kirian, who had recovered after cancer, came. “This is the Canaries I want,” said Tenerife’s majority shareholder, Rayco García.

In the seats set up on the pitch, Tenerife’s players and De Miguel’s family sat, their eyes heavy. The archbishop, Eloy Alberto Santiago led a mass. The club’s president and majority shareholder spoke. He promised they would never allow María, De Miguel’s widow, to be alone. He also announced they would adopt Carla, his 14-month-old daughter, supporting her economically until she is 18. Gallego addressed her, football as family meaning something. “I hope one day you can look back and see who your dad was, be proud of him, not just for the footballer he was but the person: for his humility, his goodness,” he said.

Sniffing, his voice breaking, the captain paid homage to his teammate, his strike partner, his friend. The kind of person, he said, who did not seem to be there, and definitely did not demand that people notice he was, but always was. A man, he noted, so disinclined to put anyone out that when his car broke down he walked home from training rather than bother anyone for a lift. That, he insisted, might not seem like much, but it said much. “Today we don’t want to talk only of the player; we want to talk about you, Jesús, about the person that was behind the shirt,” he had begun. “Above any game, any team, what really remains is the person and the impact you leave. And you were a very special person.”

Gallego gave way to the archbishop, orations led by Tenerife staff, and as the act came to a close, difficult days ahead, the spotlight taken elsewhere, the drums began and the fans belted out a familiar tune, once more with more meaningful than ever before:

double quotation mark We have to sing with even more strength if you’re losing

Even those who left us sing, from heaven

This will never stop

We will sing to eternity.”

Then Tenerife’s players departed. They have training on Monday and next week they play.

Sports.title: Tom Brady ends tenure as investor in Birmingham City after three years
Sports.content:
Tom Brady has ended his three-year involvement as a ⁠minority investor in Birmingham City, the English second-tier club said on Monday, ⁠thanking the seven-times ⁠Super ​Bowl champion for his support.

“Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude ⁠to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the club ⁠over the last three years,” the Championship side ​said in a ‌statement.

“It was truly ‌amazing to have someone with Tom’s experience and ‌passion associated with the club, and the club looks forward to continuing to build on that foundation from the training ground to the Birmingham community.“

The club gave no reason for Brady’s ‌departure and did not specify what would happen to his stake.

The former NFL ​quarterback joined Birmingham’s ownership group in August 2023 through a partnership with Knighthead Capital Management, becoming a minority investor and chair of a new ⁠advisory board.

Brady, 49, also holds minority stakes in ​the NFL’s ​Las Vegas Raiders ​and the WNBA’s Las Vegas Aces.

His departure ​comes as ‌Birmingham enjoy ​a ​strong Championship campaign, sitting top of the standings on goal difference with 29 points after 15 matches.

Sports.title: The little-known new face called up by England: Can you name the star brought in to replace Ezri Konsa?
Sports.content:
The little-known new face called up by England: Can you name the star brought in to replace Ezri Konsa?

Thomas Tuchel has made a first-time England call-up to replace Ezri Konsa - but casual fans could be forgiven if they do not recognise the latest Three Lions addition.

He is not a widely-recognised face among the stars from the Premier League and other top European leagues in Tuchel's selection but James Hill, 24, has starred for Bournemouth in their eight-match winning run under Marco Rose this season.

The central defender, who started his career at Fleetwood Town, has enjoyed a dream few months: He married partner Tara Rose in June, welcomed his first child in August and has now had his maiden England call.

England announced today that Arsenal defender Konsa will not be in contention to face Croatia at Wembley on Thursday night - although he will be fit to potentially face Spain away on Sunday - and Hill has been called up in his place.

Hill has played for England's Under 20s and Under 21s but this is his first senior call. He was signed by Bournemouth for just £1million in 2022 - beating Sheffield United, Burnley, Leeds, Southampton, Tottenham and even Barcelona, who all checked on his progress.

Bournemouth's official X account posted today: 'Congratulations, Hilly. Our defender has earned a first senior @England call-up.'

James Hill - pictured with new wife Tara - has been called up to the latest England squad (Source: Instagram/james_hill_10)

Hill has starred for Bournemouth in their eight-match winning run under Marco Rose

Hill's route to the top is a fascinating one. He attended a trial day at Fleetwood as a 14-year-old and managed to impress them enough to earn place at their new academy.

It proved to be a shrewd piece of talent identification, with Hill later becoming the club's record sale, eclipsing the fee they received for Jamie Vardy.

And having signed for the Cherries in 2022, Hill has now established himself as a key member of Marco Rose's side.

He's played every minute of every Premier League match this season at the heart of the defence and clearly Tuchel has been impressed.

Speaking before his call-up, Hill said: 'It’s every kid’s dream, isn’t it? You grow up watching the Three Lions on TV, for the World Cup, the Euros. It’s one of the greatest honours you can have in football.'

More to follow..

Sports.title: Michael Carrick arrives early to face his fate: Man United boss drives into training at 7.15am - with Old Trafford chiefs set for Monaco summit to determine under-fire manager's future
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick’s fate as Manchester United head coach is set to be decided on Wednesday when chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox meet with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco.

Berrada and Wilcox will make their recommendation to Ratcliffe, with all the indications pointing to Carrick being sacked after United dropped into the relegation zone.

It’s understood that the Old Trafford hierarchy would want to inform Carrick of their decision face to face, so there may not be any confirmation from the club until Thursday.

The 45-year-old turned up for work at Carrington at 7.15am on Tuesday to oversee training with the players who are not away on international duty amid increasing uncertainty over his future.

The manager's position increasingly precarious after they dropped into the relegation zone despite salvaging a 4-4 draw against Aston Villa at Old Trafford on Sunday.

It left him with just one win from ten Premier League games this season – United’s worst start since Sir Alex Ferguson replaced Ron Atkinson 40 years ago.

Carrick is taking training as usual this morning - with a cut-down group of players as a number of United's stars have departed on international duty.

Michael Carrick is pictured arriving at Manchester United's training ground at 7.15am

Mauricio Pochettino is the frontrunner to replace Carrick - leaving his role as US head coach

Mauricio Pochettino has emerged as a new frontrunner to replace Carrick. The Argentine is currently in charge of the US national team, but his contract includes a £7million release clause.

Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann, who were both under consideration when United gave Carrick more time to turn the season around following a 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth last month, could also be in contention.

In the three games since then, Carrick’s side lost at Chelsea, staged a remarkable comeback to beat Roma in the Champions League in midweek and then fought back again to draw with Villa.

Although it’s understood that no final decision has been reached over Carrick’s future and insiders say that speculation over his sacking is premature, the expectation within Old Trafford is that a new man will be in charge for the visit to Anfield a week on Sunday.

Carrick replaced Ruben Amorim in mid-January and the former United midfielder was handed a two-year contract in May after guiding United to a third-place finish and qualification for the Champions League, losing just two of his 17 games as head coach.

But this season has unravelled alarmingly for United with his only two wins in 15 games in all competitions coming at home to newly promoted Ipswich and Sabah of Azerbaijan.

Asked after Sunday’s chaotic draw with Villa if he would consider quitting, a defiant Carrick said: ‘That's not going to happen.

‘We’re in November. I don’t like this situation and where we are. But we can do something about it. I'm quite clear with what direction the club needs to go in, and it's got to win games.’

Avram Glazer and Sir Jim Ratcliffe, co-owners, are pictured at Old Trafford in September

Sacking Carrick would leave United searching for their eighth permanent manager or head coach since Ferguson retired 13-and-a-half years ago.

Pochettino was strongly linked with the job when Erik ten Hag was appointed in 2022 and again when the Dutchman was sacked two years later.

The 54-year-old has extensive Premier League experience at Tottenham, Chelsea and Southampton and was also in charge at Paris Saint-Germain.

Howe was previously seen as the favourite but it’s understood there has been no contact between United and the former Newcastle boss.

It would cost United around £3million in compensation to appoint the 48-year-old under the terms of his departure from St James’s Park in July.

Nagelsmann is available after leaving his role as head coach of the German national team in the summer when they were eliminated from the World Cup following a penalty shootout defeat by Paraguay in the round of 32.

NOW READ: Ian Ladyman on what Man United, with their seemingly addictive habit, must do now once Michael Carrick is sacked

Sports.title: Forget Eddie Howe or Julian Nagelsmann. Man United need a boss with clout, class, gravitas and trophies... and that's Carlo Ancelotti, the Godfather of management
Sports.content:
Well intentioned though they might have been, there was a deadening familiarity about Harry Maguire’s soundbites after last month's 3-0 Old Trafford catastrophe, against Bournemouth, amplifying a sense of Manchester United being stuck in a godforsaken failure loop.

Maguire’s ‘look in the mirror’ and ‘take accountability’ and ‘wearing this shirt’ mantras were the kind of words he and Luke Shaw have been trotting out for years. It’s white noise, now. None of this stuff makes the blindest difference.

But it was by the law of unintended consequences that Maguire revealed how Michael Carrick, a nice guy in a fix, simply doesn’t exude the authority required to command United. ‘Michael turned our season on its head last season,’ the defender observed after the humiliation by the Cherries.

Never, in the days when United were a force in football, would the manager be described as ‘Alex’ or, decades earlier, ‘Matt’. Sir Alex Ferguson and Sir Matt Busby simply wouldn’t tolerate that kind of familiarity.

Judging by the names emerging as possible next inheritors of this most poisoned chalice – Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann – there is no appreciation that monumental authority, self-assurance and powers of persuasion are required here, and that this is not just another turn in the annual game of managerial swings and roundabouts.

United require a manager capable of instilling calm in the madhouse, standards where they are missing, and fashioning an environment in which no one would dare contemplate acts of vicious mutiny from the likes of Bruno Fernandes. The less widely appreciated point is that United require a manager capable of inspiring the kind of players the club need to join this ship.

The words of Harry Maguire (above) in support of Michael Carrick gave away a familiarity between players and manager that Sir Alex Ferguson, for example, would never have tolerated

The next manager must be able to dazzle and impress targets as well as have authority within the Old Trafford dressing room. Carlo Ancelotti, a stellar competitor, fits the bill

United have cut player salaries hard within an extremely constricted budget under Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos and the name of Manchester United, starved of the biggest trophies for so long domestically and on the European stage, no longer carries the old cachet.

The next manager must be able to dazzle and impress targets. With the greatest respect, Howe and Nagelsmann just won't do.

There has been a sense for weeks now that Carlo Ancelotti is the individual United have needed all along. A stellar competitor who has lifted five Champions League trophies and league titles in five countries, but who has ridden the rollercoaster for long enough to brush off the kind of vicissitudes which have destroyed so many at United.

He does not emit a lot of visible heat or light. There’s little of the rage from him in the technical area we see in Jose Mourinho, whose Real Madrid side’s victory in Sunday’s El Clasico led some to suggest he still has what United need. But the most combustible players certainly know who’s boss when Ancelotti's around.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic tells of the ‘Ancelotti eyebrow’, which put in an appearance on a bitterly cold night at Evian, during the player and coach’s time together at Paris Saint-Germain. As Ibrahimovic tells it, the pitch was terrible and PSG were not playing well.

‘At half-time, you always know when something is going on because that one eyebrow goes up. As I sat down I thought, “Now he’s angry”.

'There was a box in front of him and from nowhere he kicked it and it flew through the air and hit me on the head. “Jesus,” I thought. “Now he’s really angry”.’

Ibrahimovic adored Ancelotti. So did David Beckham, another who knows, from their time together at PSG, that the Italian can explode at times. ‘Scary,’ he called it.

Ancelotti with Zlatan Ibrahimovic in their PSG days. The Swedish striker was full of admiration for his manager

Does Eddie Howe really have the charisma or clout of five-time Champions League winner Ancelotti?

A book discussing the Italian's methods, which Ancelotti co-wrote with Mike Forde, his former sporting director at Chelsea, was entitled Quiet Leadership and in his preface he referenced Vito Corleone and The Godfather.

‘When you watch Corleone, do you see a weak quiet man?’ he wrote. ‘Or do you see a calm powerful man, in charge of his situation?

'My approach is born of the idea that a leader should not need to rant and rave or rule with an iron fist, but rather that their power should be implicit. It should be crystal clear who is in charge, and their authority must result from respect and trust, rather than fear.’

At Chelsea, he flourished in the face of bedlam. Roman Abramovich, the owner, suggested Ancelotti favoured English players, demanded he be ‘tougher’ with the dressing room and, on one occasion, summoned the manager to his London apartment for a 'dressing down’ after a 6-0 victory against West Bromwich Albion. He shrugged all this off.

When Abramovich demanded that Ancelotti ‘find a playing identity for the team’ he put Michael Essien in the playmaker role, to immense effect, and took the team to a Premier League and FA Cup Double in 2009-10.

‘He brought the best out of us and made us feel 10-feet tall,’ John Terry said of Ancelotti. ‘You know his training is excellent because he’s coached the best teams in the world – but it was the personal touches which lived with me.’

Ancelotti is coach of the Brazil team, of course, and it would be costly to extract him from that post, though there was always a sense with him of unfinished business in the Premier League. He was disappointed when Abramovich sacked him after two years and coveted the Liverpool job which Jurgen Klopp got instead.

Ancelotti led Chelsea to a Premier League and FA Cup Double in 2009-10 despite the meddling of Roman Abramovich

Ancelotti is coach of the Brazil team but there is a sense with him of unfinished business in the Premier League

The prospect of helicoptering around Howe and Nagelsmann, who would both be receptive to United, or Antonio Conte, whose temper would make him a disaster at the club, feels rather like Groundhog Day – taking United back to the dither of 2024, when they stuck with Erik ten Hag, despite the availability of the proven, far better Thomas Tuchel, whom they’d actually interviewed at that time.

Ancelotti or Howe to get a tune out of an imbalanced squad that has been patched up with cheaper options and, given the limited money available in January, will be little improved on? It’s obviously no contest.

In Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's time as manager from 2018, assistant manager Mike Phelan used to shout the word ‘standards’ down the corridors at the training ground and that’s what United need restoring again now.

More immediately come fixtures against Liverpool, Sporting Lisbon and Brentford. It will require no little personality and authority to deal with that lot.

Sports.title: Racing world mourns as promising young jockey dies after suffering horrific fall on her horse during race
Sports.content:
Apprentice jockey Izzy Neale has died in hospital days after she suffered a fall during a weekend race.

Neale, 22, was on board Marnoo when she and another rider fell 400m from the finish line during race six at Warren Racecourse, about 100km from Dubbo, on Sunday.

Racing NSW said she was knocked unconscious and airlifted to Dubbo Hospital, where her family rushed to her bedside.

The sporting authority shared a joint-statement on Tuesday with Ms Neale's family to confirm she had died.

'It is with deep sadness and broken hearts that we announce the passing of our beloved Izzy, surrounded by her closest family and friends,' the family said.

'Izzy rode horses before she could walk. Her love of horses was a lifelong passion that, more recently, had grown into a love of racing.

Apprentice jockey Izzy Neale (pictured) has sadly died after suffering a fall during a race

Izzy Neale won her first metropolitan race in July on It's A Tata (both pictured)

'Through organ donation, Izzy will give others the chance of life, bringing some comfort to our family amid this devastating loss.

'We are deeply grateful for the love, kindness and support shown to Izzy and our family by her friends, the racing community and everyone who has been by our side during this heartbreaking time.'

'We would like to thank Racing NSW and the NSW Jockeys Association for their care, compassion and support during this incredibly difficult time.

'We also extend our heartfelt thanks to the medical staff who cared for Izzy with such compassion.

'As we come to terms with our loss, we ask that our family's privacy be respected. Izzy was dearly loved and will forever be in our hearts.'

The Kieran Hazelton-trained Marnoo suffered a near foreleg injury and was later euthanised.

A race meet set to be held at Scone on Monday was postponed following consultation with jockeys and trainers.

Scone is Neale's home track in the NSW Hunter Valley, where she grew up.

The 22-year-old was a promising apprentice jockey having won 88 races

A day before the fall in central-west NSW, Neale was riding at Rosehill's Five Diamonds Day

'The thoughts and heartfelt support of Racing NSW and the entire community are with Izzy, her family, friends and colleagues during this extremely difficult time,' a previous Racing NSW statement read.

The other jockey involved, Diego Montes de Oca, was also taken to Dubbo Hospital with a suspected broken foot.

The incident has rocked the racing world.

'Tough day to be a jockey when things like this happen,' Melbourne Cup winner Robbie Dolan wrote after the accident.

Former jockey Melinda Turner added: 'Praying for a miracle. A terrible day for our industry.'

Just a day earlier, Neale was racing in Sydney at Rosehill's Five Diamonds Day, where she told Sky Racing that she was due to settle on the purchase of her first home this week.

She won 88 races from 699 starts.

Neale recorded her first metropolitan win in July on It's A Tata in the Highway Handicap at Rosehill.

Sports.title: West Ham wipe Russell Brand from their history after years of getting VIP treatment and kissing their managers in post-match interviews - as he's jailed for 10 years and six months for rape and sexual assault
Sports.content:
West Ham wipe Russell Brand from their history after years of getting VIP treatment and kissing their managers in post-match interviews - as he's jailed for 10 years and six months for rape and sexual assault

West Ham have removed references to Russell Brand from their website after the actor and comedian was found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.

Brand, a prominent West Ham supporter who regularly featured on the club's official channels, was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison on Monday.

The 51-year-old was cleared of two further counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault after a jury deliberated for eight-and-a-half hours. His four-week trial concluded at Southwark Crown Court last Thursday.

Brand is also facing further rape allegations from two women and has already been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Metropolitan Police said its investigation 'remains ongoing'.

West Ham appear to have distanced themselves from Brand, who grew up in east London and inherited his support for the club from his father, following the guilty verdict.

Among the references removed from the club's website is a 2023 article published after West Ham's Conference League triumph, which stated that 'comedian and actor Russell Brand, a globally recognised Hammers fan, documented himself watching the game live'.

Brand, a prominent West Ham fan who regularly featured on the club's website, was sentenced to ten-and-a-half years in prison on Monday (above kissing former boss Sam Allardyce)

References to Brand have been removed from West Ham's website following the guilty verdict

Brand was frequently given VIP access by the club which he supported from childhood (pictured above with Hammers legend Trevor Brooking)

In an interview with FourFourTwo magazine in February 2009, Brand spoke of his admiration for former West Ham captain Mark Noble, saying: 'I can snog Pink or throw Christina Aguilera around a bit. But when Mark Noble comes in, I get tongue-tied. Now how does that work?'

Brand was frequently granted VIP access by the club and conducted post-match interviews in which he kissed former managers Sam Allardyce and Slaven Bilic.

Daily Mail Sport understands that Brand is not a season ticket holder and has never held any formal relationship with the club.

The removal of references to Brand from the club's website comes after publishers confirmed they had withdrawn his books from sale.

Hodder & Stoughton, which published Brand's best-selling memoir My Booky Wook, is one of several publishers who have confirmed it has withdrawn his titles from sale.

My Booky Wook was the UK's Christmas No1 best-seller in 2007 but returned to the spotlight during the trial, when jurors were shown extracts in which Brand boasted about his sexual exploits and attitudes towards women.

Prosecutors argued the passages supported the accounts of several of his accusers.

In one extract read to the jury, Brand said he would not have stopped until he got his 'birthright orgasm'.

Brand pictured with former West Ham midfielder Enner Valencia and Noel Gallagher after a Premier League match between West Ham and Man City at Upton Park

The removal of references to Brand from the club's website comes after publishers confirmed they had withdrawn his books from sale

Pan Macmillan, one of Britain's largest publishers, also said it was in the process of withdrawing Brand's books.

On Thursday, Brand was found guilty of raping a 21-year-old fan after meeting her at a 2009 stand-up show at the Hammersmith Apollo.

He was also found guilty of groping another MTV worker during a party at a Soho bar in 2004, but not guilty of orally raping her in a toilet.

Jurors found Brand guilty of sexually assaulting a Capital Radio worker after meeting her in a corridor in 2005 and guilty of sexually assaulting a Channel 4 worker during a forced massage in 2009.

He was cleared of raping a woman he met at a cabaret show on the fringes of the 1999 Labour Party conference in Bournemouth and was found not guilty of trying to drag an MTV worker into a toilet to indecently assault her in 2001.

The judge, Mr Justice Bentham, told him: 'You've been convicted of a number of offences including rape. The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term.'

A conviction of rape can carry a life sentence, with standard maximum determinate sentences often reaching up to 19 years depending on the severity and guidelines.

Sexual assault convictions, meanwhile, carry a maximum sentence of ten years per count.

Sports.title: Darts star Gerwyn Price sparks backlash after appearing to back Russell Brand with post claiming there was 'zero evidence' against rapist after he was jailed for 10½-year term
Sports.content:
Darts star Gerwyn Price sparks backlash after appearing to back Russell Brand with post claiming there was 'zero evidence' against rapist after he was jailed for 10½-year term

Darts player Gerwyn Price has drawn criticism after sharing a social media post which appeared to support convicted rapist Russell Brand.

The 41-year-old, ranked fourth in the world, shared a picture on Facebook suggesting there was 'zero evidence' against Brand, who was last Thursday found guilty by a jury at Southwark Crown Court in London of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

The post compared Brand's sentence to 21-year-old Hamoud Al Soaimi, who was given a two-year suspended sentence for three counts of sexual assault and one assault by penetration of a 13-year-old in 2024.

Al Soaimi was 15 when he committed the offences between 2018 and 2019, and was handed a more lenient sentence compared to his co-defendants due to how the sentencing guidelines handle offenders under the age of 18.

The co-defendants in the same Newcastle grooming gang case, Omar Badreddin, Mohamad Badreddin and Huzaefa Alaboud, were sentenced to immediate prison terms of 18 years, 13 years and five-and-a-half years respectively.

The post shared by Price placed Al Soaimi's picture next to Brand's. Under Al Soaimi's name it read: 'Convicted of three sexual assaults and one count of assault by penetration of a child under 13.

Price shared a picture on his Facebook which suggested there was 'zero evidence' against convicted rapist Russell Brand (source: Facebook/Gerwyn Price)

Price has drawn criticism for the post which appeared to omit fundamental legal context

Brand was sentenced on Monday for the rape of a fan at his home in Hampstead, north London, in 2009 when she was 21, and for the sexual assault of three other women

'He received a two-year prison sentence suspended for two years, plus 180 hours unpaid work.'

Beneath Brand's photo, the post stated: 'Three counts of "sexual assault" and one count of "(grape emoji)" of a fan who had a threesome with him three days prior. 0 evidence. 17-22 years later.'

In the comments, Price wrote: 'Not saying anyone is innocent just highlighting the two tier justice system we have to deal with.'

One social media user addressed the 'omitted legal context' in the comments, highlighting that the 'graphic omits that Al Soaimi was 15 years old when he committed the offences'. Others appeared to criticise the suggestion that Brand was not guilty.

It isn't the first time that Price has posted about Brand, sharing a photo of his television showing the Channel 4 Dispatches investigation when it first aired in 2023 with the caption 'speaking up on certain topics, now this'.

The former darts world champion has also used his social media to collar support for Reform UK, as well as claiming support for the party was surging across Wales.

In one post earlier this year, Price wrote: 'The amount of people I know that are voting Reform is unbelievable, first time I’ve ever voted in my life as well… if they don’t win there’s definitely something fishy.'

Brand was sentenced on Monday for the rape of a fan at his home in Hampstead, north London, in 2009 when she was 21, and for the sexual assault of three other women, one in a bar and two in the workplace.

Police have received 'multiple reports' of sexual abuse since the disgraced 51-year-old comedian and actor was convicted, it can now also be revealed.

Former girlfriend Jemima Goldsmith, 52, is the latest to come forward, accusing Brand of 'violence, coercive control and abuse'. She said she was so terrified after a 'violent incident' in 2014 that she called police to remove him from her £15million Cotswolds mansion.

Price shared a photo of his television showing the Channel 4 Dispatches investigation when it first aired in 2023 (source: Instagram/gerwynpriceiceiceman180)

Two people held a banner outside Southwark Crown Court which appeared to compare Brand with the crucifixion of Jesus Christ

Brand now faces the prospect of a second trial as police sift through a raft of new claims, and prosecutors are expected to decide within weeks whether to charge him with two further alleged rapes, including an attack on a 16-year-old.

On Monday Mr Justice Bennathan said Brand had harboured a 'casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you', telling him: 'About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous, you were clever, and in many people's eyes you were funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator.'

The judge blasted Brand's 'staggering arrogance' and belief that his 'status protected' him after he resorted to smearing journalists when they first exposed his attacks in 2023. He also criticised Brand's entourage for indulging 'dreadful behaviour' after assaults took place in front of staff who laughed or did nothing.

He paid tribute to the 'determination and bravery' of the victims. 'All those women had to face being confronted and being told they had lied, or twisted the truth and, or, they had agreed to your sexual demands: that was all done because of you, on your instructions,' he said.

Mr Justice Bennathan made a point of condemning rape myths after Brand's defence barrister came under fire for reeling off a series of stereotypes, suggesting the victims should not be believed because they did not scream more, kick or slap him.

The judge said: 'Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.'

Sports.title: Man United's new boss contenders: Mauricio Pochettino tops the bookies' favourites ahead of Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann on 14-man list of top candidates
Sports.content:
Man United's new boss contenders: Mauricio Pochettino tops the bookies' favourites ahead of Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann on 14-man list of top candidates

Mauricio Pochettino is the bookies' leading candidate to replace under-fire Michael Carrick as Manchester United head coach should the latter get sacked.

As reported by Daily Mail Sport late on Monday night, Carrick is facing the sack during this November international break as a result of United's disastrous season so far.

Scrutiny on his role has intensified with the Red Devils now in the relegation zone despite salvaging a 4-4 draw against Aston Villa at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino is currently in charge of the US national team, but his contract includes a £7million release clause. However, it is yet to be determined the true value of prising Pochettino out as that figure doesn't include buying out his backroom staff.

It is also believed within Pochettino's deal that there is another clause which would allow him to leave his US role for particular high-profile jobs, such as at Old Trafford.

And Betfair have the Argentine as the favourite to succeed Carrick should he be dismissed within the next fortnight before United travel to bitter rivals Liverpool on November 22.

Mauricio Pochettino is the bookmakers' favourite to become the next Man United head coach

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick is expected to get the sack after a poor start

As of 8.12am on Tuesday morning, they have him at 4/7 with out of work trio Eddie Howe (5/2), Julian Nagelsmann (5/1) and Didier Deschamps (15/2) the next favourites.

Antonio Conte and Aston Villa manager Unai Emery (both 9/1) follow the aforementioned quartet in the odds.

Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler, Kieran McKenna, who worked with Carrick as an assistant manager to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, and ex-England manager Gareth Southgate are all 20/1.

Southgate's successor Thomas Tuchel is 28/1 alongside Diego Simeone, Sebastian Hoeness and Cesc Fabregas.

Nottingham Forest head coach Oliver Glasner is 33/1 too.

As Daily Mail Sport detailed, although it's understood that no final decision has been reached over Carrick's future and insiders say that speculation over his sacking is premature, the expectation within Old Trafford is that a new man will be in charge for the visit to Anfield a week on Sunday.

Carrick replaced Ruben Amorim in mid-January and the former United midfielder was handed a two-year contract in May after guiding United to a third-place finish and qualification for the Champions League, losing just two of his 17 games as head coach.

However, he has only won three of 15 games in all competitions. Breaking it down even further, the 45-year-old has overseen United's worst top-flight start since Sir Alex Ferguson replaced Ron Atkinson 40 years ago - with one victory in 10 matches.

NEXT MAN UNITED BOSS ODDS Mauricio Pochettino - 4/7 Eddie Howe - 5/2 Julian Nagelsmann - 5/1 Didier Deschamps - 15/2 Antonio Conte - 9/1 Unai Emery - 9/1 Gareth Southgate - 20/1 Fabian Hurzeler - 20/1 Kieran McKenna - 20/1 Thomas Tuchel - 28/1 Diego Simeone - 28/1 Sebastian Hoeness - 28/1 Cesc Fabregas - 28/1 Oliver Glasner - 33/1 Odds correct as of 8.12am on November 10, 2026 from Betfair
