Sports.title: Can Hamilton and Verstappen fight back for F1 Brazilian GP victory?
Sports.content:
With Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen 20th and 21st on the grid of the Brazilian Grand Prix, Sunday’s Formula 1 race promises to be fascinating – regardless of weather conditions.

Hamilton and Verstappen happen to be two drivers who performed memorable recoveries at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace, a track where overtaking has always been easier than most.

Back in 2021, the seven-time world champion was excluded from qualifying results due to a technical breach, meaning he started the sprint from last; he fought his way up to fifth. With a five-place grid drop for a new engine, Hamilton was 10th on the grid for the grand prix but battled to the front and came out on top in a titanic duel against Verstappen.

Three years later, the Dutchman was eliminated in Q2 on a wet Sunday morning and also took a five-place grid penalty for his sixth internal combustion engine, ending up 17th on the grid. The rain also impacted the race, but Verstappen rose to the occasion and comfortably overtook Esteban Ocon for victory.

But the DRS device had facilitated Hamilton’s exceptional drives, and the overtake mode that now features on F1’s new power units instead isn’t as decisive; the Interlagos layout might actually make it worse.

When asked how easy overtaking would be compared to 2021, the Ferrari driver replied: “Harder, because back then we had, obviously, a very long straight, and if you got close, you had the DRS, and maybe a car wouldn't have it – whereas now, everyone is just opening up their wings.

“I think overtaking will be very, very, very hard. I'm not sure you're going to see the same sort of races that you've seen in the past. But maybe the wet conditions will change that.”

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

“Now we don't have DRS anymore,” Verstappen concurred. “And the overtake mode is very limiting around here because of the long straight, everyone is draining the battery. So, your speed difference on the straight is going to be a lot less – a bit like Mexico, really. So, it will be quite a lot harder to pass than normal.”

So what will Hamilton’s strategy be? “I don't have one,” he responded. “Try to win, somehow.”

Verstappen, meanwhile, is banking on a number of incidents if he is to be a contender for victory. “Lots of safety cars, so they can't pull away, it keeps coming back to me,” the Red Bull racer said. “We'll see. I don't really think about it too much. I'll just go from lap one and see where I end up.”

He added: “I hope [with Lewis] we can clear the cars in front of us as quickly as we can.”

Across 19 grands prix so far in F1 2026, just two races have been won from outside the front row. Verstappen prevailed from fifth on the grid in Mexico, though he was virtually in the lead on lap one, and Antonelli remarkably triumphed from 19th in Italy. But if the expected rain impacts the race, then 2026’s dry-weather history will be meaningless.

Additional reporting by Isa Fernandes and Federico Faturos

Sports.title: The wet-weather challenges thrown up by Brazilian GP qualifying
Sports.content:
One hour, 23 minutes. You could've squeezed most of a football match into the rain delay during Formula 1 qualifying for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, and it looked for all the world like the session wouldn't actually get going again.

A repeat of 2024, where qualifying was squeezed onto Sunday morning, looked likely. Yet, a saviour arrived when a break in the clouds emerged, and the circuit had dried just enough for safety car specialist Bernd Maylander to give his approval of the conditions. It scarcely stopped a handful of drivers from having a moan about the visibility, but they soon accepted that they needed to lock in and focus up on getting around the track.

This meant the use of the lesser-spotted full-wet tyre, or the "x-wet" per the F1 lexicon. Often derided as a tyre only fit for bumbling around on behind the safety car, the blue-walled Pirelli was actually holding up pretty well and proved perfect for the level of standing water around the circuit. Aquaplaning, where the tyre struggles to break the surface tension of the water on-track, was nonetheless prevalent - but water dispersal as the rain held off soon brought the track to a more driveable state.

The downside of using the extreme wet tyre lies in the greater water dispersal (according to Pirelli, around 85 litres of water per second) which drastically cuts visibility as the spray rooster-tails out the back of the car. Yet, the dispersal is a necessary evil: without it, the circuit would just remain wetter for longer.

Although the rain lights ensure that the driver behind has at least some level of visibility, selecting your braking zone remains tricky; poor visibility means the driver must find a reference point in their immediate circle of vision. Stopping distances are also considerably longer, so a driver needs a different marker to their usual point of pedal application in the dry.

Considering all these climatic challenges, it's small wonder why race control takes a more tentative approach to wet conditions. Hence, it was a welcome surprise to see the session reopened - even if the circuit was still sodden with the afternoon downpour. Carlos Sainz reckoned that it was a "punchy" call from the FIA - but it only took a couple of laps to ensure the cars were more stable.

"It felt a bit punchy when we left on the x-wet because we were aquaplaning in sixth and seventh gear down the straights. And if you lose the car at those speeds, it's always going to be a big one," Sainz concluded after the session.

Carlos Sainz, Williams Photo by: James Sutton / Formula 1 / Formula Motorsport Ltd via Getty Images

"Also, very little visibility when you were running close to a car, but we were not forced to run close to cars in quali, so you can create a bit of a buffer to see. But it was very sketchy for two laps.

"Then we managed to create that little bit of dry line and the tyres started working, the aquaplaning started to go away. Everyone managed to keep the car on track until the end of Q1, which was a bit of a surprise, to be honest."

Liam Lawson agreed with Sainz's view of the session, stating that "when we started, it was extremely sketchy - I think we were definitely pushing it. But I like the fact that we were out there and not in the garage; I think obviously it is risky, but there weren't that many incidents."

As expected, the wet conditions delivered chances to those usually not accustomed to fighting at the top; the free practice performance-chasing was effectively rendered obsolete and the power units had slightly more parity as the effects of top-end performance and acceleration were mitigated by the low-grip track conditions.

This put a bit more of a premium on low-speed downforce and, crucially, keeping the tyres warm across Q1 - although Fernando Alonso nonetheless noted that "the engine is very important in terms of drivability and the way it behaves in the corners, and we still have a little bit of an issue there".

The approach through Q1 was, initially, simply about trying to set clean laps and hope that the progression of the circuit and the tyres would yield a lap-on-lap improvement.

Of course, each driver was tested on their reaction times in the event aquaplaning occurred, and the 2026 power units and the control over the rear brakes added another hurdle to overcome. But each driver (largely) became increasingly dialled in, watched as the laptimes improved, and then started to push the braking zones a little bit more as the circuit dried up.

There was a transition point in Q2, however, as the intermediates soon became the tyre to be on. With less standing water, the full wet was starting to overheat and was giving up performance in the middle part of the lap, initially enough to perhaps offset the dampness through the first and final sectors, before all three became much more suitable for the intermediate overall.

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

This meant that they could chase the track grip more, and it was evident that the times had begun to peak at the end of Q2 as the circuit approached its best conditions under the downpour. Getting the intermediate timing right, which Lawson reckoned he and his Racing Bulls team had nailed, was key to getting a couple of quicker laps in without risking the threat of falling off the circuit.

A few drivers struggled at this crossover, particularly with harvesting and braking into Turn 12 - Sainz and Ollie Bearman both had offs here, as newcomer Rafael Camara couldn't get the car to slow down enough before he careened into the barrier at the close of Q2.

With more rain impending during Q3, it was more about a mad dash to get a clean lap in, rather than watching the progression. That's perhaps when it felt most like 'normal' qualifying, as the tyres were effectively good enough for one lap with the expected downpour setting something of a timer.

It appeared that the majority of the drivers genuinely enjoyed the rare chance to tackle properly wet conditions, although some had a few qualms about the session restarting. George Russell surmised that "I love driving in the rain - but at some point, if that was a race, that was no way we should be driving in it - the chances of seeing a really, really horrific incident is very, very high."

Perhaps there's a bit of a split of opinion between the younger and older drivers; both Lewis Hamilton and Nico Hulkenberg expressed their enjoyment of wet conditions, while new champion Kimi Antonelli labelled them "the wettest conditions I've ever driven [in]. So it was not the nicest of experiences"; both he and Bearman said that the circuit was over the limit at the Q1 restart, although the latter conceded that the early running did at least contribute to the circuit improving.

Regardless, it was valuable data for each of the drivers ahead of Sunday's race - where inclement weather is expected to play a role once again. And so begins the overnight discussions: does anyone risk a pit-lane start for a set-up change?

Sports.title: No F1 engine manufacturers to get extra upgrades after FIA’s third ADUO evaluation | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The FIA will not to offer any engine manufacturers the chance to perform extra power unit upgrades following its latest Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) evaluation.

Under new rules introduced as part of Formula 1’s 2026 power unit regulations the sport’s governing body controls how often manufacturers can upgrade their internal combustion engines.

The evaluations take place periodically throughout the season. The FIA has completed its third such evaluation and, as was the case during the second, determined no further engine homologation opportunities should be offered.

The third evaluation period concluded after the United States Grand Prix last month. The second followed the Hungarian Grand Prix.

The first evaluation period, which ran from the start of the season to the Canadian Grand Prix, remains the only time any additional upgrade opportunities were awarded. On that occasion Red Bull-Ford were found to have the top-performing power unit.

Audi, Ferrari and Honda’s units were found to be more than 4% less powerful. They were permitted two extra homologation opportunities this year and two more next year. Mercedes were found to be within 2% and 4% of the leading power unit and therefore received one extra upgrade this year and next.

Separately, in May the FIA changed the ADUO rules to allow any manufacturer which was 10% off the leading design to spend more money. The revision was expected to assist Honda following their poor start to the season.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Some have likened F1’s ADUO to the World Endurance Championship’s heavily-criticised Balance of Performance regulations. The FIA’s single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis defended the regulations but indicated they may be revised in coming seasons.

“Based on the quality of the data and the robustness of the assessment process, we are confident in our findings and the conclusions reached,” he said.

“The first year of implementation has also reinforced our belief that the ADUO concept is the right one for Formula 1. However, it is important that the system continues to evolve to ensure it remains efficient, relevant and fit for purpose.

“To that end, we have been working closely with the power unit manufacturers and teams to explore refinements to the methodology that will support the continued effectiveness of ADUO in future seasons.”

Sports.title: “The car is steering by itself, don’t you see it?”: How handling trouble baffled Antonelli | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli looked on course to win his first race as the new world champion as he pulled out an eight-second lead over his pursuers over the opening 12 laps at Interlagos.

But he reported something felt wrong with his Mercedes’ handling soon after switching to slick tyres and spun off, allowing Lando Norris through into the lead. The two Red Bull drivers passed him and by lap 34 Antonelli was 17 seconds off the lead.

Antonelli’s exchanges with race engineer Peter Bonnington underline how he was mystified by his car’s handling. Bonnington kept him supplied with notes on where he could find more time but it was only after he swapped his flat-spotted set of slicks for a fresh set that he began to show more competitive pace.

Unfortunately for Antonelli, the rain returned soon afterwards. He pitted for intermediates again – collecting a penalty for an unsafe release as he did – and the early leader had to settle for a fifth-place finish.

Sports.content: The Formula 1 world championship began in 1950 and is considered the world’s leading form of single-seater motorsport. The 2025 F1 season is the 75th time the championship has been held. [caption id="attachment_530322" align="alignright" width="470"] The 2025 Formula 1 season started in Australia[/caption]A world drivers’ champion has been crowned every year since the series began. Since 1958 a world constructors’ championship title has also been awarded. The most successful F1 drivers in history are seven-times world champions Lewis Hamilton and Michael Schumacher. In 2021 the former became the first and so far only driver to date to win 100 grands prix. While Schumacher retired from F1 at the end of 2012, Hamilton continues to race. His rival world champions in the series are Max Verstappen and Fernando Alonso. There are 10 teams active in the championship, each of which field cars for two drivers. Each team is required to design and build the majority of its cars but may source some parts including engines, gearboxes and certain other components. Lewis Hamilton could have avoided his high-speed spin when the rain returned in the latter stages of the Brazilian Grand Prix.

His Ferrari team summoned him into the pits before he began the lap. Liam Lawson immediately in front of him did pit but Hamilton stayed out. But the conditions had deteriorated and he spun on his next lap.

Hamilton made a strong start to the race from 20th and briefly ran as high as ninth. But Max Verstappen overtook him and Ferrari then told him to let Oliver Bearman past.

Ferrari made this call because Hamilton went off the track when he passed Bearman on the first lap. However the stewards later ruled Hamilton had not gained an advantage by doing this.

Excerpts from Hamilton’s Brazilian GP radio messages

Lap: 8/71 HAM: 1’30.578 Hamilton Understood. Okay.

Sports.title: Russell explains pit exit spin: ‘I took too much risk because I saw a chance to win’ | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell says he spun in the pit lane exit during the Brazilian Grand Prix because he thought he had a race-winning opportunity.

The Mercedes driver was running third early in the race as the track was drying. He was within 10 seconds of race leader Andrea Kimi Antonelli when he came in to swap his intermediate tyres for slicks on lap 17.

However Russell spun when he reached the pit lane exit. The error cost him around 16 seconds and dropped him behind several of his rivals.

“Obviously it was a bit of an up and down race,” said Russell, who eventually finished fourth. “I’ve no idea what happened on that pit exit, I probably just took too much risk because I was seeing an opportunity to go for the win at that point, but it happened.”

Russell was one of few drivers who only made two pit stops during the race, keeping his set of slick tyres on until the rain returned in the closing stages.

“Ironically, because that happened, I then didn’t pit for another set of slick tyres and it kind of put me back in the same position as I was before the incident,” he acknowledged.

The Mercedes driver set the second-fastest time in qualifying, and believed he could have been quickest had he not aborted his final run under instruction from his race engineer. He said he was satisfied with his performance.

“I’m probably more happy coming away from the weekend because the performance was good,” said Russell, who started seventh following a penalty for replacing his engine. “At this stage I care more about the performance and I care about the result because that’s what’s been my weak point.

“The performance yesterday was great, the performance on the soft tyre was really great today but obviously I did make that mistake. But it probably would have been a different picture if we’d have started P2.”

Sports.title: Piastri splits from Webber’s management team | Formula 1
Sports.content:
McLaren driver Oscar Piastri has confirmed he is no longer being represented by Mark Webber’s management team.

Webber, who won nine grands prix during his 12 seasons in Formula 1 , has guided Piastri’s career since 2019. Piastri made his F1 debut with McLaren in 2023 and led much of last year’s championship before slipping to third place at the end of the season.

Piastri issued a statement saying he had split from the management team led by Webber and his partner Ann by mutual arrangement.

“I’d like to thank Mark and Ann for all their support and advice over the years,” said Piastri. “Their guidance has been invaluable, particularly in navigating the beginning of my F1 career. I wish them all the best going forward.”

Webber said he and Ann were “proud to have played a pivotal role in the formative years of Oscar’s career and to have placed him in F1 so that he could compete at the front so early on.

“Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close. This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure, and for us to embark on our new ventures. We wish Oscar all the very best for a long and successful career.”

Sports.title: Conor Benn’s 40 Million Problem: Zuffa’s Make-Or-Break Crossroad
Sports.content:
Chris Mannix estimates Conor Benn will clear upward of $40 million across the Regis Prograis win, his knockout loss to Ryan Garcia, and a third bout. If that figure holds, Zuffa’s next move is simple: decide whether Benn is a long-term commercial asset worth rebuilding, or a depreciating commodity to cash out before the floor gives way.

Cheap preliminary bouts can shave operational overhead, but cost-cutting does not rescue a main event that draws too few buyers to carry elite purses. Denzel Bentley is a clean, in-house booking on paper, yet he brings virtually no promotional leverage outside hardcore circles. If Benn stumbles against a rugged domestic contender, his headliner status evaporates on a Tuesday-level attraction.

“Conor Benn in the last three fights, I would estimate he has made. Well, the last two and then there’s one coming up. He’s going to make north of $40 million. Very few fighters make that in their career,” said Mannix.

A third meeting with Chris Eubank Jr. remains a dependable box-office draw across the UK, but it offers zero forward momentum. Without a world title or fresh bad blood, a trilogy simply taxes the same domestic consumer base a third time. It functions as a lucrative exit strategy rather than a platform to expand Benn’s brand.

Shakur Stevenson provides stateside name recognition, yet the financial and stylistic variables work against Zuffa. Stevenson is a naturally smaller fighter moving up in weight. A Benn win does little to erase the Garcia beatdown, while a calculated twelve-round schooling by Stevenson leaves Zuffa covering two astronomical purses for a clinic that actively turns off casual ticket buyers. That dilemma also complicates distribution, as an American-led Stevenson bout targets a prime U.S. broadcast window, whereas an Eubank card requires a UK primetime slot to secure the gate.

If Zuffa intends to actually rehabilitate Benn, it needs a recognizable, established welterweight willing to stand in the pocket. The play is an opponent who commands respect on the marquee, yet offers the stylistic openings Benn requires to deliver a highlight-reel finish that makes his next event an easy sell.

Sports.title: David Benavidez Gives PBC a Condition for Staying
Sports.content:
David Benavidez is prepared to re-sign with Premier Boxing Champions following his December 5 bout against Michal Cieslak, provided his contract permits regular cross-platform appearances.

In an interview with Chris Mannix, Benavidez revealed he launched his own promotional banner, outlining an aggressive roadmap targeting Jai Opetaia in May followed by Oleksandr Usyk in September. The true worth of any future contractual commitment rests entirely on delivering those marquee bouts without bureaucratic delay.

“As long as we’re able to move freely and fight whoever, whatever network we want to do, then we can stay here,” Benavidez stated. “I want these fights to happen immediately.”

Benavidez gives PBC credit for letting him shop around on other networks. He needs that kind of leeway if he wants major unifications, simply because the money has to come from rival platforms or deep-pocketed outside backers.

Starting his own promotional company lets him push for co-promotional billing, a say on fight dates, and a piece of the TV rights. Still, none of that matters unless the opposing camps and money men sign off. Making a fight with Opetaia is one thing; putting together the numbers for a monster event with Usyk is a totally different ballgame.

Despite turning 29, Benavidez carries the mileage of a thirteen-year professional tenure. Eliminating the harsh cut to 175 pounds undoubtedly preserves his conditioning. Yet his relentless, close-range combinations naturally expose him to heavy return fire from full-sized cruiserweights. A punishing clash with Opetaia in May could result in facial cuts, orthopedic damage, or an abbreviated summer training camp ahead of a proposed September date with Usyk.

With Benavidez, the facial wear is catching up to the odometer. He turned pro at sixteen, but the real mileage is the gym work. His whole identity in camp has always been grueling, high-volume sparring where he plays the hammer, walking guys down and eating clean shots just to deliver five of his own. You can get away with that in your early twenties when the recovery is instant, but that kind of daily collision accumulates on a guy’s face and joints.

The weight shifts do not help either. Spending a decade draining a massive frame down to 168 pounds, ballooning between camps, then cutting to 175, and now suddenly filling out toward 200 changes facial structure dramatically. Once a fighter stops that severe water depletion cycle and carries heavier, solid mass into his late twenties, the baby fat is completely gone, and the facial tissue hardens up fast.

The real giveaway will be the first time he faces genuine adversity at cruiserweight. When guys age overnight on the outside, you watch the legs and the punch reaction. If the feet look heavy early or the reflexes to slip counters are a fraction of a second slower against a puncher like Cieslak or Opetaia, that weathered look in camp ceases to be cosmetic and becomes a fighting reality.

Sports.title: Gene Tunney’s Only Loss Explains His Greatness
Sports.content:
Gene Tunney’s best case for greatness is what he did after Harry Greb handed him his only professional defeat. Greb took Tunney’s American light heavyweight title in 1922 by setting a pace Tunney could barely withstand. Three years and four rematches later, Tunney was landing body shots that forced Greb to hold.

The first fight at Madison Square Garden showed how far Tunney had to go. Greb threw from awkward angles and took control in the late rounds as Tunney tired. Bloodied and exhausted, Tunney stayed upright through the 15th. Two days later, he went to the athletic commission’s office to seek a rematch.

Tunney regained the title by decision in February 1923, though many ringside reporters thought Greb had done enough to win. Tunney won their third meeting that December. Their fourth fight, in September 1924, ended without an official decision. The Cleveland Plain Dealer favored Greb, while The New York Times reported that most ringside writers saw an even fight. More than two years after the first bout, Greb was still giving Tunney trouble.

By their fifth meeting in March 1925, Tunney weighed 181 pounds to Greb’s 168. He used those extra pounds to do damage at close range. The Associated Press reported that Tunney concentrated his attack on the body and cut short Greb’s attempts to rally. Greb, who had poured on punches late in the first fight, spent much of the fifth holding. The weight advantage belongs in the story because Tunney had found a way to make Greb feel it where he had once been most dangerous.

Tunney stopped Tommy Gibbons later that year and took the world heavyweight title from Jack Dempsey by decision in September 1926. Dempsey dropped him in the seventh round of their rematch a year later, then delayed the referee’s count by failing to go promptly to a neutral corner. Tunney rose and made it through the round. In the eighth, he dropped Dempsey on his way to another decision. Tunney stopped Tom Heeney in July 1928 and retired as champion.

The Long Count still invites people to imagine what Dempsey might have done with those extra seconds. The Greb series shows what Tunney did with four more chances against a man who had already beaten him. The first rematch gave him his title back, but the disputed decision left plenty to argue about. By the fifth fight, the clearest evidence was in the way Greb fought. The man who had set the pace over 15 rounds in 1922 was holding to buy himself a few seconds at a time.

Sports.title: Willy Hutchinson Has the Belt and the Style Canelo Hates
Sports.content:
Willy Hutchinson offers Canelo Alvarez an intriguing path toward an undisputed crown at light heavyweight, along with the precise movement that historically gives Canelo fits. After Hutchinson claimed the vacant WBC belt against Joshua Buatsi, Chris Mannix proposed the pairing, prompting Sergio Mora to wonder about the logic behind it.

Mora highlighted Hutchinson’s slick jab, deceptive rhythm, and southpaw looks, arguing that if Canelo wants to spend twelve rounds chasing an elusive stylist, he might as well target Dmitry Bivol directly.

“It’s the movers, the guys that don’t engage, the tricky guys,” said Mora on Mannix’s YouTube channel, who pointed to Hutchinson’s jab, timing and habit of switching southpaw. If Canelo is prepared to deal with that style, Mora would rather see him fight Dmitry Bivol again.

Mannix’s pitch carries clear tactical purpose. Should Canelo defeat Hutchinson while Bivol retains the remaining straps, their second meeting would crown an undisputed champion. Capturing the WBC strap gives Canelo fresh leverage after dropped rounds in their initial encounter. The cost, however, involves chasing a rangier opponent who rarely plants his feet long enough for return fire.

Against Buatsi, Hutchinson demonstrated his ability to reset aggressive opponents. He scored with his lead hand from distance, slipped away before Buatsi set his base, and tied up on the inside. While Christian Mbilli offered Canelo a stationary target, Hutchinson could force him to spend full minutes fighting into close quarters, only to wrap him up before the Mexican star digs into the ribs.

Stylistically, Hutchinson brings every single attribute that gives Canelo severe problems. Canelo has always struggled against slick, disciplined movers with active lead hands and sharp ring generalship. Floyd Mayweather wrote the blueprint, Dmitry Bivol executed it with physical authority, and Terence Crawford exploited those exact gaps in mobility and lateral footwork.

Hutchinson takes that exact stylistic formula and backs it with genuine light heavyweight size. At 6-foot-1 with a 73-inch reach, he is not an undersized fighter moving up; he is a natural 175-pounder in his physical prime. As he proved against Joshua Buatsi, he can switch stances seamlessly, snap a long jab, control distance, and disengage before an opponent can set their base to load up power shots.

For an aging Canelo whose foot speed has noticeably slowed and who relies heavily on opponents standing in the pocket to trade, chasing Hutchinson around the ring for 12 rounds would be an absolute nightmare. From a risk-versus-reward perspective, it is even worse for Canelo.

Hutchinson possesses world-class talent and now holds a major belt, but he does not carry the mainstream American pay-per-view profile to deliver a massive blockbuster gate. If Canelo wins, critics immediately dismiss it by claiming he merely defeated an opponent without marquee status. If Canelo loses or gets thoroughly outboxed, his aura and marketability take another massive hit against a fighter most casual fans are just learning about.

If Turki Alalshikh put an obscene sum on the table for Willy Hutchinson, Canelo and Eddy Reynoso would probably have a private conversation behind closed doors that sounds very different from what they would say into a microphone.

Their internal calculation would break down into two stages. For starters, Reynoso would likely watch the tape and spot every red flag imaginable. Reynoso is a meticulous matchmaker who protects the Canelo brand with extreme precision. He knows Canelo’s legs are not what they were five years ago, and he knows how much trouble tall, athletic switch-hitters who move laterally cause his fighter. Reynoso’s immediate coaching instinct would be to steer Canelo away from a nightmare style that yields minimal glory.

From there, Canelo’s response would depend entirely on what that number looked like. Canelo has reached the point in his career where he views himself as an enterprise. If the money was merely “great” ($40 million to $50 million), Canelo would casually brush it off. He would tell Turki that Hutchinson brings nothing to the gate, has no real profile in North America, and does not deserve to share the ring with him. He would counter by asking for that same bag to fight someone like Chris Eubank Jr. or another name who actually comes forward to trade.

If Turki offered an absurd, once-in-a-lifetime figure, say, $100 million or more with full guarantees, Reynoso and Canelo would pause. But even then, they would attempt to alter the playing field before signing anything. They would push for a catchweight, demand strict rehydration stipulations, or try to impose terms designed to drain Hutchinson’s mobility and take the spring out of his legs.

If Turki insisted on a straight 175-pound fight with zero compromises, Canelo would almost certainly pass. At this stage of his career, with his financial empire secure, taking a guaranteed boxing lesson against a young, 6-foot-1 mover for any amount of money is not worth watching his aura evaporate in front of the world. Canelo would smile, thank His Excellency, and ask to fight a brawler instead.

Sports.title: Canelo Plans to Renew Turki Deal After March Fight
Sports.content:
Canelo Álvarez plans to renew his deal with Turki Alalshikh after his March fight, trainer Eddy Reynoso says. His decision win over Christian Mbilli may have strengthened the case for another deal, which would keep Saudi backing in play for a Terence Crawford rematch.

“It’s the last one [the fight in March], but we’re going to renew. There are very good plans for Saúl. He already spoke with Turki, and there are good plans to continue his career,” said Reynoso, in comments to La Afición translated and shared by EverythingBoxing’s Darshan Desai.

What Turki Could Get From Another Deal

Some fans saw the Mbilli win as Canelo’s best performance since he stopped Caleb Plant in 2021. Canelo still fought in bursts, but he had to keep finding clean shots against an unbeaten contender who pressed him for 12 rounds. That gave Alalshikh a fresh performance to judge alongside Canelo’s name and drawing power. Reynoso gave no indication of how much the win figured in their talks.

Crawford offers the biggest commercial reason to renew. The first fight gives the promotion an obvious question to sell. Can Canelo reverse the result? Saudi backing helped make the first fight happen, and a renewed deal would give Canelo a direct route back to the same financier. The boxing problem remains. Crawford could still use his jab and reach to score from outside and make Canelo follow him. Beating Mbilli, who came forward, tells us little about how Canelo would close distance on Crawford.

Hamzah Sheeraz offers a different kind of event at 168 pounds. His British following gives the promotion a second market, and his height and reach give it something to sell beyond Canelo’s name. Sheeraz has less experience at that level, though. Compare that with IBF champion Osleys Iglesias, a dangerous southpaw whose belt gives Canelo a sporting reason to fight him. Sheeraz gives Alalshikh an easier fight to market, especially if the aim is to put on an event that can draw in Britain as well as with Canelo’s audience.

A return to 175 pounds would open up two more fights. Dmitry Bivol already beat Canelo, so a rematch comes with a result to avenge and a clear question about whether Canelo can get past Bivol’s jab and footwork. Artur Beterbiev would be a first-time opponent. The sell there is whether Canelo can hold his ground against a naturally bigger puncher who can force him to work at a pace he would rather set himself. Both fights depend on Canelo being willing to go back up to light heavyweight.

Reynoso named no opponents for an extension and gave no terms. If the deal goes through, Crawford would offer the biggest event, while Sheeraz would give Alalshikh a way to build one around Canelo at 168. Bivol and Beterbiev only enter the picture if Canelo wants another fight at 175.

For Canelo’s camp, Crawford, 39, is the ideal financial play with almost zero physical danger. He is a smaller guy who relied on running, movement, and potshots to nick rounds. He was never going to walk Canelo down or smash him up. There is zero wear and tear on Canelo’s body in that matchup compared to getting in the trenches with a relentless slugger or moving back up to 175.

If Crawford came out on the back foot the first time, a full year sitting on the couch is not going to turn him into a pressure fighter. Ring rust makes guys even more defensive. If he gets pried out of retirement by a massive Saudi check, he will likely double down on the track shoes, look to survive on points from the outside, and avoid any inside trade.

For Reynoso and Canelo, it represents a massive payday without the physical toll. The only hurdle is whether Turki actually wants to cough up another nine-figure purse to finance a fight that already lacked real fireworks.

Sports.title: Alycia Baumgardner Outclasses Turhan, Then Gets Called Out By Caroline Dubois
Sports.content:
On Sunday night, November 8th, at MVPW07, in her lightweight debut, Alycia “The Bomb” Baumgardner put her boxing skills on display as she outclassed Elif Turhan (14-1, 8 KOs) and won the IBF world title.

Baumgardner was elusive; she touched the body, and her power shots were sharp and accurate. Turhan couldn’t find the range to land her right hand, and she failed to make any in-ring adjustments.

In the opening round, Baumgardner set the tone as she fired the jab and followed it up with a three-punch combination. Round two featured back-and-forth action as Baumgardner’s shots were landing and Turhan was missing wildly.

At the 1:05 mark of the third round, Baumgardner landed a big right hand that knocked Turhan off-balance. As the third round was coming to a close, Baumgardner hurt Turhan, but the referee prematurely stepped in to stop the action.

The referee made a significant error when she stopped the action because she thought the ten-second bell was the final bell, which is the one that officially ends the round.

During the first four rounds of the fight, the hard-hitting Turhan was routinely off the mark when she threw her power shots. In the 5th round, Turhan finally experienced success when she was able to land the uppercut.

The second half of the fight featured Baumgardner working off the jab and landing a variety of punches. Baumgardner exposed Turhan as she made it apparent that we were viewing a matchup between a highly skilled boxer and a one-dimensional fighter.

At the conclusion of the 10-round contest, the scorecards reflected the dominance that took place inside of the ring. All three judges scored the bout (100-90) in favor of Baumgardner.

With the victory, Alycia Baumgardner (19-1, 7 KOs) won the IBF title and became a two-division world champion. Following the impressive victory, Baumgardner was confronted by WBC/WBO lightweight champion Caroline Dubois.

After Baumgardner conducted her post-fight interview, Dubois left her ringside seat, grabbed a mic, and addressed Baumgardner. While standing by the ring, Dubois issued a challenge to the new IBF lightweight champion.

“I handle my business; you handled yours. Are we fighting?” Dubois asked. “Are we fighting champ? Are we fighting champ? Are we fighting champ? That’s all you got to say. That’s all you got to say. Why you’re not looking at me champ? Why you’re not looking at me champ? Let’s go. Undisputed.”

Caroline Dubois pulled a bold move based on the fact that she was scheduling a fight for undisputed status while her February 2027 opponent, the WBA lightweight champion Stephanie Han, was sitting one seat away from Dubois at ringside.

During the verbal exchange, Alycia Baumgardner was advising Dubois to focus on her next opponent as opposed to looking ahead to a fight for undisputed. However, if Dubois is successful on February 20th, a Baumgardner vs. Dubois bout would be the 2027 fight of the year for women’s boxing.

Sports.title: Dana White Says Zuffa Will Work With Sanctioning Bodies Case by Case
Sports.content:
Dana White plans to treat boxing sanctioning bodies as optional business partners, dealing with them when convenient and bypassing them when they become an obstacle. Denzel Bentley found out firsthand what that freedom costs the athlete, surrendering his WBO middleweight championship to face Shane Mosley Jr. under the Zuffa Boxing banner.

“We’re sort of dealing with that on a case-by-case basis, and if we can work it out, we’d like to for the fighters. If we can’t, then we won’t,” White said at Saturday’s post-fight press conference.

In mixed martial arts, White operates an enclosed system. He picks the challengers, dictates the schedule, and awards the internal championship hardware. Boxing strips away that total control. Zuffa can stage any pairing it likes, but an external regulatory body controls the hardware. That gives the sanctioning body immediate leverage over the athlete, even if it cannot stop the promoter from opening the arena doors.

Bentley attempted to negotiate a delay, asking the WBO to permit an interim defense against Mosley before facing mandatory challenger Yoenli Hernandez. The sanctioning body held all the leverage. Warriors Boxing had already claimed the promotional rights to the Hernandez fight with a $200,000 purse bid, guaranteeing Bentley a $150,000 payday. The WBO denied the exception and stripped Bentley on October 30. Zuffa staged the Mosley bout regardless, eight days later in London.

That sequence exposed the sharp divide between promotional convenience and fighter interest. Bentley walked away from a locked-in six-figure purse and the regulatory leverage of a world championship belt. While his London compensation remains undisclosed, losing the belt permanently damages his future bargaining position at the elite level. For Zuffa, the upside was immediate and clear. Keeping Bentley in London retained two in-house fighters for its own platform instead of sending its champion to perform on a competitor’s broadcast.

The WBO acted out of institutional preservation. Once a purse bid concludes, allowing a champion to pivot to an unapproved bout undermines the entire mandatory framework. Permitting Bentley to delay would have shelved Hernandez and made a mockery of Warriors Boxing’s winning bid. Enforcing the vacancy was the only way the organization could protect its authority and the credibility of its bidding process.

London proved Zuffa can run standalone events without the approval of an alphabet organization. The breaking point will arrive when White tries to stage an undisputed championship or a major unification. Stripping one titlist instantly evaporates the historical premise of a unification bout. When the hardware itself is the primary selling point for the global audience, White will either have to accept the rules of the boxing establishment or abandon the pursuit of true world titles altogether.

Sports.title: Anthony Yarde In Line For WBC Title Shot After Benavidez Knockout Loss
Sports.content:
Anthony Yarde was knocked out by David Benavidez and spent a full year on the shelf. Somehow, his reward could be an immediate crack at a world title. Frank Warren is considering using Yarde for Willy Hutchinson’s first WBC light heavyweight title defense in March, effectively granting him championship access without the burden of winning an eliminator.

Hutchinson had to go through the fire with Joshua Buatsi across two fights to capture the vacant belt. Yarde, meanwhile, might walk directly into the challenger’s corner coming off a stoppage defeat and twelve months of inactivity. What has Yarde done since Benavidez demolished him to justify cutting to the front of the line? Nothing inside the ring. His entire argument is built on name recognition and the equity of older wars.

Warren was open about the option on talkSPORT Boxing: “Anthony Yarde was in the ring. I don’t know where we’re going to go with that one. We’ll see if we can agree terms. That’s something we may consider as well.”

Casual British fight fans recognize Yarde from his past encounters with Benavidez, Artur Beterbiev, and Sergey Kovalev. That name value makes him infinitely simpler to sell to television buyers than a high-risk contender like Albert Ramirez. If the WBC blesses a voluntary defense and numbers make sense, Warren converts Hutchinson’s hard-won triumph into a profitable domestic event. If Hutchinson retains, he collects a marquee domestic scalp. If Yarde pulls it off, Warren crowns a long-tenured in-house headliner.

The timing also plays directly into Hutchinson’s hands. Yarde carries sufficient power to make Hutchinson pay if he retreats into the ropes, but Hutchinson possesses the footwork to keep Yarde turning. Forcing Yarde to reset his base prevents him from sitting down on heavy bursts. As the rounds wear on, Yarde faces the grueling reality of sustaining hard combination punching over twelve rounds after such a protracted layoff.

The commercial logic is obvious. The sporting logic is nonexistent. A tune-up win would establish what Yarde has left after the Benavidez beating. Under Warren’s plan, Yarde could skip that test and answer the question with a world title on the line.

Ghana News.title: Richmond Adu-Poku: Record labels are dead in Ghana
Ghana News.content:
Ghana has become exceptionally good at producing music stars. We churn out hit songs, manufacture viral sensations and export artistes who command attention beyond our borders.

But when it comes to building the powerful businesses that turn these stars into sustainable commercial empires, our performance has been rather less impressive.

We have the talent, the sound, the audience and the occasional international breakthrough. Yet, somewhere between the recording studio and the international bank account, the money seems to lose its way home.

Perhaps it is time to bring back an old friend we have neglected for too long: the Record Label.

This is not an invitation to resurrect an era when artistes needed permission from a label executive to sneeze, let alone release a song. It is about rebuilding the business infrastructure that makes music commercially sustainable.

From Gramophones to Global Highlife

Ghana's recording industry did not begin with Spotify, TikTok or an artiste discovering the magic of a digital distribution account. Its history stretches back nearly a century.

In the 1920s, recording companies such as Zonophone and His Master's Voice were already documenting Ghanaian music for commercial distribution. Among the pioneers was Kwame Asare, popularly known as Jacob Sam, whose 1928 recording of Yaa Amponsah became a landmark in recorded highlife.

In 1948, Decca established a permanent recording studio in Accra, widely recognised as the first of its kind in West Africa. It became an important recording centre for influential musicians, including E.T. Mensah's Tempos, King Bruce's Black Beats and E.K. Nyame's Guitar Band.

By the 1960s and 1970s, Ghana had developed a formidable recording and manufacturing ecosystem. Ambassador Records, Record Manufacturers Ghana and the Ghana Film Studio contributed to production, while local studios and vinyl-pressing facilities helped take Ghanaian music to commercial audiences.

In other words, we were doing more than making music. We were manufacturing records, employing people, distributing products, developing businesses and exporting culture.

Highlife was not just a sound. It was an industry, complete with machinery, investment and commercial ambition.

When the Vinyl Stopped Spinning

Economic difficulties, declining local pressing facilities and the popularity of cassette duplication weakened the old system from the late 1970s into the 1980s.

The industry adapted. Cassettes became the new currency, while businesses such as Frimprince Music, Prince Dave Records, Megastar and Soul Records helped keep Ghanaian music commercially alive.

Later, labels such as Slip Music became important players in highlife, gospel and popular music.

The packaging changed, the technology evolved and distribution found new routes. But one principle remained constant: music needed investment, organisation and businesses willing to take risks.

Somebody understood what we occasionally forget today: a microphone can create a star, but it takes a business to build an empire.

The Modern Label Era: Building Stars and Brands

The emergence of hiplife and contemporary Afropop introduced another generation of producer-led and artiste-led music companies.

Lynx Entertainment, founded by Richie Mensah in 2006, became a notable example of structured talent development, contributing to the careers of artistes such as Asem, Eazzy, MzVee, KiDi and Kuami Eugene.

Other notable players included Samini Music, Black Avenue Musik, BBnZ Live, Highly Spiritual Music, Legacy Life Entertainment, Sarkcess Music and Burniton Music.

These companies understood that releasing songs was only the beginning. There was branding, artist development, production, promotion, management and commercial partnerships to consider.

Some have evolved, others have scaled down, while most have disappeared from the industry's spotlight. The problem is not that every label has vanished. It is that Ghana has not built enough strong, sustainable music businesses to match the extraordinary talent it produces.

We have plenty of people interested in discovering the next superstar, but far fewer adequately capitalised institutions willing to invest in what happens after the discovery.

Distribution Is Not the Music Business

Digital technology has made it easier than ever for Ghanaian artistes to take their music global. Today, an independent musician can release a song without waiting for a traditional executive's blessing. That is progress, and nobody should romanticise unnecessary gatekeeping.

But let us not confuse access with capacity.

Having a distribution account does not automatically make someone a music entrepreneur. Uploading songs and chasing streams are one thing; financing campaigns, building brands, negotiating licensing deals and turning music catalogues into wealth are entirely different ball games.

That is where modern record labels become relevant.

Artistes may not need old-fashioned record deals, but they certainly need transparent partnerships that provide investment, expertise and commercial muscle.

Independence is beautiful, but being your own artiste, accountant, lawyer, marketer, distribution manager and CEO can quickly turn musical freedom into corporate slavery.

Even stars need a team!

Let's Celebrate the Businesses Behind the Music

The Telecel Ghana Music Awards should seriously consider restoring its Record Label of the Year category. Stars do not magically manufacture themselves, and the businesses investing behind the hits deserve their moment in the spotlight.

The Ghana Association of Phonographic Industry must also reposition itself to champion modern labels, distributors, music rights and stronger industry partnerships.

Beyond awards and applause, Ghana needs investment, better contracts, effective copyright protection and locally owned music catalogues. International partnerships are welcome, but Ghanaian businesses must develop enough commercial muscle to negotiate from positions of strength.

We must stop exporting our talent while importing the business power to profit from it.

More Than Hitmakers

Ghana does not lack musical talent. What we lack are sufficiently strong institutions capable of turning that talent into enduring commercial power.

We need labels that think beyond the next release, executives who understand intellectual property and investors who recognise that music catalogues can be valuable assets long after the latest hit has disappeared from the charts.

Our history proves that we have built such structures before. Our contemporary successes prove that the talent remains.

What is missing is the ambition to connect the two.

Because an industry that can produce stars but cannot build businesses around them will spend its lifetime celebrating other people's commercial victories.

After nearly a century of making music, Ghana deserves more than applause. It deserves ownership, investment and power.

Ghana News.title: Mahama directs Roads Minister to mark designated contraflow lanes in Accra – Ayariga
Ghana News.content:
President John Mahama has directed the Minister for Roads and Highways, Governs Kwame Agbodza, to identify and mark key roads in Accra for contraflow operations to improve traffic management in the capital.

Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Mahama Ayariga, disclosed this while discussing the contraflow arrangement on Joy FM's Super Morning Show on Tuesday, November 10.

He said the President had instructed the Roads and Highways Minister to ensure that roads designated for contraflow operations are clearly marked to inform motorists and other road users.

"He [The President] directed the Roads Minister to make provisions in the new reconstructions that are taking place. Proper marking of the contraflow sides so that the public is aware that that side of the road, during certain peak hours, will be available for buses that will be moving in the opposite direction," he said.

According to Mr Ayariga, the markings will help motorists identify lanes reserved for the Ayalolo buses to prevent any chaotic situation.

He explained that the move forms part of broader measures to improve the efficiency of the contraflow system and ensure that the buses can transport commuters without unnecessary interference from other vehicles.

The intervention is part of the government's efforts to improve public transportation and ease traffic congestion in Accra.

Ghana News.title: Makeup Ghana, University of Ghana launch first beauty and wellness industry report
Ghana News.content:
Makeup Ghana, a professional body that advocates for the development of the beauty and wellness industry in Ghana, in collaboration with the University of Ghana College of Humanities, has launched the first-ever report to address challenges that have stalled the industry.

The report, which seeks to sanitise the operations of practitioners, building their capacity is expected to bring new reforms to the sector.

The Ghana Beauty and Wellness Report 2026, the first comprehensive, evidence-based national study of the sector, was launched at the 10th Ghana Beauty Awards in November 2026.

CEO of Makeup Ghana, Rebecca Donkor, delivering her opening remarks

The report answers long-unanswered questions such as who buys, what they pay, who sells, who trains, who regulates, and what it would take for the industry to employ more young people and earn more for Ghana.

It was commissioned by Makeup Ghana, marking its tenth year, and produced by an independent steering committee chaired by Professor Sheena Lovia Boateng of the University of Ghana Business School.

The evidence rests on 1,250 face-to-face consumer surveys across ten regions in October 2026, fifty in-depth interviews, and submissions from 27 institutions, including the Food and Drugs Authority, the Ghana Standards Authority, the Ghana Revenue Authority, the Bank of Ghana and two commercial banks.

It also included the first public registers of the industry: 118 manufacturers, 982 cosmetics retailers in all 16 regions, and about 160 spas, wellness businesses and aesthetic clinics.

Everyone in Ghana can see the beauty industry.

It is on every street, in every market and in most homes. Until now, nobody had counted it.

Demand is strong and growing. Eighty-six per cent of buyers say they spend more on beauty than five years ago, and 94 per cent expect to spend the same or more in future.

This is a cash and mobile money economy of small, frequent payments, led by hair. Hairdressing dominates spending, and three quarters of buyers pay in cash.

Trust travels through people, not platforms. Family and friends inform 76 per cent of buyers, television 66 per cent, and influencers only 3 per cent.

Safety has a gap. Three in four buyers have heard of the FDA's registration mark, but only one in five checks it when buying. When something goes wrong, complaints go to the salon, not the authority.

In June 2026, a one-week FDA exercise seized 4,504 unregistered cosmetic products.

On trade, Ghana imported about US$95 million of cosmetics in 2025, against exports of US$6.6 million in 2023.

Yet the Ghana Export Promotion Authority lists cosmetics among its priority export sectors.

The sector also trains itself. Associations and colleges report over 3,000 trainees a year, on national credential pathways that already exist.

The report argues this makes beauty one of Ghana's readiest youth employment channels.

Professor Sheena Lovia Boateng

Speaking at the launch, Professor Boateng said the evidence was always here, but it had never been brought together.

She highlighted three findings. First, this is a hair economy.

Braiding and wash-and-set each reach more than seven in ten of the women who buy."If you work in hair, you are not part of this industry.

You are its center," she said.

Second, customers are spending more, even inside tight budgets. Third, trust travels person to person. “Your best  is a satisfied customer walking out of your door," she said.

Boateng was plain about what the report cannot say. It is a baseline, not a census.

The report closes with 14 actions, each assigned to a named institution. They include a sector council, an enforcer for service standards that already exist on paper, and licensing tiered by risk so that small operators are helped into the formal system rather than driven out of it.

It also calls for a 2027 edition to measure what this baseline could only outline.

For an industry long seen but never counted, the report offers Ghana its first clear picture — and a starting point for policy, investment and jobs.

Ghana News.title: Tiwa Savage gives Siifa’s ‘Slim Girl’ the superstar stamp of approval
Ghana News.content:
Afrobeats singer Siifa has received a boost to his rising career after Nigerian superstar Tiwa Savage was spotted vibing to his latest single, ‘Slim Girl.'

The moment, which has sparked conversations on social media, has brought additional attention to the emerging singer and his growing musical catalogue.

For Siifa, having a respected music icon such as Tiwa Savage connect with his sound is an encouraging development. Widely celebrated for her musical achievements and influence, Tiwa’s moment with the song represents a significant milestone for the emerging artiste.

According to Siifa, ‘SLIM GIRL’ celebrates the beauty and captivating curves of women while creating an energetic, feel-good atmosphere. He describes the track as an ideal soundtrack for dancing, entertainment and celebrating the confidence and beauty of femininity.

Beyond the attention surrounding ‘SLIM GIRL’, Siifa has continued to demonstrate his versatility through other releases. His previous single, ‘Soro’, is available on major digital streaming platforms, further expanding his catalogue.

Another notable release is ‘Leave You’, featuring Ghanaian singer Olivetheboy. The song explores the emotional experiences of a woman battling insecurity and the fear of losing her partner. In response, her lover reassures her of his genuine affection and commitment, promising not to abandon her.

Siifa’s musical journey began at a young age. He discovered his passion for singing at just 12 while participating in the choir alongside his cousin, Ifeanyi, popularly known as Ipro Boy, at Pool of Healing Church in Aba, Abia State. During his time at the church, he also developed his musical abilities by playing different instruments.

The singer draws creative inspiration from his personal experiences and the environment around him, using music as a platform to communicate relatable stories, emotions and life lessons.

His musical journey has also seen him collaborate with Ghanaian artiste FBS. Their collaboration, titled ‘Odogwu’, has gained visibility, with its official music video reportedly receiving television airplay, while the audio is available on digital streaming platforms.

A major turning point in Siifa’s career came with his signing to McNeil Musik. After years of seeking sponsorship and the right support to advance his music career, the record deal represents an important step towards achieving his professional ambitions.

With the attention surrounding ‘SLIM GIRL’ continuing to grow, Siifa is steadily positioning himself in the Afrobeats space. From his early beginnings in the church choir to collaborations with Ghanaian artistes and his latest record deal, his journey reflects his determination, consistency and passion for music.

Tiwa Savage’s moment with ‘SLIM GIRL’ has given Siifa another opportunity to introduce his sound to a wider audience.

Ghana News.title: Women’s Development Bank applies to BoG for banking licence – Vice President
Ghana News.content:
The proposed Women's Development Bank has submitted an application to the Bank of Ghana (BoG) for a banking licence, marking a major step towards its establishment.

Vice President Professor Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang says a dedicated committee tasked with developing the institution has completed its work and submitted the application through the Ministry of Finance for regulatory consideration.

Speaking at the 15th Ghana Economic Forum organised by the B&FT, she said the bank is being designed to address persistent financing challenges confronting women-owned businesses, particularly those operating in the informal sector.

She explained that the institution will adopt a different approach from conventional banks by bringing financial services closer to women entrepreneurs and traders.

"We therefore constituted a dedicated committee that brought together market women, susu collectors, representatives of women's business associations, financial sector professionals and other key stakeholders," she said.

The Vice President noted that the committee's work was guided by the need to ensure that the bank reflects the actual experiences and financial needs of women.

"My conviction has always been that an institution established to serve women must be shaped by the experiences, aspirations and everyday realities of those very women," she added.

Professor Opoku-Agyemang cited Ghana Statistical Service data indicating that women manage nearly 60 per cent of micro-establishments but account for less than 10 per cent of large businesses.

She said the disparity highlights the need for targeted financial interventions to help women-owned enterprises expand and become more competitive.

"This bank is not meant to be just another financial institution. It is conceived as a last-mile bank designed to bring financial services closer to the women whose enterprise and hard work sustain our markets and local economies," she stated.

Ghana News.title: Government considers moving Ashaiman–Atimpoku road project to Big Push
Ghana News.content:
Roads and Highways Minister Governs Kwame Agbodza

The government is considering transferring the 64.4-kilometre Ashaiman Roundabout–Atimpoku Junction road project to the Big Push programme to address funding challenges affecting its construction.

Roads and Highways Minister, Governs Kwame Agbodza, said the proposed move would not affect the project's design, scope or nature of the ongoing works, but would change its source of funding.

He disclosed this during an inspection of road projects, adding that the Tema–Aflao road, being constructed by BHM Construction, and the Bolgatanga–Bawku–Pulmakom road were also being considered for the funding arrangement.

According to the Minister, the move is intended to ensure a more consistent flow of funds and prevent financing difficulties from further delaying construction.

Mr Agbodza attributed the delays affecting the Ashaiman–Atimpoku project and other roads financed through loans to the impact of the Domestic Debt Exchange Programme (DDEP), which disrupted government-backed financing arrangements.

He said transferring the projects to the Big Push framework could help address the funding constraints and support their completion.

“I am going to make a recommendation to the government to migrate the project onto the Big Push. The scope will not change, and the terms of the actual work will remain the same. It is only the source of funding that will change,” he said.

Ghana News.title: Cities and businesses drive global climate action, but major gaps remain
Ghana News.content:
Climate action led by cities, regional governments, businesses and civil society organisations is making progress in translating global climate commitments into practical action, although significant gaps remain in efforts to address the climate crisis, according to a new report by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).

The 2026 Yearbook of Global Climate Action, launched by UN Climate Change on the opening day of the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, highlights progress across 44 global indicators aligned with the outcomes of the first Global Stocktake under the Paris Agreement.

The report points to growing renewable energy capacity, slowing deforestation and increased implementation of various adaptation measures as evidence of momentum in global climate action.

However, it identifies persistent gaps, particularly in reducing methane emissions from the oil and gas sector and addressing food loss. It also highlights the absence of global indicators across some important areas as a limitation to tracking progress and strengthening accountability.

UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said the report demonstrates how climate commitments are increasingly translating into tangible outcomes for communities and economies.

“This Yearbook shows how businesses, cities, communities, and more are turning global commitments into change that people are seeing, feeling and benefiting from,” he said.

Stiell stressed that the pace and scale of implementation must increase, urging countries and stakeholders to use COP31 to expand existing solutions, mobilise climate finance and extend the benefits of climate action to more people.

He said the world could and must go much further and faster, adding that COP31 should help scale up solutions, mobilise finance and ensure more people benefit from climate action.

Businesses and communities demonstrate growing climate action

The 2026 Yearbook presents the latest available data and trends across 96 global socio-economic indicators aligned with the first Global Stocktake.

Structured around the six thematic priorities of the COP31 Action Agenda, it examines developments in climate action while highlighting initiatives by businesses, sub-national governments and other non-Party stakeholders.

The indicators are intended to strengthen transparency and make it easier to compare progress over time, while identifying areas where implementation is advancing and where additional efforts are needed.

The report also draws on a record number of progress reports submitted through the UNFCCC's Non-State Actor Zone for Climate Action (NAZCA), an online platform that tracks climate initiatives undertaken by businesses, organisations, cities, regions and other sub-national governments.

A total of 83 Cooperative Climate Initiatives (CCIs) submitted reports detailing more than 200 actions.

According to the Yearbook, these self-reported activities demonstrate how collaborative initiatives can measure and showcase concrete results, strengthen transparency and support the wider implementation of climate action.

The findings also indicate progress under the Action Agenda's Plans to Accelerate Solutions (PAS), which are multi-stakeholder workplans outlining key actions and voluntary commitments to speed up implementation.

After one year of implementation, 84 per cent of the reported PAS initiatives indicated progress, suggesting that the Action Agenda is beginning to translate commitments into implementation.

Marrakech Partnership marks 10 years

The release of the 2026 Yearbook coincides with the 10th anniversary of the Marrakech Partnership for Global Climate Action, established in 2016 to strengthen collaboration between governments and non-Party stakeholders.

The partnership operates under the leadership of the Climate High-Level Champions and provides a platform for governments, cities, regions, businesses and investors to work together on climate action.

The initiative builds on the recognition, during the adoption of the Paris Agreement in 2015, of the important contributions that non-Party stakeholders can make towards addressing climate change.

At COP29, the mandate of the Climate High-Level Champions was renewed until 2030. A five-year vision covering 2026–2030 was subsequently launched at COP30 to guide their work and accelerate climate action implementation.

The partnership is expected to remain an important component of efforts to advance climate solutions alongside formal negotiations between governments.

Yearbook to be updated with COP31 outcomes

COP31, taking place from 9 to 20 November 2026 in Antalya, Türkiye, is expected to place strong emphasis on accelerating real-economy climate action through the Global Climate Action Agenda.

The agenda is designed to complement the formal negotiation process by supporting practical implementation among governments and non-Party stakeholders.

Unlike previous editions, the 2026 Yearbook has been launched in a new online format. UN Climate Change says the publication will be updated to reflect key outcomes on Global Climate Action emerging from COP31.

Published annually, the Yearbook provides an assessment of progress and gaps in global climate action, while documenting concrete initiatives by non-Party stakeholders to encourage wider participation and raise ambition.

Ghana News.title: How fragmented health data systems take time away from patient care
Ghana News.content:
A health worker in a busy facility has patients to attend to, medicines to monitor and records to update. But when different health programmes operate separate reporting systems, the work of documenting patient and service information can become repetitive.

Information collected once may have to be submitted several times through different platforms to meet the requirements of different authorities.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) says this fragmentation is adding to the administrative workload of health workers in African countries, with implications for the time they can devote to caring for patients.

Team Lead for Health Information, Knowledge Management, Digital Health and Artificial Intelligence at the WHO Regional Office for Africa, Dr Benson Droti, said some countries had allowed individual health programmes to develop their own information systems, resulting in duplicated reporting.

“Because of the fragmentation at national level… health workers collect data once; they report it so many times,” he said in an exclusive interview with JoyNews Mahmud Mohammed-Nurudeen.

He explained that some donor-supported programmes operate outside national health information frameworks because development partners have specific reporting requirements.

Different technologies and the absence of common standards also make it difficult for the systems to exchange information.

Dr Droti said limited coordination by central government had compounded the problem, allowing different programmes to establish systems that sometimes collect similar information without communicating effectively with one another.

“We often say in WHO that data should be collected once, reported once and used several times,” he said.

He stressed that the solution does not necessarily require every country to operate a single information system. Different platforms can serve different purposes, he said, provided they can communicate and avoid collecting the same information repeatedly.

“What is important [is that] they should not be collecting the same information and they should be able to speak with each other,” he said.

When reporting competes with patient care

For health workers, the problem is experienced at facility level, where information may have to be submitted to several authorities even when it has already been recorded.

Dr Droti said this creates an additional reporting burden for staff who should be able to devote more time to patients.

“What we want health workers to spend more time on is caring for patients rather than spending time reporting data to different people,” he said.

The WHO official's account also points to a governance problem. Where national authorities cannot coordinate the development and operation of health information systems, programmes may continue to introduce separate reporting arrangements.

That can make it harder for health managers to access a complete picture of services and use information across the health system.

The reporting burden is linked to a wider problem of information that is collected but cannot easily be shared or used where it is needed.

Dr Droti said African countries had made progress in data availability, quality and use over the past five to ten years. However, he said many systems remained fragmented, poorly integrated and inaccessible to some of the people who need the information to make decisions.

He gave the example of a rural health facility running out of essential medicines. If stock information is not updated promptly or connected to the supply chain, authorities responsible for replenishment may take longer to identify the shortage.

He also described a district-level situation in which delayed reporting of rising malaria cases could slow the response by national authorities.

“Behind every missing data point could be a patient who is not receiving the care that they need,” he said.

He added that decision-makers who cannot access reliable information may also struggle to distribute health resources equitably.

The case for connected health information systems

The First Africa Health Data Forum, scheduled for Nairobi, Kenya, from November 10 to 12, 2026, is expected to address some of these challenges.

The forum's concept note identifies fragmented information systems, parallel reporting requirements and limited interoperability as persistent obstacles to strengthening health data across the region.

It will bring together governments, development partners, technical institutions, academia, civil society and private-sector organisations to discuss country priorities and practical ways to improve health data systems.

For Dr Droti, the priority is to build integrated systems that allow information from different sources to be connected and made available to authorised users.

He said he would like to see African countries move from fragmented data systems to integrated health intelligence systems by the time the forum meets again in 2028.

That change, he said, should include stronger national coordination, better interoperability and greater use of information in decisions about resource allocation, workforce planning, disease prevention and service delivery.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
