World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Moroccan trio make African Player of Year shortlist as Salah absent
World.content:
Achraf Hakimi will hope to defend his title of African Footballer of the Year on December 2 as he leads a trio of Moroccan players on the shortlist, which does not feature Egyptian star and former winner Mohamed Salah.

Morocco captain Hakimi is joined by Brahim Diaz and Ismael Saibari on the 10-man shortlist released by the Confederation of African Football (CAF) last week.

The trio led Morocco to a controversial Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) title in January. Although Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 after extra time in the final, Morocco were subsequently awarded the title after Senegal walked off the pitch over a disputed penalty. A decision on Senegal’s appeal over being stripped of the title will be made ⁠⁠at the end of ⁠⁠November.

The three players also helped Morocco reach the quarterfinals of the World Cup, where Saibari was the country’s top scorer with three goals while Hakimi scored one.

At the club level, Saibari shone with Bayern Munich after they signed him for a hefty 50-million-euro ($56m) transfer fee this summer while Diaz continued to prove his worth with Real Madrid.

Hakimi, meanwhile, helped Paris Saint-Germain to their second consecutive Champions League title.

In 2025, he became the first Moroccan since 1998 and the first defender since 1973 to win Africa’s most prestigious award, finishing ahead of Salah and Nigeria striker Victor Osimhen, the 2023 winner.

The other players on the African Footballer of the Year shortlist are Amad Diallo (Ivory Coast); Yoane Wissa (Democratic Republic of the Congo); Antoine Semenyo (Ghana); Ismaila Sarr, Pape Gueye and Sadio Mane (Senegal); and Teboho Mokoena (South Africa).

Salah’s absence from the list has raised eyebrows because the Egyptian forward is widely recognised as a generational talent and one of Africa’s top players.



The former Liverpool star, now with the Turkish side Trabzonspor, took home the award in 2017 and 2018. Mane won the subsequent two awards.

World Cup heroics reflected in nominations

Notable names in the coach category are Egypt’s Hossam Hassan, who was subsequently sacked by the national team over a marital scandal, and DR Congo’s Sebastien Desabre, both of whom led their side to historic runs to the World Cup round of 16.

The Moroccan duo of Mohamed Ouahbi, who led the team during the World Cup, and Walid Regragui, who was the coach during qualification, were also nominated for their country’s success at the tournament while Cabo Verde’s coach Pedro Leitao Brito has made the shortlist for helping the island nation make its World Cup debut.

Goalkeeper Vonzinha, who became an overnight global sensation due to his World Cup heroics, is among the 10 nominees for goalkeeper of the year alongside Egyptian pair El-Mahdi Soliman and Mostafa Shobeir.

Morocco’s Yassine Bonou remains a leading contender after his performances at the World Cup and AFCON.

The World Cup also saw several young stars shine on the international stage, earning them places on the shortlist for Young Player of the Year. Ghana midfielder Caleb Yirenky scored a dramatic stoppage-time winner against Panama in the Black Stars’ opening match while Morocco’s Ayoub Bouaddi starred as a breakout defensive midfielder.

Bouaddi became the first African teenager to make five World Cup appearances and was signed by Manchester City in August. He is accompanied by compatriot Abdellah Ouazane on the shortlist.

Cameroon dominates women’s award

Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) winners Cameroon have dominated every award category on the women’s side.

Midfielder Monique Ngock, 22, was named player of the tournament while Michaely Bihina was recognised as best goalkeeper. Marie Ngah Manga scored twice in Cameroon’s 3-0 final victory over Malawi.

Her brace tied her for most goals at a WAFCON (five) alongside Zambia’s Barbra Banda, 2024 winner of CAF Women’s Footballer of the Year, and Malawi’s Temwa Chawinga. All three along with Chawinga’s sister Tabitha feature on this year’s shortlist.

South Africa’s Thembi Kgatlana, who scored four WAFCON goals, is also a top contender for the accolade.

Standing out in the goalkeeper shortlist is Cameroon’s Michaely Bihina, who won the Golden Glove at WAFCON, and Malawi’s Mercy Sikelo.

Competition is also stiff for the women’s Young Player of the Year, which includes Cameroon’s Maeva Nyadjou, a breakout defender at the tournament.



Malawi’s Rose Kadzere scored in her side’s quarterfinal victory over Ghana to reach the semis and help secure qualification for the women’s World Cup.

World.title: France summons Iran’s ambassador over supermarket fridge ‘sabotage’
World.content:
The French government said it is seeking tough sanctions to deter further cyberattacks across Europe.

France says it has summoned Iran’s ambassador to Paris “to lodge a very strong protest” after it accused Tehran of carrying out a major cyberattack targeting supermarket fridges last month.

“It marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation’s interests and the security of the French people,” Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Tuesday.

“I can also tell you that we rule nothing out and will take all measures – including those we may not disclose publicly – that we deem proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks,” he added.

Barrot, speaking on France Info ‌‌television, said the government would push for European Union sanctions in response to what he called an “attack of unprecedented scale and aggression in our country”.

He said firm measures would be taken “to deter anyone who might be tempted, in Iran or elsewhere, to do it again”.

On Monday, Barrot said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was behind cyberattacks targeting more than 700 French supermarkets on October 11 and 12, when refrigerators were remotely accessed “to initiate abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles”.

Raised temperatures in fridges forced the supermarkets to throw away all perishable food.

Millions of euros’ worth of food was spoiled, according to retailers. In some cases, the raised temperatures sparked fires or melted equipment.

French supermarket groups E-Leclerc, Intermarche, Carrefour, Monoprix and Cooperative U were all hit.



Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said on Monday she had opened an investigation into Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit of the IRGC, over the attacks.

The prosecutor’s office has requested international arrest warrants be issued for two Shahid Kaveh officials.

Similar incidents have since been reported in other European countries.

In a suspected cyberattack on November 2, temperature spikes were recorded in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden.

Jody Westby, chief executive of Global Cyber Risk LLC, said tracking down the group directly responsible for the attacks is “very difficult” because of poor cooperation on international cybercrime investigations.

“It’s been a problem for 20 some years, and now it’s a little better, but only marginally so,” Westby told Al Jazeera. She said that it was difficult to track and trace the origin of such attacks “because of the nature of packet switching”.

In recent days, European air traffic has also been disrupted by false bomb alerts against dozens of flights, although the origin of those threats has yet to be determined.

World.title: UK author M John Harrison’s End of Everything wins Booker Prize
World.content:
Harrison, 81, becomes the oldest winner of the prestigious prize, whose previous winners include Salman Rushdie and Margaret Atwood.

British ‌‌author M John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize ⁠⁠for his ⁠⁠dystopian satire novel, The End of Everything, becoming ⁠⁠the oldest winner in the literary award’s history.

The Booker judges unanimously selected the 198-page book on Monday, saying it can be read as a “thriller, a mystery, a satire, a dystopia, a road novel, a work of realism”.

The novel, whose themes of “catastrophe and apocalypse” chime with our uneasy times, is the first work of science fiction to win the prestigious literary award.

Harrison beat five other finalists, including previous winners Douglas Stuart and Marlon James. He was awarded the 50,000 British pound ($67,000) prize at a ceremony in London.

The End of Everything is set on the southeast English coast in the near future, after an unspecified calamity shattered society and brought an influx of enigmatic alien entities to Britain. It centres on a beachcomber who lives with his gun-toting aunt and discovers a puzzling, shape-shifting artefact on the shore.

“It’s a grim world, and it’ll keep on being grim. And it’s weird. But at the end of things, there may be some kind of – I wouldn’t say hope, or closure, but there might be some kind of relief,” Harrison said, when asked what he wanted to convey to readers.

The 81-year-old author is the oldest writer to win the Booker, two years older than Margaret Atwood when she won in 2019.

Previous winners also include Salman Rushdie, Ian McEwan and Arundhati Roy. Last year’s winner was Flesh by Hungarian-British writer David Szalay.



‘Fantastically exciting’

Critics have praised the book’s dark humour, though some have been confused by its elusive narrative.

Mary Beard, who chaired the judging panel, described the book as “the politics of now seen through the lens of the future”, saying it depicts a society grappling with ⁠⁠a catastrophe its inhabitants do not fully understand.

“What he does is to say, when the catastrophe comes, you won’t know what’s happening,” the historian said. “And there are bits where you, the reader, are with the characters in not fully understanding. Now, I think that’s fantastically exciting.”

Harrison’s win marks a rare moment of mainstream recognition for the science fiction genre. He previously said he had been “working for 40 to 50 years to shift the balance, both as a novelist and as a critic. Why shouldn’t a well-written [work of science fiction] be considered to be literary fiction?”

Beard said Harrison’s win was “recognition of what some people would see as the blindingly obvious, that you find great books in every genre.”

Founded in 1969, the Booker Prize is open to English-language novels from any country published in the UK and Ireland and has a reputation for transforming writers’ careers.

World.title: What is Hasina’s game plan as she seeks a passport to return to Bangladesh?
World.content:
The ousted leader faces the prospect of being hanged upon return for her violent suppression of the 2024 uprising that killed more than 1,400 people.

Share What is Hasina’s game plan as she seeks a passport to return to Bangladesh? on social media

Dhaka, Bangladesh – Bangladesh’s ousted leader Sheikh Hasina wants a new passport to return to the country next month, more than two years after fleeing to India following a mass uprising that forced her from power.

The 79-year-old former prime minister was sentenced to death in absentia last year for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on the student-led protests in 2024, a charge she denies.

She faces the prospect of being hanged upon her return, as the government that succeeded her remains a staunch political opponent.

Dhaka has already rejected the passport request and has challenged Hasina to seek extradition from India if she is serious about returning home.

“Bangladesh does not give passports to terrorists who kill thousands of people and flee. It will work under the current extradition arrangements with India to pursue and get the terrorist Hasina handed over,” State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir told Al Jazeera.

On Tuesday, the Bangladeshi prosecutor Md Aminul Islam, who secured the death sentence for Hasina at the Dhaka-based International Crimes Tribunal, said she will be executed if she returns home.

“Sheikh Hasina has no option but to face the execution of the verdict,” Islam told reporters.

So, what led Hasina to approach the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi, seeking a new passport and a national identity card since her existing documents have been revoked, and what is her game plan?

‘She knows what her fate is’

Hasina ruled Bangladesh with an iron fist for nearly 20 years and still enjoys support among a section of its population, while many others want to see her hanged.



Her return could worsen political tensions as Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s government tries to restore ‌‌stability two years on from the 2024 uprising that led to the killing of more than 1,400 people, according to the United Nations.

But analysts question whether Hasina genuinely intends to return to face the law, or is using the promise to revive her political fortunes from self-imposed exile in India.

For Zillur Rahman, president of the Centre for Governance Studies, a Dhaka-based think tank, Hasina’s passport request is less about an imminent plan to return and more about keeping herself politically relevant as she tries to retain control of her Awami League party.

“I think she knows what her fate is. But what she wants is to keep Awami League leaders and activists politically engaged,” he said, referring to Hasina’s party, which was founded by her father and Bangladesh independence movement leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.

“As far as I understand, she does not want to hand over the party’s leadership to anyone else under any circumstances. I think that is a major problem for her and for the party. Otherwise, the party might have tried to find a way to survive.”

Jon F Danilowicz, a retired United States diplomat who once served as deputy chief of mission at the US embassy in Dhaka, was more categorical.

“There is zero chance that Hasina will return to Bangladesh in December. In my view, this has all been a bluff intended to rally her supporters and shift the narrative regarding her increasing irrelevance at home,” he told Al Jazeera.

Faiz Sobhan, senior research director at the Bangladesh Enterprise Institute research centre, also sees Hasina’s promise as an effort to lift the morale of her party, which is now banned, with many of its leaders in jail or in exile.

“The announcement keeps Sheikh Hasina politically relevant and lets her gauge the mood at home,” he said. “An actual return seems inconceivable, since it would mean facing the gallows or spending the rest of her life behind bars.”

Despite analysts casting doubt on the prospect of Hasina’s return, her announcement appears to have energised some Awami League leaders and supporters.

“Our leader will return. They have tried to stop her before, but they could not stop her. They are conspiring against her again, but she will overcome these conspiracies and return,” an organising secretary of the party’s central executive committee told Al Jazeera, speaking on condition of anonymity from exile in India.



When asked how Hasina would return and what steps the party was taking to facilitate it, many Awami League leaders and supporters said they had no clear idea about her game plan.

“But she has announced that she will return, and I believe she will come back in December, no matter what,” Arman Rahman, a Dhaka-based Awami League activist and former leader of its student wing, told Al Jazeera.

The India question

Hasina’s future is also tied to India’s calculations.

New Delhi, her close ally for decades, has sheltered her since she fled Dhaka in August 2024. But her continued presence has become a point of contention between the two countries.

Dhaka has repeatedly sought Hasina’s extradition under a bilateral treaty. New Delhi says it has been examining the requests, with India’s foreign ministry in April saying it wants to “engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties”.

Meanwhile, both countries have signalled an interest in repairing strained ties.

Sreeradha Datta, professor of international affairs at O P Jindal Global University near New Delhi, told Al Jazeera that India regards Hasina as a longstanding friend, even as it tries to separate her presence in the country from its diplomatic engagement with Dhaka.

“Sheikh Hasina is a very good friend of India. [New] Delhi looks at her as a friend whom it will always support. That is our official position,” she said.

Former US diplomat Danilowicz believes New Delhi is increasingly aware of the diplomatic cost of continuing to host Hasina, but is “unlikely to facilitate” her return to Bangladesh.

“While there may be some in India who still believe that Hasina and her party provide them leverage, by now the [Narendra] Modi government must understand the damage that her continued presence in New Delhi is doing to efforts to normalise relations with Bangladesh,” he said.

“I am certain the Modi government would love to see the Hasina problem go away, including by having her find a third country to reside.”

Rahman, of the Centre for Governance Studies, offered a different explanation for why India may continue to shelter Hasina despite the diplomatic complications.

“I think India is finding it difficult to digest her presence, but at the same time, it cannot let her go either,” he said.

“If India does not take responsibility for protecting her now, its other allies in South Asia and elsewhere may lose trust in New Delhi. They may feel that India does not ultimately protect those who have stood by it.”

Rahman believes India may continue to offer Hasina refuge, but is unlikely to help restore her political domain in Bangladesh.

“I don’t think India will abandon her. But at the same time, I don’t think it will provide her with all forms of political protection, particularly by helping her return to Bangladesh and reestablish herself here,” he said.

Datta, meanwhile, does not expect imminent improvement in relations between the neighbours. “I don’t think Bangladesh-India relations will return to normalisation very soon,” he said.



Is a deal with BNP possible?

Many are also asking if Hasina could enter into some kind of a political understanding with the governing Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), now controlled by Prime Minister Rahman, son of Hasina’s longtime rival, Khaleda Zia, who passed away a year ago. Rahman himself lived in exile in London when Hasina was in power.

But analysts see little possibility of such a deal, with the Bangladesh Enterprise Institute’s Sobhan describing the idea as a “non-starter”.

“The BNP has little to gain and much to lose from any accommodation with the Awami League. Its base spent 16-plus years being jailed, harassed and sidelined [by Hasina], and any hint of a deal would be seen as a betrayal,” he told Al Jazeera.

On Monday, BNP acting secretary general and Prime Minister Rahman’s political adviser, Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, also dismissed the prospect of Hasina’s return.

“She is deluding herself if she thinks she can return, reimpose fascism and reclaim her throne,” Rizvi said at an event in Dhaka.

Sobhan said the BNP government had little room to act outside the verdict delivered by the International Crimes Tribunal.

“A broader settlement to stabilise the country is hard to imagine, and reconciliation without accountability or an apology is harder still,” he said.

Extradition was the “only formal route” available to Dhaka, Sobhan added. “And it means being dragged back [to Bangladesh], not choosing to return.”

World.title: Nvidia spy scandal fuels debate over chip exports to China
World.content:
US lawmakers call for tighter restrictions on chip sales amid inquiry into Nvidia CEO’s relationship with alleged spy.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s intimate relationship with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy has highlighted divisions in Washington over the export of advanced chips to China.

Huang, the head of one of the most critical firms in the global artificial intelligence race, has long been among Silicon Valley’s most powerful voices arguing against restrictions on high-end chip sales.

For years, the tech executive lobbied United States President Donald Trump to loosen export controls, finding allies in sympathetic administration figures such as David Sacks, Trump’s former AI tsar.

Whereas hawkish voices argued that Beijing should not have access to cutting-edge US technology on national security grounds, Huang and like-minded executives argued that China already had the computing power to make strides in AI and that wider uptake of US technology would help maintain its dominance in the field.

Jensen Huang’s lobbying now faces intense scrutiny following claims that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang — with whom he had an affair — was an intelligence agent recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has denied the allegations, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.

Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims, which The New York Times and the Financial Times first reported, citing unnamed US intelligence officials.

Nvidia’s board of directors on Sunday launched an inquiry into Jensen Huang’s relationship, pledging to examine “all available information” while also expressing confidence in the CEO.



Jensen Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993, has pledged to cooperate fully with the inquiry and expressed his commitment to protecting Nvidia and US national security.

Trump has meanwhile said the FBI too is investigating whether Huang’s affair led to any compromise on US national security.

Already, US lawmakers have invoked the controversy to push for tighter restrictions on China’s access to US chips.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren and Republican Senator Jim Banks on Monday called on the US Congress to take “decisive action” and pass their AI Overwatch Act, which would empower lawmakers to scrutinise and potentially halt exports of advanced chips to China and other adversaries.

“The Commerce Department should complement these efforts with immediate action to close export control loopholes and ensure that advanced AI chips are not going to China’s military,” Warren and Banks said in a joint statement.

Democratic House Representative Bill Foster also cited Jensen Huang’s relationship in a statement on Monday in which he called on his fellow lawmakers to get his Chip Security Act “across the finish line”.

The legislation, cosponsored by Republican House Representative Bill Huizenga, aims to prevent illicit smuggling to countries such as China by implementing measures to track the location of chips sent overseas.

Advocates of tighter restrictions now have a “much stronger political argument” and are likely to make use of it, said Rui Ma, a tech industry consultant and founder of Tech Buzz China.

“Chip exports to China have been deeply divisive in Washington, and Huang has been one of the strongest advocates for keeping that market open,” Ma told Al Jazeera.

“If his influence is diminished by this investigation, regardless of its eventual findings, those pushing for tighter restrictions will be in a much stronger position,” she said.

Trump, who has forged a close relationship with Jensen Huang since returning to the White House, has taken several actions to make it easier for chip makers to do business with China, while also maintaining significant export controls.

In May last year, the US Department of Commerce announced that it would scrap the previous Biden administration’s “AI Diffusion Rule”, which would have imposed caps on chip exports to more than 100 countries, including some US allies.

In December, Trump said he had granted Nvidia approval to sell its second-most powerful chip, the H200, to China under an arrangement that would see 25 percent of sales paid to the US government.



Nvidia, which controls an estimated 80 to 90 percent of the market for graphics processing units (GPUs) used to run frontier AI, welcomed the decision at the time, saying it would “support high-paying jobs and manufacturing in America”.

On the other hand, Trump has resisted calls to allow exports of Nvidia’s top-of-the-line Blackwell chips, which deliver about 2.5 times the performance of the H200.

“I think recent events likely increase attention on export control loopholes, and add momentum to bills already being discussed in Congress, like the Chip Security Act,” Erich Grunewald, a senior researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, a Washington, DC-based think tank, told Al Jazeera.

While export controls have spurred contentious debate, their effectiveness has been called into question amid China’s steady advances in AI development.

Authorities and analysts have documented widespread smuggling of restricted chips into China, mainly through Southeast Asia.

Chips with compute power equivalent to 1.6 million Nvidia H100s made their way to China in violation of export restrictions up to the end of 2025, according to an estimate by Epoch AI.

Chinese companies have also been able to bypass US law by remotely accessing compute capacity supplied by Nvidia-powered data centres in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.

Gabriel Wildau, managing director at global business advisory firm Teneo, said claims that Huang had been ensnared in an espionage campaign deserved to be treated with skepticism given the anonymous leaks and motives to discredit him and his company.

“President Trump shows no sign that he intends to disrupt the current US-China rapprochement, but he may face new pressure from Congress and hawkish voices inside his administration to address the remote access issue,” Wildau, who focuses on political risk analysis in China, told Al Jazeera.

Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping have already met twice this year: The US president visited Beijing in May, and the Chinese leader reciprocated with a state visit to Washington in September. They are scheduled to meet again next week when Trump visits Shenzhen for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. And they are expected to meet a fourth time in 2026 in December, when Trump hosts the G20 summit in Miami.

“The risk is that Washington acts to close this loophole [in the aftermath of the Huang controversy], and Beijing regards the action as a violation of the bilateral truce,” Wildau said, referring to the trade truce Trump struck with Xi during their summit in South Korea last year.

Chris Clague, an associate fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London, said the revelations about Jensen Huang would inevitably undermine the “legitimate” argument in favour of allowing tech transfers between the US and China.

“This has made it a little bit easier for his detractors to poke holes in that,” Clague told Al Jazeera. “It’s indicative of the tensions that exist between the US and China, which are never going away, but it shouldn’t derail efforts at finding some sort of compromise.”

World.title: Three workers die at Tata’s iPhone parts plant in India’s Tamil Nadu
World.content:
The workers had inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank, a district official says.

Share Three workers die at Tata’s iPhone parts plant in India’s Tamil Nadu on social media

Three contract workers have died at a Tata Electronics plant producing components for Apple iPhones in the southern Indian state of Tamil Nadu, the latest incident involving the US tech giant’s supply chain in its most important manufacturing hub outside China.

The deaths occurred at a site in Hosur, in the Krishnagiri district, late on Monday.

The workers were among a group assigned to clean an effluent treatment plant (ETP) at a facility in Hosur, senior district official Dinesh Kumar told The New Indian Express.

Kumar said the deaths occurred when the workers inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank.

The three workers were taken to a private hospital, where doctors declared them dead on arrival, TNIE cited Kumar as saying.

The salt-to-aviation Tata Group’s electronics unit accounts for roughly 40 percent of iPhone assembly in India, and Foxconn makes up ‌‌the rest. Tata has in recent months faced many challenges as its iPhone-making operations have been hit by a ransomware attack and concerns about water pollution.

Over the years, as Apple expanded manufacturing beyond China, India has emerged as a key hub, which now accounts for roughly 25 percent of the world’s iPhones.

Industrial hub

Tamil Nadu is a key industrial hub in India, hosting factories ⁠⁠of many global giants, such as Foxconn, Hyundai, VinFast and BMW.

The state’s minister for industries, Virudhai Magal Keerthana, said in a post on X that the worker deaths will ⁠⁠be “thoroughly investigated and appropriate action will be taken based on the findings”.



Tata’s Hosur site has faced repeated setbacks: a fire halted production ‌‌at the components plant in 2024, and state authorities warned of a shutdown over alleged groundwater contamination this year before dropping the matter.

Separately, a ransomware breach at an adjacent iPhone plant in the same ‌‌compound ‌‌leaked documents linked to Apple’s then-unreleased iPhone 18 Pro, the Reuters news agency reported previously.

World.title: Are your supplements fake?
World.content:
NewsFeed Are your supplements fake?

That protein powder in your cupboard might not be all protein, and those creatine gummies might be candy. How are manufacturers duping customers? Al Jazeera’s Basel Ghazoghli explains how you can protect yourself.

World.title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.

"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Speaking later at a White House press briefing, Trump told reporters, "I know the FBI is looking into" the affair but did not give further details on the investigation, or confirm when it was launched.

Trump added he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.

The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.

Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology.

The revelations knocked about $250bn (Â£190bn) off Nvidia's value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%.

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang.

According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

World.title: Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say
World.content:
Trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have begun in Abu Dhabi.

Although expectations for a breakthrough that ends Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine are low, US officials said yesterday that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would control Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario.

Jared Kushner - Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the US delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff - said the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.

"An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war," Kushner wrote on X.

Ahead of the meeting, the two US envoys met Ukrainian and European and Nato officials in Abu Dhabi, and French Foreign Minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot was adamant that France, the UK and Germany "will indeed be in the meeting room".

European officials are wary of Russia trying to secure a deal with the US on future "collective security" without them, and Moscow and Kyiv's positions on ending the conflict are still far apart.

A key area of disagreement between the two involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is by now mostly occupied by Russia.

Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk which it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security.

While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".

However, he acknowledged that the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".

"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."

For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it's attacked again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from eastern Europe â which would be alarming to Europeans.

The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.

World.title: 'There is no justice' - Epstein survivor on how model agency sent her to abuser's home
World.content:
If you are outside the UK, please watch on YouTube, external

An email in the DOJ files, from Fuller to Epstein, makes clear the close ties between the agency and the financier.

"Had it not been for you, we would have fired her months ago," Fuller writes of another model in March 2012. "And I would be careful as she blabs about things," he says.

A month after Epstein's second arrest in 2019, MC2's US branch was dissolved and Fuller opened a new agency, The Source Models, which is still operating. The BBC has found that 50 models from MC2 were transferred to his new agency.

We asked The Source Models to comment on our findings - it did not reply.

Model agencies were useful to Epstein, says Sigrid McCawley, the lead lawyer for more than 100 of Epstein's victims.

"Epstein said to many people he wanted three different girls a day. Think about those numbers... The [model] scouts were really critical because they were the ones who were identifying the type of woman that Epstein liked."

In the case of former agent Ramsey Elkholy, BBC Eye has discovered he tried to connect 34 women to Epstein, including an 18-year-old who was still in school.

The experience of one of the women highlights how assistants would be co-opted into the structure of the abuse.

Elkholy, the DOJ files show, suggested to Epstein that one of the financier's female assistants befriend this woman, before introducing her to Epstein.

We spoke to this woman, and she revealed that at her first meeting with Epstein, aged 19, he sexually abused her in his New York townhouse.

Ramsey Elkholy told the BBC: "I completely reject any allegation that I knew of or facilitated abuse of any kindâ¦ At the time, I had no knowledge of any abuse and I knew only his own [Epstein's] account of his 2008 [legal] case, which I misguidedly believed."

He continued: "The record and published reporting show that women were often groomed by other women in his inner circle. I was never part of that circle, or indeed of any such activityâ¦ my intention was to help models find professional opportunities by introducing them to an extremely well-connected individual."

If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence, information and support is available at BBC Action Line

Lawyer Sigrid McCawley says these female assistants would have had "no choice" in how they conducted themselves.

"These young survivors were being abused regularly. Their livelihoods were being threatenedâ¦ They had to do what they were being told to do."

Another model we have spoken to, Simona (not her real name), from eastern Europe, told us Epstein had raped her more than 200 times.

"People think that we gained something, that we agreed on this abuse in order to gain something, whether it's monetary or influential, but it's not true. We're left with deep trauma," says Simona.

She says the first time she met the financier, aged 20, she was already signed with a model agency in New York, and he offered to introduce her to his "good" friend Faith Kates.

At the time, Kates was the head of Next Management, one of the world's biggest model agencies. She stepped down from that senior executive position in December last year, but is still legally listed as a director of the company.

World.title: Police officer dies and another injured after backpack explosion in Oviedo
World.content:
A police officer has died and another has been injured in the northern Spanish city of Oviedo after an explosive device went off at the scene of a shooting.

The blast happened when officers from Spain's canine unit and explosives disposal unit arrived and examined a suspicious backpack following reports of a dispute between neighbours on Tuesday morning.

A woman who had been shot and the injured officer have been taken to hospital for treatment.

The suspect fled the scene and is still at large, police said.

Spanish police paid tribute to the dead officer, who has been named as Juan JosÃ©, in a statement on X and said: "Our hearts are with his family, friends, colleagues and loved ones."

Officers attended the scene early after receiving reports of an argument between neighbours and upon arriving found a woman who had sustained gunshot wounds, police spokesman Pedro Aguado said.

While searching for the suspected attacker, officers found a suspicious backpack with a flashing light and contacted both the bomb disposal unit and canine unit.

"While the package was being moved outside to ensure the safety of the residents, an explosion occurred," Aguado added.

The explosion left a member of the canine unit dead and an officer from the bomb disposal unit seriously injured, he said.

A three-year-old police dog named Deny was also killed in the explosion.

A widespread police operation is ongoing near the scene of the explosion and officers are continuing to hunt for the suspect.

Taking to social media, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said he was "deeply shocked" by the fatal incident and paid tribute to the officer injured in the explosion.

"Your dedication and courage deserve the gratitude of an entire country," he said.

Spanish opposition leader and President of the People's Party Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o said: "What happened in Oviedo is heartbreaking.

"My condolences to the family of the officer who died and my best wishes for the recovery of the one who was seriously injured.

World.title: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
World.content:
A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.

The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.

Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".

The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said.

"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".

Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.

The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.

Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.

Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (Â£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website.

"For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.

However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.

While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.

CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.

It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.

Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".

The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.

As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.

It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".

The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.

World.title: DR Congo sentences 66 soldiers to death for being 'cowards'
World.content:
At least 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in the Democratic Republic of Congo for cowardice, mutiny and refusing to obey orders, local media report.

The sentences followed a trial of 71 soldiers before a military court in Walikale, in North Kivu province, in eastern DR Congo. Four soldiers were acquitted, while another was sentenced to 10 years in prison.

The army said the trial was intended to improve discipline among troops as they battle armed groups in eastern DR Congo.

The region has endured decades of conflict, with fighting continuing between government forces and the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), a rebel coalition that includes the M23 group.

The soldiers were reportedly arrested on 20 October in Walikale, where they were accused of abandoning their positions and fleeing during clashes with FRN fighters.

The Congolese army's campaign against armed groups, including the M23, has long been undermined by poor discipline and disorganisation within its ranks.

The government has repeatedly accused neighbouring Rwanda of supporting the M23, an allegation denied by both Kigali and the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.

The army has faced persistent criticism over its lack of professionalism and disciplined, while soldiers have complained of poor pay and inadequate equipment.

Last month, another 27 soldiers were sentenced to death on similar charges of cowardice after reportedly withdrawing from the frontline during clashes with rebels.

In March 2024, DR Congo lifted a 20-year moratorium on the death penalty, citing the need to remove "traitors" within the army.

The government said capital punishment would also apply to people involved in armed groups, insurrection, as well as committing treason and war crimes.

The decision to reinstate the death penalty was widely criticised by rights groups. However, no formal executions have been carried out since the moratorium was lifted.

Since the beginning of 2025, at least 507 soldiers have been convicted, including 381 death sentences, according to figures compiled by French broadcaster RFI.

In October 2025, former Congolese President Joseph Kabila was sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself. He has since been named as the FRN's leader.

World.title: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
World.content:
A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution.

"By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorisation, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said.

The effort will likely fail, as Republicans remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says the effort is aimed at pushing President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.

Hegseth has called the impeachment effort a "sham" and defended his record.

"You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said in a video statement last week. "It's not going to work. We will not back down."

He called Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" and said he was not concerned about the impeachment effort. In the video, Hegseth defended his leadership of the department and listed ways he has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda.

Massie formally introduced his articles of impeachment in a resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon. The move starts a 48-hour clock for the chamber to take up the measure. Lawmakers could vote on the resolution directly, vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside.

"I'm doing this because it's the right thing to do," he told reporters after introducing the articles.

Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it started nearly nine months ago. He has previously garnered headlines over demanding the Trump administration release the files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and has now brought them back in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections.

He has said the effort was aimed at preventing a Democrat spectacle next year when they have control of Congress. He said he hoped to force Trump to name a replacement, who could be quickly confirmed while Republicans have power.

"My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials."

Democratic leadership has signalled openness to such an effort against Hegseth once they take control in January.

Asked about the effort on Monday, Hegseth said, "We're not worried about that".

He said he planned to hold a news conference on Tuesday to discuss the subject.

President Trump has indicated that he plans to stick by Hegseth, praising his leadership in the US capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro earlier this year and defending his work during the war in Iran.

"We've made the world a lot safer place. Why haven't we gone after all these other people that ran wars and lost?" Trump said on Monday at the White House.

He also touted recruitment numbers under Hegseth.

"The soldiers, the actual soldiers, the great people that do the work, the great patriots, they love Pete Hegseth," he said. "He's done a very good job."

Impeaching a cabinet secretary is rare. It must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office.

Trump was impeached by the House twice in his first term in office but was cleared by the Senate after two trials and not removed.

As with the presidential process, the House would first hold a vote on charges against Hegseth and the Senate then would conduct a trial to decide whether to acquit or convict.

The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not convict either one.

While impeachment has been "an incredibly rare process", it has become far more normalised since the House impeached President Bill Clinton in 1998, said Paul Gowder, a law professor at Northwestern University in Chicago.

He said it has become "much more common as the country has become more politically polarised," adding a prediction that several more of Trump's cabinet members may face impeachment over the next two years.

Massie told reporters he was not sure if the measure had sufficient backing to pass. It would need a majority to pass the House and even with all Democratic support, it would still likely need some Republican support as the party holds a slim majority.

Peter Loge, a professor of public affairs at George Washington University, told the BBC that he believed it was likely to pass due to those slim margins.

"There are enough angry Republicans that more than enough Republicans are gonna simply not show up to vote," he said.

Currently, there are 218 Republicans and 214 Democrats in the House.

While the House requires a simple majority to pass articles of impeachment, the Senate mandates a two-thirds vote to convict, threshold that is difficult to meet in the current congressional term.

When Democrats take over in January, they are likely to have at least 54 Senate seats - though two races do not yet have winners due to slim voting margins. A total of 67 votes will be required to convict and remove an official from office.

- 10/11/2026 - This story was updated to reflect that 67 votes in the Senate are needed to remove an official from office

World.title: Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
World.content:
Donald Trump has said "Iran militarily is effectively over", and said that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict.

"We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."

Trump's comments came after he met the Qatari prime minister. Qatar is a US ally in the Gulf region, and one of Iran's neighbours, which has been a key mediator in efforts to end the war.

Addressing reporters in the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.

Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about Trump's prior comments about resolving the conflict.

This is not the first time that Trump has said the Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.

The president has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President JD Vance blamed on the Iran war.

Ahead of the midterms, Trump had said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz. However, in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said that he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the conflict.

Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the war, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression.

"We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," he said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.

Global oil prices, which have fallen sharply since the midterms, dipped further after Trump's comments.

On Tuesday afternoon in Asia, Brent crude was more than 1% lower at $91.50 (Â£52) while US-traded was down by 1.2% at $85.82.

World.title: NIJ Alumni Association congratulates Akodu on election as NUJ Lagos chair
World.content:
The Nigerian Institute of Journalism Alumni Association (NIJAA) has congratulated Adewale Akodu on his election as the chairman of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ), Lagos State Council.

The association, in a congratulatory letter dated 10 November 2026, issued and signed by its Global Secretary, Dimeji Kayode-Adedeji, said that Mr Akodu, as an alumnus of the institute, is a source of pride for the association.

“On behalf of the executive and the entire members of the Nigerian Institute of Journalism Alumni Association (NIJAA), I write to heartily congratulate you on your well-deserved election as Chairman of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ), Lagos State Council,” Mr Kayode-Adedeji wrote.

The letter emphasised that the association is proud that Mr Akodu has been found worthy by his colleagues to have been elected to lead the largest and most vibrant council of the great union.

‘Your victory is not only a personal triumph, but a thing of pride to all of us at NIJAA. That a proud alumnus of the Nigerian Institute of Journalism has been found worthy by colleagues to lead the largest and most vibrant council of the great union is a testimony to your competence, character, humility and years of dedicated service to journalism,” the letter read.

“We have noted, with great delight, your acceptance speech and your three-point agenda of welfarism, professionalism and capacity building, as well as your commitment to members’ welfare, dignity, security, regular payment of salaries, improved working conditions and respect for journalists’ rights. These are values the Nigerian Institute of Journalism has always stood for, and we are confident you will live up to them,” he added.

“NIJAA assures you of our full support and partnership throughout your tenure. We are ready to collaborate with your executive in the areas of training, mentorship, capacity building, ethical re-orientation and welfare of members, particularly young journalists who look up to leaders like you,” Mr Kayode-Adedeji wrote.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“We also urge you to be a chairman for all — to extend a hand of fellowship to all contestants and members, and to run an inclusive, transparent and unifying administration, as you have already promised,” the letter added.

“Once again, congratulations, our dear alumnus. We wish you a peaceful, successful and impactful tenure. May your leadership bring renewed pride to the NUJ Lagos State Council and to the NIJ family at large. Please accept the assurances of our highest regards.”

World.title: Customs hands over intercepted LPG consignment to NMDPRA
World.content:
The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) has handed over an intercepted consignment of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) to the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA).

The handover took place on Friday at the warehouse of the Customs Cross River/Calabar Free Trade Zone/Akwa Ibom Area Command.

It was witnessed by Acting Customs Area Controller, Deputy Comptroller Nkeiruka Nwala, and NMDPRA State Coordinator, Joy Okor-Odey.

The National Coordinator of Operation Whirlwind, Mahmood Bello, said the exercise demonstrated Customs’ commitment to preventing illegal diversion of petroleum products.

He said the products were intended for legitimate domestic consumption and that their diversion threatened national economic security.

Mr Bello disclosed that the exercise also featured the public auction of 245 jerry cans of petrol, containing 6,125 litres.

He said the products were intercepted at identified flashpoints, including Ekairoa, Sakansi, Abaka and Yukongo.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to him, the auction had a total duty-paid value of N6.135 million.

Mr Bello said the interceptions and subsequent handover aimed to ensure petroleum products were transported, distributed and utilised according to established regulatory guidelines.

He warned that illegal diversion and smuggling threatened national economic security, distorted legitimate supply chains and encouraged economic sabotage.

The national coordinator commended the Comptroller-General of Customs, the Office of the National Security Adviser, NMDPRA and Operation Whirlwind personnel.

He urged operational commanders to strengthen surveillance and intelligence gathering amid reports of possible increased petroleum product diversion and smuggling.

Also speaking, Ms Nwala said the handover formed part of efforts to strengthen inter-agency collaboration and combat petroleum product smuggling.

She emphasised sustained cooperation among relevant agencies to protect national economic interests and ensure compliance with petroleum regulations.

Ms Nwala said the formal transfer of the LPG consignment underscored regulatory compliance, accountability and effective coordination within the petroleum sector.

She commended NMDPRA representatives and other stakeholders for partnering with Customs to tackle economic crimes.

‘LPG is not just a product’

In her remarks, Mrs Okor-Odey described the handover as a practical demonstration of inter-agency cooperation and regulatory responsibility.

She said the exercise would help ensure LPG reached legitimate domestic, commercial and industrial consumers.

She said: “LPG is not just a product; it is energy for homes, businesses and industries.

“When LPG is diverted or illegally transported, it can have serious consequences for consumers and the economy.”

Mrs Okor-Odey warned individuals and companies involved in illegal petroleum product diversion that the authority would not tolerate activities undermining product availability.

She disclosed that preliminary investigations had been completed and the concerned company had paid the applicable administrative penalty.

The coordinator assured that the handed-over LPG would be handled professionally in accordance with established safety standards.

She cited the product’s volatile nature as a reason for strict adherence to safety requirements.

Mrs Okor-Odey pledged continued collaboration with Customs and other security agencies to strengthen intelligence sharing and petroleum regulatory enforcement.

(NAN)

World.title: PANDEF condemns political violence in South-south, urges parties to hold rallies in secured venues
World.content:
The Pan Niger Delta Forum (PANDEF) has condemned the spate of political violence recorded in the South-south region ahead of the 2027 general elections, urging political parties to organise rallies in secured venues to prevent further attacks.

PANDEF, the apex socio-political organisation representing Nigeria’s South-south geopolitical zone, described the incidents as a threat to peaceful coexistence and democratic values in the Niger Delta.

The National Chairman of PANDEF, Godknows Igali, stated this in a statement on Monday, warning political actors against thuggery, intimidation and violence.

Mr Igali said the people of the South-south were traditionally known for their peaceful disposition, urging political stakeholders to preserve the region’s culture of tolerance and coexistence.

“PANDEF wishes to restate that violence, intimidation and political thuggery are alien to the spirit, values and traditions of peaceful coexistence, tolerance and political forbearance for which the people of the South-south are known. This is what we inherited from our founding fathers and must be sustained,” he said.

He urged political party leaders to demonstrate maturity in resolving political differences and embrace peaceful coexistence rather than encouraging their supporters to engage in violence.

“The Forum reminds all leaders, supporters and stakeholders of political parties to demonstrate maturity and embrace the spirit of sportsmanship in resolving political differences where they arise.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The leaders of political groups must recognise their sacred responsibility to guide their followers and discourage every form of inflammatory rhetoric, provocation and conduct capable of triggering violence,” he added.

PANDEF also cautioned youths in the Niger Delta against allowing themselves to be used as political thugs during and after the elections.

“PANDEF hereby makes a special appeal to the youths of the Niger Delta not to allow themselves to be used as cannon fodder, instruments of political violence, thuggery or intimidation.

“Our young people, as the primary focus of our democratic governance, are the future of our region and should channel their energy and zeal towards peaceful and constructive political activism. This must not be sacrificed on the altar of the depraved interests of a few selfish political actors,” he said.

The condemnation comes amid a series of violent incidents involving political supporters in parts of the South-south region in recent weeks.

In September, suspected political thugs reportedly disrupted a mobilisation rally involving supporters of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, Peter Obi, and his running mate, Rabiu Kwankwaso, in Warri, Delta State.

Esther Umoh, a photographer associated with Mr Obi, alleged that the attackers opened fire on members of the campaign team, including the entourage of the party’s Delta State governorship candidate. The circumstances surrounding the incident were not independently established.

Mr Obi’s convoy was attacked on 4 November around Watt Market Roundabout in Calabar, Cross River State, while he was returning from the palace of the Obong of Calabar to the Metropolitan Hotel, where a presidential town hall meeting was scheduled to be held. Suspected hoodlums reportedly attacked the vehicles with sticks and machetes, smashing some of their windscreens.

The Cross River State Police Command subsequently arrested a 27-year-old suspect, Victor Duke, in connection with the incident and said investigations were ongoing to identify other suspects.

On 7 November, a political procession organised by supporters of the NDC and the Obidient Movement along Nnebisi Road in Asaba, Delta State, turned violent, leaving one person dead and five others injured, according to the police.

The Delta State Police Command said it had received intelligence suggesting the possibility of violence before the procession and had advised the organisers against holding an open-road rally, recommending a designated venue instead.

The incident has generated controversy, with the state government criticising the organisers for allegedly disregarding police advice, while political actors have called for investigations into the violence.

Call on security agencies

The PANDEF chairman called on the Nigeria Police Force, the State Security Services (SSS) also known as the Department of State Services and other relevant security agencies to thoroughly investigate the incidents, identify those responsible and prosecute them to deter future occurrences.

“Regarding what has happened, we urge the Nigeria Police Force, the Department of State Services (DSS) and other relevant security agencies to undertake urgently, thorough investigations in the various locations to identify and apprehend the perpetrators and masterminds, and ensure that they are brought to book,” he said.

Mr Igali also advised political parties to organise campaigns and rallies in secured locations with adequate security arrangements to prevent further violence.

“We advise that political parties and their leadership should, as much as possible, organise rallies and large gatherings in properly walled or secured venues, with adequate security arrangements whenever transit movements become necessary. This will facilitate better crowd control, minimise the risk of clashes and ensure the safety of all concerned.

“We therefore call on all stakeholders to place the collective interest of our region above partisan considerations and work together to preserve peace, protect lives and property, and sustain the values of mutual forbearance that bind us together as a people.”

World.title: Abia criminalises removal of manhole cover
World.content:
The Abia State Government has declared the unscrupulous removal of manhole covers in different parts of the state a criminal offence.

The Commissioner for Information, Okey Kanu, disclosed this on Monday while briefing reporters at the Government House, Umuahia, on the outcome of the State Executive Council meeting.

Mr Kanu said the unwholesome practice endangers people’s lives and warned that anyone caught vandalising the facilities would be prosecuted.

He said the Ministry of Works had so far installed reinforced concrete slabs over 120 open manholes and drains across Aba and Umuahia.

He expressed concern that some unscrupulous persons have continued to remove the covers despite the government’s efforts to secure them.

The commissioner also cautioned against the unauthorised construction of speed bumps on public roads, saying these structures, when improperly constructed, contribute to the rapid deterioration of roads.

He advised communities to obtain approval from the Ministry of Works before constructing such bumps to ensure compliance with approved standards.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Abia to host 27th Africando Conference

Mr Kanu announced that Abia would host the 27th Africando Conference from 17 November to 19 November to provide opportunity for local businesses to connect with international investors.
