World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: 66 Soldiers Sentenced to Death for Cowardice
World.content:
Dozens of defendants were put on trial over accusations that they abandoned their posts and refused to follow direct orders.

Some 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in DR Congo on charged of cowardice, mutiny, and failure to obey orders. The sentence was handed down by the Goma Garrison Military Court.

At least 71 members of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) were arrested in several separate incidents related to the fierce fighting between the military and rebel groups near the country's borders with Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi.

They were arrested on allegations of abandoning their posts or running away from clashes with FRN rebels. Prosecutors had sought capital punishment for 70 of the defendants, while asking for a 10-year jail term for an intelligence officer. The court, however, acquitted four defendants,



Major Dieudonné Kasereka, head of communications for FARDC in the affected region, said that the charges were necessary to reinforce discipline in the country's embattled North Kivu and South Kivu regions.

What is the FRN?

The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation is an umbrella group of rebels that also includes the March 23 Movement (M23) and Alliance River Congo (AFC).

The group's origins can be traced back to the Rwandan genocide in 1994 and the ensuing ethnic conflict, as it emerged from the Congolese Tutsi militias of the time.

It is led by former DR Congo President Joseph Kabila. When current President Felix Tshisekedi came into power in 2019, Kabila found himself increasingly ostracized politically and went into self-imposed exile in an area occupied my what was then M23. Further complicating the conflict is the involvement of the FDLR rebel group, an ethnic Rwandan Hutu militia also active in South Kivu.

Although Rwanda's strongman president Paul Kagame denied involvement in the conflict, both DR Congo and many in the international community held that evidence of Rwandan involvement was clear. Indeed, Rwanda was involved in the 2025 US-brokered peace deal — which was seen as mostly serving US economic interests and doing little to resolve the long-running conflict.

Earlier this year, the United Nations condemned FRN and Rwandan soldiers for "murder, torture and other ill-treatment, corporal punishment, forced unlawful recruitment and abusive labor, and use of child soldiers."

Edited by Kieran Burke

World.title: Somalia: U.S. Airstrikes Target Islamic State Positions in Somalia's Puntland Region
World.content:
Bosaso — A series of airstrikes targeted suspected Islamic State positions in Somalia's northeastern Puntland region overnight, with the strikes hitting areas in Qandala district, security sources said.

The bombardments mainly struck the areas of Dabablayaal and Hal Baalade, east of Dhaadaar, near key positions held by Puntland's regional security forces around the Togga Jaceel Sare area, according to local security information.

The strikes were reportedly carried out by US forces supporting operations against Islamic State fighters in the Cal Miskaad mountains, where Puntland forces have been conducting a prolonged campaign against the group. There was no immediate official confirmation from US Africa Command or Puntland authorities.

Security information gathered over the past four weeks indicated that Islamic State operatives, particularly members involved in operational activities and planting landmines, had been gathering in Hal Baalade and Dabablayaal, according to local sources.



The fighters were also reportedly active near the Wangable well and the settlements of Goob and Gardaadin, all within Qandala district. Some of the militants had previously operated east of the Togga Jaceel area, where Islamic State maintained bases and strategic positions.

The latest reported strikes come amid continued efforts by Puntland forces, backed by US air support, to weaken the group's presence in the rugged Cal Miskaad mountain range. The area has served as a major stronghold for Islamic State's Somalia branch.

The group last carried out direct attacks in the Dasaan area on September 27, using explosive-laden drones, according to security information. The incident highlighted its continued ability to deploy improvised aerial weapons despite sustained military pressure.

On September 5, a landmine explosion that was reportedly unsuccessful occurred between Sheebaab and Dhaadaar, killing one Islamic State member, according to the same sources.

Islamic State maintains a smaller presence in Somalia than Al-Shabaab but has established networks in the mountainous areas of Puntland, where it has faced repeated military operations by regional forces and US support.

The number of casualties and the extent of damage from the latest airstrikes were not immediately known.

World.title: Kenya: Millions Spent, No Flights - Ruto Makes Fresh Promise On Kisii Airport
World.content:
Nairobi — President William Ruto has renewed his promise to transform Suneka Airstrip into a fully operational airport, years after millions of shillings were spent on the facility without delivering the commercial flights residents have been waiting for.

Ruto said his government would partner with Kisii Governor Simba Arati to expand the runway and upgrade the facility to accommodate bigger aircraft.

The President made the announcement on Tuesday while addressing residents during the third day of his Gusii region tour in Bonchari Constituency, where the airstrip is located.

"I want to tell the people of Bonchari as well, and Simba, that we are going to build that new airport," Ruto said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He acknowledged that the facility had experienced numerous challenges but said he had reached an agreement with Arati to address them and ensure the project is completed.

"That airport had many challenges, but I have agreed with this Simba that we are going to build that new airport," he said.

Ruto said the two leaders would work on extending the runway to allow bigger aircraft to land in Kisii, reducing residents' dependence on airports in neighboring counties.

"He will plan with me how we will extend that runway so that the big aircraft can land here for the people of Kisii," he added.

The latest promise comes after years of uncertainty, stalled construction and changing government plans that have left Suneka Airstrip struggling to achieve its ambition of becoming a commercial aviation hub.

Millions spent but airport remains unfinished

Suneka Airstrip first received major rehabilitation in 2015, when a Sh52 million project was launched to improve its facilities.

The first phase included a passenger lounge designed to accommodate 200 people, toilets, a car park, an administration block, a perimeter fence and runway markings.

The Kisii County Government announced the works in February 2015, saying the improvements would boost tourism and business in the region.

However, the bigger ambition of accommodating commercial passenger and cargo aircraft required further investment and runway expansion.

In 2020, the national government allocated an additional Sh300 million towards expanding the facility to accommodate larger aircraft.

The Kenya Airports Authority subsequently undertook Phase II runway rehabilitation works under a contract initially valued at Sh134 million before being revised to approximately Sh129.2 million.

But the project stalled after the contractor abandoned the site.

According to the authority's 2021/2022 audited accounts, construction had reached only 58 per cent before the contractor demobilized equipment in April 2022.

Ruto previously announced plans to close the airstrip

Close 

In August 2023, Ruto announced plans to decommission Suneka Airstrip, citing insufficient land for the Kenya Airports Authority to undertake the required expansion.

The announcement dealt a major blow to residents and local leaders who had pushed for years to have the facility upgraded.

However, the government later changed direction.

In August 2025, Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba announced that the government was moving to recommission the airstrip following consultations between Ruto and Gusii leaders.

Ogamba said the President had directed leaders to review the facility's status and facilitate the resumption of construction.

The revival efforts received another boost in July 2026 when Interior Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo announced that a new contractor had taken over the stalled project.

Omollo said the previous contractor had encountered challenges and that the necessary documentation had been completed to allow construction to resume.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Nine Zimbabwean Nationals Appear in Gauteng Courts Over Alleged Attempt to Join Russia-Ukraine War
World.content:
Nine Zimbabwean nationals on Monday appeared in two separate Gauteng magistrates’ courts after their arrest over an alleged attempt to leave South Africa to participate in the Russia-Ukraine war.

The nine men were arrested on Sunday following an intelligence-driven investigation, according to the National Prosecuting Authority (NPA).

Five of the accused appeared before the Kempton Park Magistrates’ Court after being arrested at OR Tambo International Airport.

They have been identified as Weight Mudhanyane, 23, Javangwe Munyaradzi, 41, Wesley Sothole, 24, Abel Muchenje, 40, and Knowledge Ndunduma, 46.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The remaining four accused, Bobo Chinhondo, 43, Batsirai Shereni, 24, Liberty Shereni, 44, and Niobe Zhou, 37, appeared before the Johannesburg Magistrates’ Court following their arrest at a hotel in Bruma.

All nine face charges of contravening the Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act 15 of 1998.

In a statement released on Monday, the NPA said a multidisciplinary team conducted the operation after gathering information during the investigation.

“The arrests were effected on November 8 2026 following an intelligence-driven investigation. Acting on information gathered during the investigation, a multidisciplinary team conducted an operation that resulted in the arrest of the accused. It is alleged that the accused intended to leave South Africa to participate in the Russia-Ukraine war,” said the prosecuting authority.

The matter involving the five accused who appeared in Kempton Park was postponed to November 10 to allow them to secure legal representation.

The four accused who appeared in Johannesburg are expected back in court on November 12, also to allow them to obtain legal representation.

All nine accused remain in custody.

World.title: Africa: Model Citizens - 23 African-Born Immigrant Win in U.S. Elections
World.content:
blog

The growing political visibility of recent African immigrants in the United States is a standing reproach to dated conceptions of belonging back home.

Members of the Democratic Party are not the only ones celebrating the party's stunning victory in last week's midterm elections. Across Africa, where the exploits of African-born Americans are closely monitored, the outcome of the elections has generated considerable excitement. The reaction in Nigeria to the success of fourteen Nigerian-Americans in various state-level elections--incidentally all on the platform of the Democratic Party--is typical. Nigerians in Diaspora Commission chairperson Abike Dabiri-Erewa went on social media to congratulate the victorious cohort, making sure to append a graphic vividly displaying their names, headshots, and respective constituencies.

In all, a record twenty-three African-born immigrants from at least ten African countries spread across thirteen U.S. states won their respective races to become lawmakers in various American federal and state legislatures, extending a run that had seemed to reach a highwater mark back in January when Ugandan-born Zohran Mamdani became New York's youngest mayor in over a century.



The feeling of pride among Africans is both justified and understandable. For many, the fact that African-born immigrants are finding their feet and flourishing across various walks of life is a welcome rebuke to racial bigots of all stripes who equate blackness with underachievement. For such Africans, there is a special gratification in seeing recent African immigrants atop the totem pole across American industry, higher education, medicine, technology, and, not to forget, sports and entertainment. Recent African immigrants from Cameroon, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa rank among the most educated and highest paid immigrant groups across the United States. The average Nigerian-born immigrant (immigration to the United States from Nigeria is heavily dominated by Yorubas and Igbos from the southern region of the country, but still) boasts more degrees than a thermometer. According to the Washington-based Migration Policy Institute, 61 percent hold at least a bachelor's degree, "compared with 31 percent of the total foreign-born population and 32 percent of the U.S.-born population."

Unsurprisingly, in the same way that they use the United States itself as a mostly favorable point of reference, Africans also use the success of recent African immigrants to the United States to call attention to yawning and recurrent gaps in everyday life across Africa on the one hand, and the delinquencies of African leadership on the other. For many, the fact that someone would have to leave Africa in order to find personal and professional fulfillment, taking all their talent and expertise with them, and the lack of urgency by African leaders in response to this ongoing hemorrhaging of human capital, is an indictment of the situation in a majority of African countries.

All things considered, the noted feeling of pride at the increased political visibility and general success of African-born Americans is tinged with not a little anguish that Africa basically continues to give away what it cannot afford to lose.

None of this is to downplay the enormous social challenges that recent African immigrants themselves continue to confront. The case of Deqa Dhalac, the first African-born female mayor who, earlier this year, announced that she would not run for reelection into the Maine (Portland) House of Representatives because, according to her, "Throughout my tenure, I have experienced persistent racism, harassment, and threats that reflect a broader national pattern targeting Black and Brown elected officials," is a reminder that, for many, the path to political visibility can be quite rocky, and that, when it comes to full acceptance, it is definitely not yet uhuru.

That said, it cannot be denied that, in the final analysis, the United States continues to offer (political) possibilities that are not available to these recent African immigrants back home in Africa. The explanation for this is as follows: The conception of citizenship that prevails, albeit imperfectly, in the United States, is modern, vis-à-vis the regnant conception across Africa, which is predominantly static. Whereas, in principle, American citizenship is open to anyone who is born in, emigrates to, and is dedicated to the foundational tenets of the United States, citizenship in many African countries is still framed and invariably weighed down by the logic of autochthony. As President Trump stated during a naturalization ceremony in January 2019, echoing a belief that has served as a beacon to successive generations of Americans, "The beauty and majesty of [American] citizenship is that it draws no distinctions of race, or class, or faith, or gender, or background. No matter where our story begins, whether we are the first generation or the tenth generation, we are all equal. We are one team and one people proudly saluting one great American flag" [PDF].

Contra the American promise, quaint and often ridiculous markers, particularly regarding ethnicity, religious affiliation, caste, and gender, continue to animate politics across many African countries. The most profound--and, from a certain perspective, the most tragic--testament to this is the situation in South Africa (for anyone who may be interested, my three-part essay on the country's struggles is available here), where the collective mentality lags behind a constitution whose liberalism ordinarily puts it on par with the Constitution of the United States. In Nigeria, the heartland of regressive nativism, social discourse continues to be dominated by demeaning and ultimately meaningless conversations about one's "state of origin." In different ways, both South Africa and Nigeria demonstrate the inflexibility of political identity in Africa.

Which should ordinarily change the level of concern if, say, your African citizenship, parsimonious as it is, secured you some benefits. Just the opposite. In the words of Cornell University political philosopher Olufemi Taiwo, "the non-responsive and non-responsible character of African governments" effectively means that "most nationals of African countries do not enjoy the most basic privileges of citizenship in their homeland: protection from the predations of their fellows and the overreaching of state functionaries; the provision of basic amenities for the citizens; a minimum standard of living that keeps them above subhuman levels with some luxuries thrown in for good measure; and the privilege of having a hand in the constitution of the government that rules them."

The role played by this denuded form of citizenship in forcing African nationals to consider the exit option has been remarked. What could do with more attention is the opportunity that the modern form of citizenship affords for self-discovery and self-fashioning for the potential immigrant. As many immigrants to the United States understand, American citizenship opens up opportunities that would be otherwise permanently foreclosed, precisely because the United States is the one country where, at the end of the day, political modernity currently finds its fullest fulfillment. I know from personal experience that immigration advocates in the United States have little appreciation of this nonmaterial dimension of immigrant quest for the American dream, reducing immigration to the impact of climate change and whatnot.

Close 

In the meantime, what this means for diasporic Africans is clear enough. As we continue to redeem the promissory note of modernity across Euro-America, it is incumbent on us to affirm and invest in ideas and policies that advance and strengthen the same across Africa. The easiest and costless way to do that is to stop treating Africa and Africans, not as moral aliens, but as a region and people subject to the same rules and expectations of dignified treatment that apply to human beings everywhere. To refrain, as many do, from criticizing human rights violations in Africa under the pretext of not wanting to patronize African leaders is to assume that Africans are not mature enough to be approached and treated as adults. It is hypocritical to demand--as we should--access to the rights and privileges of modern citizenship across Western countries, while ignoring the entrenched violation of the same rights and privileges in Africa.

And for my African compatriots: It is not enough to celebrate the fact that Africans flourish outside of Africa. All of us must commit to the imperative of making Africa itself livable for anyone who desires to make a home there.

Imagine a time in the not-too-distant future when the mayor of Abuja is a Norwegian-born Nigerian, and the mayor of Johannesburg just so happens to be a Russian-born South African, both with equal and unfettered access to the respective bounties and prohibitions of Nigerian and South African citizenship.

Imagine that.

Nathan Schoonover contributed to the research for this article.

World.title: Nigeria: U.S. Trade, Security Partnership Could Create Opportunities in Nigeria
World.content:
U.S. Air Force Gen. Dagvin Anderson, commander of U.S. Africa Command, conducts an interview with Olivia Burrows, reporter for Citizen TV Kenya, in Nairobi, Kenya, July 28, 2026.

analysis

Washington is linking commerce to security. For Nigeria, the measures are market access, non-oil exports, investment and jobs.

Nigeria's ambition to expand non-oil exports and attract investment provides a practical test of Washington's effort to connect commercial engagement, diplomacy and security across Africa.

Following the Africa Strategic Dialogue at the National Defense University in Washington on 29 October, senior US officials explained how their institutions were approaching those connections. US Africa Command commander, Dagvin Anderson, identified Nigeria among the countries where he had encountered interest in constructive American economic engagement.

US Department of State's Bureau of African Affairs Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Frank Garcia Jr. framed the approach as an economic partnership, with benefits required on both sides.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"It has to be a good deal for African partners and a good deal for the US taxpayers and industry," Mr Garcia said.

He also identified the conditions companies need to operate.

"Conflict impedes companies from building, hiring, growing," he said.

Mr Anderson approached the relationship from the security side, explaining why cooperation needed to extend beyond military activity.

"And so we can't just focus on the security piece," he said. "We have to look at how we bridge into that stability and investment."

However, the commercial relationship has its own institutional foundation and explicitly stated national priorities.

The US-Nigeria Commercial and Investment Partnership was established through a five-year memorandum signed in July 2024. Its working groups began meeting in June 2025 across agriculture, the digital economy, and infrastructure, bringing government and private-sector participants together to identify obstacles to trade and investment.

Those activities predate the latest AFRICOM dialogue. The bilateral partnership is a commercial framework, not a military programme directed by the command.

At a ministerial meeting in Lagos in January, Nigeria's Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Jumoke Oduwole, emphasised export diversification and access to the American market.

She said "a central priority for us is to accelerate non-oil export diversification and to ensure that more Nigerian businesses can access U.S. markets in a way that is competitive, sustainable, and inclusive," according to the US Mission's published account.

Her formulation supplies a Nigerian measure of success. Expanding opportunities for American companies in Nigeria and helping Nigerian businesses compete in the United States are related ambitions, but they require different results.

The partnership's working groups were tasked with identifying barriers other than tariffs and recommending solutions to policymakers. By the January ministerial, they had developed proposals intended to improve the business environment and facilitate private-sector activity.

That work provides a setting in which to assess the wider language of mutual benefit. For a Nigerian exporter, progress means more than an announcement of interest. It means being able to compete, secure customers, and deliver products into a market on commercially workable terms.

At the October discussion, Mark Mitchell, the Commerce Department's deputy assistant secretary for the Middle East and Africa, Global Markets, described commercial-support activity across technology, energy, manufacturing, critical minerals and infrastructure.

He distinguished formal Commercial Advocacy cases from the department's broader support for business engagement.

That distinction matters when assessing the scale and status of commercial opportunities. A prospective procurement, an awarded contract, an approved financing package, and an operational project represent different stages. They should not be presented interchangeably as completed investments or demonstrated local benefit.

In a written statement following the roundtable, the US Department of Commerce said, "The Department of Commerce is focused on the mutual wins of trade relationships and commercial deals that can deliver economic prosperity and security. We are working toward a long-term partnering relationship through trade."

The statement makes the intended connection explicit.

The US Department of Energy was also represented in the October discussion by William Schirano, the Energy Department's deputy assistant secretary for multilateral engagement and market development. He described energy access and technical cooperation as foundations for broader economic activity.

A public G20 energy ministers' statement issued in September provides one example of that wider agenda. It calls for financing, stronger distribution systems, and local and regional value chains for clean cooking, while recognising that countries will choose different technologies according to their circumstances. It includes liquefied petroleum gas, electricity, natural gas, and other options. The statement is a multilateral commitment, not an announcement of a Nigeria-specific project.

AFRICOM's organisational developments show how the military side is approaching economic engagement.

Recent reporting suggests that the command had established a Defense Economics Office to examine how economic, commercial, and financial activity could produce security effects. Mr Anderson identified Joshua Stinson, a colonel, as the command's lead for defense economics.

The reported remit extended beyond investment promotion. It included infrastructure and access, critical mineral supply chains, and efforts to disrupt adversaries' revenues. The office's emergence formed part of a wider setting in which the United States, China and Russia compete for influence and access across Africa.

"We're not looking to replace what Commerce does, by any means," Mr Anderson said, according to publicly available news reports.

That boundary is important. Security priorities may influence American engagement, but commercial negotiations, financing decisions, and Nigerian economic policy retain separate responsibilities.

Mr Anderson acknowledged another limit during the October exchange. Providing access to the American economy was not his direct responsibility, but he could help connect African requests with relevant institutions and convene discussions.

Close 

His military resources had been "reduced," he said, making coordination with other agencies part of his explanation of how AFRICOM could continue pursuing security objectives.

The approach, therefore, joins institutions around potentially overlapping interests without making those interests identical.

Ms Oduwole's stated priorities concern a more diversified Nigerian economy and stronger opportunities for Nigerian businesses. Washington's stated objectives include American commercial gains and security benefits from more durable relationships.

For Nigerian businesses, results would be visible in barriers removed, financing secured, contracts performed, and exports delivered. For households, the relevant consequences include employment, affordable services, and opportunities to participate in productive economic activity.

Nigeria has articulated what it wants from the commercial relationship. The task now is to assess whether the institutions pursuing partnership can translate those objectives into results--and distinguish opportunities being discussed from benefits already delivered.

Pearl Matibe is a Washington, D.C.-based correspondent and geopolitical analyst covering US-Africa relations, defence, diplomacy, and international security. She reports across print, broadcast, and digital platforms, including The Shaka Spear, examining how policy decisions affect African countries and their publics. She regularly covers the Pentagon, State Department, and White House. Follow her on X: @PearlMatibe.

World.title: PAUL MAURO: Sanctuary states have a DMV problem — and Trump can demand answers
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Democrats have captured both houses of Congress and are gleefully announcing, "woke is back." But there’s one inconvenient detail: President Donald Trump still controls the executive branch.

Why does that matter?

Because Ryan O’Shea mattered.

ICE LODGES DETAINER FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED IN WRONG-WAY MARYLAND CRASH THAT KILLED MOM, DAUGHTER

On October 16, 21-year-old Ryan O’Shea, a University of New Haven hockey captain studying criminal justice, was driving home from a game when a pickup truck traveling the wrong way on Connecticut’s Interstate 91 slammed head-on into his car. Ryan was killed instantly.

Police say the other driver was Guillermo Carmona-Lopez, who is a Mexican national who DHS says had already been removed from the United States twice. Somehow, he was back.

ILLEGAL ALIEN'S ‘INEXCUSABLE’ CRIME SPARKS INTERSTATE CLASH BETWEEN GOP SEN, DEM GOV: ‘YOU SHOULD BE ASHAMED’

The story circulated widely on social media, but received limited mainstream coverage. One needn’t wonder why. Ryan was not a member of any of our media’s preferred victim classes, he wanted to go into law enforcement, and he was allegedly killed by someone who the feds say shouldn’t have been here.

Three strikes.

But his death raises a larger question: How is it possible that so many foreign drivers are permitted — or even assisted — in getting licensed to drive on our roads? Is there more going on here?

Examples similar to Ryan’s are legion. In July, Uzbek national Bekhzod Asrarov, who had entered the U.S. legally, allegedly killed 21-year-old college soccer player Tobias "Toby" Forsythe when his tractor-trailer slammed into the young man’s car. Asrarov, who held an Ohio CDL, reportedly couldn’t communicate with police without Google Translate, failed an English-proficiency test and allegedly attempted to conceal evidence, including his electronic driving logs.

Then, on September 2, Indian national Manjit Singh, whom DHS identified as illegal, was involved in another fatal Ohio crash that killed 50-year-old Brenda Watson. Singh held a California CDL and has been charged with aggravated vehicular homicide.

We could go on. Ohio has at least moved to tighten the loopholes that allowed this. Too late for two Americans.

TRUMP PROMOTES FREEDOM HAULERS INITIATIVE TO FAST-TRACK MILITARY VETERANS INTO TRUCKING JOBS

But that’s more than blue states are willing to do. So in September 2025, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced emergency restrictions on CDLs issued to foreign drivers after a nationwide audit uncovered widespread fraud.

In New York alone, Duffy’s audit found that over half of commercial trucking licenses went to illegal drivers — and those drivers hit the roads across the country. In one case, investigators found that a Chinese national accused of causing a fatal highway pileup in Tennessee was illegally issued a New York State driver’s license.

In California, the audit found that 25% of CDLs were unlawfully issued — with a stated policy that California will not enforce federal English proficiency rules.

So this year, Duffy began the process of cracking down on the practice nationwide. He withheld $73 million from New York State, which refuses to comply (and is suing in response).

But more significantly, the feds announced "Joint Task Force Crossroads of America," a nationwide initiative targeting fraud and criminal activity regarding CDLs.

DEADLY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TRUCK CRASH EXPOSED FAILURES ON THE ROAD AND AT THE BORDER: KEY SENATOR

How widespread is the problem? The task force started with more than 1,000 leads and inspected more than 200 driving schools across 23 states. Multiple criminal investigations have already been opened.

It’s a start. But let’s recall: Guillermo Carmona-Lopez, who allegedly killed Ryan O’Shea, did not have a CDL.

DOJ ESCALATES BLUE-STATE ICE STANDOFF AFTER STATES REFUSE KEY FEDERAL REQUEST

So limiting the task force to just CDL enforcement is a mistake. Because somewhere in the DMV systems of our states there are officials issuing licenses to applicants who not only likely couldn’t pass the driver’s tests we’ve all taken — they cannot even read the exam. Or our road signs.

And someone is recruiting these drivers, getting them here, corrupting the DMVs and facilitating their placement onto our roads.

This is activity squarely within the province of the federal executive. Our newly woke Congress can bemoan investigating it… but Congress cannot stop it. And targeting the scheme also has the advantage of opening another front on immigration enforcement that doesn’t involve highly visible ICE sweeps. The Trump administration just got some good news on this front. In a major November 6 federal court ruling, Judge Lewis Kaplan ordered New York City to comply with an ICE subpoena seeking information about migrants with serious criminal histories at a Bronx shelter.

Game-changer.

The administration can now build on that reasoning by pursuing targeted, court-enforced subpoenas for New York DMV records to identify criminal aliens who have obtained driver’s licenses — and then deporting them.

The administration should go all-in on this over the next two years. Because there’s also this: At least 17 states, plus Washington, D.C., both permit illegals to obtain driver’s licenses or driving-privilege cards, while also operating automatic voter-registration systems for license holders.

The administration has received little credit for recognizing the illegal driving problem (arguably, another failure in messaging on good policy that has plagued Trump 2.0). And the standing up of the Crossroads of America task force is a good start. But this initiative could go further. Successfully enforced, it would serve as one of the ways red states demonstrate the superiority of a little common sense. So, New York Governor Kathy Hochul has gleefully announced that "75% of Americans will be governed by DEM Govs." Fair enough — the electorate spoke.

Now the other 25% should demonstrate what makes them different by cooperating with the feds to keep illegals off the roads, penetrate the criminal networks running this trafficking and disincentivize others from accessing this pipeline to enter the country illegally.

While the new task force uses this recent federal judge’s decision to issue subpoenas, identify illegals in our DMV systems and bring sanctuary jurisdictions back in line with the Constitution.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Then maybe at least some of today’s left, so intent on resurrecting our open border madness, will recognize that young men like Ryan O’Shea are not just collateral damage for their Woke 3.0 ambitions.

World.title: Kushner enters Ukraine peace talks as Trump eyes securing safeguards against another Russian invasion
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Russia and Ukraine will finally return to the negotiating table Tuesday for their first trilateral peace talks with the U.S. in nine months.

Ahead of the talks, officials said both Moscow and Kyiv have shown "a little bit of flexibility privately" on territorial disputes that have long stood in the way of reaching an agreement.

U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will sit down with Ukrainian intelligence chief Rustem Umerov and Putin aide and veteran negotiator Vladimir Medinsky in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday.

The Trump administration has asked Russia to accept an "Article Four and an Article Five-like security guarantee" for Ukraine that would be "effectively very similar to NATO," a U.S. official said Monday on a background call previewing the negotiations.

President Donald Trump has not yet decided what security guarantee the U.S. itself would provide, the official said, describing an American guarantee as a "really, really big deal" that would ultimately have to be worked out between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

RUSSIA'S NEIGHBOR REVEALS PERSONAL APPEALS TO TRUMP AS US WEIGHS NATO TROOP PULLBACK IN EUROPE

A lot has happened on the geopolitical stage since the latest trilateral talks happened in Geneva, Switzerland, in February. The first being the inception of a new conflict between the U.S. and Iran — and the second being the 2026 midterm elections, which saw a sweeping rebuke of Republicans with a blue wave taking the country by storm.

The latest round of talks will also mark the beginning of structured negotiations over territory.

Russia continues publicly to demand all of Donetsk, while Ukraine has pushed for freezing the conflict along the current line of contact. But behind closed doors, "both sides have shown a little bit of flexibility privately," the official said.

UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY OPEN TO FREEZING FRONT LINES IN CEASEFIRE WITH RUSSIA

Trump also suggested in a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday that Ukraine’s borders could ultimately change under a peace agreement, saying the country could emerge from the war with "a little bit different shape."

U.S. negotiators do not expect to resolve the territorial dispute in Abu Dhabi. Instead, officials say the goal is to clarify where each side stands, identify the remaining gaps and begin exploring potential compromises that can ultimately be taken back to Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelenskyy.

The administration increasingly views the territorial question and postwar security arrangements as inseparable.

Officials believe neither Russia nor Ukraine will make the concessions needed to settle the territorial dispute until each understands what the security landscape will look like after the fighting stops.

INSIDE MELANIA TRUMP'S SECRET DIPLOMATIC ROLE IN THE RUSSIA-UKRAINE CEASEFIRE DEAL

Before sitting down with Russia and Ukraine, U.S. negotiators will meet with national security officials from Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy, along with NATO, the European Union and Ukraine, to discuss security guarantees and a broader postwar security architecture.

Washington then hopes to persuade Russia to join a broader multilateral negotiating process involving European governments.

"We need Europe at the table," a U.S. official said, arguing that direct negotiations between Russia and European countries will ultimately be necessary for a durable settlement.

Among the ideas under consideration is reviving the NATO-Russia Council, which the administration wants to make a more robust forum for communication, de-escalation and resolving future disputes.

Officials are also exploring crisis communications, greater military transparency and reciprocal measures intended to reduce the risk of another conflict.

The administration's goal in Abu Dhabi is not a final agreement. Officials instead hope the talks can establish a framework for more frequent negotiations and eventually move the process from a U.S.-Russia-Ukraine format to broader multilateral talks involving Europe.

The administration also sees sanctions as potential leverage in enforcing an eventual agreement. A U.S. official suggested sanctions on Russia could potentially be eased over time while retaining the ability to "spring back in place" if Moscow violates a peace deal.

Witkoff and Kushner, the son-in-law of the president, are also considering returning to meet Putin and Zelenskyy soon, depending on the outcome of the Abu Dhabi talks.

"This is the first time I feel like we see real desire on the Russian side to finish," the official said.

But officials acknowledged the negotiations remain highly uncertain, with deep distrust between Moscow and Kyiv and major decisions on territory and security still unresolved.

The immediate test in Abu Dhabi will be whether the private flexibility U.S. negotiators say they are seeing can translate into something concrete once Russia and Ukraine are back in the same room.

But the Abu Dhabi talks could also set the stage for higher-level diplomacy.

U.S. officials said Witkoff and Kushner are considering returning to meet Putin and Zelenskyy soon, depending on the outcome of the two-day negotiations.

Trump is also preparing to travel to China for the APEC summit next week, where he said Sunday he expects to meet Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Discussions about a potential three-way meeting are underway, though no summit has been finalized.

World.title: Sarah Ferguson in touch with ex-Prince Andrew as expert warns royal downfall 'has further to go' after arrest
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor may have lost his royal titles, but the scandal surrounding his ties to Jeffrey Epstein continues to follow him — and his ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson.

People magazine reported that while it's unclear whether the former Duchess of York has seen her ex-husband recently, the two remain in contact.

"They have an ongoing cordial and supportive relationship as co-parents and co-grandparents," a spokesperson for Ferguson told People.

FORMER PRINCE ANDREW, SARAH FERGUSON DUBBED ROYAL FAMILY’S ‘BONNIE AND CLYDE’ AS EPSTEIN FALLOUT GROWS: AUTHOR

Fox News Digital reached out to Ferguson's spokesperson for comment.

"It is not surprising," royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "If Andrew came to court, she might well be called as a witness. Much depends on whether the police in Britain can obtain the unredacted Epstein files. But there is no way back for Andrew. He hasn't helped the FBI. He has no support. He has no reputation to lose. It can't get much worse. His fall is unique. It has further to go."

Andrew has been issued a witness summons in a civil fraud case, marking what is believed to be the first such summons issued to a member of the British royal family since 1870, The Associated Press reported.

WATCH: SARAH FERGUSON DENIES TELL-ALL BOOK AMID ROYAL FAMILY CONCERNS: EXPERT

The summons comes after a High Court judge in London ruled in October that Andrew could be called to testify about a payment he received in connection with the case. Andrew may apply to have the summons set aside, so there is no guarantee he will testify, the AP reported.

The lawsuit was filed by Turkish national Nebahat Evyap Isbilen, who alleges that her former advisor, Selman Turk, misappropriated tens of millions of pounds of her money. As part of the case, she says Turk misled her about a 750,000-pound (approximately $1 million) payment he arranged for her to make to Andrew in 2019. The younger brother of King Charles III repaid the money in 2021, and he is not a party to the lawsuit. Turk denies dishonesty.

Police Scotland confirmed to Fox News Digital that active inquiries are underway into information concerning Andrew and Epstein at Balmoral Castle, the royal family's Scottish estate. They noted that the inquiries are at a "very early stage."

The confirmation follows a report by the Scottish Daily Express that police inquiries concern allegations that women were trafficked to the royal estate, where Andrew hosted Epstein and his longtime associate, Ghislaine Maxwell.

"We have received information and active enquiries are ongoing, but these are at a very early stage," a Police Scotland spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "All enquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those enquiries. We would never confirm details of ongoing enquiries, and it would be inappropriate to comment further."

Police declined to specify the focus of the inquiries or whether Andrew is the subject of an investigation. Fox News Digital reached out to Andrew's attorney for comment. A spokesperson for Buckingham Palace told Fox News Digital the palace does not speak on Andrew's behalf because he is no longer a working royal.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Andrew lives in seclusion on the king’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk. A spokesperson for Ferguson told People that she has been spending time with their daughters, Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie, and her five grandchildren since returning to the U.K. in late August.

"She's resettling here, lying low while she looks at the next stage. She's happy spending time with her family and focusing on her relocation," the spokesperson said.

People reported that Ferguson is renting a house in the Home Counties, a region of counties surrounding London. She previously spent time in the Austrian Alps.

"Sarah Ferguson will be deliberately lying low to allow any tension involving the royal household to die down," royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital. "Right now, Sarah is probably staying away from Sandringham to avoid adding to the melodrama. Obviously, Sarah is concerned about Beatrice and Eugenie. Any repercussions attached to her may fall on their shoulders too."

"The Andrew and Sarah story and their continued love for each other have always been strong," Turner said. "Most days, when they were living together at Royal Lodge, they would make time for each other."

On Feb. 19, Andrew's 66th birthday, Thames Valley Police arrested him on suspicion of misconduct in public office following allegations that he shared confidential information with Epstein while serving as a British trade envoy. He has not been charged. The investigation followed the king's decision in 2025 to strip his brother of his remaining royal titles and honors over his ties to Epstein.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

On Oct. 8, Andrew secured a legal victory when a High Court judge in London ruled that search warrants used to raid two properties linked to him were unlawful because police had relied on the wrong legal provisions. The judge, however, said "the fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring an investigation to an end, or mean that the whole of the investigation was unlawful."

Andrew has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein.

Ferguson retreated from public life after the release of Epstein-related documents renewed scrutiny of her past relationship with the convicted sex offender. She has not been accused of any wrongdoing in connection with the financier, who died in federal custody in 2019.

Emails released as part of the Epstein files revealed that Ferguson continued to praise the convicted sex offender even after his 2008 conviction, including referring to him as a "supreme friend," renewing scrutiny of their relationship.

"For 30 years, Sarah Ferguson and Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor sold us the much-debated story: Married. Divorce. Living together at Royal Lodge. Co-parenting. The 'happiest divorced couple in the world,'" British broadcaster Helena Chard told Fox News Digital.

Chard believes Ferguson is prioritizing her family even as her relationship with Andrew remains "publicly cordial for their daughters but privately fractured."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Sarah is loyal," Chard said. "However, she is also loyal to herself and will do what she needs to spring back. She realizes her own Epstein emails, calling him a 'supreme friend' and more has cost her charities, book deals, her title. Her much-needed invitations also dried up, although she still has a close circle of friends."

On Oct. 29, Ferguson made a rare public appearance alongside her daughters at a memorial service in London for her former boyfriend and longtime friend, Paddy McNally, who died in July at age 88.

"It was no coincidence," Chard said. "Paddy was the one who helped her navigate her most trying time living away from her loved ones, in the Austrian Alps, in exile, cut off from royal life. His guidance, his support, his belief in her gave her the strength to come back to the U.K. to resettle and rebuild. Paddy's legacy is still carrying her through."

Ferguson's plans for the future remain unclear, People reported. While she is looking to "forge an independent life," her spokesperson told People she is not working on a tell-all memoir. Ferguson has written several books.

Andrew has also remained largely out of public view as he faces an ongoing police investigation and a witness summons in a separate civil fraud case.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"As long as Sarah is tied to Andrew, a comeback with King Charles, Prince William and Princess Catherine is almost impossible," Chard said. "William is reportedly taking an even tougher line. With her daughters, grandchildren and close friends around her, she no doubt is plotting her public revival. Her Falklands hero and exiled ex Prince Andrew will not be in tow."

World.title: Reporter’s Notebook: House leadership up for grabs as GOP reckons with devastating losses
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Internal House and Senate party leadership elections are some of the most fascinating exercises to unfold on Capitol Hill.

Both House and Senate Democrats and House and Senate Republicans will choose their leaders in the coming days. And the changes are going to be seismic.

But not everyone is on board with heir apparent leaders. That’s what makes this process so intriguing. However, there are only two rules in leadership elections: You can’t beat someone with no one. And — perhaps more importantly — it’s about the math.

Republicans are up first with elections in both chambers starting Tuesday morning.

THE HITCHHIKER’S GUIDE TO WHAT HAPPENS NEXT ON CAPITOL HILL

For Minority Leader, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., is running against Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio. Current House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., is not seeking to stay in leadership once his party isn't in charge anymore.

If Democrats have 260 seats, Republicans would have 175. All incoming House Republicans (including non-voting delegates from U.S. territories) are allowed to vote in conference. The selection of Minority Leader does NOT go before the entire House like Speaker. So, the winning candidate only needs a simple majority. That would be 88.

The same for the race between House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., and Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, for Minority Whip.

Senate Republican leader John Thune, R-S.D., is running to keep his leadership position for the party in the new Congress.

Meanwhile, Democrats will begin elections for their House leader on Wednesday where Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is expected to secure that nomination. No internal Democrat Senate leadership election date has been set.

There are some progressives and Democratic Socialists of America-affiliated Democrats who will be House Members next year who want someone other than Minority Leader Jeffries keep his position.

Who do they want instead? Well, no one has said. Again, you can’t beat someone with no one. And frankly, it’s hard to believe that Democrats would not elect the first Black Speaker of the House.

But drill down on the math.

For the sake of argument, let’s say Democrats have 260 House seats in the new Congress. First, Democrats must tap a nominee for Speaker in their Caucus. That needs a simple majority. So surely Jeffries will score at least 131 votes in a private ballot for Speaker.

The Speaker of the House is the Constitutional officer for the legislative branch of government – much like the President is for the executive branch and the Chief Justice of the United States for the judicial branch. Thus, the ENTIRE House votes for Speaker when it convenes the new Congress at noon on January 3.

There are 435 Members. If all Members cast ballots, Jeffries simply needs 218. Jeffries could lose 40 votes or so and still prevail. So that is not going to happen. He might not even lose more than a couple votes, frankly.

The Senate Democratic Caucus and Republican Conference work much the same way as the House. A simple majority wins for Majority Leader in the Democratic Caucus and Minority Leader in the Republican Conference. However, the selection of Senate Majority Leader is not a vote which plays out on the floor. The concept of "Senate Majority Leader" has only been around since the early 20th Century and is not mentioned in the Constitution. Remember what we said about the House Speaker being the head of this branch of government.

It would be hard to envision a scenario where Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., would not become Majority Leader after Democrats flipped the Senate in a beat down.

First, who else is running? Well, Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, is very popular among Senate Democrats. But he’s running for Majority Whip to succeed retiring Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin, D-Ill. One could see Democrats defaulting to Schatz if something happens with Schumer.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., said he wants to look at his options and endorsed Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., for Majority Leader. But Van Hollen isn’t running. Sen.-elect Annie Andrews, D-S.C., told colleague Bret Baier she wants a "generational change" in leadership. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, D-Maine, and Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., both said they would oppose Schumer.

But again, you can’t beat someone with no one.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOW MIDTERMS MAY CHANGE THE HOUSE IMPEACHMENT EQUATION FOR HEGSETH

Here’s the math:

Let’s say Democrats do win Mississippi and Alaska, giving them 56 senators who caucus with the Democrats. All Schumer needs is 29 Democrats to support him in Caucus and he’s the next Majority Leader.

There has not been as much rumbling about the future of Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D. Heretofore, President Trump has not called for new leadership in the Senate. But a group of Senate Republicans are calling on a delay in leadership elections slated for Tuesday. Senate Republicans would choose Thune or anyone else on a secret ballot in the Senate GOP Conference. A simple majority would win. If Republicans are down to 44 seats, the winner would just need 23 votes.

So for the next couple of weeks, there’s a lot of counting. Counting about votes for impeachment. Counting in leadership elections. And next year, counting votes as Democrats try to enact their agenda.

Democrats will say voters are counting on them. And Republicans, well, they may be counting the days.

Everything in the new Congress will come down to the math. And there's the issue of impeaching Pentagon Chief Pete Hegseth.

But forget about Democrats pushing the move next year. Try Republicans — THIS year.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., is reintroducing articles of impeachment for Pentagon Chief Pete Hegseth this week. The chances are increasingly high that the House could in fact impeach Hegseth.

Why?

Massie tried to impeach Hegseth before the midterms. But the House adjourned a day early in September. That nixed Massie’s effort. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) condemned the effort by the Kentucky Republican. But Johnson insisted that he didn’t send Members home early because of fear that the House had the votes to impeach Hegseth.

Massie attempted to execute a parliamentary move which would compel the House to consider the impeachment articles right away. But they expired once the House went out of session. But Massie will resuscitate them.

GOP LAWMAKER SAYS MORE QUALIFIED OFFICIALS SHOULD LEAD PENTAGON, QUESTIONS HEGSETH'S 'MORAL COMPASS

Massie authored a total of eight articles of impeachment, ranging from the "kidnapping" of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro to how the Pentagon is running the war in Iran.

It’s possible the House could move to table the articles, or send them to committee, euthanizing the effort. But a growing number of House Republicans are grumbling about Hegseth. Any effort to dismiss the articles in the House might not work.

It’s about the math.

All Democrats are likely to vote to impeach Hegseth. Some Republicans are exasperated by Hegseth and have said privately they’d like to impeach. There are even more Republicans trying to build distance between themselves and President Trump after the midterms. That’s augmented by the fact that Republicans believe the war in Iran cost them control of Congress. Thus, even more Republicans may be willing to impeach. Finally, the GOP may have attendance problems. Republican Members who lost – or were shocked that they lost – might not show up. In other words, there may be more Democrats in the House than Republicans. And don’t forget that some Republicans are now looking for a scapegoat after the election.

A simple majority is necessary to impeach.

If adopted, the House would send the articles of impeachment to the Senate. Under Senate rules of impeachment, the Senate must at least receive and consider the articles. But it could move quickly to dismiss. That’s what happened when the Senate considered articles of impeachment for former Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas a few years ago. The bona fide "trial" part of the process never happened where the Senate heard arguments, listened to witnesses and took evidence.

It takes a simple majority to dismiss such articles. Believe it or not, this could happen under a Republican-controlled Senate. But how might outgoing Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Bill Cassidy, R-La., vote? That’s to say nothing of Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, John Curtis, R-Alaska, Todd Young, R-Ind., and others.

It takes a two-thirds vote to convict and remove in a Senate impeachment trial.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In addition, unlike legislation, articles of impeachment carry over into the new Congress. Would a new Democratically-controlled Senate want to get bogged down in an impeachment trial from the start? Especially when new Democrats want to vote on affordability and health care?

Or, would a Democratic Senate embrace the idea of a full-blown impeachment trial for Hegseth – especially since the execution of the war in Iran seems to be one of the main reasons for this week’s electoral shellacking?

Some of this hinges on who both parties in each body select as their leaders.

Quiet serial killers may be hiding in plain sight, an expert warns, after new DNA technology helped unmask a Pennsylvania man authorities say killed at least two women in the 1970s.

At a Thursday news conference, Pennsylvania State Police identified James Richard Clark Sr. as the man who sexually assaulted and strangled Brenda Ritter, 18, and Susan Rush, 21, in the 1970s.

Rush vanished on Nov. 24, 1976, after leaving a shopping mall, according to the City of Washington Police Department. She was supposed to meet her family at church but never arrived. Her brother spotted her car along a street the next morning, Thanksgiving Day, and her body was discovered in the trunk.

TED BUNDY LINKED TO ANOTHER DECADES-OLD HOMICIDE NEARLY 40 YEARS AFTER HIS EXECUTION

Ritter disappeared from her boyfriend's house in 1977, police said. Her body was later found on a hillside, and authorities determined she had been sexually assaulted and strangled.

The suspect, Clark Sr., died at 66 on July 17, 2023 of natural causes.

DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON

In late 2028, evidence from Ritter's killing was sent to the state police crime lab, which produced an unknown male DNA profile. The DNA was put into an FBI database, CODIS, which was searched weekly with no match. In May 2025, testing at Cybergenetics' laboratory showed the same man was responsible for the deaths of both women.

Clark left DNA at both crime scenes, according to police, and advances in testing at several labs, including Identifinders International, helped investigators zero in on him before more testing sealed the match.

Police said Clark would have been 20 at the time of Ritter's homicide, and 19 when Rush was killed.

Pennsylvania State Police Cpl. James Petrosky said he thinks there may be more victims.

World.title: Popular cooking methods may destroy key health benefits of broccoli, experts warn
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Not all methods of cooking broccoli are created equal, and some simple tips can ensure you get the most nutrients out of it.

Whether it's steamed, roasted or added to a stir-fry, broccoli is a healthy option packed with vitamins such as A, C and K, minerals such as calcium, potassium and iron, fiber and even a potentially cancer-fighting compound, the Washington Post recently reported.

But certain ways of cooking broccoli can ensure you get the most out of the cruciferous vegetable and preserve those compounds.

YOU'RE PROBABLY COOKING RICE WRONG, AND CHEFS REVEAL THE SIMPLE MISTAKE TO AVOID

Boiling broccoli can cause water-soluble nutrients and compounds to leach into the cooking water, while prolonged or high-heat cooking, including roasting, can reduce antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and cancer-fighting properties.

"Boiling causes the most loss in nutrients," Sol Figueroa, a Florida-based registered dietitian nutritionist with Mochi Health, told Fox News Digital. "Vitamin C and glucoraphanin dissolve in water, so a lot of them end up in the cooking water that gets poured down the drain."

NATURAL COMPOUND IN BLUEBERRIES AND GRAPES MAY UNLOCK FAT-BURNING PROCESS IN MUSCLE CELLS

Glucoraphanin is a natural compound found in cruciferous vegetables and, when it is digested, it can be converted into sulforaphane, a compound studied for potential antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects and possible benefits for liver, metabolic and gut health, as well as cancer prevention.

Figueroa offered several tips to help get the most out of your broccoli. One way to preserve some of the nutrients is to use as little water as possible when boiling, she said.

Another is to sprinkle mustard powder on cooked broccoli. Mustard seeds contain myrosinase, an enzyme that helps convert glucoraphanin to sulforaphane and that can be lost during cooking.

COMMON GRILLING MISTAKE COULD STRIP FISH OF KEY NUTRIENTS AND RUIN YOUR MEAL, EXPERTS WARN

Some simple prep also may help preserve sulforaphane, according to Figueroa.

"We can't say broccoli prevents disease, but the findings are promising."

"Chopping the broccoli and letting it sit for about 30 to 40 minutes before cooking gives sulforaphane time to form first," she said.

FOUR COMMON KITCHEN HABITS THAT CHEFS SAY HOME COOKS NEED TO STOP DOING IMMEDIATELY

Most of the research related to broccoli's health claims has been conducted in labs and animals, Figueroa added.

"We can't say broccoli prevents disease, but the findings are promising," she said.

Steaming is one of the best ways to preserve broccoli's enzymes, and while the method often reduces vitamin C in other foods, research shows broccoli might be an exception, the Washington Post reported.

Quickly microwaving broccoli may help preserve nutrients, according to the outlet, and using broccoli's cooking water in soup or stew can help retain some water-soluble vitamins.

CLICK HERE TO 

Felice Kaufman, a Florida-based food blogger at Cooking in the Keys and former New York Whole Foods Market chef, said she usually steams broccoli, cutting the florets into similar sizes and checking for doneness after about three minutes.

"Taste a piece. If you'd eat it right then, take it out of the pot," Kaufman told Fox News Digital. "The heat keeps cooking the broccoli after it comes out of the pot."

Kaufman also recommends using the stalk, which she trims, slices and cooks with the florets.

"The stalk is the best part," she said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

She prefers steaming to boiling, in part to preserve vitamin C, but said that's not always possible.

"If the sink is full — it happens — I'll throw the broccoli straight into the boiling water," she said. "One less thing to wash."

No matter how it's served, getting some broccoli into your diet is key, experts agree.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The most important thing is eating broccoli at all," Figueroa said.

If roasting is the way your family likes it best, do that, she added.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Kaufman echoed that advice, saying, "Five ounces of broccoli, organic, conventional or frozen, is better than any processed food you can eat."

World.title: GOP senator withholds support for Thune as leadership showdown looms
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

FIRST ON FOX: A Senate Republican isn’t ready to support Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., to stay as the top Republican as the GOP’s leadership elections fast approach.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., in an interview with Fox News Digital, argued that whoever would be the next to lead the Senate GOP and earn his vote in the process needed to lay out a plan on how Republicans would pass key agenda items heading into the lame-duck session of Congress before Senate Democrats take control in January.

Thune plans to run again for another term as the GOP leader, but Scott and a cohort of others want to delay Tuesday morning’s leadership elections to debrief after stunning losses across the board on Election Night. Whether he’ll support Thune for another term depends on his pitch.

SENATE GOP REBELS MOVE TO DELAY LEADERSHIP VOTE, DEMAND RECKONING AFTER MIDTERM DISASTER

"I don't want to put the cart before the horse," Scott said. "I mean, I think the first step is what do we want to accomplish? And then anybody, including John Thune, if they want to be that, the first thing I have to say is, ‘Do they want to do that?’"

"If that's not what they want to accomplish, then why would we elect them? But if that's what they want to accomplish, then tell us why they're the best at it," he continued.

Senate Democrats flipped the upper chamber with wins in red states across the country, clinching a 54-seat majority that could grow even more depending on the outcomes of outstanding races in Mississippi and Alaska.

STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

That gives Republicans little time with a trifecta in government to ram through key remaining agenda items before Democrats officially take over.

Thune still plans on running for leader, too, despite the grumbling among Republicans. He said on Monday after lawmakers returned to Washington that he expected a "very engaged conversation" ahead of the leadership election.

"We'll see where it goes from there, but, yeah, I'm running for leader, and I think it's important that we have that discussion, and we will," Thune said.

Scott said that he wants the candidates to be "specific" on how they can balance the budget and pass a slew of legislation, including a stock trading ban for lawmakers, permitting reform, the National Defense Authorization Act and the SAVE America Act.

SCHUMER TANKS POPULAR INSIDER TRADING BAN IN DEM EFFORT TO DERAIL REPUBLICAN'S AGENDA AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

All of that, he said, would be a show that Republicans are listening to voters after getting pummeled in the midterms.

"Back home, they don't care about anything other than do we make their lives better," Scott said.

Thune is so far running unopposed for the top job — Scott reiterated that he had no interest in running again, trying twice for the gig, once against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022, and in 2024 when Senate Republicans were searching for McConnell’s replacement.

When asked if he would like to see someone else jump into the fray, Scott said, "Oh, I wouldn't do that to anybody."

Scott and Sens. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., Ted Budd, R-N.C., John Kennedy, R-La., and Mike Lee, R-Utah, all signed onto a letter demanding that Republicans meet before holding their leadership elections and delay voting until they have a full debrief on the midterm losses and what comes next.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

They’re joined by Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Dave McCormick, R-Pa., who called for the elections to be delayed but did not sign onto the letter pushing leadership for a meeting.

When asked how long he’d like to see the leadership elections delayed, Scott said, "I think this first step is how long is it gonna take us to agree on what our path should be?"

"If we can get that done quickly, then we can, you know, have elections after that," he said. "And then people that want to run with that agenda in mind, saying they believe in that agenda and will work hard to get that agenda accomplished, then that's how we would decide how we vote."

World.title: Gas prices fall below $4 per gallon for the first time since July
World.content:
The average nationwide price for regular gasoline on Tuesday fell below $4 per gallon for the first time since July 20, according to data from AAA.

The drop comes as oil prices have plunged, with President Donald Trump repeatedly playing down the prospect of a renewed war with Iran, and pushing for progress between Russia and Ukraine in new trilateral talks.

Still, gas prices remain elevated by more than 30% since the war with Iran started on February 28, and around 40% since the beginning of the year.

The drop in pump prices came after oil futures plunged 13% last week. For the global crude oil benchmark Brent, it was its biggest one-week percentage drop since April 2020, when the Covid pandemic began shutting down the global economy and demand for oil rapidly declined. Oil prices slid by another 5% on Monday, to their lowest point since August 31. And on Tuesday they briefly fell below $90 a barrel.

The slide in oil prices started after Trump told NBC News last week that he did not plan to attack Iran. The fall continued after Democratic candidates put up commanding vote totals in Tuesday’s midterm elections, which some called a “blue tsunami.”

Markets quickly began betting that Democratic control of the House and Senate would put a cap on some of Trump’s most economically-disruptive policies, such as the Iran war.

“Given the Democrats’ control of Congress, there will likely be more scrutiny over the war, while funding it could become more difficult,” said ING commodities strategists in a note. “The outcome of the elections means there could be more pushback from the Republican Party, too.”

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vice President JD Vance wrote in a post on social media in the wake of the results on Wednesday morning. Vance added that “any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

For traders, Vance’s acknowledgment of the unpopularity of the war bolstered the case for lower oil prices. But on Friday, Trump was briefed on a narrow window for a potential new military campaign against Iran, sources told NBC News. No decision has been taken, the officials also said.

Trump on Monday again reinforced that he was leaning against a major escalation. “Iran militarily is effectively over,” the president told reporters at the White House. “We’re just keeping it the status quo.” He said there was there was “positive momentum” in talks and that he saw a “good chance” that the war “could get ended.”

He added that “The military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing, but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes.”

World.title: Inflation likely took a breather last month as fuel prices fell
World.content:
Americans are tired of inflation, as last week’s election results showed, but there may have been some relief last month as gasoline, diesel and jet fuel prices eased.

The consumer price index, which is scheduled for release at 8:30 a.m. ET on Tuesday, is expected to show an increase of 0.3% month-over-month, according to a survey of economists conducted by Bloomberg. Economists also project that so-called core inflation, which does not include food or energy prices, rose 0.2%.

In September, the CPI report showed prices grew 0.6% from August along with a 3.7% increase from a year earlier. (The October data will not include a year-ago number after the U.S. government shutdown disrupted the agency’s data collection, forcing it to skip the October 2025 CPI report entirely.)

Even with some relief, the October data is set to illustrate the price pressures on consumers — a big factor in the Democrats’ sweeping victories in the congressional midterm elections last week. Eighty-four percent of voters told NBC News’ Exit Poll that they believed higher prices were a result of President Donald Trump’s policies, and 39% said the economy was their No. 1 issue at the ballot box, according to the exit poll.

Those policies include global tariffs that add to the cost of products imported into the United States, as well as the war in Iran. Launched in February, that conflict has driven regular gas prices up 40%. Diesel fuel prices are 70% higher than at the start of the year.

That, in turn, pushed inflation higher across the U.S.. Economists have warned that the rise in this commercial fuel can quickly ripple across the economy. Diesel is a major input cost for the transportation industry that delivers goods, such as groceries, to store shelves around the world.

Gas prices declined last month, as Americans either voted early or geared up to cast their ballots on Election Day. On Oct. 1, the AAA national gas price average was $4.41 per gallon. At the end of the month, it was $4.18, a more than 5% drop.

As a result, Citigroup economists predicted that Tuesday’s data will show “stabilizing and falling airfares, and limited pass through of higher energy costs into goods prices.” They also said shelter inflation and services prices could also show some slowing.

Gas prices have continued trending downward in November, falling to $4 on Monday — although it’s still significantly higher than before the Iran war.

Even as the oil price surge takes a breather, it may not last long. Throughout the Iran war, countries that are members of the International Energy Agency have released 400 million barrels of crude and related products, such as diesel, into the global market. “Restocking those inventories will create a floor under prices once the current conflict in the Middle East has faded,” said Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG.

Given inflation’s overall stubbornness, economists believe the Federal Reserve will remain on track to hike rates for the second time this year. The Fed’s next two-day interest rate meeting will take place Dec. 8-9, right before the next inflation reading on Dec. 10.

Market odds for a December hike sat at 85% Monday afternoon.

“Still, details of Q4 data will be important for shifting inflation risks into 2027,” Citi economists wrote.

Bank of America economists agreed, predicting that the report would be “a cooler start to fall,” after multiple months of rising inflation.

Meanwhile, AI is also stoking inflation in other parts of the economy. In August, JPMorgan estimated that memory costs were on track to rise more than 400% from the end of 2024 through the end of 2026.

Tech companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data centers and the equipment that fills those facilities, pushing memory prices higher. Those costs are being passed down to consumers. Consumer tech companies, including Apple, have raised their prices as a result.

World.title: California voters reject new tax on billionaires in a blow to the left
World.content:
California voters have rejected a ballot measure that sought to impose a one-time tax on the state’s billionaires, NBC News projected Monday, dealing a blow to progressives who championed the proposal.

Proposition 40 sharply divided Democrats in the state and nationally as the party figures out what direction it wants to take heading into an open presidential contest. It also faced a barrage of ad spending funded by the billionaires it would have affected, particularly in Silicon Valley.

The ballot initiative proposed a 5% tax on the assets of state residents who have net worths of more than $1.1 billion, with the option for a smaller, phased-in tax for those worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion. It would require California to spend 90% of the created revenue on healthcare. The taxes would apply retroactively to anyone living in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026.

Proposition 40 would have been the first enactment of a billionaire tax in the U.S. But many progressives who support increasing taxes on the wealthy in general came out against it because it was a one-time tax, rather than a permanent one, and it primarily benefited one policy area, healthcare.

Critics in both parties argued that the tax would prompt wealthy Californians to flee the state in droves, which would dry up broader tax revenue streams and create more budget problems.

Democratic opponents included outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom, a possible 2028 presidential contender, and Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra. Many of California’s largest unions and Democratic-aligned advocacy groups also opposed the measure.

Meanwhile, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., another potential White House hopeful, were among its notable backers, holding several rallies in the state ahead of Election Day.

Opponents of Proposition 40 held a staggering upper hand on the airwaves. In late October, they were outspending supporters 250 to 1 on ads, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

The biggest spender, “No on Prop. 40,” was a coalition that included the California Teachers Association, the California Medical Association and Planned Parenthood and received contributions from several billionaires. Other groups got millions from Google co-founder Sergey Brin and the California Business Roundtable.

The “Billionaire Tax Now” campaign, championed by the Service Employees International Union, said the matter is not over.

“The billionaires may have bought themselves a temporary victory at the ballot box, but they have not bought themselves an end to this debate, and this is only round one,” Suzanne Jimenez, a sponsor of Prop 40 and chief of staff at the union, said in a statement Monday.

Opponents of the billionaire tax also placed two dueling initiatives on California’s ballot — Proposition 41 and Proposition 42 — that would have effectively nullified Proposition 40.

Proposition 41 sought to require the state auditor to review new special tax measures and that any new tax be counted toward a voter-approved state spending limit. Proposition 42 proposed banning any new taxes on assets, including investment accounts and property and restricting increases in retroactive taxes. Both would have gone into effect by earning just one vote more than Proposition 40, even if it passed.

World.title: Republicans, reeling from an election drubbing, will choose their leadership in Congress
World.content:
WASHINGTON — After a blue tidal wave swept them from power, House and Senate Republicans will try to pick up the pieces Tuesday and select their leadership teams for the new Congress.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has already heeded his party’s call for new blood, announcing he will forgo a bid for minority leader and step down from leadership. But other GOP leaders in both chambers are fighting to hang on to power in the wake of last week’s historic midterm drubbing.

The House: Scalise vs. Jordan

In the House, Johnson’s decision has triggered a two-person race for minority leader.
