More communication skills from Life Kit

4 habits of highly effective communicators. Called 'supercommunicators,' these people have the exceptional ability of creating authentic connections with others — just by listening and talking.

Sponsor Message

Good conversations take time and attention. Here's how to have better ones. Having good conversations is an art form. Former NPR host Sam Sanders tapped longtime radio host and podcaster Celeste Headlee for her tips for really listening and connecting.

4 negotiation tactics to try in everyday life. People often use negotiation tactics in business environments. But you can also use them to get your roommate to clean up, figure out where to eat for dinner or decide on which car to buy.

How to receive critical feedback. Receiving feedback doesn't necessarily have to be terrifying, according to Shanita Williams, a feedback coach, professor and author of Feedback Mentality. In this episode, Williams and Stacy-Marie Ishmael, a writer and editor, provide five tips to make receiving feedback a little less scary.

This story was edited by Malaka Gharib. The visual editor is CJ Riculan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.

World.title: How word of mouth is helping an Amish community's fight against measles
World.content:
How word of mouth is helping an Amish community's fight against measles

toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR

Measles spreads incredibly fast. For the last few months, so has Dale Weiser's phone number.

Weiser is the clinical services supervisor for the Chester County Health Department in south-central Pennsylvania. Since August, she's been driving out to Amish homes to vaccinate people against measles. She says it usually starts with a phone call.

"I was at a house, like, at 4:30 in the afternoon, and I had a phone call at 8 the next morning saying, 'hey, I heard you were down the street. Can you come do that at my house?'" she says of a typical request she gets from Amish families. So far, she's administered more than 400 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine in Amish homes.

Sponsor Message

The house calls are part of the state of Pennsylvania's strategy to wage war on measles by flipping the script on traditional public health messaging. Instead of advertising vaccinations loudly, health officials have launched a quiet word-of-mouth campaign designed to win the trust of the state's Amish community, which has been particularly hard hit by the country's worst measles outbreak in 35 years. The state has confirmed six measles-related deaths and more than 1,500 cases so far — though the true count is likely much higher, since many people who get sick don't seek medical care.

Lower vaccination rates

Surveys suggest only about a third of Amish families in the region vaccinate their children. That's left the Amish community especially vulnerable to measles, one of the most contagious diseases.

There's no religious edict against vaccination among the Amish. It's very much seen as a family and individual choice, says Weiser. Often, she says, these decisions are driven by practical and cultural factors.

toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR

"They don't have health insurance. They're not interacting with the mainstream medical society. And measles wasn't a problem for 30 years, so there was no real risk to not being vaccinated, at least for measles," Weiser says.

But as measles cases have piled up in Pennsylvania, Weiser says many Amish families have changed their minds about getting the MMR vaccine. And when they do, she hops in her car and brings the shots to them.

Sponsor Message

"When I arrive at their home, there's usually a small child that will run from the back of the house to the barn to tell the men that there's somebody strange in the driveway, or that the nurse is here," she says.

A patient, personalized approach to outreach

Some days, Weiser will vaccinate a single family in their kitchen. Other times, she'll find dozens of people gathered to get the shot. She's also fielded a lot of questions. Some, like what's in the vaccine and potential side effects, are things anyone would ask, she says.

"But I was caught off guard when I was asked if there were tracking chips in the vaccine, and I was like, whoa. Flashback to COVID. Where did you hear that?" she recalls.

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

As with the general population, vaccine misinformation has made its way to the Amish community. And when she encounters it, Weiser takes the time to explain why the rumors are false.

Chester County Public Health Director Jeanne Franklin says this kind of patient, personalized approach has helped build trust among the local Amish – who, along with conservative Mennonites, are known as the Plain community because of their simple way of life.

toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR

"That's why we said it has to be boots on the ground in the communities. It's not just because they were a Plain community, it was because we needed to be seen as caring people," Franklin says.

Instead of relying on traditional top-down, rigid public health messaging, her staff has spent a lot of time quietly visiting Amish church leaders and businesses, introducing themselves and asking community leaders if they would hand out flyers advertising vaccine clinics. "One of them said, 'Come on back with a clinic' at his restaurant. And he helped spread the word," Franklin says.

Sponsor Message

Vaccine questions and misinformation

When I stopped by the restaurant, Honey Brook Barbecue in Honey Brook, Pa., an area with a sizable Amish community, I found the manager grilling chicken in an outdoor tent. Like many Amish people NPR talked to, he spoke on the condition of anonymity in keeping with his community's tradition of not drawing attention to oneself.

toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR

The manager says 24 people showed up to get vaccinated at his restaurant back in August, all drawn by word of mouth. He says he decided to host the clinic for two reasons: to protect the general public and to protect his own community. He said he didn't want people blaming the Amish for spreading measles.

But he says other people in the Amish community who don't regularly interact with the public aren't getting vaccinated. For some, it's because of cultural reasons, but he says others are concerned about what they've heard is in the MMR vaccine.

"In my community, a lot of it has to do with what people think is in it," the manager says of the MMR vaccine. One concern he's heard repeatedly is that the vaccine contains parts of aborted fetuses.

That is a myth often repeated by anti-vaccine forces, and it is one heard in conversations with Amish people in Lancaster County, home to around 45,000 Amish people. It's also the county with a third of the state's measles cases — more than 500 confirmed cases.

At the Amish-owned Gordonville Book Store, where a buggy is parked outside, I meet a shopper named Lydia Esh. She says she, her husband and six adult children had all previously been vaccinated against measles. But none of her 13 grandchildren have gotten the shot, because their parents had heard that the MMR vaccine had changed and now contained aborted fetus parts — which is false.

toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR

There is some evidence that anti-vaccine groups have been targeting the Amish in recent years, says Steve Nolt, a professor at Elizabethtown College who has written numerous books about Amish history and culture. For example, he points to an  questioning the safety of childhood vaccines published in The Pennsylvania Busy Beaver, an advertising publication with a large Amish readership.

Sponsor Message

But in conversations around Lancaster, I also find evidence that public health outreach efforts are working. One member of the Plain community, a visibly pregnant woman outside an Amish-owned hardware store, says her husband and two children recently got vaccinated to protect her and her unborn child. She asked NPR not to use her name, as did an Amish man working at a produce stall in an Amish market. He says he recently got vaccinated because "measles is scary."

Linda Beth Fisher, an 18-year-old Amish woman behind the counter at the Gordonville Book Store, says she is concerned that several Amish people in her area have died in the measles outbreak, but she's not sure what to believe about the MMR vaccine.

toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR

"Personally, I'm kind of leery of it. I'm not sure why," Fisher says. "I guess I've just kind of heard that they're not good, but I've also heard that they are good. So I just feel like it's two sides of the story. Would you encourage people to get it?"

"They almost always come back"

These types of concerns often surface at pop-up vaccine clinics like one recently hosted at the Christiana Fire Company in Lancaster County. The Pennsylvania Department of Health hosts these events in Lancaster three or four times a week — all advertised by word of mouth, says Dr. Jennifer Wallace. As medical director for the department's Bureau of Community Health Systems, she oversees pop-up clinics and outreach to vulnerable communities across Pennsylvania.

toggle caption i Daniel Vasta for NPR

Wallace says when members of the Plain community come with questions, "We're here to give them that information and then let them ponder it. They can ask any questions they want to and then let them either get vaccinated if they choose or take that information home. Think about it. Talk with their bishops. Talk with their community. They almost always come back."

Sponsor Message

Wallace says many who end up coming are families with multiple children. Tables set up around the firehouse are strewn with crayons, coloring books and bubble wands to keep young ones entertained while parents fill out paperwork.

"And then you see the kids get vaccinated and you can almost see the mother's shoulders relax over time as each child gets that shot," she says. "We've had some mothers cry afterwards because they're just so relieved."

The state health department says 30 people attended the Christiana firehouse clinic, 24 of whom got vaccinated. That included a father and his three sons who arrived for their second doses.

World.title: The Democratic Party gained power across the country in the midterms. Now what?
World.content:
The Democratic Party gained power across the country in the midterms. Now what?

toggle caption i Win McNamee/Getty Images

Two years ago, voters sent Democrats a message when they ousted them from power in Washington. At first glance, last week's midterm results sent a new one.

Democrats will enter the next Congress with one of the largest majorities in a generation, flipping dozens of House districts and at least seven Senate seats in mainly Trump-won communities. The party now controls a majority of governorships, and gained control of several additional state legislative chambers.

"I think one of the big surprises for me on Tuesday night was just how deep and wide our election results were," Democratic National Committee Chairman Ken Martin said in an interview with NPR. "This was the biggest election cycle for Democrats in the history of our party."

Sponsor Message

Martin, who has faced criticism from some inside the party throughout his term as chairman, said that the stunning Democratic victories across the country were the result of his party's focus on issues like affordability and ending the war in Iran.

He said the midterms were bigger than politics and bigger than party, and acknowledged the results were just as much about serving as a "massive repudiation of Donald Trump and the MAGA Trumpers and the Republican Party." "I think it's an admonition for Democrats, for sure: Now that we're in power, we have to deliver," he said. "But it was a complete message to Republicans. You had the ability to help us and you did nothing."

Blue tsunami in the South

With an expanded Congressional majority and a lame duck president, one of the frontlines for figuring out if the Democratic party's power will hold will be in the South, Martin said.

"Six of the 10 fastest growing parts of the country right now are below the Mason-Dixon line, and 40% of the U.S. population is going to live in the South after the next Census," he said. "As we go into 2032 and there's a realignment with the reapportionment, states like Minnesota, Michigan, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, New York, Rhode Island, Illinois and California are all going to lose electoral votes and congressional votes to the South."

Sponsor Message

Last week's midterms brought the region's power – especially with Black voters – more squarely into focus. Turbocharged Black voter turnout helped elect the country's first Black female governor in Georgia and may elect the first Black U.S. Senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction.

A slew of Republican-led states seeking to redraw House maps for partisan advantage backfired, as Democrats gained several seats across the region.

Georgia Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock said in an interview with NPR that Democratic victories in 2026 were a "proof of concept" that the South is central to the future of American politics.

toggle caption i Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

"You saw a multiracial coalition of voters stand up on Tuesday night beyond anything I had even hoped for, and they offered a silent rebuke of where we are now," he told NPR. "It's now up to us to provide the leadership, even as we listen to people, and point the way forward into how we build an economy that works for everyday working families."

Warnock said Democrats' direction in the next two years should aim to serve as a cure for the last decade of Trump-dominated politics that has been defined more as top versus bottom rather than left versus right.

"Ordinary people have had their hopes dashed time and time again, cycle after cycle, across Republican and Democratic administrations," he said. "They've seen the widening chasm between the haves and the have nots."

He called the midterms a "moral moment" that will help determine what kind of nation America wants to be.

Looking ahead to 2028

In the early days after the 2026 elections, a look ahead to the 2028 presidential race finds both parties with the potential to see crowded fields of candidates in several new lanes reacting to signals sent by the electorate.

That includes Warnock, who will be up for reelection in 2028 and is among names floated as a presidential contender, along with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, California Rep. Ro Khanna, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, former Vice President Kamala Harris and others who have spent significant time in the South campaigning for other Democrats.

Sponsor Message

As new members of Congress descend on Washington for their orientations, competing visions for Democratic governance are on display with postmortem event panels called "What Worked" and "What Just Happened?" and event names like "What's Next" as party strategists argue online about which wing of the party was the most successful.

2026 victories also scramble the traditional map of swing states, Martin said, suggesting that Democrats would start off competitive in places like Florida and Texas and as favorites to win the White House.

"Texas is no longer a red state. It is a blue state. They didn't even go from red to purple to blue, which is a normal sort of progression," he said. "If Texas is now a blue state, and you look at Georgia and you look at other parts of the South, how do the Republicans get to 270 votes?"

World.title: California voters defeat billionaire tax proposal that divided Democrats
World.content:
California voters defeat billionaire tax proposal that divided Democrats

toggle caption i Jae C. Hong/AP

Midterms coverage: Live results | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

California voters have rejected a proposal to charge billionaires a one-time 5% tax on most of their wealth, according to a race call by The Associated Press.

Proponents said the tax could raise $100 billion for healthcare. Led by a union that represents healthcare workers, the SEIU-UHW, advocates of the tax said the Republican-controlled Congress cut healthcare programs to give tax breaks to the wealthy, so it was time for the wealthy in California to fill the gap. The state has more than 200 billionaires, according to estimates, with some putting the number at a few hundred.

Sponsor Message

Opponents argued that the proposal, known as Prop 40, would just drive the wealthy out of California, costing the state revenue and harming its economy.

But the measure divided Democrats in a state where they heavily outnumber Republicans.

Loading...

The state's Democratic Party favored Prop 40, as did Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who went to the state to campaign for it. But Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed the tax, saying it would be better to have a national tax on the wealthy. The Democratic candidate for governor, Xavier Becerra, also opposed it.

A leading teachers union also opposed the proposal, which would have set aside just a small portion of the resulting revenue for schools. And Google co-founder Sergey Brin led other wealthy Californians in a surge of campaign spending opposing the measure. At least five times as much was spent opposing the measure as favoring it.

Brin also drove a campaign that put two other proposals on the ballot to block the billionaire tax from taking effect, had it been approved by voters.

World.title: Specialized burn treatments deployed for soldiers injured in Alberta military base fire
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Survivors of the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta are being treated with RECELL, a spray-on skin product. Canadian military nurses, medical centres and labs across Canada are contributing to their care.

Experts across Canada are taking extraordinary measures and using the latest medical techniques to care for soldiers burned at a fire at CFB Wainwright last month.

In Alberta, 21 soldiers remain in hospital, with nine in critical condition and 15 on ventilators to help them breathe, according to Acute Care Alberta.

“It has been ... all hands on deck across Canada to provide that support to the front-line staff to be able to provide this care, and part of this has been tapping into the best products and instruments that are out there,” Acute Care Alberta's interim CEO Dr. Sayeh Zielke said in an interview with CBC News in late October.

Spray-on skin

One product being used is called RECELL, a device that makes spray-on skin in minutes.

Doctors put a very thin piece of a patient’s healthy skin into the device, which breaks down the cells and turns them into a suspension that can be sprayed over a burn.

It’s unlicensed in Canada, but Health Canada used the Medical Devices Special Access Program to bring it into the country.

Dr. Julia Slater, medical director at the burn centre at the University of Kansas Health System, demonstrates how a RECELL kit works. (Supplied by University of Kansas Health System)

Dr. Julia Slater, medical director for the Burnett Burn Center at the University of Kansas Health System, has frequently used RECELL over the last five years; it was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2018.

Slater said burn centres can easily get overwhelmed by mass casualty incidents like the one at CFB Wainwright on Oct. 17, when an out-of-control grass fire killed four soldiers and injured dozens more. She commended Health Canada for taking quick action.

“I think it shows how quickly your system was able to recognize how big of a deal this was to have that number of patients with this severe of injuries.”

When a high proportion of a patient’s body is burned, there may not be much donor skin available, Slater said in an interview from Kansas City. RECELL turns a small graft into a spray that can cover a larger surface area.

The entrance of CFB Wainwright as seen in the early hours of Oct. 18, 2026, the day after a fatal grass fire on the military base. (Julia Wong/CBC News)

And the RECELL suspension can be made in the operating room in roughly 30 minutes, compared to weeks for lab-grown skin, Slater added.

“In my practice, it has just revolutionized how we can treat patients with large burns, getting them out of the hospital sooner, less surgeries, getting them healed faster.”

In a statement, AVITA Medical, the company behind RECELL, said its staff travelled to burn centres in Calgary and Edmonton to help surgeons who were using the device for the first time.

Allograft donation

Other provinces also jumped into action to help Alberta hospitals with treatment.

Shared Health, Manitoba’s health authority, provided allografts — tissues harvested from living or dead donors — from Oct. 19 to Oct. 27.

“Provinces really come together in situations like this,” said Nicole Sneath, interim vice-president of quality, patient safety and operations.

“We see how important collaboration across the country really is when there’s some of these unprecedented events that happen and for us to be able to respond and mobilize quickly.”

‘Major team effort’

Burn care typically involves skin grafts, changing dressings and monitoring for signs of infection, Zielke said.

Dr. Sayeh Zielke is the interim CEO of Acute Care Alberta. (Google Meet)

“Multiple surgeries happen thereafter to replace the skin with either artificial skin, or allografts, cadaver skins, until we [are] able to provide the patient with their own lab-grown skin tissue.”

As of Monday, 25 soldiers who were injured at CFB Wainwright were still hospitalized nationwide, the Department of National Defence said.

Last week, four were transported from Alberta to hospitals in B.C. and Ontario, to be closer to family.

At the Ross Tilley Burn Centre at Sunnybrook Hospital in Toronto, medical staff are working around the clock on two soldiers, while a third is an outpatient, said surgeon Dr. Alan Rogers.

He said he estimates that patients with major burns will stay one to two days in hospital for every percentage of their body surface that was affected.

Dr. Alan Rogers is a burn surgeon at the Ross Tilley Burn Centre at Sunnybrook Hospital. (Maxime Beauchemin/Radio-Canada)

“It’s a major team effort to get these patients through effectively," Rogers said. "Each day can bring new challenges for these patients and ultimately we’re trying to get good quality [skin] coverage of large areas so that they can rehabilitate effectively.”

Recovery will take months to years, he said.

“It is arguably one of the most painful experiences a patient can endure,” Rogers said. “Patients will still require a number of operations and once they’ve had all their wounds closed with their own skin, they will have various challenges in terms of restoring function.”

He said the long-term goal is to get the soldiers to a place resembling their lives before the fire — “returning them to their place in the world … to be as close to the people they were before, physically [and] emotionally.”

World.title: Where Trump goes now on the big 3: tariffs, Iran war, immigration
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After his party's calamitous loss in the midterms, a looming question is whether U.S. President Donald Trump will shift course on any of his three biggest initiatives since returning to the White House: tariffs, the war with Iran and immigration enforcement.

Trump has come across as somewhat subdued in his public appearances over the past week.

Yet in both his words and actions, Trump has shown defiance in the face of the results, which saw the biggest drop in Republican House candidates' share of the vote in any election since the Watergate scandal of the early 1970s.

He named Stephen Miller — the chief architect of Trump's hard-line immigration policy and the driving force behind much of his unprecedented use of executive orders — as his new chief of staff, the most powerful adviser to the president.

Many observers see the move to elevate Miller as a signal that Trump intends to double down on immigration enforcement rather than ease off.

Then, during an unscheduled briefing Monday afternoon in the White House, Trump mostly brushed aside the issues that drove the vote swing against the Republicans, declaring the war in Iran "effectively over" and describing the U.S. as "doing better than it's ever done before."

With the firm caveat that Trump is often highly unpredictable, here's what analysts expect from the president on his three key initiatives in the wake of the midterms.

WATCH | Despite Republicans' heavy midterm losses, Trump sets combative tone: Trump loyalists gear up for a fight after Democratic ‘blue-nami’ | Duration closed caption 2:50 U.S. President Donald Trump is setting a combative tone in the wake of dramatic Republican setbacks in the midterm elections, as the administration also faces fire from within.

Tariffs

Trump's long-standing love affair with tariffs is no secret. Even though tariff-driven price increases played a significant role in the Republicans' midterm drubbing, the president appears highly unlikely to toss out the policy entirely.

But some observers do see room for Trump to back down on select tariffs, particularly ones that are politically unpopular, as tariffs on Canadian goods proved to be in border states like Michigan and Maine during the election campaign.

Barbara Weisel, an international trade and investment policy adviser, says there's potential for Trump's team to fine-tune its tariffs, using them in a more strategic and targeted way.

"The scale of the Democratic wave and public anger may prompt the administration to rethink its approach, and it can do so without completely abandoning Trump’s beloved tariffs," Weisel wrote in a post-midterm article published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Drew Fagan, professor at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, says much will depend on whether Trump and his top advisers "actually want to solve the problems that they've created."

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, seen here with U.S. President Donald Trump in the Oval Office on Sept. 28, has been one of the chief backers of Trump's tariff strategy. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

"He's in denial with regard to the degree to which voters saw the economy, inflation, the weakness of their paycheques versus cost as the fundamental issue, and tariffs were part of this," Fagan told CBC News Network on Monday.

One data point that could signal whether Trump intends to shift his trade agenda will be whether any of the top advocates for tariffs in his administration either leave or get pushed out, chiefly Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick or U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

War with Iran

Senior members of the Trump administration, including to some extent the president himself, are acknowledging the war's impact on gas prices hurt Republicans in the midterms.

While Trump and his team continue to defend the decision to go to war with Iran, they are signaling they want it to end. However their path to doing so remains anything but clear.

"W e're seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it's going to be ending fairly soon," Trump said during the Monday briefing.

Trump has said for months that the war would end soon.

The question becomes whether the end will be found through a peace deal or military escalation.

WATCH | Why Trump's move to name Stephen Miller as chief of staff matters: Trump names hardliner Stephen Miller chief of staff after midterm blowout | Duration closed caption 2:46 U.S. President Donald Trump promoted trusted, hardline adviser Stephen Miller to chief of staff on Friday, in a sign he may come out swinging after the Democrats' resounding victories in Tuesday's midterm elections.

A diplomatic agreement could "reinforce perceptions that his war was an unmitigated disaster that damaged U.S. national security, the Republican Party’s electoral prospects and his personal legacy," said William F. Wechsler, a former Pentagon official responsible for special operations and combating terrorism.

"The only way out, Trump may therefore conclude, is to win the war. That could lead to a decision to restart major combat operations, if not immediately, then in the months to come," Wechsler wrote in a piece for the Atlantic Council, a Washington, D.C.-based think-tank.

Immigration enforcement

In his interview with 60 Minutes, recorded Friday, Trump said the administration may have been too tough in its deportation policy.

But when asked during Monday's briefing whether he has told Miller he wants changes to immigration enforcement, Trump's response suggests there won't be a substantial shift.

"We have a very strong deportation policy ," Trump said. "M y policy hasn't changed."

Earlier this year, after federal agents in Minneapolis shot and killed two American citizens, the administration toned down the high-profile, aggressive nature of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) tactics.

However, ICE actually stepped up its overall pace of detentions to hit record highs in the summer, according to analysis by the Deportation Data Project, based at the University of California Berkeley and UCLA.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents detain a man outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs building during a protest in Portland, Ore., in June 2025. (Jenny Kane/The Associated Press)

Sarah Binder, a professor of political science at George Washington University, is skeptical that Trump will move in any significant way toward softening his immigration policy.

"It doesn't seem likely, not with this decision to have Stephen Miller running the show," Binder said Monday in a post-midterm briefing organized by the Brookings Institution, a think-tank in Washington.

Yemisi Egbewole, who served as chief of staff in former president Joe Biden's press office, says it's hard to reconcile Trump's appointment of Miller as chief of staff with his claim to 60 Minutes that he's willing to reach a compromise with the Democrats on immigration.

"That really speaks to the duality of the president. He says one thing, but then his actions deliver another totally different result," Egbewole told CBC News Network on Monday.

"There are ways to find common ground, but the president has to drive the conversation there and not let Stephen Miller enact his own agenda," she said.

Trump's willingness to make deals with the Democrats on immigration — or any other major policies — is almost certain to dwindle if the party follows through on threats to launch Congressional investigations into allegations of corruption against the president's family and inner circle.

World.title: Why Danielle Smith wants to give a subsidy to the oilpatch despite near-record profits
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Alberta government is preparing to unveil new subsidies later this month for oil companies to ramp up production in order to help fill the province's proposed Pacific Link pipeline to the West Coast.

The incentives would come as the largest oil producers are posting billions of dollars in profits in their latest financial results and the industry as a whole is experiencing one of its most lucrative years over the last decade.

Suncor Energy, Cenovus Energy, Canadian Natural Resources and Imperial Oil posted combined profits of more than $12.5 billion in recent quarterly earnings reports. The Canadian oil and gas industry is forecast to post revenues of more than $200 billion in 2026, according to Studio Energy, after oil prices climbed above $100 US per barrel several times this year amid the U.S.-Iran war.

That's why some industry experts question why new subsidies are needed.

"What kind of incentives does the oil and gas sector really need?" said Janet Annesley, a former executive with Husky Energy and Shell Canada, on CBC Radio's Alberta at Noon.

"They've got money, they're buying back shares, they're flowing lots of dividends to shareholders. So what really more do we Albertans have to do to get them to make investments here and have more projects?"

Premier Danielle Smith, Annesley said, will have to "prosecute the case with Albertans about why we should be giving more incentives to oil companies."

LISTEN | Digging into the Pacific Link pipeline: West of Centre 32:08 Pacific Link: A pipeline in whose interest?

Oil production is already at record levels, but with several new and expanded pipeline projects in development, there is uncertainty whether the industry will pump out enough crude to justify beginning construction on the Pacific Link — for which Smith wants construction to begin in fall 2027.

The province is seeking to create an "alternative enhanced royalty structure," according to Smith, to incentivize companies to commit to growing oil production.

"We hope that once that is on the table and they know all of the factors that would go into it, I suspect that you're going to see a lot of interest in being able to fill that pipeline," Smith told journalists in Fort McMurray, Alta., in September.

More oil wanted

The new subsidy is expected to be aimed at the oilsands sector, since that is the source of most oil production in the province and new projects are often large enough to noticeably increase overall production levels.

The Alberta government already provides a financial incentive to oilsands companies to build new projects, since they pay much lower levels of royalties to the government during the first few years of operation.

A view of Suncor's Base Plant oilsands mine. Suncor is one of the companies considering whether to proceed with expanding production in the oilsands. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

Already, some companies are hinting at potentially moving quicker to build new projects.

Imperial Oil was considering a decision to proceed with its Aspen oilsands project by the end of the decade, but chief executive John Whelan said that could occur sooner.

"We are looking at do we want to bring it forward," he said, during a conference call with analysts on Oct. 30, while acknowledging the company is encouraged by steps taken by the provincial and federal governments to support the sector.

Suncor executives are looking at their growth plans over the next several years and contemplating how they could potentially move faster, if they decide to, said chief executive Rich Kruger.

"We're asking ourselves and doing some preliminary work," he said, during a conference call with analysts on Nov. 4.

"We're all anxiously waiting to hear more from the province on royalties and incentives there. The parties are all sleeves rolled up, meeting endlessly, working hard together."

The Oil Sands Alliance would not comment on the proposed Alberta incentives until an actual announcement is made.

Introducing a deadline

Some oil companies could be hinting at possible growth plans as a way to alert investors and gauge their interest. Despite lucrative oil prices, many investors would rather oil companies continue to produce hefty profits for shareholders, as opposed to spending billions of dollars to invest in new projects.

Many investors are enjoying the robust profits and are reluctant to give up the cash they collect, says Mark Little, the former chief executive of Suncor.

The company leaders are "testing investors' appetite for expansion," said Little, to hear if they will support growth plans or if they warn not to do it.

"To me, the biggest uncertainty on growth isn't the [federal government], it's not the province, it's not money," said Little, "It's whether the investor will support it."

Former Suncor executive Mark Little, pictured in 2022, says the current Alberta royalty system works well. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

The last large oilsands project to be constructed was nearly a decade ago, which is why Little says it's important for the industry to make investments to ensure the sector's long-term future.

"I almost call it the 'liquidation phase' because all we've been doing is basically producing, spending as little as possible, and handing the cash back to the shareholders," he said.

An aerial view of an oilsands mine north of Fort McMurray, Alta. Oil production continues to increase as companies expand and improve existing facilities. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

The Alberta government's move to introduce a new incentive is "mystifying," said Little, since the current royalty system is already sophisticated, flexible and works well. However, he could see merit in the provincial government introducing a deadline for companies to develop the properties they own.

Production from the oilsands continues to increase as companies invest in expansion projects and find ways to improve existing operations.

Lennie Kaplan, who previously served as a senior manager with the Treasury Board, estimates that some level of incentives are necessary for companies to spend billions of dollars to build new large-scale oilsands projects.

"These projects are very capital intensive," he said, about the level of investment required.

For the Alberta government to reach its goal of doubling oil production, Kaplan's calculations estimate the government would need to provide $115 billion of incentives between 2027 and 2050, which includes $95 billion of royalty relief and $18 billion of additional construction subsidies. Under that scenario of normal oil prices, as forecast by Alberta Energy, the government would collect an additional $250 billion in royalties.

However, in a scenario with low oil prices, the government would need to provide $240 billion of incentives and yet experience a net fiscal loss of $80 billion.

Kaplan's modelling does account for other considerations, including a rising industrial carbon tax, which he said is important considering the Alberta government still pledges to be net-zero by 2050.

World.title: Military budget squeeze limits paid Remembrance Day participation in Ontario
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A military reserve unit in southwestern Ontario has imposed a cap on the number of soldiers it is willing to pay to attend Remembrance Day services this year, CBC News has learned.

A series of leaked internal emails involving members of 31 Canadian Brigade show internal budget restraints imposed across the military have forced local commanders to limit paid attendance to 50 troops per unit.

The brigade, which is headquartered at Wolseley Barracks in London, Ont., has 13 units, which are sprinkled across the region, including St. Thomas, Waterloo and Hamilton.

The decision means 650 soldiers out of a total strength of 2,400 can participate in local ceremonies. Troops who contacted CBC News say maximum participation was encouraged in the past.

The reservists normally get a half-day's pay for ceremonial events, said one of the internal emails.

The decision is not going over well among troops, many of whom have reached out to CBC News.

Originally, it seems, the plan had been to fund fewer than 50 soldiers per unit. But in an Oct. 9 internal email, the brigade commander, Col. Blair Ashford, wrote that he had decided to increase the allotment and that it was a "defensible number" because it matched the number of soldiers that turn out for exercises.

He alluded to having to make a final choice between ceremonies and the one day a week of training units are expected to complete.

Talk of cutting training

"We cannot take from other buckets of money/time for ceremonial events — cancelling Thursday nights or weekend training to get time and money for ceremonial events," Ashford wrote.

He added that the continuing budget squeeze could mean "there is also the possibility that we will be cutting Thursday night training as well if we do not get our pressures relieved."

Last month, CBC News reported that the Canadian military was in the midst of another round of internal belt-tightening, despite an enormous influx of cash from the federal government.

It is a combination of past and current budget initiatives colliding with the expectations and demands associated with higher defence spending.

The Department of National Defence was told to focus its billions of extra dollars on priority areas, including the purchase of much-needed new combat equipment.

WATCH | Nov. 2025: More about the Canadian military buildup: Feds set aside additional $81.8B over five years to build up Canadian military | Duration closed caption 11:19 The federal government is describing this budget as a 'blueprint' to defend Canada's 'sovereignty.' Defence Minister David McGuinty says it's 'hard to predict' whether Canada is on track for its NATO targets.

At the same time, it is still subject to the demand for operations and maintenance reductions announced by the Trudeau government in 2023 and enacted in the 2024 federal budget.

As complaints from reservists filtered out and CBC News asked questions of the Department of National Defence, the chief of staff for the brigade — Lt.-Col. Anthony Ross — wrote a follow-up note on Oct. 27 describing the cap as necessary "in light of financial pressures."

He said it had come to his attention that some "personnel are speaking negatively to the media about this cap."

Ross emphasized that troops "are still free to attend ceremonies in uniform in the crowd on a voluntary unpaid basis."

A spokesperson for the Defence Department said Remembrance Day "holds a sacred place in Canada’s military tradition" and is a "deeply personal and solemn" occasion for troops.

Andrée-Anne Poulin said the 2nd Canadian Division, the parent unit of 31 Brigade, "has not issued a division-wide direction restricting members, including reservists, from attending or participating in Remembrance Day ceremonies."

She said the department stands behind the brigade commander, who is trying to balance operational and training requirements with ceremonial responsibilities.

"This means that there is no change to our usual posture on this sacred day," Poulin said.

"Members who are not otherwise occupied with operational imperatives, or officially tasked to support Remembrance Day ceremonies, are fully expected to take part in ceremonies in their local communities of their choosing."

World.title: These domestic violence shelters can hardly keep up with the cost of groceries
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At Nova Scotia’s largest shelter for women and children fleeing domestic violence, many clients arrive at the door having made the decision to leave a dangerous situation, while not necessarily knowing where their next meal will come from.

“It’s very difficult to raise a family or even be on your own as a single woman,” said Rachel Shepherd, executive director of Bryony House. “And so it’s a big factor and it’s a big barrier for people considering accessing services or leaving an abusive relationship.”

While the cost of living soars and survivors of abuse face the daunting task of trying to start fresh, the people who run women’s shelters are finding it increasingly difficult to ensure their residents have enough to eat.

A new report by Women’s Shelters Canada surveyed shelter organizations and transition houses across the country about how the high cost of groceries is impacting their operations.

Among the 239 respondents, 96 per cent of shelters feel their community is facing a food insecurity crisis, while 75 per cent said it’s become more difficult over the past year to make sure there’s enough food to go around.

“That financial pressure that they’re feeling is really putting strain on the workers,” said Robyn Hoogendam, senior research and policy manager at Women’s Shelters Canada. “They’re having to do more to fundraise, to build new partnerships and anything else that’ll just ensure that food keeps coming into the shelter.”

Hoogendam said while there have been significant investments in gender-based violence initiatives, particularly since the Mass Casualty Commission that examined Nova Scotia's 2020 mass shooting, funding is not keeping pace with inflation.

At Bryony House, which can house 40 women and children at a time, residents are given three meals per day, plus snacks. Shepherd estimates their food costs have increased at least 25 per cent over the past year.

She said funding from the provincial government is not enough to cover their groceries. The shelter relies on donations from Feed Nova Scotia — which delivers to Bryony House three times per week — and other local charities.

Shepherd said staff are finding ways to get creative. They’ve started a food program for outreach clients where they gather for weekly crockpot cooking classes and try to “make a meal on a dime.”

At the Cape Breton Transition House, director Jodi McDavid said food is important because many women and children arrive at the shelter already hungry. Some survivors have been living in poverty, while others have had their access to food limited by their abusers as a form of control.

McDavid said in recent years, the shelter spent $27,000 annually on groceries, but this year they’ve already spent $35,000. She’s had to reallocate money and apply for more grants as a result.

Jodi McDavid, director of Cape Breton Transition House, says they've already gone well over budget for groceries this year. (Kyle Moore/CBC)

“We go around, try to trim the fat, right? But there’s not a lot of fat in a non-profit,” said McDavid. “So you just kind of look at other things where you’re like, ‘OK…feeding people is more important than Christmas.’”

She said cutting back on holiday gifts and staff training are among the hard decisions she’s had to make to afford groceries.

Both Bryony House and the Cape Breton Transition House received thousands of dollars from a provincial initiative that saw profits of American alcohol sales go toward local charities and food programs.

They said it was a massive one-time boost, but worry that things will be even tighter next year without the extra cash.

A spokesperson for the Department of Opportunities and Social Development and the Nova Scotia Status of Women Office said “we recognize that rising food costs are creating real pressures for women, families and the organizations that support them.”

“While the province doesn’t have a dedicated food-security funding stream specifically for women’s shelters, we are responding to the rising costs these organizations face,” said Nicole MacDonald in a statement.

She pointed to a $17.9 million investment in 2025 to stabilize operations at 10 transition houses and respond to the cost of living. MacDonald said that’s in addition to $17.6 million annually in core funding for transition houses and women’s centres to cover salaries, staffing levels and operating costs.

But for those on the front lines, it feels like more money is always needed.

Shepherd and McDavid said it’s not just about supporting women as they flee from an abusive situation, but also in the months and years that follow as they work to rebuild their lives and provide for their families.

“We need long-term support for survivors of intimate partner violence, and it’s not going to suffice to just have one year or maybe two years of support,” said Shepherd.

“It’s a long-term commitment that we need to make to women so they can stay on their feet — not just get on their feet — but stay on their feet.”

For anyone affected by family or intimate partner violence, there is support available through crisis lines and local support services. ​​If you're in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911.

If you or someone you know is struggling, here's where to get help:
