World.title: Lions and tigers are kept legally in Ontario backyards. No one knows how many there are
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Mark Tardif, the chief bylaw officer in Wainfleet, Ont., shares photos and stories from some of his most memorable calls, including a lynx tied up like a dog, a runaway water buffalo and two tigers that wouldn't take their eyes off him.

People can legally keep lions or tigers in Ontario backyards, but provincial authorities don't know how many of the predators live in captivity across the province.

Ontario is the only province in Canada that has no licensing or permit system for keeping non-native wild animals, leaving it up to municipalities to decide what species residents can own.

In Wainfleet, Ont., a rural municipality 43 kilometres southwest of Niagara Falls, dangerous exotic animals became such a persistent problem that the township wrote its own rules in 2018 to give local authorities the tools to address the issue.

Enforcing it all falls to chief bylaw officer Mark Tardif, whose work has included policing a veritable Noah's Ark of exotic animals, from primates and sugar gliders (a type of exotic gliding possum), to pythons and tigers.

"A lot of tigers, probably five, six tigers, a jaguar, lemurs, kangaroos, water buffaloes," he said. "Snakes, unfortunately, lots of snakes."

Among his cases were dozens of animal escapes from a roadside zoo called Ringtail Ranch and, this spring, a Wainfleet resident who kept several tigers on a local property.

Zohaib Masood is shown with a juvenile tiger he kept on a property in Wainfleet along with two adult tigers and a hyena. The juvenile tiger and hyena were seized by Ontario's animal welfare services inspector. (Submitted by Zohaib Masood)

Whenever he deals with a call involving big cats, Tardif says he leaves himself an escape route.

"I usually leave my vehicle running and the door open, in case I have to bolt."

He says his protective vest was never designed for those kinds of encounters.

"I don't know how well this would hold up on a tiger bite," he said. "I want to go home at the end of the day. I have a family. So I do what I need to do."

Big cats, missing numbers

Wainfleet's bylaws require owners to register their exotic animals with provincial animal welfare authorities, but getting a clear picture of provincewide exotic animal ownership and related incidents from government records has proven difficult.

While Ontario allows people to keep dangerous predators, there is no provincewide system to account for them.

Two privately-owned tigers, seen here in an enclosure in Wainfleet, Ont. There are no federal or provincial rules when it comes to the ownership of dangerous exotic animals in Ontario, leaving monitoring and enforcement up to municipalities. (Mark Tardif/Township of Wainfleet)

Emergency responders might arrive at a property without knowing a lion or a tiger is present and when a municipality forces an owner out, they simply move their animals to another community.

CBC News asked Ontario for records of complaints and seizures invovling privately-owned big cats, as well as any statistical reports on those animals between January 2020 and May 2026. The Ministry of the Solicitor General said the records aren't kept in a single database and estimated the work would cost $1,050 — the equivalent of 35 hours of search time at Ontario's standard FOI rate.

"The records responsive to this request are not maintained as a single centralized dataset," the ministry said in a letter to CBC News, indicating the data was scattered across multiple systems, files and departments.

The Ministry of the Solicitor General said the OPP has "no classification system that captures occurrences involving 'exotic or dangerous animals.' "

A serval lies in the hay within its enclosure at Roaring Cat Retreat in Grand Bend, Ont., in this June 2019 Instagram photo. (Roaring Cat Retreat/Instagram)

An access-to-information request to the RCMP by CBC News about any information tracking big cats in private ownership also returned no records.

The only federal agency that tracks big cats is Environment Canada and Climate Change Canada.

It said in an email that two live tigers were imported into Ontario between 2022 and October 2026. Import applications must identify the animals' intended destination, but tracking ownership transfers, births and deaths is "typically the purview of provincial authorities," the department said.

'Giant gap' in rules

Once lions and tigers are in Canada, Kendra Coulter, a professor at Huron University College who heads the Animal Ethics and Sustainability Leadership program, says Ontario has no provincewide system to track who keeps them, where they end up or how many are born here.

"Falling through the cracks would imply that there was a floor in place, that there's some sort of structure or infrastructure around these animals and around the public," said Kendra Coulter, a professor of management and organizational studies at Western University's Huron University College, where she heads the Animal Ethics and Sustainability Leadership program.

"This is a giant gap that needs to be addressed," she said.

Kendra Coulter is a professor at Huron University College and co-ordinator of the school's Animal Ethics and Sustainability Leadership program. (Submitted by Kendra Coulter)

Coulter says because Ontario lacks any rules about exotic ownership, there are "covert networks" where people knowingly buy, sell and give away dangerous animals.

"We have no firm evidence, though we have reports" from law enforcement and people speaking off the record to researchers, she said. "Law enforcement has told me that some of this is happening online with commercial trading sites, but often in code."

CBC has not idependently established that animals are traded through coded listings.

Exotic animal owners are often reluctant to speak about it publicly. CBC News approached two private owners and Bervie Zoological Park, a roadside zoo near Kincardine, about 220 km west of Toronto — all recently had big cats seized by provincial authorities. None agreed to speak about the issue on the record.

When such animals are seized, they are often handed over to accredited zoos by the province. Many of those facilities were also reluctant to discuss the issue on the record. Some representatives contacted by CBC News said they feared confrontations with owners seeking to reclaim their animals.

Jungle Cat World Wildlife Park, a roadside zoo in Clarington, declined an interview and tour, but owner Peter Klose agreed to answer questions from CBC News by email.

"We believe that zoological facilities and research institutes with wildlife should be subject to provincial third-party oversight to ensure high animal welfare standards for all wildlife in captivity," he wrote when asked if Ontrario should introduce legislation governing the ownership of dangerous animals such as lions and tigers.

One town's ban, another town's problem

For Erin Ryan, the wildlife campaign manager at the animal welfare non-profit World Animal Protection, the bigger question is how those animals end up in private hands in the first place.

"Without any type of zoo licensing system or any type of permitting scheme, there's no requirement to show that you have the expertise, the facilities or the resources to keep either the animals or the public when safe when these animals are transferred to new places," she said.

Big cats peer through a fence at Roaring Cat Retreat in Grand Bend, Ont., in 2019. (Colin Butler/CBC)

In 2018, Ringtail Ranch's animals moved from Wainfleet, in the Niagara Region. In 2019, the owner resurfaced in Grand Bend in southwestern Ontario. After a battle with municipal officials there, the owner moved to Maynooth, in southeastern Ontario the following year.

In 2022, when four of the ranch's lions killed and ate a tiger, the owners were allowed to choose where the surviving animals would be relocated.

Brent Ross, a spokesperson for the Ministry of the Solicitor General, said the animals " were rehomed in appropriate settings to ensure their well-being. The location of the animals remains confidential for the same reason."

"They simply pack up shop and just move somewhere else where there isn't a bylaw," Ryan said. "Municipal rules can force an owner to move. They don't establish whether the next property is equipped to take the animals."

For Ryan, the question is what happens when the animals get to the next address.

"Municipal rules can force an owner to move. They don't establish whether the next property is equipped to take the animals," she said.

Coulter and her research assistants at Huron University College examined the bylaws of all 444 Ontario municipalities in 2020. At the time, half had no mention of ownership of non-native wild animals.

"You move 15 minutes west into the next county and there's no prohibitions," she said. "You can keep a tiger in your backyard."

In other words, municipalities can force dangerous animals out by creating bylaws, but without provincial laws governing where they're allowed, enforcing a bylaw in one town often shifts the responsibility to another place, resulting in a patchwork of rules.

Proposed rules, but no progress

There was an attempt to introduce a clear set of rules for Ontario in 2025 through Bill 35, a Liberal private member's bill that would require zoo licences, annual inspections and inventories recording births, deaths and transfers of non-native animals.

Under the proposed legislation, existing owners would be allowed to keep their animals, but would have to register them and undergo annual inspections. The legislation appears to have stalled. According to the Ontario legislature website, Bill 35 hasn't advanced beyond first reading since May 29, 2025.

CBC News reached out to Kanata-Carleton Liberal MPP Karen McCrimmon who sponsored the bill. Her office said it remains "in limbo" and they don't know if it will move forward in this legislative session.

Back in Wainfleet, Tardif stops short of saying whether the province needs clearer rules to govern the private ownership of exotic animals.

"I have no control over what the federal government does and provincial government does," he said. "It makes everyone's job hard, but these are the tools we have to work with and the legislation we have to work under."

World.title: Why health care for Canadian women veterans is falling short
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It started with the boots.

Wanda Motard is a size five-and-a-half in women's footwear. But when she was in basic training at Saint-Jean Garrison in Quebec in 2002, the only options were men's boots that didn't even begin to fit.

So despite the August heat, Motard says she would double up on thick wool socks and try to make do.

"I was constantly tripping over my feet, had rolled my ankle a few times, [which] led to a sprain," she told Dr. Brian Goldman, host of White Coat, Black Art . "With the forced marches, it became really, really difficult once I had my rucksack on."

The ill-fitting backpack left Mortard hunched over, compounding her struggles.

"But you know, the military is: one man, one kit."

Motard says she coped by getting off-the-shelf insoles, loading up on anti-inflammatory meds and icing her feet every night.

LISTEN | Motar's search for answers: White Coat Black Art 26:30 20 years of pain: A woman veteran’s search for answers

Halfway through her basic training, Motard got boots that fit. But those early experiences were just the beginning of a series of problems that — more than two decades after she first joined Canada's Armed Forces (CAF) — have left the 47-year-old veteran with complex physical and emotional health problems, including chronic pain.

She's not alone. Roughly half of all veterans live with chronic pain, which for women veterans is more than double the number among Canada's general population, according to a joint report from the Chronic Pain Centre of Excellence for Canadian Veterans and the Canadian Pain Society.

The report, which came out in June, called for "urgent, co-ordinated action" to address gaps in care.

"We know that women veterans have different health outcomes from women civilians," said Alice Aiken, founder of the Canadian Institute for Military and Veteran Health, and professor of physiotherapy at Dalhousie University in Halifax.

While the report on chronic pain didn't explain the causes, said Aiken, it's important to monitor "because it can be a gateway for disability."

WATCH | Resignations rock Women Veterans Council: Nearly half of Women Veterans Council resigns in protest | Duration closed caption 2:13 Five of the 12 members of Canada’s Women Veterans Council — set up to deal with gender inequality in the military — have resigned in protest. One former member says they were unable to make any change and there was a lack of communication with the government.

Aiken, who has a PhD in health policy and is herself a veteran, said military jobs can be "very physically demanding" and come with more opportunities for injury and other sources of physical pain.

And she says many female members of the Forces have experiences similar to what Motard went through with ill-fitting equipment.

"A lot of the uniforms were not and are not designed specifically for women. They don't fit properly," said Aiken. "And so they're also then subject to potentially more injury and more reasons for chronic pain."

Not enough research

But there's a gap in research about women's experiences. Aiken says less than 10 per cent of publicly funded research dollars go to health research specific to women and research on women veterans is even more sparse.

When the House of Commons standing committee on veterans affairs released its 2024 report Invisible No More about the plight of women veterans, the first of its 41 recommendations was to launch a comprehensive research program, notes Aiken.

Additionally, there can be a tough transition in terms of where veterans find care.

While they're in the Forces, people receive their health care from a separate military system, which Aiken describes as "probably one of the best health systems in Canada."

Soldiers board a CC-150 Polaris aircraft at CFB Greenwood in Nova Scotia in October 2014. (LS Eduardo Jorge/Combat Camera/Canadian Forces)

In that system there's a more interdisciplinary approach, in which any clinician can refer a patient to other health professions, says Aiken.

Once they leave the military, though, veterans are left navigating the health-care system in their province or territory.

Aiken praises publicly funded health care but says it "doesn't recognize, necessarily, the unique health needs of veterans and in particular women veterans."

Help from a private clinic

Into that gap has sprung at least one private clinic where a longtime military doctor, Dr. Markus Besemann, opened Beechwood Physical Medicine in Ottawa in 2022.

Besemann is a physiatrist, an expert in rehabilitation medicine. His 37-year career in the Forces included being chief of its rehabilitation program from 2008 to 2023.

When Besemann retired from the military, he and chiropractor Dr. Geoff Outerbridge founded Beechwood "to look after many people in pain but, amongst others, to focus on veterans and chronic pain," he said.

Dr. Markus Besemann, a longtime military doctor, opened Beechwood Physical Medicine in Ottawa in 2022, along with chiropractor Dr. Geoff Outerbridge. (Brian Goldman/CBC)

For some services the clinic offers, patients may be able to seek funding from Veterans Affairs Canada (VAC), but for others they'll need to pay out of pocket or seek reimbursement through any group health benefit programs they have access to.

Motard is one of their patients. She says she was put on a waitlist for a physiatrist in the public system after she left the military, but started searching online for other options during her wait.

Motard, who lives in the region of Gatineau, Que., across the river from Ottawa, says that search led her to Besemann, whose patient she'd been for five years when they were both in the military.

She says she was drawn to the integrated care Beechwood offered, where clinicians ranging from physicians to physiotherapists to psychologists and acupuncturists are together under one roof.

The mental health side of what they do is important, says Besemann.

"The simple sentence, I think, that says everything is, medicine is all about 'What's wrong with you? What's the diagnosis?' And trauma-informed care, I think, is 'What happened to you?'"

Sexual harassment a factor for many

Aiken said that while there isn't research on Canadian veterans specific to this topic, research on U.S. veterans suggests "military sexual trauma can also be a contributor to chronic pain."

To that end, Motard says the support she's had from Beechwood clinic includes seeing psychotherapist Mary Marcolin to address problems that include sexual harassment.

While in the Forces, Motard says the harassment she experienced "ranged anywhere from inappropriate comments, unwelcome comments, to inappropriate touching, pressure to enter into sexual relationships, right up to threats and stalking, essentially," Motard said.

She was a member of a class-action lawsuit against the Department of National Defence (DND) for sexual misconduct, which was settled in 2019 , with the federal government agreeing to compensate those affected and take steps to make the military a safer and more respectful workplace.

In 2021, the Forces, the federal government and the DND issued a public apology.

A 2025 report found the military made significant progress in changing the culture around sexual misconduct, though it said more work is needed to make those changes last.

DND said in an email to CBC News that it is "addressing sexual misconduct through a sustained culture change effort."

It also said, among other things, that "a contoured combat uniform designed around female morphology" will begin to go into service in 2027, with similarly updated body armour to follow in 2028.

A spokesperson for Veterans Affairs says the department recognizes the complex needs of veterans living with chronic pain, and offers coverage for a range of physical and mental health services.

The spokesperson also said VAC is working to address gaps in care and in research on the health of women veterans.

World.title: U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine begin in Abu Dhabi
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the head of Kyiv's delegation said.

The two-day session in the UAE's capital, Abu Dhabi, is the first such meeting since February. It will focus on security guarantees, the White House said before the discussions. Russia sees NATO as a threat, and Ukraine wants to prevent future Russian invasions.

There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks took place against a backdrop of new long-range strikes between Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line.

Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's air force said.

WATCH | Ukraine, Russia both say they were hit by cyberattacks : Ukraine, Russia both say they were hit by cyberattacks | Duration closed caption 3:58 Ukraine's emergency alert system sent out fake warnings about nuclear and chemical attacks on Sunday. Hours later, Russia said its emergency alert system had also been hacked.

Russia attacked 10 ‌Ukrainian regions overnight, hitting ​five major ​energy substations that ​transmit electricity between ⁠regions, ⁠Ukrainian ‌Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi ⁠said on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, Russia's Ministry of Defence said that its forces shot down 155 Ukrainian drones overnight above eight Russian regions, as well as the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

The U.S. is renewing a push to end the war between Moscow and Kyiv after three rounds of negotiations earlier this year. The conflict, Europe's biggest since the Second World War, began after Russia's all-out invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.

U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on X that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were working on a "negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment."

Russia and Ukraine hold to their divergent demands

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, noted at the start of the talks that the Russian delegation "has become bigger and more professional."

He expressed hope that the meeting "will allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine."

WATCH | How involved is Melania Trump in the push for peace in Ukraine? : How involved is Melania Trump in the push for peace in Ukraine? | Duration 2:28 Melania Trump is earning praise and awards for her so-called peace in Oleshky, Ukraine. But why is the U.S. first lady getting credit for securing the ceasefire?

Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, said that the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the U.S. envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission.

Russia has objected to the Europeans' involvement in the three-way talks, but said that EU representatives could join at a later stage.

The Russian and Ukrainian governments remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal to end the full-scale war, now nearing its five-year mark.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson -- the four regions that Moscow illegally annexed in September 2022 but never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.

Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won't agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that it would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles. He has warned that Russia will achieve its goals by force if Kyiv refuses to meet its conditions for peace.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was visiting Denmark on Tuesday, rejects Putin's demands to voluntarily cede territory that Russia hasn't been able to take on the battlefield. Zelenskyy also rejects any limits on Ukraine's military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.

Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled.

LISTEN | Reuters correspondent Dan Peleschuk on Ukraine conscription controversies: Front Burner 21:55 Ukrainian conscription in the crosshairs

U.S. says broader European security deal needed

Last week, Trump declared that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, describing it as "a big agreement" that is "going to involve more than Ukraine."

Kushner said Monday on X that a "comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them."

Just before Moscow launched the all-out invasion in 2022, it demanded that NATO roll back its deployments in the alliance's member countries in Central and Eastern Europe, seeing their presence as a security threat. Similar demands will likely be part of any comprehensive peace deal proposed by Russia.

WATCH | This is how residents of the besieged town of Oleshky stayed alive : This is how residents of the besieged town of Oleshky stayed alive | Duration 2:32 Buses full of residents from Oleshky arrived in northern Ukraine's Chernihiv region on Oct. 31 after a marathon journey from the besieged Russian-occupied town through Russian-annexed Crimea, and Belarus. Residents have been struggling with severe food shortages, mined routes and drones in recent months. Melania Trump, wife of U.S. President Donald Trump, is credited with brokering the rare, limited ceasefire earlier in October. Some residents would only provide their first names due to safety concerns.

The Russian and Ukrainian delegations include senior officials who have attended previous rounds of talks.

Russia's chief negotiator is Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky, who has led Moscow's team since the first direct peace talks with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022. The Russian delegation also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and deputy chief of the General Staff's operational department, Yuri Zhigarlovsky.

Apart from Umerov, the Ukrainian delegation also reportedly includes Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy, Sergiy Kyslytsya, and Davyd Arakhamia, the parliamentary faction leader of Zelenskyy's Servant of the People party.

While the ground battles have morphed into a war of attrition along the 1,200-kilometre front line, Russia and Ukraine have ramped up their long-range strikes with drones and missiles.

Russia has intensified its air campaign against Ukraine's power grid, seeking to weaken the country's resolve as winter sets in. Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine's shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors.

Ukraine, meanwhile, has escalated its drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: View From Inside the Taxi, Havana, Cuba – Photo of the Day
World.content:
View From Inside the Taxi, Havana, Cuba. By: Andrew Cannon (Canada). Camera: iPhone13

HAVANA TIMES – This year our Photo of the Day section will be celebrating its eighth anniversary. Many Havana Times readers have shared their pictures with us and with all of you.

Thanks to this section, we have discovered how much hidden talent exists among our subscribers. We renew our invitation to share space with the best images taken in different parts of Cuba, Latin America, United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Japan, Ireland, France, and many more.

World.title: Ladies in White Leader Released After Two Days in Detention
World.content:
Berta Soler was injured in her right foot as a result of violence during her arrest. / Facebook/Ángel Moya

Berta Soler was subjected to violence during her arrest, confined to a dark cell, and interrogated by State Security.

By 14ymedio

HAVANA TIMES – Berta Soler, leader of the Ladies in White, was released on Monday after being held by State Security for 46 hours, during which her whereabouts were unknown. Her husband, Angel Moya, announced the news on social media: “Released bearing the marks of violent repression.”

Moya reported that Berta Soler was released at around 10 a.m. “on a public street, near the headquarters of the Ladies in White,” in the Havana neighborhood of Lawton. In his post, Moya provided details about an injury the activist sustained to her right foot as a result of the violence during her arrest.

Soler was taken to the Aguilera police station in Diez de Octubre and later transferred to the Cotorro police station, where, according to the activist, she received medical attention before being confined to a dark cell.

According to Moya, before her release, Soler was interrogated by an officer from the State Security Investigation Department at Villa Marista. The officer questioned her about what had happened during the peaceful protest at which she was arrested, reminded her that she was under a precautionary measure of house arrest and that the measure could be revoked, and warned her that she would soon be summoned for questioning.

The post included photographs of the injury Berta Soler sustained to her foot during her arrest. Hours earlier, Moya had denounced her detention, saying he had overheard police officers mention that they had seen his wife “walking with a painful limp.”

According to activist Blanca Reyes, Moya went that same day to the Revolutionary National Police (PNR) station on Aguilera Street, in Lawton, in Havana’s Diez de Octubre municipality, to find out where the opposition leader was being held, “since she was beaten and no one knows whether she is at a police station or in a hospital.” Reyes stated: “Our sister’s situation is worrying.”

According to Moya’s account, on Saturday, two days after Soler had been arrested for several hours alongside fellow Lady in White Mara Cristina Labrada — the same Thursday that Yoani Sanchez, director of 14ymedio, was also arbitrarily detained — Berta Soler joined a “public and peaceful protest” with about 20 women from Lawton who were suffering from a lack of water.

The water shortage, Moya claims, is “intentional,” caused by the state-run company Aguas de La Habana to harm the Ladies in White headquarters and the area “within a 50-meter radius.”

Shortly after 10 a.m. that day, “several high-ranking State Security repressors” arrived at the scene and spoke with the protesting women, while the security operation was reinforced over the following hours.

“At noon, representatives of the state-run company Aguas de La Habana arrived and offered an explanation that also failed to convince the protesting women,” Moya recounted. His impression was that the authorities “had no intention of resolving the underlying cause of the problem, which is the deliberate manipulation of the water supply valve.”

With no satisfactory response, half an hour later the demonstrators blocked traffic on Porvenir Avenue, “using their own bodies as barriers.”

Moya said he did not witness the end of the protest because he had already been arrested by the political police and taken to the Aguilera station, where he overheard that his wife was walking in pain and that she had subsequently “been taken in a patrol car to another location,” which was not identified.

After an eight-hour interrogation, Moya was released, but his wife was not. The activist also clarified that “with the exception of Berta Soler, none of the women participating in the protest belong to organizations opposed to the Cuban communist regime. They are working women.”

The regime has intensified its persecution of activists and journalists on the island in recent weeks. Also on Saturday, dozens of residents took to the streets in El Cobre, Santiago de Cuba, to demand the release of Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano, a young activist known for his community work who had been detained hours earlier by State Security in an operation involving armed agents.

As for independent journalists, before Yoani Sanchez’s detention, Adelth Bonne Gamboa and Camila Acosta, both contributors to CubaNet, had also been arrested during the same week.

Meanwhile, Rolando Pérez Lora, an evangelical pastor known as the Preacher of Christ, was forcibly transferred from Havana to Las Tunas, where he was released on Monday, with a pending police summons.

According to reports from the Cuban Observatory for Human Rights and the Alliance of Christians of Cuba, Perez Lora had been detained while providing pastoral support to a young Christian member of the religious organization, who was also arrested.

In mid-September, State Security also detained Henry Constantin, director of La Hora de Cuba. In his case, rather than being released like the other journalists mentioned above, he was transferred to Kilo 7 prison in Camagüey, where he remains in pretrial detention on a charge of disobedience.

First published in Spanish by 14ymedio and translated and posted in English by Havana Times,

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Serbia’s Student Movement: From Protest to Power
World.content:
By Andrew Firmin (IPS)

HAVANA TIMES – On the night of 25 October, tens of thousands filled the streets of Belgrade and other cities, as they’d so often done in protest over the past two years. But this time they came out to celebrate. In that day’s National Assembly election, Student List, a slate of political newcomers, defeated Aleksandar Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), in power since 2012. The student-led movement behind the protests, which rose up against corruption, has given Serbia the opportunity for a democratic reset.



From grief to protest

Serbia became steadily more autocratic under Vučić. Public institutions served ruling-party interests amid a web of corruption, patronage, coercion and impunity. Public media became a ruling party mouthpiece.



Civic freedoms deteriorated dramatically. In 2018, the CIVICUS Monitor rated Serbia’s civic space as narrowed, meaning that fundamental rights were broadly respected. By the end of Vučić’s rule, the rating had collapsed to repressed, meaning that criticizing those in power carried severe risks. The state used violence against protests and treated civil society as a security threat, targeting it with spyware and subjecting organizations to raids and police investigations.



The seismic shift began in November 2024 with the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second-largest city. Sixteen people died. The government insisted it was a tragic accident, but the station had only recently been renovated and, with construction contracts shrouded in secrecy, many suspected corners had been cut. For protesters, this was a lethal symbol of the costs of corruption, negligence and impunity. No one has been held accountable.



Students held vigils and mass protests on a scale unseen since 2000, when demonstrations ousted Slobodan Milošević, the infamous authoritarian leader and accused war criminal. This time, their most effective tactic was a months-long education strike in which they blockaded and occupied universities.



As the protest movement grew it connected with existing groups, including environmental and legal aid organizations, independent media and, crucially, academics, university administrators and education unions, who took solidarity strike action. This built wider public support, backed by a ‘students in every village’ campaign that saw students meet with rural communities to ask about what mattered most to them.



State attempts to suppress the movement failed, including mass arrests, violence by security forces and gangs of ruling-party supporters and an extensive campaign of disinformation and smears. Vučić vilified protesters as agents of foreign powers bent on subversion and the government fired education sector employees for taking part in strikes.



Change on the cards



Ultimately, the protests forced Vučić’s hand. Constitutionally barred from seeking a third term as president, he announced an early parliamentary election in June and stood down as president in September, making clear his intention to hold onto power as prime minister. He presumably gambled that a skewed playing field, characterized by intimidation and biased coverage, would let him win again and unleash an even fiercer crackdown.



The gamble failed because of the movement’s discipline and the smart choices it made. Throughout, students resisted opposition parties’ attempts to co-opt them, insisting that deeper change was needed to re-establish the rule of law, free public institutions from political capture and tackle corruption. From its early days, the movement practiced internal democracy, taking decisions in university plenums, open assemblies where people debated, learned and decided together. When it decided to field a slate of candidates, it used the same method to select them. Students didn’t put themselves forward, choosing instead public figures untainted by association with established politics and likely to command broad support. Those who’ve won seats include academics, actors, former sports stars and medical professionals.



The result surpassed all predictions. According to projections based on the preliminary count, Student List has around 53 per cent of the vote, which would give it a clear majority of 141 of the National Assembly’s 250 seats. The SNS-led bloc trails on around 39 per cent. The margin was such that Vučić had to concede quickly.



Challenges of power



After the euphoria comes the challenge of moving from protest to power. A movement that has refused to have formal leaders must now unite behind a prime minister. Once the National Assembly convenes, Student List will have 90 days to form a government. Its deliberately broad campaign focused on major questions of national renewal but offered little detail. This strategy papered over political differences among representatives who range from nationalist to more liberal, which can be expected to surface if the incoming government succeeds in restoring the space for normal political debate. There’s also the question of how those elected will relate to the student movement.



As in Hungary, where long-term autocratic leader Viktor Orbán finally fell to electoral defeat in April, the new government will face the difficult task of reorienting state institutions that have bent to the former ruling party’s interests. An early sign of change came when the public broadcaster apologised to viewers for its bias towards the SNS, something that also happened in Hungary. The government will need to repay voters’ faith by rooting out corruption, which will mean overhauling institutions including the judiciary and police. All this will unfold alongside a presidential election that’s due by the end of the year.



Challenges lie ahead, but a population that has rediscovered the power of collective action can face them with confidence. Serbia also offers a vital source of international inspiration. Together with Hungary’s example, it shows there’s nothing permanent about autocratic rule. The world’s many Gen Z-led movements that have self-organised to demand a fairer distribution of economic and political power, and civil society more broadly, can take heart. Serbia has shown that organising and protesting works, and change is possible.



Andrew Firmin is CIVICUS Editor-in-Chief, co-director and writer for CIVICUS Lens and co-author of the State of Civil Society Report.

World.title: International News Briefs for Monday, November 9, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Monday, November 9, 2026.

Democrats Build on Sweeping Gains in Midterm Elections, Claiming 254 House Seats

Nov 09, 2026

Democrats are continuing to build on their sweeping gains in last week’s midterm elections as votes continue to be counted. They can now claim 254 House seats, compared to 162 for Republicans, with 19 House races yet to be decided. Democrats will also control at least 30 governorships and will control both legislative chambers and the governor’s office in 23 states — up from 16 before the election. Democrats also broke Republican “trifectas” in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and in Texas, where 87-year-old Houston Democrat Senfronia Thompson says she has the votes to become the first woman and first Black speaker of the Texas House of Representatives. Retired Navy Vice Admiral Nancy Lacore, who was abruptly fired from her post as chief of the Navy Reserve by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in August 2025, won election to the House of Representatives, flipping a seat in South Carolina held by the GOP. According to Axios, the House is poised to impeach Hegseth this week.

Meanwhile, Houston, Texas, Mayor John Whitmire announced Friday the city would start limiting the collaboration of local law enforcement with ICE during traffic stops. The announcement comes amid pressure from activists and as Republican Governor Greg Abbott prepares to leave office. Abbott previously threatened to revoke more than $110 million in public safety funding to Houston over a policy granting officers discretion over whether or not to contact ICE. Houston has seen mounting violent incidents involving ICE agents during traffic stops and car pursuits, including the fatal shooting of Mexican father Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July. This is Houston Mayor Whitmire.

Mayor John Whitmire: “This morning, I have directed the chief and HPD, through an executive order, that we will change our policy in regarding contact with ICE. I do this to begin a healing process, reduce fear and anxiety across our community. I also do this knowing that elections matter.”

Trump Replaces White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller

Nov 09, 2026

President Trump has replaced White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, the chief architect of his mass deportation policy, days after Republicans lost control of Congress. In a statement, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, Democratic Congressmember Robert Garcia, said, “Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down. Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families. Stephen Miller should lawyer up.” Attorney General Todd Blanche responded on Fox News that quote “Stephen Miller has a lawyer, it’s me”. This is Blanche on CNN.

Attorney General Todd Blanche: “The Department of Justice represents members of the executive who are brought in front of Congress, so there is nothing unique to me saying that every attorney general in history represents members of the administration. And this idea that Congressman Garcia comes out and says, ‘Oh, no, no, Stephen Miller needs his own personal lawyer,’ I would suggest he read the Constitution.”

In that interview, Blanche also repeatedly dodged questions about whether he’d investigate Democratic members of Congress, after President Trump ordered probes against congressional Democrats for calling for the impeachment of certain Cabinet officials. Soon after, Democratic Congressmember Robert Garcia issued this response to Blanche.

Rep. Robert Garcia: “We have the attorney general saying to the American public that somehow he’s going to defend administration officials, when his job is to defend the Constitution and the Department of Justice to be the people’s lawyer.”

Meanwhile, President Trump offered the press secretary job to Ultimate Fighting Championship, UFC, chief Dana White. Trump later said that he was only kidding, but White is set to meet with Trump today at the White House.

Former Top Federal Health Official Accuses Wiles of Putting Lobbyists and Campaign Funds Ahead of Public Health

Nov 09, 2026

Calley Means, a top federal health official who resigned two weeks ago, went on Joe Rogan’s podcast to accuse outgoing Chief of Staff Susie Wiles of prioritizing lobbyists and campaign funds over public health initiatives. Means claimed Wiles refused to back his push for healthier children’s diets because she wanted the sugar industry’s money, and says her team pushed for more flavored vape approvals and looser restrictions on the largely unregulated drug kratom. Means said, “Susie said to me many times: ‘We need money for the midterms, Calley. We need money for the midterms.’” Calley Means also alleges that companies hiring Wiles’s daughter, a lobbyist, got special priority.

Petition Urging Jeffries to Remove Himself from Race to Become House Speaker Surpasses a Million Signatures

Nov 09, 2026

Calls from progressives demanding new leadership in Congress continue to grow. An online petition urging Democratic Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries to remove himself from the running to become the next House speaker has surpassed 1 million signatures. Jeffries has faced mounting opposition over his pro-Israel interests and continued acceptance of corporate PAC money, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, AIPAC. Incoming Congressmembers-elect Chris Rabb, Melat Kiros and Darializa Avila Chevalier, all members of the Democratic Socialists of America, DSA, have already declined to pledge support for Jeffries if he’s up for House speaker.

Chuck Schumer is facing similar calls to step down as Senate Democratic leader. Senators-elect Peggy Flanagan, Troy Jackson, Abdul El-Sayed, Juliana Stratton and Adam Hamilton have all said they won’t support Schumer.

30 People Killed in Yemen in Missile Attack

Nov 09, 2026

In Yemen, at least 30 people were killed and more than three dozen injured on Friday as a missile slammed into a market in the southwestern province of Taiz. Women and children are among the dead. Yemen’s Saudi-backed government blamed the attack on fighters with Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthis, while a Houthi-linked television channel reported the attack was carried out by Saudi warplanes. This follows the deadliest month of attacks on Yemen since 2017. According to the Yemen Data Project, Saudi-led attacks killed 426 civilians in October — almost a quarter of them children.

Meanwhile, a missile fired by Houthi fighters struck an administrative building run by the state oil giant Saudi Aramco in Riyadh on Sunday, shattering windows on several floors of one of the tallest buildings in the Saudi capital’s King Abdullah Financial District.

Israeli President Herzog Picks Opposition Leader Eisenkot to Form Next Government

Nov 09, 2026

In Israel, President Isaac Herzog has picked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government, passing over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Sixty-seven lawmakers, including from Arab-led parties, backed Eisenkot, while 46 backed Netanyahu. Eisenkot has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension, to build what he calls a “national emergency government,” but his bloc is divided over allying with Arab-led parties, which won a historic 19 seats in elections last month.

Israeli Forces Release Palestinian Journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh

Nov 09, 2026

Israeli forces have released Palestinian journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh without charge, five days after armed police and Shin Bet agents raided his Jaffa home. Police accused the +972 Magazine contributor of “contacting a foreign agent” after he interviewed exiled former lawmaker Azmi Bishara in Qatar ahead of Israel’s election last month. Adalah, a legal group that supports Palestinian citizens of Israel, said, “The message to Palestinian citizens is unmistakable: a public conversation with a political figure can land you in a cell. This is political persecution carried out through criminal law.”

Storm Triggers Mass Flooding in Gaza, Killing 5 Palestinians, as Israel Bars Imports of Shelter

Nov 09, 2026

In Gaza, health authorities say heavy rains collapsed a sandbank onto tents in Deir al-Balah, killing at least five people, including four children. Gaza’s Government Media Office says the storm flooded at least 70,000 tents, and the U.N. says about 950,000 displaced Palestinians live in areas exposed to flooding. Ahmad Alhendawi of Save the Children said, “This is not simply the result of bad weather. Tents, shelter kits and fuel are waiting at Gaza’s borders while children sleep in floodwater, because the Israeli authorities are blocking their entry. This is a choice, and children are paying the price.” This is a displaced Palestinian woman.

Olfat Magdoub: “This is the first day of rain, and of course we are already flooded. What will happen if it rains again the next day? This is only the first day, and we’re already overwhelmed. Two weeks ago, when it rained, I swear to God, I spent four days sleeping on blankets spread on the floor because the rainwater had flooded the bedding. Same now, the mattresses are wet, so we sleep on the ground.”

Hundreds of Thousands March in Amsterdam Demanding Action to Stop Gaza Genocide

Nov 09, 2026

In the Netherlands, more than 200,000 protesters marched through Amsterdam on Sunday demanding the Dutch government take action to halt Israel’s attacks on Gaza. Protesters wore red, many of them carrying signs reading “Stop the Genocide.” They’re demanding a halt to all direct and indirect arms trade with Israel, an expanded import ban on products from illegal Israeli settlements and for Dutch leaders to exert more political and diplomatic pressure on Israel to end its illegal occupations.

Protesters Take Direct Action to “Stop Dirty Data Centers” in Europe

Nov 09, 2026

In more news from the Netherlands, over 100 protesters broke into a construction site of a Microsoft data center in the ​outskirts ​of Amsterdam on Friday. It was the first of many direct action protests held across Europe in 16 countries over the weekend by the “Stop Dirty Data Centers” coalition. Protesters are calling for a large-scale pause on new data center construction.

bq. Protester: “There’s for sure a lot of opposition. I think it would be good for governments to do more research into what the people actually want. There’s very much opposition against Big Tech, against their surveillance, against the power that they have over democracies. And they should not be able to get away with that, especially since the people don’t agree.”

Nvidia Share Prices Plummet as CEO Jensen Huang Admits to Affair with Alleged Chinese Spy

Nov 09, 2026

The billionaire tech CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an extramarital relationship with a business executive who U.S. intelligence determined was a Chinese spy. On Sunday, the chip maker Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into Huang after he apologized to his colleagues, his wife and their children. The New York Times reports Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation that sought to convince him to lobby U.S. officials to allow the export of advanced computer chips to China. According to the New York Times, President Trump eased some of those limits on the sale of advanced chips to China after Huang’s lobbying. Jensen Huang is a close ally of President Trump, and Nvidia is currently one of the world’s two largest publicly traded corporations, along with Apple. Nvidia’s stock tumbled on the news, wiping hundreds of billions of dollars from its nearly $5 trillion valuation.

U.S. Is Absent as United Nations Climate Talks Open in Antalya, Turkey

Nov 09, 2026

In Turkey, world leaders, delegates and climate activists are convening in Antalya today to mark the start of another round of U.N. climate talks. Heads of governments and officials from more than 190 countries are expected to attend — with the glaring absence of the United States, after President Trump last year withdrew the U.S. from the Paris Climate Agreement for the second time.

Nations in the Global South are again expected to pressure richer countries responsible for the climate crisis to commit to more financing of a loss and damage fund that was established at the U.N. climate summit in Egypt four years ago to cope with climate-related disasters. Though Turkey is hosting the U.N. talks, Australia is presiding over the negotiations.

Disgraced Paraguayan Ex-President Charged with Corruption over Bank Collapse

Nov 09, 2026

In Paraguay, former president and Trump ally Santiago Peña has been impeached and charged over his alleged role in the collapse of the major digital lender Ueno Bank. Pedro Alliana has been sworn in as interim president of Paraguay as Peña remains under house arrest. Alliana served as vice president under Peña. The collapse of Ueno Bank left at least 3 million people — nearly half of Paraguay’s population — without access to their money and froze hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds, including state pension money.

Cinthia Vargas: “I had my entire life savings in Ueno Bank. I’d been saving there for five years, and overnight I lost everything. I was left with nothing. Five years of savings, five years of honest work. I never stole from anyone, never bothered anyone. What for? So that Santiago Peña and his whole gang of criminals could come and rob us?”
