World.title: Warum strategische Investitionen jetzt wichtiger sind denn je
World.content:
Die Diskussion um die Zukunft des Wirtschaftsstandorts Deutschland wird häufig von vielseitigen Herausforderungen dominiert: Energiepreise, geopolitische Spannungen, Fachkräftemangel oder die Transformation hin zu einer klimaneutralen Wirtschaft. Diese Faktoren stellen Unternehmen vor große Aufgaben. Die Wettbewerbsfähigkeit Deutschlands hängt jedoch nicht allein davon ab, wie auf aktuelle Entwicklungen reagiert wird – sondern vor allem auch davon, ob Unternehmen bereit und in der Lage sind, zukunftsorientiert zu investieren.

Investitionen als Fundament für Wachstum

Investitionen sind ein zentraler Treiber wirtschaftlicher Stärke. Sie schaffen Produktionskapazitäten, fördern Innovationen, modernisieren die Infrastruktur und sichern Arbeitsplätze – und legen so den Grundstein für nachhaltiges Wachstum und gesellschaftlichen Wohlstand. Doch vorausschauende Investitionen entstehen nicht zufällig. Sie brauchen Unternehmen mit einem klaren Zukunftsverständnis und politische Rahmenbedingungen, die über Jahre hinweg Planungssicherheit bieten.

Entscheidungen werden mit Blick auf Generationen getroffen, nicht auf Quartalsergebnisse.

Gerade in Zeiten wirtschaftlicher Unsicherheit gewinnt diese Weitsicht an Bedeutung. Es braucht Unternehmen, die über kurzfristige Marktzyklen hinausdenken und investieren. Sie stärken damit nicht nur ihre eigene Wettbewerbsfähigkeit, sondern leisten zugleich einen wichtigen Beitrag für den Wirtschaftsstandort insgesamt.

Denken in Generationen statt in Quartalen

Als Familienunternehmen verfolgt Mars seit jeher genau diesen Ansatz. Entscheidungen werden mit Blick auf Generationen getroffen, nicht auf Quartalsergebnisse. Diese Perspektive prägt auch das Engagement des Unternehmens in Deutschland. Seit rund 70 Jahren ist Mars hierzulande als Investor, Arbeitgeber und Hersteller aktiv. Deutschland ist dabei nicht nur ein bedeutender Absatzmarkt, sondern vor allem ein zentraler Produktions- und Innovationsstandort innerhalb des europäischen Netzwerks des Unternehmens.

Dieses andauernde Bekenntnis zeigt sich beispielsweise in den Investitionen der vergangenen Jahre. Zwischen 2021 und 2027 investiert Mars insgesamt mehr als 235 Millionen Euro in seine deutschen Standorte. Mehr als 150 Millionen Euro wurden bereits getätigt, bis Ende 2027 sind weitere Investitionen von rund 85 Millionen Euro vorgesehen. Die Mittel fließen in moderne Produktionsanlagen, neue Technologien, Automatisierung, Nachhaltigkeitsmaßnahmen und die Weiterentwicklung von Mitarbeitenden.

Viersen und Verden: Industrielle Stärke aus Deutschland

Ein Schwerpunkt liegt dabei auf den Produktionsstandorten Viersen und Verden. In Viersen, Nordrhein-Westfalen, produziert Mars international bekannte Marken wie Twix und Balisto – Letzteres ausschließlich in Deutschland – sowie Komponenten für Celebrations. Allein rund 60 Millionen Euro wurden in den vergangenen vier Jahren (2022 bis Ende 2026) in die Modernisierung und Kapazitätserweiterung des Standorts investiert. Weitere Investitionen sind bereits geplant, um Produktionsprozesse zu optimieren, die Qualität zu verbessern und die Fabrik auf zukünftige Anforderungen vorzubereiten.

Zwischen 2021 und 2027 investiert Mars insgesamt mehr als 235 Millionen Euro in seine deutschen Standorte.

Auch der Standort Verden in Niedersachsen steht beispielhaft für die industrielle Bedeutung Deutschlands. Dort werden bekannte Tiernahrungsmarken wie Whiskas, Sheba und Cesar produziert. Gleichzeitig ist Verden das globale Forschungszentrum von Mars für Nasstierfutter. Produktion, Forschung und Innovation greifen hier unmittelbar ineinander und schaffen einen Standort, der sowohl regionale Wertschöpfung als auch internationale Innovationskraft vereint.

Produktion in Europa stärkt Wettbewerbsfähigkeit und Resilienz

Die Bedeutung solcher Investitionen reicht weit über einzelne Standorte hinaus. Europa braucht eine starke industrielle Basis, um wirtschaftlich erfolgreich zu bleiben. Produktionskapazitäten, technologische Kompetenz und Innovationskraft sind zentrale Voraussetzungen dafür.

Mars verfolgt dabei den Ansatz, möglichst nah an den Verbraucherinnen und Verbrauchern zu produzieren. Bereits heute werden 85 Prozent der in Europa verkauften Produkte innerhalb Europas hergestellt. Deutschland spielt in diesem Netzwerk eine zentrale Rolle und fungiert als wichtiger industrieller Pfeiler für Produktion, Forschung und Export. Produkte aus deutschen Mars-Standorten werden in zahlreiche europäische Märkte und darüber hinaus weltweit geliefert.

Wettbewerbsfähigkeit und Nachhaltigkeit sind dabei keine Gegensätze – moderne Produktionsstandorte müssen beides leisten. Investitionen in neue Technologien ermöglichen es, Ressourcen effizienter zu nutzen, Produktionsprozesse zu verbessern und die Umweltbelastung zu reduzieren. Nachhaltigkeit wird so zunehmend zum Wettbewerbsfaktor, der Innovationen fördert und dauerhaft Resilienz schafft.

Verlässliche Rahmenbedingungen als Schlüssel

Genau deshalb sind verlässliche Rahmenbedingungen für Investitionen so wichtig. Unternehmen benötigen Planungssicherheit, Zugang zu qualifizierten Fachkräften, wettbewerbsfähige Energie- und Infrastrukturangebote sowie regulatorische Stabilität. Nur unter diesen Voraussetzungen lassen sich strategische Investitionsentscheidungen treffen, deren Wirkung oft erst Jahre später sichtbar wird.

Bereits heute werden 85 Prozent der in Europa verkauften Produkte innerhalb Europas hergestellt.

Zugleich verfügt Deutschland über zahlreiche Stärken: Exzellente industrielle Kompetenz, eine starke Forschungslandschaft und eine leistungsfähige Infrastruktur. Diese Voraussetzungen bieten eine gute Grundlage, um auch in Zukunft Investitionen anzuziehen und industrielle Wertschöpfung im Land zu halten. Gleichzeitig bleibt es eine gemeinsame Aufgabe von Wirtschaft und Politik, die Rahmenbedingungen kontinuierlich weiterzuentwickeln und die Wettbewerbsfähigkeit des Standorts langfristig zu stärken.

Langfristige Investitionen entstehen dort, wo Vertrauen in die Zukunft besteht. Sie fördern Innovationen und stärken wirtschaftliche Resilienz. Für Unternehmen wie Mars sind sie Ausdruck einer Verantwortung, die über kurzfristige Geschäftsergebnisse hinausgeht. Und für Deutschland sind sie eine entscheidende Voraussetzung, um auch künftig Wachstum, Wohlstand und industrielle Stärke erfolgreich miteinander zu verbinden.

World.title: US demands a seat for Europe at Ukraine peace talks
World.content:
European governments and EU institutions will likely not have long to decide who they want at the negotiating table on their behalf. Kushner and Witkoff want to step up the pace of the talks and for this week’s meeting to be the last without Europe’s full participation, the same officials said.

“We need Europe at the table,” one of the officials said. “So our proposal is to bring the Europeans into the discussion after this trilateral.”

The officials welcomed the fact that the leaders of Finland and Norway called Russia’s Vladimir Putin directly on Oct. 27 and said more outreach is necessary. “We need a lot more European discussions with Russia so that they could be hearing what we’re hearing and the message that they’re conveying to us they could be conveying to Russia directly.”

The question of who speaks for Europe — and whether Ukraine’s European allies should even be speaking to Putin at all — has been deeply divisive. EU leaders will discuss the topic at an informal summit in Dublin later this week.

Ever since Trump returned to the White House last year, EU officials and diplomats have been fretting about being left on the sidelines while the U.S. talks directly to Russia to negotiate an end to the war.

Senior European officials are due in Abu Dhabi for the meetings this week but, although Kushner and Witkoff are expected to consult them, they will not be involved in the main negotiations due to Russian objections. Those present include security advisers from the U.K., Germany, France, as well as officials from Italy, NATO, the European Commission and European Council.

World.title: Return of Spanish right risks reigniting Catalan separatist flame
World.content:
“We know that they are certain to cut back our self-governing powers and intervene in Catalan society in a very heavy way,” Francesc-Marc Álvaro, a candidate for the Senate in the upcoming election for the Catalan Republican Left (ERC), said. “This would amount to throwing gasoline on Catalan society.”

Lawmaker Míriam Nogueras from the pro-independence Junts party said Catalonia had “never been respected by any Spanish regime or government,” and the next would be no exception. “Whatever its political color, the next Spanish government will be exactly the same as the previous one on one fundamental issue: Catalonia,” she said, adding that “the independence movement will regain momentum, and it will do so with renewed strength, because Catalonia’s dependence on Spain makes everyone poorer.”

For Madrid, the stakes are economic as well as political. Catalonia is Spain’s second-biggest autonomous region after Andalusia, representing about 19% of the national economy and 16.5% of the population.

End of Sánchez era

Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez took office shortly after a failed independence drive in 2017 saw several nationalist politicians flee abroad and nine others jailed.

In contrast to the PP’s uncompromising approach to Catalonia, Sánchez negotiated with pro-independence parties, making concessions in exchange for their parliamentary support.

An amnesty benefiting Catalans involved in the secession attempt angered the Spanish right but helped calm the political atmosphere in the region, eliminating a major nationalist grievance.

World.title: Why the Democrats’ midterm blowout is making Burnham’s Labour nervous
World.content:
A Labour MP, granted anonymity like others in this article to speak frankly, said their own engagement with Democratic New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s team had hammered home “the politics of trying.”

“If people think you’re not even trying, which obviously is what they thought about Trump, then you’re just going to get blown away,” they said. By making small adjustments, the MP argued, Burnham has begun to “develop a coherent argument — which is actually voters have to see you trying on the cost of living.”

Yet beyond this apparent vindication of the PM’s basic strategy, members of his party see clear warning signs for the incumbent British government in the U.S. political shift. An administration only just coming out of a dire stretch in public opinion polls, they worry, could take the wrong lessons from the Dems’ triumph across the pond if they don’t heed the deep anti-incumbent sentiment that drove it.

Reasons to be fearful

Burnham has badged his fledgling administration as a “cost of living government” since he replaced Keir Starmer at the top of Labour earlier this year.

Yet he has faced criticism from some quarters that a government-wide budget unveiled last month lacked real ambition — and now the pressure is on to deliver before a general election, due by 2029.

Claire Ainsley, a former adviser to Starmer who works for the Progressive Policy Institute think tank on both sides of the Atlantic, told POLITICO that, despite arguments about the future direction of the Democratic Party, “what they’ve all had in common is a real focus on affordability.”

World.title: Europe needs Nvidia. It’ll take more than a spy scandal to change that.
World.content:
A German government spokesperson said Monday in response to a barrage of questions on the upheaval at Nvidia that it "does not comment on the media reports," and that "we always adhere to the highest standards, including when agreements are being reached." A European Commission spokesperson also had no comment on the matter.

In both Silicon Valley and Washington, investigators are already busy. Nvidia has opened an internal investigation into whether its CEO was targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation, after Huang developed an intimate relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of trying to funnel intel on U.S. chips to Beijing. Huang has admitted publicly to having an affair.

The U.S. Congress, particularly its factions wary of China, is also set to take action. “The U.S. should immediately pause the shipment of advanced AI chips to China until we can get to the bottom of this incident and ensure our national security is not being undermined,” Rep. Michael McCaul, a Republican from Texas, and former chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said on X.

In Brussels, the blow to the Silicon Valley giant might appear to be good news for those who warn of U.S. tech dominance in the AI race. But as with the recent results of the midterm elections, the woes at Nvidia don't change Europe's reality because the bloc is so reliant on the company's AI chips.

"We don't have any alternative, the design [of chips] is almost entirely U.S.," said Dutch European Parliament lawmaker Bart Groothuis, one of the negotiators of the bloc's latest chipmaking plan.

Groothuis decried Nvidia's "bizarre monopoly position."

World.title: EU capitals fail to reach a deal on nicotine taxes
World.content:
The European Commission proposed increasing levies on cigarettes and setting minimum rates on newer products like vapes, heat-not-burn tobacco and nicotine pouches in July last year.

The tax hikes are designed to wean smokers off cancer-causing tobacco while also preventing younger people from taking up addictive nicotine products, which affect brain development in teens and increase cardiovascular risks.

Harris, who was chairing the talks, said he would bank the “significant progress” made on Monday, adding: “I intend to return to this issue” to get the file over the line.

Inching towards a deal

Taxes on nicotine pouches have been a perennial issue throughout months of talks among finance ministers in the Council of the EU — and ended up being kicked down the road again.

Ireland began negotiations Monday with a proposed €20 per kilogram in the latest compromise. An earlier draft proposed starting with €30 per kilogram and rising to €80 per kilogram by 2032. This was watered down to a target rate of €50 per kilogram, before Monday’s draft cut it to €20 with a final higher rate to be determined later.

It looked like this rate might succeed. Sweden, which had been the holdout over high nicotine pouch duties, agreed to the compromise. But then Finland opposed. Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Riikka Purra regretted that the level of ambition for pouches “has been totally removed.”

World.title: Aerial footage reveals devastation after deadly Bulgaria highway crash
World.content:
Aerial footage shows the aftermath of a deadly multi-vehicle pile-up on a highway in southeastern Bulgaria, where 11 people were killed and dozens injured, according to state media.

 

The crash involved dozens of vehicles and occurred in thick fog near Yambol, on the highway connecting the capital Sofia with the Black Sea city of Burgas.

Images from the scene show extensive vehicle wreckage scattered across the road, as emergency vehicles arrive to respond to the incident.

World.title: Portugal on alert as storm Charles brings red warnings to Madeira
World.content:
Two storms, Charles and Bruna, are expected to bring a sharp turn in the weather to Portugal, hitting the Atlantic archipelago of Madeira from late on Tuesday and the mainland throughout Wednesday.

 

The Portuguese government has issued a warning on social media. “Only go out if it is really necessary”, it said, “especially during peaks of rain and wind”. Anyone who has to drive should do so “with maximum caution”.

The authorities also advised people to keep torches or another source of light and charged devices such as power banks close at hand.

Portugal’s weather service, the Instituto Português do Mar e da Atmosfera (source in Portuguese) (IPMA), has issued orange warnings for rain, wind and rough seas in several mainland districts. They are Lisbon, Évora, Faro, Setúbal, Santarém, Leiria, Beja and Castelo Branco.

IPMA said the effects of Charles were expected to be felt on the mainland from late Tuesday morning, with rainfall “at times heavy over most of the territory”. Gusts could reach 120 km/h and waves up to six metres.

Red warning in Madeira

In Madeira, a red warning, the highest level, is in force for the mountains and the south coast from 9pm on Tuesday until 6am on Wednesday. It will then drop to orange until 9am.

Madeira’s north coast is under an orange warning from 9pm to 9am, and the neighbouring island of Porto Santo is under a yellow warning for the same period.

IPMA is forecasting rain or showers from Tuesday afternoon, at times heavy and persistent, and possibly thunderstorms. Winds could reach 130 km/h on high ground, and waves on the south coast could reach 4.5 metres.

The government warned of the risk of flooding, landslides, collapsing structures, falling trees and objects, and accidents on the coast. Power and communications could be cut at times.

How to prepare

The government is urging people to clear drains, gutters and channels of water and debris so they do not get blocked, and to remove anything else that could stop water flowing away.

People should stay away from rivers, streams and places that have flooded before. The government warns that “water hides holes and open manholes and can sweep away people and cars”.

Beaches, cliffs, breakwaters, piers, riverbanks and anywhere else water could overflow are also dangerous.

Drivers are advised not to park in flood-prone areas, in underground car parks or under trees. Scaffolding and other structures that could fall should be properly secured.

The government also warned that drainage systems will not be able to cope with the amount of rain expected, so several places, including towns and cities, will flood.

130 incidents in Lisbon overnight

Lisbon’s fire brigade, the Regimento de Sapadores Bombeiros (RSBL), dealt with 130 weather-related incidents between midnight and 6am on Tuesday. Most involved flooding in homes and public spaces, and none caused significant damage.

“We had some situations with roads closed in the area of the Segunda Circular, in Campo Grande, and in Prior Velho and Olivais, but these have already been resolved”, a source from the brigade told Portuguese news agency Lusa. Three trees also came down, without harming people or property.

Portugal’s National Authority for Emergency and Civil Protection (ANEPC) was due to give an update on the storm’s effects at a press conference at 8:30am on Tuesday.

World.title: Five EU countries demand UK pays for electricity market access
World.content:
Five EU countries have called for the UK to pay for access to the EU's internal electricity market, adding a financial and political dimension to negotiations ahead of the EU-UK summit on November 20, according to a letter seen by Euronews.

 

The leaders of Belgium, Germany, Denmark, Luxembourg and the Netherlands have urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa to make Britain's integration into the EU electricity market conditional on contributions to the bloc's regional development funds.

"An agreement on an appropriate financial contribution by the UK towards reducing economic, social and territorial disparities between the regions of the Union should be linked with the integration of the UK into the EU electricity market," reads the letter.

The five countries want to ensure that Britain does not enjoy the economic benefits of closer integration without making a financial contribution in return, potentially turning electricity cooperation into a wider debate over the terms of the UK's post-Brexit relationship with the EU.

The letter was signed by Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten — emphasising a push that appears to be backed by EU leaders.

A draft joint EU-UK statement, also seen by Euronews, suggests that EU leaders broadly support the principle of a British contribution to the bloc's cohesion funds. The text could still change before the November 20 summit.

UK Under Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net-Zero Martin McCluskey recently said the UK is negotiating to understand the EU's proposal and that no amount or contribution has been agreed.

McCluskey stressed that any payment would have to deliver value for money for Britain.

However, Britain could emulate Norway's model.

One possible model is Norway, which participates in the EU's internal market through the European Economic Area and contributes to grants supporting economic and social development in less prosperous European regions.

Oslo contributes roughly €391 million annually through these cohesion grants, according to the Norwegian Mission to the EU.

EU leaders see the UK's linking to the EU's internal electricity market as an enabler of enhanced energy security, decreasing reliance on fossil fuels, improving electricity trading and facilitating cross-border cooperation projects, particularly in the North Sea.

North Sea energy opportunity

The five EU countries signatories, all closely connected to the North Sea energy system, argue that a deal would provide greater predictability for businesses and investors while allowing the EU to exploit the North Sea's enormous offshore wind potential.

The letter points to ambitions to develop up to 100 GW of joint projects and 300 GW of offshore wind energy.

Related EU energy ministers pledge to boost offshore wind power in North Sea

"An agreement on electricity market integration is crucial, in order to provide clarity and predictability for stakeholders from both the UK and the EU. This is necessary to unlock the full potential of the North Sea area and transform it into the largest clean energy hub in the world," reads the letter.

The five EU leaders described the UK as a close partner in the energy transition and noted that negotiations have already started on its integration into the EU's internal electricity market, as agreed in the EU-UK Common Understanding.

“We call on you and the UK to agree during the Summit on a path towards the conclusion of these negotiations,” the letter reads.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 10th, 2026 – Midday
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: EU candidates will not have a say on anti-Orbán safeguards
World.content:
The EU is discussing stronger safeguards for new member states, including the possibility of suspending voting rights, with Montenegro first in line. But candidate countries face a take-it-or-leave-it deal.

 

Last month, the European Commission proposed a 15-year probation period for newcomers, designed to allow swift action against those that violate EU values and the principle of sincere cooperation.

The proposal stems from requests by five of the EU’s founding members to draw lessons from the experience of Hungary’s Viktor Orbán, who for years blackmailed the bloc into concessions by wielding his veto over major decisions.

“When I mentioned this for the first time, I said: no new Trojan horses in the European Union. This was still before the elections in Hungary. Today I can say no more Viktor Orbáns,” Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told reporters presenting the measure.

There is only one catch: candidate countries have no say in these institutional safeguards. They must accept them as they are or walk away from the prospect of EU membership altogether.

For Montenegro, the most advanced candidate, walking away is hardly an option after well over a decade of investing massive administrative capacity, not to mention the political capital of pro-EU forces, in joining the bloc.

Yet changing the terms of membership at the last mile leaves a bitter aftertaste for Montenegrin officials, who are careful not to criticise the measures openly for fear of derailing the process.

“It was always the case. Safeguards were always a bit one-sided,” a senior EU official told Euronews on condition of anonymity.

Safeguards per se are not new: they featured in the accession treaties of Croatia, Bulgaria and Romania. But those covered potential breaches of economic, internal market and justice rules.

Now, drawing on Orbán’s experience, Brussels is discussing going as far as suspending a country’s voting rights. Here, too, there is a major difference from the rest of the accession process, procedural as much as political.

Normally, a chapter is opened once the candidate meets the EU’s initial conditions. The candidate then implements the required reforms and meets any interim targets and, once all requirements are fulfilled, the EU agrees to provisionally close the chapter.

This time, Montenegro is not asked to submit a negotiating position, nor to meet any targets beyond accepting what is on the table, making the safeguards effectively non-negotiable.

The Commission is currently preparing EU common positions under Chapters 34 and 35, including draft treaty provisions on institutional safeguards.

Last month, it sent a first draft of the safeguards to be included in Montenegro’s accession treaty to member states for feedback. The Irish presidency of the EU Council is now collecting governments’ views and aims to send a consolidated position at ambassador level next week.

Once EU countries finalise their position, which is more general on safeguards for candidate countries, the Commission is expected to reflect it in Montenegro’s treaty.

In other words, Podgorica’s best chance of influencing the outcome is to lobby member states: once the EU position is set, there will be hardly any way to move it.

Three issues dominate the debate: the measures the safeguard could trigger, such as suspending voting rights for the most serious offences; its duration, which candidate countries consider too long at 15 years; and governance, as the proposed decision-making method would give the Commission significant sway.

Some EU capitals are sympathetic to the candidates’ arguments and want to distinguish between the political demand for stricter safeguards and a legal text that can be enforced.

Italy, a member of the so-called Friends of the Western Balkans, has pushed for respecting the equality of member states and for safeguards that are proportionate and tailor-made for each candidate.

The Netherlands, by contrast, has championed no differentiation between EU hopefuls. But whichever worldview will eventually prevail is fully outside Montenegro’s hands.

World.title: Europe must stop 'begging' for seat at Ukraine peace talks, ex-NATO chief warns
World.content:
Europe must stop begging for a seat at the table in US-brokered peace talks between Russia and Ukraine and instead prove its relevance, former NATO Secretary-General Anders Fogh Rasmussen told Euronews.

 

“Europe is already in a weak position. Europe is begging for a place at the table,” he said. “You have to make yourself indispensable by bringing assets to the table, so I hope Europe will now wake up.”

Rasmussen was speaking as Russian, Ukrainian and US negotiators meet in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday for talks aimed at ending Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Senior European officials, including representatives from the European Union, NATO, Britain, Germany, Italy and France, will also travel to the United Arab Emirates for separate discussions but will not take part in the main trilateral meeting.

Their presence reflects Europe's determination to have a say in negotiations whose outcome could reshape the continent's security.

Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law and adviser, said last week that a “new European security architecture” would be a focus of the talks. Russian officials have used similar language in calling for a reduced NATO presence in Europe.

“We have seen US President Donald Trump chose Moscow,” Rasmussen said, “and siding with Putin.”

“This is a situation we have to take seriously. The Europeans must wake up. If we don't, we will be sleepwalking into a permanent war on the European continent.”

A 90-minute phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, initiated by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, exposed divisions among Nordic leaders and highlighted Europe's struggle to speak with one voice.

The call prompted criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who questioned the decision to engage Moscow without consulting other European leaders.

"I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland. It was not coordinated with any of us," Frederiksen said shortly after the call became public.

Rasmussen, who served as Danish prime minister from 2001 to 2009, said it was a “good thing” to talk to Russia but stressed that such initiatives should be coordinated.

“And we should understand that we in Europe cannot be neutral mediators. We will side with the Ukrainians,” he said.

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski has argued that Eastern European countries must have a voice in potential peace talks, as the region is particularly exposed to the spillover effects of Russia's invasion.

“The last thing we want is Western Europe dealing with Russia, over the heads of the east Europeans," he said last week.

Rasmussen led the NATO alliance from 2009 to 2014. Just before his tenure, in 2004, the Baltic nations of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania joined both NATO and the European Union.

Asked whether their security interests should be taken into account in the negotiations, Rasmussen said: “We should have listened to the Eastern Europeans.”

Beyond the peace talks, Rasmussen criticised Washington's delays in approving the delivery of US-made air-defence missiles to Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in late October that he had been waiting almost a month for US approval of Patriot and NASAMS missile deliveries.

The delays have raised concerns about Ukraine's ability to repel Russian ballistic missile attacks and other aerial threats, which continue to batter the war-weary capital, Kyiv. Rasmussen described the delay as “damning” for Ukraine's defences.

“I'm so disappointed that the Americans have not delivered what they have promised to deliver. I'm not going to guess about the reasons why, but it just underlines the need for us in Europe to be able to stand on our own feet,” he said.

Asked whether he had ever seen NATO as divided as it is today, amid US troop reductions, Trump's threats to withdraw from the alliance and tensions over Greenland, Rasmussen replied: “Not at all.”

“It was an era where we could trust the American ally,” he said.

“When push comes to shove the Americans will come to the aid of Europe, but we have to be able to stand on our own feet. It's high time that we take decisions in Europe irrespective of who is residing in the White House.”

World.title: Stocks rally as investors snap up tech shares at lower prices
World.content:
European shares were higher on Tuesday, following gains in Asia and a rally in US stocks, while investors awaited October US inflation data.

 

European stocks rose in early trading on Tuesday, extending Monday's jump. A little after the open, the UK’s FTSE 100 was up 0.73%, France’s CAC 40 gained 1.20%, and Germany’s DAX advanced 1.14%.

US futures edged higher, and oil prices fell at the same time.

“It’s quite remarkable to think investors were showing signs of panic less than a week ago, and now markets are merrily pushing higher as if there’s nothing to worry about,” says Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell.

Previously in Asia, AI-linked firms led gains across stock markets, in stark contrast to the battering they took following last Tuesday's Democratic sweep of Congress, which stoked regulatory concerns.

However, traders remained concerned about profitability given the vast sums pumped into the sector. They were also watching Nvidia following reports of an investigation into whether chief executive Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

Nvidia’s shares traded 1% higher in pre-market trading despite the US president saying the FBI was looking into CEO Jensen Huang’s involvement with an alleged Chinese spy.

Commenting on the rise, Mould said: “Certain investors might have taken the view that whatever happens to Jensen Huang, the company will continue to dominate the AI chip space.”

Tech giants including Amazon, Microsoft and Apple were among the big gainers on Monday in New York as tech bounced back with help from bargain-hunting, with observers pointing out that confidence in the AI outlook remained solid.

Global demand for AI chips remains robust. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC), which makes chips used in AI systems, reported on Tuesday that its October revenue rose 59.7% from a year earlier.

Taiwan's Taiex jumped 2.5%. South Korea's benchmark Kospi surged 4.5%, thanks to strong advances in chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung, while Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 closed 2.9% higher on the back of rallies in Kioxia and Tokyo Electron.

Shares in OpenAI investor SoftBank Group jumped 13.9% ahead of the company’s earnings release later in the day. Its share price had fallen to its lowest level in a year on Monday.

Stock indices in Hong Kong and Shanghai were also higher.

China’s exports in October climbed 35.2% from a year earlier, while imports grew 41.6%, according to customs data released on Tuesday.

That put the country on track for another record annual trade surplus, with the total for the first 10 months of 2026 already exceeding $1 trillion (€893bn).

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 rose 1.1%, while markets in India were closed for a holiday.

However, SPI Asset Management's Stephen Innes said the gains did not suggest markets were back in rude health.

"The market rallied because the sellers stepped away, not because the entire buy-side suddenly rediscovered its courage," he wrote in a commentary.

"For the second consecutive session, the companies receiving the enormous capital expenditure cheques dramatically outperformed the businesses writing them. That is a potentially important development after last week's indiscriminate liquidation," he said.

"The hyperscalers remain central to the AI investment cycle, but the market is increasingly questioning the returns on the extraordinary sums being committed to new infrastructure.

"Equipment providers, optical networking companies and selected data-centre suppliers can still benefit from existing spending programmes, even as investors become more selective about the ultimate economics for the companies funding those projects."

In other dealings, early Tuesday, the US dollar rose to 157.91 Japanese yen from 157.90 yen. The euro slid to $1.1249 from $1.1266.

Oil falls on Iran peace hopes

Oil prices continued their retreat on hopes of an end to the Iran war.

Both main contracts fell more than 2.5% by 10:30 CET on Tuesday, extending Monday’s losses, when Brent dropped almost 6%. Brent was trading at around $90 a barrel, while the US benchmark WTI stood at about $84.70.

Both have lost around 20% this month as traders bet on a resolution to the more than eight-month-old conflict, which has sent inflation soaring and prompted central banks to raise interest rates.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday there was "positive momentum" towards ending the war after meeting Qatar’s prime minister at the White House. He said further strikes were "quite unlikely", although he kept the option open.

“Markets are increasingly taking the view that Donald Trump needs to forge a new path if he wants to save face from the midterm election washout, and that might mean finding a way to end the Iran war,” Mould said.

He added that this would, in theory, help lower energy costs, bringing relief to consumers and businesses.

World.title: Japan to supply Philippine military with coastal radar and drones
World.content:
Japan agreed on Monday to give the Philippine military a coastal radar system and surveillance drones to help it track ships, in a grant worth 4.3 billion Japanese yen (€24 million).

 

Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro and Japan’s ambassador Katsuro Kitagawa signed the agreement in Manila. The radar will go to the Philippine Navy and the drones to the Air Force.

Japan’s foreign ministry said the equipment would also help protect shipping routes important to Japan, including those through the South China Sea and the Luzon Strait, between the Philippines and Taiwan.

Japan handed over five coastal radar systems to the Philippines in February under a 2023 grant. Tokyo says the new radar will be the first complete defence system it supplies under its Official Security Assistance programme.

Beijing has criticised the programme since its creation, calling it an attempt to build a security network around China under the cover of development aid.

The Philippines and China both claim Scarborough Shoal, where China’s military said it sent ships and aircraft on patrol on 30 October.

In a phone call on 3 November, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi urged Manila to act cautiously over the dispute. Lazaro described their conversation as “frank and constructive” and said both sides wanted to keep talking.

Beijing has separately described Japan’s expanding military role in the South China Sea as destabilising, and has accused Tokyo of using its security partnerships with regional states to advance US strategic interests.

China claims historic rights to resources across much of the South China Sea. In a case brought by the Philippines, an international tribunal ruled in 2016 that those claims had no legal basis where they exceeded the rights granted by the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Beijing has rejected the ruling.

Japan and the Philippines are also discussing transferring an Abukuma-class destroyer to the Philippine navy.

Their defence ministers said in October that they wanted the handover to take place as soon as possible after Japan retires the ship, which it expects to do in the coming years. Philippine crews would receive training first.

The EU approved a separate €15 million package in July to help Philippine forces monitor the country’s waters.

Its first grant to the Philippines under the European Peace Facility will fund coastal radar, infrared surveillance equipment and training.

World.title: Macrons file new defamation lawsuit against US podcaster over transgender rumours
World.content:
Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron filed a new defamation lawsuit in the United States last week against right-wing influencer Candace Owens, who claims the French president's wife is a transgender woman.

The Macrons filed suit in a federal court in the southern state of Tennessee, where Owens resides, arguing that the conservative podcaster has "used this false statement to promote her independent platform, gain notoriety, and make money".

Owens confirmed the lawsuit Monday, writing on X, that the "Macrons have indeed filed a NEW set of claims against me".

To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable  tracking and audience measurement. Accept Manage my choices

The latest filing comes after a judge limited the scope of their previous complaint at the end of October, for a case that was filed in Delaware in 2025.

Read moreMacrons file defamation suit against US podcaster over transgender rumours

In the Delaware case, the judge dismissed the case against Owens, as an individual, on jurisdictional grounds but allowed proceedings against her companies to continue.

In the latest suit, the Macrons accuse Owens of "unequivocally" doubling down after the first lawsuit was filed.

"She has continued to use her podcast to expand her lies about the Macrons, sell merchandise making fun of the Macrons, and collect donations based on her 'reporting' on the Macrons," according to the 411-page complaint.

While the Macrons called Owen's content "verifiably false and devastating lies", they noted "there is nothing shameful or defamatory about being a man, being transgender, or being gay. Owens' statements are defamatory because they accuse the Macrons of lying to France and to the world, for decades, about who Mrs. Macron is – and of committing crimes to conceal that supposed lie."

Brigitte Macron, 73, has also taken to the courts in France to combat claims she was born a man.

Two women were convicted in September 2024 of spreading false claims after they posted a YouTube video in December 2021 alleging that Brigitte Macron had once been a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her brother.

The fake news about Brigitte Macron has regularly resurfaced on French social media since her husband's first election in 2017.

But it flourished abroad and particularly in the United States after Owens seized on it in March 2024, creating social media content and a video series titled "Becoming Brigitte".

"These claims are demonstrably false, and Owens knew they were false when she published them," the court filing said.

"These lies have caused tremendous damage to the Macrons. Defendant has subjected the Macrons to a campaign of global humiliation."

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

World.title: Turkey courts Egypt to tip the scales in eastern Mediterranean power game
World.content:
This week’s joint naval exercises between Turkey and Egypt in the eastern Mediterranean are the latest move in a burgeoning partnership, as Ankara intensifies its efforts to draw Cairo closer and loosen its bonds with Turkish rivals Greece, Cyprus and Israel.

Advertising

The "Sea of Friendship 2026" naval drills, held from 4-9 November off the coast of Alexandria, follow five years of rapprochement after nearly a decade of mistrust sparked by the 2013 ouster of Mohamed Morsi, a close ally of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, by Egypt's President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.

It is the second year in a row that Turkey and Egypt have held the joint drills, after a 13-year break.

“I think it's already a sign that the two countries are getting closer,” said Africa expert Elem Tepecikoglu of Ankara’s Social Sciences University. In her view, the naval exercises are part of an evolving partnership.

“This normalisation process started five years ago in the diplomatic realm,” she explained. “And then we see cooperation in the security domain as well. So this is why I say I'm optimistic that Egypt might come closer to the Turkish side.”

The strengthening alliance between Turkey and Egypt is stirring unease in Israel, at a time when Israeli-Turkish relations are already frayed by the war in Gaza and Ankara’s support for Hamas.

“Obviously, Israel does not see this as necessarily positive, because of the heightened tensions between Israel and Turkey,” warned Turkey analyst Gallia Lindenstrauss of the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

She noted that Israel is growing ever more wary of Turkey’s expanding reach in the eastern Mediterranean. “There is concern that Turkey and Egypt can cooperate in ways that will squeeze Israel’s room to manoeuver, politically but also militarily.”

Lindenstrauss said she does not see this as a likely scenario, affirming that the 1979 peace agreement between Israel and Egypt is “still very much in place, despite many geopolitical turnovers”.

“But there was always a fear that the other countries surrounding it would unite and act against Israel,” the analyst added.

Lindenstrauss believes Egypt’s strong ties with Turkey’s rivals, Greece and Cyprus, allay fears of Israeli encirclement. “It is very important that this relationship keeps going ahead because it is a source of stability in the eastern Mediterranean,” she said.

Houthi war risks dragging Israel and Turkey into Horn of Africa standoff

Turkish leverage

Egypt, Greece, Cyprus and Israel are bound by a tightly knit strategic energy alliance centred on the Eastern Mediterranean Gas Forum, a regional organisation formed in 2020 that has its headquarters in Cairo.

Just last month, they stood united in condemning the Libyan parliament's ratification of a maritime deal with Turkey that encroached on Greek and Egyptian waters.

Still, Jalel Harchaoui, a regional expert at the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank, observes that Turkey and Egypt are forging ever-closer collaboration on issues ranging from Libya to the Sudanese civil war to the Horn of Africa. Harchaoui suggests this growing cooperation is steadily boosting Ankara’s leverage over Cairo.

“I think observers should ask, can Egypt afford to do without Turkey? And the answer is probably no, and Turkey probably is aware of it,” he said.

Even so, Harchaoui doubts Cairo is ready to pivot fully toward Ankara. “If [Egypt] switches 180 degrees, it would be a disaster for the other side. I'm talking about Greece and Cyprus and Israel. So you could also ask yourself, can Egypt afford to anger its traditional friends?”

Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean

Egypt's balancing act

Ankara is stepping up its diplomatic courtship of Cairo, hoping to lure Egypt away from its longstanding partners.

But Turkish ambitions stumbled when Egypt declined to join the Mecca Defence Alliance with Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August. Analyst Lindenstrauss sees this as a clear sign of the boundaries in Turkish-Egyptian ties.

“Egypt has already moved closer to Turkey than was imaginable a few years ago,” she said. “However, at the end of the day, there are limits to how much it can accept greater Turkish influence. I think Turkey pretty much reached where Egypt is willing to agree to, and it will not give Turkey concessions in the eastern Mediterranean that will endanger its relationship with Greece and Cyprus, or its peace agreement with Israel.”

Lindenstrauss believes that despite diplomatic tensions with Israel over the war in Gaza, it still remains in Egypt’s interests to maintain ties with all sides. “Because of Egypt's importance in the region, I think it can definitely go ahead with this balancing act. It gives it all the gains and the risk is relatively low compared to having Egypt choose sides,” she added.

Ankara stands ready to ramp up its campaign to win over Cairo as the battle for influence in the eastern Mediterranean intensifies. In the unfolding rivalry between between Turkey on one hand and Greece, Cyprus and Israel on the other, Egypt is emerging as the pivotal player.

World.title: Borussia Dortmund's Felix Nmecha and the question of religion
World.content:
Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.

"Faith does not justify exclusion. Faith does not justify division. Borussia Dortmund is a club for everyone," read a statement after the Bundesliga club beat Elversberg, a game in which Nmecha scored twice. Nmecha's first documented "Crowns down celebration" was at the 2026 World Cup, for which "The King's Return" campaign was launched.

"In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players. We remain committed to this approach," the statement continued.

"However, when it comes to our club's values, discrimination, and the question of what view of humanity is fostered within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent."

The fan club states their issue is not with Nmecha being a devout Christian, but rather his public support for "The King's Return" campaign, which the supporters club said "gives us cause to reassess the situation."

This campaign, according to research by German public broadcaster ARD in the summer of 2026, was designed by the "Ballers in God" (BIG) network. BIG was founded in 2015 by footballer John Bostock, a devout Christian who wanted to create a community where professional footballers could strengthen each other in their faith, pray together, and read the Bible. In over a decade since, the BIG community has grown to nearly 800,000 followers on Instagram.

Nmecha issued a response on social media not long afterwards, writing:

"I've been told that my most recent goal celebration has led to some misunderstandings," Nmecha wrote.

"My message was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form. As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for every person—regardless of where someone comes from, what they believe in, or what worldview they hold."

Reports suggest that both the board at Dortmund and Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp will speak to Nmecha on the matter in the coming days.

Connections to US evangelical nonprofit in question

The fan club say their criticism is "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalized because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices... When religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, that is where our tolerance for intolerance ends."

Here, they are referring to the recent ARD investigation. That work revealed the homepage for "The King's Return" campaign featured a link to a live counseling chat run by US-based evangelical nonprofit Groundwire. During the investigations, counselors told reporters that abortion is "Satan's plan" and that homosexuality is a sin.

Borussia Dortmund's statement of core values commits the club to diversity, human rights, and inclusion regardless of gender, sexual orientation, faith, or background. The club's largest and most influential fan group also promotes progressive, anti-fascist, and inclusive values. It is also part of a wider fan landscape in Germany where club members are more involved in club decisions than in many other countries. This was evidenced when the club signed a deal with arms manufacturer Rheinmetall two years ago and in the case of Nmecha as well. When the midfielder signed for Dortmund in 2023, many of the club's fans protested because the player had previously shared or liked several transphobic and homophobic posts on his Instagram account. In response, Nmecha deleted some posts and instead issued a statement emphasizing "I do not discriminate against anyone."

Felix Nmecha first displayed the "Crowns down celebration" at the 2026 World Cup Image: Christian Kolbert/kolbert-press/picture alliance

Law guarantees freedom to chose religion

Article 4 of German Basic Law guarantees that each individual is allowed to decide how strongly, why and which god to believe in. In football, players cannot display political, religious, or personal slogans, statements, or images on their jerseys, undershirts, or gear. However, physical gestures are allowed so long as they don't delay the game or antagonize the crowd.

The use of physical religious gestures has history in sports, as professor Paul Putz described in his book "The Spirit of the Game: American Christianity and Big-Time Sports". Putz describes how the the pioneers of the Christian athlete movement realized they: "could influence others to Christian ideals more effectively on the field than in the pulpit."

And yet, such gestures can also be at odds with the atmosphere of modern sports arenas, particularly football. In their book "Sports and Christianity: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives", Nick J. Watson and Andrew Parker explain how modern sport has become a substitute for traditional faith.

"Sport seduces the teeming 'global village'; it is the new opiate of the masses; it is one of the great modern experiences … Sport, for many, has replaced religion as a source of emotional catharsis and spiritual passion," they wrote.

With the 26-year-old Nmecha a key player for both club and country, the conversation around faith and football looks set to continue for some time yet.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: Spain: Police officer killed in Oviedo after neighborhood dispute escalates with explosion
World.content:
At least one officer was killed and another injured as a fight between two families became increasingly violent.

A national police officer was killed in Oviedo, Spain on Tuesday following an explosion in the Villafria neighborhood. Another is being treated for serious wounds in a nearby hospital.

According to local media, the officers were responding to an escalating dispute between two local families in which a woman was shot by a man early in the morning. She is reportedly expected to recover, though it remains unclear what prompted the attack.

Suspect fled the scene

The two officers — a member of the elite TEDAX explosives unit and a canine handler — approached a suspicious backpack at the scene, which then detonated before it could be neutralized.

Police union JUPOL expressed its "deep sorrow and dismay" over the incident.

The area surrounding Rafael Urrusti Street has been cordoned off. Spanish daily El Pais reported that Oviedo Mayor Alfredo Canteli is heading to the scene to try and settle some of the confusion surrounding the attacks. The newspaper also wrote that a 64-year-old suspect, a Spanish national, is still at large. He reportedly has a history of petty crimes. He wife has been detained as part of the investigation.

World.title: Fact check: Online disinformation rife after Krakow mass shooting
World.content:
Fake and AI-manipulated images spread online in the hours after the Krakow attack, fueling false narratives about the mass shooting. DW Fact Check examined what's real, and what isn't.

A gunman killed six people in a shooting spree in Krakow's Old Town on Saturday, before being shot and detained by police. The gunman, who is also suspected of killing three family members before the attack, later died in hospital.

On Monday, Poland's national prosecutor's office announced a formal investigation .

Nevertheless, much is still unknown about the details of the crime, leaving social media users to fill the information vacuum with fake images of the attacker and alleged screenshots of his online profile. DW Fact Check breaks down the developing story.

Are these genuine images of the attacker?

Claim: A viral picture has been circulating on social media claiming to be the real image of the suspected attacker.

DW Fact Check: Fake

In the post, the image is posted with the caption, "[…] The perpetrator of the attack in Krakow is a 25-year-old Polish citizen, Polish police have reported. The death toll has reached six. (…)".

But the unusual sharpness of this picture raises doubt of its authenticity. It is difficult to imagine capturing such a clear image in a chaotic situation.

The footage from X posts about the alleged shooter in Krakow is said to supposedly show the face of the shooter lying on the ground after the attack in Krakow. The face has been altered multiple times with AI Image: X

DW checked the image using two different AI detectors. Hive Moderation identified it as 99.5% AI-generated, while Google's SynthID Detector confirmed that it contains a SynthID watermark, indicating that it was generated or edited using Google's AI technology.

In our research we found several versions of the suspect image circulating online, most looking very similar. We also found a number of images and videos showing the attack.

Although DW cannot independently verify the footage, it shares similarities in terms of the people and background with some original images published by picture agencies.

It appears the AI-generated images may have been created using this footage as a reference. Some of the posts sharing these images have also been labeled as AI-generated .

One important thing to understand is that AI cannot sharpen a blurry image with correct details or recover details that are not visible in an original photograph. It can generate plausible details based on the surrounding visual information, but these are essentially guesses, not exact reproductions of what was actually there.

More about this and how users used sharpening AI tools here .

Was the shooter really a supporter of Ukraine? This claim is supposedly backed up by this picture of a post in a Telegram channel Image: X

Did the shooter sympathize with Ukraine?

Claim: "Michal Oksinski, the terrorist from Krakow who also killed his parents and sister, had a Telegram account with the Ukrainian flag. On November 3, he wrote 'Thanks, Dad, for the gun', posting this photo of himself wearing the Ukrainian flag insignia," an X user wrote in a post viewed more than 700,000 times.

DW Fact Check: Fake

This Telegram channel is almost certainly inauthentic. The account allegedly posted a photo on November 3, showing the attacker holding a gun, standing in front of a television and a Ukrainian insignia on the wall.

Another post on November 4 simply reads, "11/7/2026", the date of the attack. Both of these posts were edited on November 8, after the suspect had been apprehended.

DW verified on the Telegram app by hovering over the posts to show the edit history. The channel's photo, a Ukrainian flag, was also edited after the attack took place.

Fake: Digital AI tools indicate the image was 99% likely to have been created using AI Image: Hivemoderation.com

This is a common disinformation tactic — fake accounts will edit old posts and pictures in the days after a breaking news event to give the appearance that they've predicted or announced the event in advance.

Further proof: in Poland, the date is written first, not the month. And the photo of the alleged attacker itself is almost certainly AI-generated. HIVE Moderation said it was 99.9% likely to be created with AI.

Does the attacker have links to a group that operated in Ukraine?

Claim: "#BREAKING: The attacker in Poland had a full arsenal in this trunk! He also has forward observation group patches, an American military company active in Ukraine," reads an X post viewed nearly 100,000 times. The attached photo of the supposed "arsenal" in the trunk has been shared by several other accounts .

DW Fact Check: False

The attached photo claims to show the attacker's car with a trunk full of guns, ammunition, a helmet and a military vest.

The vest in the trunk of the car features a symbol supposedly connected to the Forward Observations Group, an American tactical training lifestyle brand that has traveled to and operated in Ukraine.

This is a photo of a trunk full of weapons — but this picture doesn't show the alleged attacker's car Image: X

The patch, however, is the Old Roger flag, a symbol commonly used in military circles. The Forward Observations Group logo is a variation of this symbol, featuring a horned skeleton holding a gun, not an hourglass.

This is also not the attacker's car from the scene of the crime. This license plate is registered with the Krakow police, indicating they likely collected evidence from the crime scene and moved it to this car.

Little details like these can help separate fact from fiction, especially in a rapidly evolving story like the Krakow shooting.

Daniel Ebertz contributed to this article.

World.title: DR Congo: 66 soldiers sentenced to death for cowardice in conflict with FRN rebels
World.content:
Dozens of defendants were put on trial over accusations that they abandoned their posts and refused to follow direct orders.

Some 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in DR Congo on charged of cowardice, mutiny, and failure to obey orders. The sentence was handed down by the Goma Garrison Military Court.

At least 71 members of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) were arrested in several separate incidents related to the fierce fighting between the military and rebel groups near the country's borders with Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi.

They were arrested on allegations of abandoning their posts or running away from clashes with FRN rebels. Prosecutors had sought capital punishment for 70 of the defendants, while asking for a 10-year jail term for an intelligence officer. The court, however, acquitted four defendants,

Major Dieudonne Kasereka, head of communications for FARDC in the affected region, said that the charges were necessary to reinforce discipline in the country's embattled North Kivu and South Kivu regions.

What is the FRN?

The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation is an umbrella group of rebels that also includes the March 23 Movement (M23) and Alliance River Congo (AFC).

The group's origins can be traced back to the Rwandan genocide in 1994 and the ensuing ethnic conflict, as it emerged from the Congolese Tutsi militias of the time.

It is led by former DR Congo President Joseph Kabila. When current President Felix Tshisekedi came into power in 2019, Kabila found himself increasingly ostracized politically and went into self-imposed exile in an area occupied my what was then M23. Further complicating the conflict is the involvement of the FDLR rebel group, an ethnic Rwandan Hutu militia also active in South Kivu.

Although Rwanda's strongman president Paul Kagame denied involvement in the conflict, both DR Congo and many in the international community held that evidence of Rwandan involvement was clear. Indeed, Rwanda was involved in the 2025 US-brokered peace deal — which was seen as mostly serving US economic interests and doing little to resolve the long-running conflict.

Earlier this year, the United Nations condemned FRN and Rwandan soldiers for "murder, torture and other ill-treatment, corporal punishment, forced unlawful recruitment and abusive labor, and use of child soldiers."
