World.title: Possible Tax Increase Looms for Croatian Private Landlords
World.content:
November the 10th, 2026 – A possible tax increase is looming for Croatian private landlords in yet another strike to their pockets. This goes alongside all of the other changes coming next year.

Croatian private landlords are facing a slew of changes in the way of registration and recording at the Tax Administration next year. As if all of what has previously been announced wasn’t enough, there’s also a possible increase in the annual lump-sum tax on the cards. Index reports that the government is now proposing automatic registration and de-registration of taxpayers who earn income from renting out their tourist accommodation, as well as an increase in the lowest tax amounts in the most tourism-developed cities and municipalities.

The final proposal of amendments to the Income Tax Act was sent by the government to the Croatian Parliament on the 5th of November, as part of the tax changes planned for 2027. One of the novelties relates to the establishment of automated data exchange between the competent institutions and the Tax Administration. On the basis of data from official records the Tax Administration could in the future independently carry out the registration and de-registration of those who earn income from tourist rentals.

official records and data should be better aligned

Until now, people starting to rent out accommodation and earn income from that activity had the obligation to report the start of performing the activity and register in the register of taxpayers. With the proposed solution part of that procedure would be taken over by the competent institutions, whereby administrative obligations should be simplified, and data in official records better aligned. Nevertheless, from the government’s proposal it does not follow that landlords would be freed from all obligations of reporting changes or submitting documentation. The scope of their future obligations will depend on the final legal solution and the rules of its implementation.

an increase in lump-sum tax…

In addition to changes in the recording of taxpayers, the government is also proposing an increase in the minimum amounts of the annual lump-sum income tax from tourist accommodation. These are amounts that are calculated per bed, or corresponding accommodation unit. For cities and municipalities in the first category of tourist development the legal minimum would increase from 100 to 150 euros per bed. In the second category an increase from 70 to 100 euros is planned. This, however, does not mean that the tax will rise by the same amount for all landlords. Local units still determine the amount of the lump-sum tax within the limits prescribed by law, so the concrete effect will depend on how much is currently paid in an individual city or municipality.

For example, a landlord who has six beds in a local self-government unit of the first category, and in which the legal minimum of 100 euros is currently applied, pays 600 euros in tax annually. According to the proposed amendments that amount would rise to 900 euros, which is 300 euros more. On the other hand, where local authorities already apply a lump sum of 150 euros or more per bed, the increase in the legal minimum does not necessarily mean an additional rise in the tax obligation.

there’s no way to avoid these tax hikes

The government’s proposal also covers the amounts that are applied in the event that city or municipal representative bodies do not make a decision on the amount of the lump-sum tax. In units of the first category of tourist development that amount would increase from the previous 200 to 225 euros per bed or corresponding accommodation unit. For the second category an increase from 135 to 150 euros is planned. In practice, this would mean that a landlord with six beds in the first category, in the case of application of that legal amount, would instead of the previous 1,200 euros pay 1,350 euros annually. These are amounts provided for in the draft law, and not already determined tax obligations for individual private landlords.

World.title: Research: Vučić Falling is More Important Than Price Increases and Protests for Croatia
World.content:
November the 9th, 2026 – Research has discovered that Aleksandar Vučić falling in Serbia is more important than the price increases and protests within Croatia.

The defeat of Aleksandar Vučić in the elections over in Serbia was the most important topic for Croatians in the past month, ahead of inflation and price increases, shows the new CRO Demoskop. Index reports that the defeat of Aleksandar Vučić in the parliamentary elections in Serbia was declared the most important topic of the past month by 21.9 percent of respondents. Inflation and price increases took second place with 14.3 percent, while street protests in several European cities were singled out by 12.4 percent of citizens.

The death of Goran Bare and Mišo Kovač was an important topic for 11.9 percent of respondents. The Nazi rampage by part of Torcida fans, arrests and threats to journalists was singled out by 9.9 percent. Problems with the remediation of illegal waste in Gospić and protests against the incineration of waste in Koromačno received 4.7 and 4.4 percent respectively.

If elections had been held at the beginning of November, HDZ would have won 24.9 percent of the votes, and SDP 17.5 percent. HDZ fell by 0.1 percentage points compared to October, while SDP lost two points and recorded the lowest support in the current term. In the last year support for HDZ has fallen by five, and for SDP by six percentage points.

This is at the same time HDZ’s weakest result since Andrej Plenković began his third premiership in April 2024. Among the four leading parties support in one month fell by a total of 2.7 percentage points, and around three quarters of that drop falls on SDP. Možemo is in third place with 13.6 percent, and Most in fourth with 9.4 percent. Those parties also recorded a slight drop, by 0.2 and 0.4 percentage points respectively. Undecided voters stand at 18.8 percent, compared to 15.6 percent in October. The research was conducted by the agency Promocija plus on a sample of 1,000 respondents. The sampling error for party ratings is ±3.53 percentage points, with a confidence level of 95 percent. The data source is CRO Demoskop for RTL.

World.title: Will New Dawn in Serbia Result in a Change of Relations With Croatia?
World.content:
November the 9th, 2026 – Will the new dawn in Serbia after the removal of Aleksandar Vučić finally result in a long-awaited change of relations with Croatia?

The fact that a new group of people with fresh policies will finally lead Serbia does not necessarily mean that it will totally abandon its old, poisonous national priorities. Zlatko Crncec reports for Novi list that the new political ruling elite in Serbia is encouragingly announcing a radical break with the foreign policy of Aleksandar Vučić. However, as in everything else, much, if not almost everything, remains rather unclear.

Both when it comes to who will make up the future Serbian Government, and what exact policy they will pursue. Because the fact that a new team is coming to the head of Serbia does not necessarily mean that it could abandon old national priorities. Between good-neighbourly relations, the protection of Serbs in the region, the constitutional issue of Kosovo and the attitude towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, space opens up for serious political uncertainties.

It is still not clear whether the victory of the Student List “Students are Winning” also means a real change in Serbia’s attitude towards neighbouring countries. Or will only the way in which the previous national and foreign policy goals are presented to the public change?

neighbourly relations…

This is especially important for Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Kosovo. These are the countries towards which Aleksandar Vučić’s policy, in various forms and intensities, has for years been burdened by unresolved issues from the past, national pretensions, the instrumentalisation of the position of Serbian communities and occasional political crises. The programme of the list and the public appearances of its leader Ilija Srdanović point to several important conclusions. First, the new political structure wants to distance itself from the personalised foreign policy of Aleksandar Vučić. Second, it does not intend to abandon traditional Serbian state priorities, especially when it comes to Republika Srpska and Kosovo. Third, it is trying to find a language that would simultaneously satisfy pro-European oriented citizens, the nationally sensitive part of the electorate and international partners. Precisely in that combination lies the greatest unknown of the new policy.

For Croatia the most important message is the one that the leader of the Student List Ilija Srdanović expressed immediately after the election victory. He announced that relations between the two countries will be based on good-neighbourliness, and not on a policy of confrontation. “Croatia will not be in any other status there except good-neighbourly relations,” Srdanović emphasised. In doing so he attributed responsibility for the deterioration of relations to the previous Serbian president. He spoke about the policy of one man who “set two peoples against each other”, emphasising that foreign policy should in the future be conducted by the government of Serbia, and not by an individual. Namely, in Serbia the government has greater powers than the president, but it is allowed that he can be a member of a party.

Vučić, at least for the largest part of his mandate, was also the president of the ruling SNS and in that way was able through party discipline to be at the same time the strongest political figure in Serbia. Therefore what Srdanović stated can still mean some progress. Vučić’s Serbia often used the Croatian state as a foreign policy opponent, and Croatian authorities as a convenient argument in domestic political showdowns.

Accusations about Croatian influence on the Serbian opposition, alleged interference in internal affairs and acting against Serbian national interests were part of everyday political life. Srdanović’s message suggests that such a practice could be abandoned. However, it is important to pay attention to his statement about Croatia, and for now much clearer regarding mere political tone than when it comes to concrete moves. Besides, at this moment it is still not clear whether Srdanović, although he was first on the list, will even be a member of the new Serbian Government. If he will be, it isn’t clear which portfolio he could take over.

minority rights

The more extensive Student List programme shows that a good-neighbourly policy does not mean abandoning issues that have traditionally burdened relations between Belgrade and Zagreb. In the part of the programme that relates to the position of Serbs in the region, the list particularly emphasises the rights of Serbs in Croatia, the preservation of their national, cultural and linguistic identity, the position of returnees, what it calls the selective application of law in certain court proceedings, and the conditions for the dignified marking of grave sites.

In doing so it invokes United Nations Security Council Resolution 1120, the Erdut Agreement and the bilateral agreement from 2004 on the protection of the rights of the Croatian minority in Serbia, and of the Serbian and Montenegrin minorities in Croatia. That part of the programme deserves a certain amount of attention. It shows that the Student List does not intend to abandon an active policy of protecting the Serbian minority outside the borders of Serbia. That in itself, of course, is not at all disputable. The protection of minority rights is a legitimate obligation of every democratic state, and Serbia and Croatia have bilateral agreements precisely so that those rights would be protected. However, a problem arises if minority issues are turned into an instrument of political pressure on a neighbouring state. Which Vučić abundantly used. Therefore for Croatia it will be important how Belgrade will concretise its demands.

Will it be a matter of institutional cooperation, exchange of information, solving the problems of returnees, protection of cultural heritage and equal treatment by judicial bodies, or will space again be opened for political accusations and unilateral interpretations of history? Particularly interesting is that the programme at the same time mentions the rights of the Croatian minority in Serbia. Which are far from what the Serbian minority has in Croatia.

However many shortcomings the model of electing three Serbian deputies in a special electoral unit has, the fact that Croatia nevertheless applies it speaks of the fact that it wants transparent and good relations. On the other hand, in Serbia there is no mechanism that would guarantee that Croats have their guaranteed representative in the National Assembly. The announcement that the Student List could work on that gives the possibility for a different and better model of mutual relations, instead of constant political competition around the position of Serbs in Croatia. If Belgrade is going to advocate for the rights of Serbs in Croatia, it should at the same time show readiness to protect the rights of Croats in Serbia without political calculations, including their cultural autonomy, representation and the possibility of participating in public life.

war crimes

The second major issue remains the wartime past and open questions from the 1990s. Srdanović has in previous appearances emphasised that the new generation does not want to be burdened by responsibility for events from a time in which its members did not participate. Such a position is politically understandable, but it is not sufficient for things to move from a standstill. In that sense more important than statements about a new beginning will be whether the new authorities will open space for a more serious attitude towards the missing, war crimes, archival material and compensation for victims. In the political confusion that currently reigns in Serbia, it is impossible to extract anything more than these genuinely encouraging wishes that Srdanović expressed in the above-mentioned and in several other public appearances.

the attitude towards srebrenica…

Bosnia and Herzegovina is perhaps the politically most sensitive issue in the entire regional agenda of the Student List. In an interview for Radio Free Europe Srdanović very clearly said that the new authorities will continue cooperation with Republika Srpska. “The continuation of cooperation with Republika Srpska is in the interest of the citizens of Serbia and the citizens of Republika Srpska,” Srdanović said.

To the question of whether Belgrade will encourage the authorities of Republika Srpska to solve problems with the institutions of the central government in Sarajevo, he answered that they will advocate for open dialogue and finding common solutions for all citizens of BiH and Republika Srpska.

Whatever that means.

The Student List does not question the special relationship of Serbia and Republika Srpska. It does not announce its reduction, redefinition or the withdrawal of Belgrade from political and institutional relations with Banja Luka. Another possibility is a change in the way that relationship is realised. Srdanović speaks of dialogue, common solutions and the interests of all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which can be read as a distancing from the policy of constant conflicts between Republika Srpska and the state institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the programme does not give a precise answer to the question of how the Student List imagines the relationship of Belgrade towards the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Serbia has special ties with Republika Srpska, which also stems from its constitutional and political framework, but at the same time has the obligation to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The new authorities will have to show whether they can reconcile those two facts without creating additional tensions. Particularly indicative is Srdanović’s answer about Srebrenica. To the question of what position the new authorities will take, he said that the issue of Srebrenica is defined by court decisions, and he mentioned the documents that the Serbian Assembly adopted back in 2010.

World.title: Zadar Airport Smashes Previous Records in 2026
World.content:
November the 9th, 2026 – Zadar Airport has smashed its previous records in 2026 despite having a somewhat weaker October than usual. A brand new route from Zadar to German will also operate next summer.

In the first ten months of this year, almost 80,000 more passengers were recorded by Zadar Airport than in the same period last year. For summer 2027, a brand new Ryanair line to Friedrichshafen has also been announced. as eZadar reports, Zadar Airport has already by the end of October surpassed the number of passengers achieved during the whole of last year. According to official statistics, in the first ten months of 2026 1,714,335 passengers were recorded, or 74,734 more than in the entire record year of 2025. Compared to the same ten-month period last year, traffic rose by 4.89 percent, or by 79,947 passengers. The new annual record was thus set while two months still remain until the end of the year.

8,000 fewer passengers in october

October itself, however, finished in a weaker way than October last year. 95,956 passengers passed through Zadar Airport, while in October 2025 there were 103,829. That is a drop of 7.58 percent, or 7,873 fewer passengers. The number of aircraft in the official records was also reduced: from last year’s 532 to this year’s 499, which represents a drop of 6.20 percent. The October result is thereby the first monthly drop in the number of passengers this year compared to 2025. All previous nine months recorded growth.

a new line for summer 2027

In addition to the traffic results, the question of the director’s mandate is currently topical at Zadar Airport. Josip Klišmanić, who has been at the head of the company since October 2017, had his existing mandate, according to data available at the Commission for Deciding on Conflict of Interest, expire on the 14th of October 2026. The government has proposed his temporary appointment for a maximum of six months, until the appointment of a director through a public tender.

This period of the year is always quieter at Zadar Airport. The direct international connection is reduced to Munich, on Mondays and Fridays. Domestic connections are maintained via Pula and Zagreb. For the next summer season an expansion of the destination network has also been announced. The Irish low-cost carrier Ryanair in the summer flight schedule 2027 will connect German Friedrichshafen with Zadar, whereby Zadar Airport gains yet another direct connection with the German market.

World.title: Estonians lose €21 million to scammers in nine months
World.content:
April was the worst month for fraud in Estonia this year, with scammers stealing more than €4 million, including €1.7 million lost by a single company in an invoice fraud scheme known as business email compromise (BEC).

Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) Director General Egert Belitšev said a BEC scheme is a type of fraud targeting businesses, in which criminals use a fake or spoofed account to convince a company that one of its regular partners has changed its bank account details. The company is then instructed to transfer payments to the new account.

Egert Belitšev. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

Overall, however, fraud statistics show slight improvement. While victims lost nearly €25 million during the first nine months of last year, losses this year were €4 million lower. Part of the decline is linked to fraud operations in Ukraine involving senior public officials that have since been uncovered.

No phone scams reported in August

More than 90 call centers were shut down in Ukraine over the summer, and the operation has had a clear impact in Estonia as well. No phone scams were reported in August.

"The troubling part is that the investigation identified various Ukrainian officials who were involved in the fraud schemes and provided protection for the scammers," Belitšev said.

Only €1 million of the more than €20 million lost this year is expected to be recovered and returned to victims. At the same time, authorities have made progress in identifying offenders. This year, 38 people have been caught, most of them money mules.

Astrid Asi. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

Most offenders are young people

Prosecutor General Astrid Asi noted that most offenders are young people.

"They were mainly recruited through social media accounts, and a large share came from outside Estonia," she said.

Some of those involved have been minors, though most have been in their 20s.

Authorities expect investment scams to become more common in the near future. Sandra Horma, head of fraud prevention at the Estonian Banking Association, said scammers typically promise extraordinary returns and often present the opportunity as a secret offer available only to a specific individual.

"They try to create the impression that the person is such a talented investor that they have been noticed, for example on social media, and are therefore receiving special offers," Horma explained.

Investment fraud caused €5 million in losses during the first nine months of this year.

World.title: Niina Petrõkina: My rivals are now jumping 1,440 degrees, so I have to too
World.content:
Estonian skater Niina Petrõkina says she will have to add a challenging quadruple jump to stay at the top, after setting personal bests in both programs and taking silver at the Grand Prix in Kelowna, British Columbia.

The two-time and reigning European champion scored a personal-best 221.07 across both programs for her second career Grand Prix medal, and now targets the round later this month and much closer to home, in Helsinki.

She improved her short-program best in Canada, then bettered her free-skate score too. "I liked that I felt so free in the free skate. I felt my character, which is written into the story of the program," she told ERR Sport.

Three years ago in the US Petrõkina, 22, became the first Estonian skater to reach a Grand Prix podium, though that time the organizers saw fit to fly the Japanese flag at the ceremony. While this time the flag was right, the Estonian said her position was not quite. "I'd like to see it in first place," she added.

Petrõkina said the nerves never go away regardless of experience, and described her routine: six minutes of warm-up, then rest, a walk, and a reminder of why she does it. Every time I skate well and feel the emotion and the audience's support, I think — that's what I do it for."

The quadruple salchow, a a figure skating jump featuring four full revolutions (1,440 degrees) in the air, is the open question. She has landed it in training, and by early information the free skate in Canada was meant to open with it, but she chose the safer option."The goal is to show that jump, but for that it has to be stable. It's not clean enough in training yet," Petrõkina went on.

She framed the choice plainly: good scores and medals, and/or the quad. "The goals are there, the competition is strong and it motivates me to put those jumps in. Everyone is starting to jump them — I have to as well."

The Helsinki GP round takes place November 20-21, and Mihhail Selevko and Arlet Levandi are also representing Estonia there.

World.title: Health Insurance Fund suspends doctor's appointment reminder service after trial
World.content:
The Estonian Health Insurance Fund has suspended its new appointment reminder service after testing revealed inaccurate patient information and duplicate notifications.

Many healthcare providers send patients an SMS or email reminder ahead of an upcoming doctor's appointment. However, not all hospitals do so, prompting the Estonian Health Insurance Fund to test sending notifications through the national health portal to ensure that every patient receives appointment information 72 hours in advance, regardless of the healthcare provider.

However, this meant that patients attending appointments at hospitals that already send their own reminders received duplicate notifications from both the Health Insurance Fund and the hospital.

Evgeni Nikolaevski, product manager of the national health portal, told ERR that the purpose of appointment notifications is to help people remember their upcoming appointments and give them enough advance notice to cancel if they are unable to attend.

"On the other hand, not all healthcare providers currently send patients appointment reminders or the notifications do not reach patients early enough. That is why we tested the option of sending notifications through the health portal, with the aim of sending patients a reminder 72 hours before their appointment, regardless of which healthcare facility they are visiting. This is intended to ensure that all patients are treated equally when it comes to receiving notifications," Nikolaevski said.

The Health Insurance Fund wanted to use the initial notifications to assess how well the system worked and gather feedback from patients and healthcare providers. Nikolaevski acknowledged that because some healthcare providers already send their own reminders, patients could indeed receive two notifications about the same appointment.

"The aim of these notifications is not to duplicate existing reminders, but to ensure that patients who do not receive notifications from their healthcare provider or do not receive them early enough also get a reminder," Nikolaevski said.

During testing, cases emerged in which appointment information submitted to the national digital appointment booking system was not entirely accurate.

"Because notifications sent through the health portal are generated based on information submitted to the digital appointment booking system, incorrect information in the original records may also appear in notifications sent to patients. For this reason, we have now suspended the sending of appointment notifications," the health portal's product manager said.

Before the Health Insurance Fund resumes sending notifications, Nikolaevski said it will need to work with healthcare providers to improve data quality and find a solution that also takes into account reminders sent by other providers.

"The goal is for patients to receive accurate, timely and clear notifications, regardless of which healthcare provider they have an appointment with," he said.

The development work cost the Health Insurance Fund nearly €4,200.

World.title: Presidential security adviser: Abu Dhabi talks unlikely to stop the war
World.content:
Ukraine, Russia and the U.S. begin talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, but Rainer Saks, security adviser to the President, says a ceasefire is unlikely at this stage.

Representatives of the United States, Ukraine and Russia are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi for talks after a long break. What should we be looking out for?

The first thing to watch out for is what topics ultimately come to the table and which issues are publicly acknowledged as having been discussed.

The Russian side has consistently stressed that these talks will deal only with what we would consider technical issues. In other words, how to ensure that, once a ceasefire has been reached, it can be maintained. How to prevent hostilities from breaking out again due to certain incidents. In the view of the Russian side, this is the main focus of the talks.

Previous trilateral talks have also focused primarily on these issues. They have also included prisoner exchanges and the return of Ukrainian children deported to Russia. In other words, humanitarian issues.

Actually, neither Ukraine nor the United States has claimed that politically sensitive issues will now be discussed. There may be some exchange of information on these matters, but it appears that negotiations on them will not take place. So it can be said that the talks beginning today are unlikely to result in a cessation of hostilities.

Rainer Saks. Source: ERR

Political observers say that Russia wants negotiations but does not want peace. Can we expect any progress toward ending hostilities from these talks?

The catch here is that unless there is an agreement on how to enforce a ceasefire, including a whole range of military de-confliction measures, it is very difficult to establish one. Ultimately, these issues also turn out to be political.

But another issue that may be discussed is security guarantees for Ukraine. This ties in with the previous question, because Ukraine and Russia alone cannot guarantee a ceasefire in the future if one is reached. There must be third-party involvement, and probably some form of military involvement as well. This is reportedly also on the agenda.

But the real reason people say Russia wants talks but not peace is that Russia is demanding additional Ukrainian territory in exchange for ending hostilities. It also wants to gain direct influence over the political process in Ukraine.

So can we conclude that there is essentially very little to expect from the Abu Dhabi talks?

There is still something to hope for in the sense that a diplomatic process toward a more stable peace could get underway. Ukraine certainly needs these talks as well, because otherwise no result will ever be achieved. But ultimately, there is really no point in getting ahead of events. Let us first see whether, after the Abu Dhabi talks, it is announced that further talks will take place at all.

Background:

Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said there is no reason to think the talks will produce a broader European peace settlement, and that the best they can achieve is a ceasefire — though he does not personally believe one will be reached in any case, as Russian leader Vladimir Putin wants to divide the West, Tsahkna said. Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart on the Donetsk oblast, with Russia demanding Ukraine cede the parts it still holds and Ukraine wanting to freeze the contact line. Some U.S. officials have said there is "a little bit of flexibility" on this matter though.

World.title: Economy minister refuses to approve Estonia's Nutri-Score law
World.content:
Minister of Economy and Industry Liina Vahtras (Reform) declined to approve a draft regulation introducing Nutri-Score food labeling, citing the need to examine alternatives and address concerns raised by food producers.

Under a draft regulation prepared by the Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture, Estonian food businesses would be allowed to voluntarily use the Nutri-Score label, which assigns foods an overall nutritional rating based on a five-letter, color-coded scale.

The system is intended to make it easier for consumers to make healthier food choices.

Liina Vahtras has now informed the Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture that the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications will not approve the draft regulation. She said the ministry supports improving the food information provided to consumers but believes the need for a specific labeling system, its alternatives and its potential impacts should be analyzed more thoroughly before it is introduced.

According to the minister, the explanatory memorandum does not sufficiently explain how objections from the industry have been addressed or what alternatives and risk mitigation measures have been considered. Food producers have strongly opposed Nutri-Score, arguing that the system is misleading and that its impact on people's health has not been scientifically proven.

Meanwhile, pediatricians have expressed support for Nutri-Score, saying they see the consequences of obesity in their work every day and that the information currently provided on food packaging is not sufficiently understandable.

Vahtras said the draft regulation's supporting documents do not adequately explain what competitive disadvantage the measure is intended to address or how much interest Estonian businesses have in using the label.

"Businesses and industry associations that have contacted the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications have so far seen no clear need to allow the use of Nutri-Score in Estonia. According to their feedback, the label would not give them a competitive advantage or an additional selling point in export markets," Vahtras said.

According to the economy minister, Nutri-Score is not used in Estonia's main neighboring markets. Nordic countries, including Sweden and Denmark, use the Keyhole label instead.

"This does not rule out the potential benefits of the label, but it highlights the need for more thorough discussions with the industry about what practical benefits the system would bring to Estonian businesses and consumers. Studies suggest that Nutri-Score can make it easier to compare the nutritional content of products, but its impact on consumers' actual purchasing decisions is modest," she said.

Vahtras noted that in an experiment involving 60 supermarkets, Nutri-Score labeling improved the nutritional quality of shopping baskets by just 2.5 percent, with the effect averaging 17 times smaller than in laboratory studies. She added that there is insufficient convincing evidence of the labeling system's long-term health benefits.

"A simplified overall rating can lead to misinterpretations: a favorable score may create the impression that a product is healthy overall, even though the label does not take into account factors such as the degree of food processing, the amount consumed or a person's overall diet," Vahtras said.

She added that a better-than-expected rating could reduce consumers' feelings of guilt, while marketing claims on packaging could weaken the deterrent effect of an unfavorable rating.

The economy minister believes these factors should be comprehensively assessed before a system is selected. It should also be clarified how the labeling system would help consumers understand nutritional information without creating a misleading impression of a food product's overall healthiness.

Vahtras said that while the draft regulation would make Nutri-Score voluntary for businesses, its use would still entail costs related to packaging changes, calculating nutritional ratings, printing and other expenses. Businesses joining the system would generally be required to display the label on all products marketed in the relevant region under the registered brand, potentially increasing implementation costs.

"Retailers' expectations could also make the use of the label effectively mandatory for businesses. We therefore consider it necessary to assess the economic impact of the labeling system more thoroughly, including implementation costs and its effect on business competitiveness," she said.

The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications believes there is no need to rush into favoring one system. Instead, Nutri-Score should be compared with other labeling systems used in Europe, while the advantages and disadvantages of waiting for a common EU solution should also be assessed.

"Especially since the question of Nutri-Score's compliance with EU law is currently before the Court of Justice of the European Union," Vahtras noted.

The Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture will present studies related to Nutri-Score on Tuesday and the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications wants to take their findings into account before making a decision.

"Given that this is not an urgent change, we believe it is reasonable to take the time to discuss the issues raised more thoroughly with businesses, consumer representatives and other relevant stakeholders before proceeding with the draft regulation," Vahtras told the Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture.

The Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture has previously said food producers' concerns are unfounded. It has emphasized that Nutri-Score is not seen as a perfect solution capable of achieving every nutrition policy objective, but that it should make nutritional information on food packaging easier for consumers to understand.

According to the ministry's analysis to date, existing scientific evidence frequently supports labeling systems such as Nutri-Score. Consumers are more likely to notice simplified labels on the front of packaging than nutritional information on the back, while color coding also helps make the information more accessible to people from different socioeconomic backgrounds.

World.title: Narva high schoolers paired with Estonian language buddies in Järva County
World.content:
A new high school elective launched this week pairs Estonian-speaking teens in Järva County with Narva peers learning Estonian as a second language.

The first-of-its kind elective got underway in Paide on Monday, when students from the two regions were randomly drawn into pairs. Language buddies will practice speaking Estonian together at least once a week before wrapping up with a final seminar in Narva in March.

During their visit, Narva students praised the Paide State High School building and the opportunity to practice their Estonian.

One teen, Elis Markova, said she enjoyed the experience.

"It's really cool, and I really like this kind of high school," she said.



Fellow student Jekaterina Bašinskaja added that "of course" she wants to learn the language, because she lives in Estonia and should be able to speak it.

Her new language buddy Valeriia Melnychenko, a student at Koeru High School originally from Ukraine, said Russian is her first language.

"We can use a mix of Estonian and Russian when we talk," Melnychenko said.

A new language buddies elective between Narva and Järva County high schoolers was launched in Paide. November 2026. Source: Olev Kenk/ERR

Paide high schooler Rasmus Kraak said that although his language buddy speaks little Estonian, they can still understand a bit and still communicate.

True to their age group, the pairs will mainly stay in touch through social media, with scheduled meetings and video calls when needed, said Koeru student Sten-Marten Raal.

A buddy for every Ida-Viru high schooler

Three schools in Järva County and three schools in Narva are taking part in the elective, contributing five students each. Every group has an assigned teacher mentor, who will monitor students' progress and help out when needed.

The program was launched by Järva Municipality, which hopes the friendships formed along the way will continue beyond the end of the elective itself.

Its longer-term ambition is to expand the initiative across the country.

"Maybe in five years, the program will grow enough that every high schooler in Ida-Viru County learning Estonian has a language buddy somewhere else in Estonia," said Järva Municipality's education and youth work specialist Piret Sapp.

World.title: Tõnu Väät: 9 out of 10 packages from Asia clear customs outside Estonia
World.content:
If we want the next logistics hub to be built in Estonia, we must adopt European regulations without adding our own extra requirements, writes Tõnu Väät.

Starting in November, every package ordered from Asia costs more, but the new customs duty and handling fee have revealed something more significant than a couple of extra euros added to each shipment: more than 90 percent of packages Estonians order from outside the European Union do not arrive directly in Estonia. Instead, they pass through warehouses in other countries and are declared there.

Estonian consumers pay a €3 customs duty on every product category and an additional €2 handling fee. If goods first arrive in another country, the country where the purchase was made receives none of the customs revenue. Twenty-five percent of the revenue goes to the country where the package is declared, while 75 percent goes to the European Union. For example, if a package is declared in Poland, Estonia receives nothing.

The sums involved are not small. Last year, Estonians purchased €5.8 billion worth of goods from online stores, 35 percent of that, or nearly €2 billion, from outside the European Union. No one yet knows exactly how much tax revenue is being lost, but it is clear that the money is bypassing Estonia.

"As a transit country, we do not appear particularly attractive to investors."

Part of the reason goods bypass Estonia is geography. We are a small market on the edge of Europe. But that is not the whole story. Asian companies establish warehouses in Poland, Germany and Lithuania partly because it is easier and cheaper to do business there. Several of those countries deliberately implement Brussels regulations at the minimum required level and do not add extra requirements of their own. VAT and other trade-related taxes are lower there than in Estonia. They also actively tell investors that their countries are good places to do business.

Estonia, by contrast, adds requirements on top of European rules and taxes trade more heavily than its neighbors. As a transit country, we do not appear particularly attractive to investors.

Shein, the fast-fashion e-commerce company founded in China, recently announced it is expanding its logistics center in Poland, where it plans to employ more than 10,000 people. The company says its European warehouse network allows for faster deliveries, with customers in some markets receiving products within 48 hours, made possible by Poland's infrastructure.

What would even a fraction of that mean for a small country like Estonia? Thousands of jobs, new buildings and equipment, and the tax revenue generated from them would outweigh any lost customs revenue many times over. Altogether, we are talking about hundreds of millions of euros.

If we want the next logistics hub to come to Estonia, we must adopt European requirements without adding our own extra conditions and begin actively inviting investors to Estonia ourselves.

World.title: International film congress in Tallinn focuses on funding and artificial intelligence
World.content:
The World Congress of Science and Factual Producers is taking place at Kultuurikatel through Thursday. Held in Tallinn to mark the 30th anniversary of the Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF), the event has attracted nearly 600 participants from more than 30 countries.

The forum, dedicated to science, history, nature and other factual content, brings together creators, producers, distributors, broadcasters and streaming platforms from around the world. One of the industry's main challenges at the moment is shrinking funding and declining budgets.

"The biggest challenge for congress delegates is finding new sources of funding. Should they move from traditional broadcasting to YouTube, become content creators themselves or seek funding from foundations? There is a huge number of challenges facing people in this industry," said congress executive producer Sara Ramsden.

Documentary film congress opens in Tallinn with 600 attendees. Source: ERR

"Every country struggles to finance large and important documentary projects. Cooperation with international partners is important both editorially and financially. Today, it is not just important, it is often the only way to bring such projects to life," filmmaker Charlotte Cayre Tisseyre said.

Another key topic at the congress is how to reach new audiences. Participants are also examining the impact of artificial intelligence, which is reshaping film production and the wider industry.

"We have four different discussions dedicated to artificial intelligence. It is a major challenge for the television sector because some broadcasters accept its use while others do not. AI is eliminating jobs across the industry. We are still trying to understand how to deal with this new, amazing but also frightening technology," Ramsden said.

Mikk Granström Autor/allikas: Erakogu

According to PÖFF CEO Mikk Granström, hosting the congress in Tallinn is both a major recognition for the festival and Estonia and a valuable opportunity for local filmmakers and researchers to establish new direct contacts.

"All the major documentary films we are used to seeing on television actually begin at congresses like this. One reason people come here is to find interesting creators from this region. The organizers have done their homework well. When we talk about digitalization and artificial intelligence, Jaan Aru is here precisely to speak about AI. Estonia is actually the first country to make this kind of artificial intelligence leap in education. Many countries have a great deal to learn from that," Granström said.
