World.title: Doha diary: A historian amid the Iran war
World.content:
(Renowned historian and author, Rila Mukherjee, was scheduled to fly from the USA to India by Qatar Airways [QA] on February 25, 2026. Her route—Shreveport–Dallas Fort Worth–Doha–Kolkata—was expected to bring her to Kolkata on the night of February 26 or in the early hours of February 27. However, as of March 8, she was still stranded in Doha. Qatar’s skies were closed due to the US-Israeli attack on Iran. QA’s commercial flights were suspended. At the time of writing, evacuation flights to India were scheduled to start soon. She reached home on 12 March.)

Today is 8 March. I am now camping out in Doha for the ninth day since 28 February. The Qatar airspace is shut and padlocked. The authorities have thrown away the key. Limited numbers of passengers are being flown to Europe and the Americas on evacuation flights (they are called ‘relief flights’) organised by QA, and relief flights to Africa and Asia will start from tomorrow. But for the time being, I am effectively marooned in Doha.

Doha is one of the largest airplane hubs in the world, and a cosmopolitan group of transit passengers has been put up by QA in the 4-star The Royal Riviera Hotel. The hotel is situated on Doha’s Corniche. It is an ageing hotel; not terribly posh, and the plumbing is a bit iffy. But it is well located, with comfortable rooms, and it is a clean and friendly hotel. I feel safe here. Its staff is composed of Asians (from Bangladesh, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Nepal), North Africans (Algerians and Moroccans mostly) and some West Asians. All of them are helpful despite the pressures they are facing. They deal gracefully with the diverse demands and complaints of the passengers.

My room faces the Corniche and I can see the Persian Gulf from my window. As a maritime historian, this makes me very happy.

This country and its national airline are looking after us very well and, really, I have no complaints. QA’s representatives visit the hotel twice daily. There is no information forthcoming on my evacuation to Kolkata, and the greater part of passenger bags are still to arrive at the hotel. My South African neighbour says one of their bags has not been delivered; perhaps it is lost.

We are largely dependent on the clothes we have on our backs and those we had in our carry-on. Most of us are washing and drying them overnight. We have to use the hair dryer if they are still not dry.

My bags came in today, i.e., 8 March.

There are some elderly travellers. Many of them say that their medicines are running out. Mine will last another week.

Will I be able to get out by then?

We are told that a limited air corridor may open today; alternatively, we may be evacuated by the land route through Saudi Arabia to Riyadh (this would take around seven hours), where a leased QA aircraft may take us to India. But we have to make our own arrangements for the Saudi e-visa and overland travel. This seems a risky enterprise. And whether this potential leased aircraft would fly me direct to Kolkata is not known. There is no clarity to date.

***

But if I was scheduled to arrive in Kolkata on 27 February (and the war broke out a day later, on 28 February), how is it that I am still in Doha

Ah, thereby hangs a tale!

It is a cautionary tale on buying air tickets with multiple connections, and what ensues when the first connection does not take off as per schedule.

***

I had spent nine weeks in Shreveport with my son and daughter-in-law and was scheduled to leave on 25 February. Unfortunately, my flight from Shreveport to Dallas Fort Worth (DFW) by QA’s codeshare partner American Airlines (AA) did not take off. We were told that the incoming flight had nose gear problems and therefore could not land. Ultimately it made an emergency landing. Fire engines, firefighters, EMTs and ambulances were standing by. Luckily, there was no fireball and there were no casualties. The vice-chair of my daughter-in-law’s department was on that flight; I bumped into him in the terminal as he deplaned, and he said that the landing had been really scary.

There were no more AA flights to DFW that day. Roo and Stephanie came back to the airport and took me home. I spent a restless night. I hate flying at the best of times.

I was put on the same AA flight the next day, on 26 February, but when I reached DFW I was told that my connection flight to Doha was full. Apparently, the AA staff at Shreveport Regional Airport knew there were no seats on that flight; nevertheless they sent me on to DFW hoping I would ‘sort out’ the matter with AA’s customer care there. The only ‘sorting out’ that AA did at DFW was to put me on a later QA flight to Doha on the same day, that is, late evening on 26 February. It was a smaller aircraft (not the Airbus 350 on which I was ticketed), the flight was cramped and some of my co-passengers were not very well behaved. One lady kept on drinking; she skipped the meal service and was quite abusive. Another one, African American, told me that as an ‘American’ she was superior to Asians. Right, I thought, we all know how you as a Black person got there!!!

In all my years of travelling I have never encountered such blatant racism.

When we reached Doha very late on the night of 27 February (almost 24 hours later due to the time difference with DFW), I had missed that evening’s flight to Kolkata!

No problem, QA’s customer care said, we’ll talk with AA as it is their problem. This took a while, so I went off to buy myself a snack at Brioche Dorée in the airport’s food court.

By then it was early morning on 28 February.

Readers, note the date!

***

AA agreed to comp me a room for the remainder of the night at The Royal Riviera Hotel. I was granted a 48-hour emergency visa by Qatar Immigration and I was shifted to the hotel on 28 February at 2 AM. QA’s ground staff helped me throughout. The room was comfortable, the bed looked inviting, and I went to sleep, confident that my Kolkata flight would take off as scheduled at 18.45 hours on that day itself (that is, 28 February). At that point, I was going to reach only 24 hours behind my original schedule.

I informed Kolkata and asked my driver to collect me from the airport accordingly.

***

On 28 February, I was woken around 8 AM by a strange sound from my cell phone. It was a very loud, continuous screech. I don’t have international roaming and I wondered who was calling me and what was happening. I saw a ‘Security Alert’ on my screen but the text was in Arabic. I started hearing thuds and bangs. Another alert, still in Arabic, came in.

What was going on? I was mystified.

I was now getting alerts in English. It said the US and Israel had jointly attacked Iran. US bases and embassies and consulates across the Gulf were vulnerable. Qatar was in this critical area. Sirens were going off. I started watching Al Jazeera and Richard Engel on NBC.

This was Day 1.

Smoke rises following an explosion, after Israel and the US launched strikes on Iran, in Tehran, Iran, February 28, 2026. PHOTO: REUTERS

By Day 2, the Gulf was not just lying in a war zone; it had been converted into a theatre of war. Doha was undergoing regular drone strikes and missile attacks.

Day 3 was relatively quiet. Apparently, Qatar and Iran had a phone conversation, and Qatar urged Iran to stop the strikes. But our temporary visas were extended by Qatar. This was an indication that the phone call was not conclusive. This war was not going to end anytime soon.

The Qatar–Iran conversation does not seem to have yielded the desired result. There is no relief from Iranian attacks. These now form the backdrop to our daily life at The Royal Riviera. Drone attacks and missile strikes re-started from Day 4. None of them target the downtown area; they target only the US base and industrial areas in Qatar. Most of the drones and missiles are successfully intercepted; the few that are not cause localised fires. The attacks usually happen around breakfast and lunch, and sometimes they occur very late at night or in the early morning hours. This means we are always in a state of extreme alert. It is jarring on the nerves. We can neither eat properly nor rest. We are getting stressed out.

But I must also mention that the attacks and interceptions sound more like Diwali patakas than the very loud explosions that one expects.

*** Days 4 till 9 (that is, till date) have seen this regional war extending from land to sea: from the Hormuz Strait to the Indian Ocean. This is now becoming very serious. Critical choke points like this strait have become a curse. Ports across the Gulf are lying idle; almost no cargo is getting through. But we have had no alerts today. Does this mean that Iran will not strike Qatar for the time being? Is this a temporary reprieve? Will relief flights be able to take off? ***

Some bags arrived at the hotel on Day 5. Mine were not among them.

By Days 6 and 7 we have more or less settled into what is turning out to be our semi-permanent home. The hotel is no longer very ‘royal’; it has taken on the character of a London bedsit. Or a council housing estate in one of the UK’s inner cities! Children play noisy games in the corridors, an oddly comforting sound among the explosions, security alerts and sirens that go on regularly.

I see an enormous solidarity among the travellers, both on my floor and when we meet up at meal times. I have a very nice South African couple next door who check on me each morning, always asking how I am faring (‘please don’t hesitate to knock if you face any difficulties’). They have even offered to take me out to buy clothes (this was before my bags arrived). Elegant MENA (Middle East North Africa) people greet me each day at breakfast, a young Pakistani financial analyst from Toronto shares his insights with me at the breakfast table, and a British couple advise me to carry my passport with me at all times (especially when I leave my room in case of an attack and subsequent fire). They kindly offered to buy me my medicines, although they are at least a decade older than me. A young school teacher from Geneva shares my table at dinner. I have not seen her lately; perhaps she has already been repatriated on one of the relief flights to Europe which started operating from Day 7. The British couple and the South Africans are still here; the Pakistani man left for Toronto early this morning. He was given only two hours’ notice and he phoned my room to say goodbye at 1.15 AM this morning.

***

What does my daily schedule look like?

It is like what I imagine a day at boarding school would be. Because it is Ramadan, the hotel starts the breakfast buffet from 3 AM, lunch is from 12 noon, and dinner is over by 7.30. The food served (although mild in taste and quasi-institutional as regards the daily menu, which does not rotate much in terms of items), is nevertheless amazingly varied as regards the cuisine: Arabic, Turkish, Italian, Spanish and South Asian (the last is not good at all). A lot of lemon is used in the preparations, but practically no onions. This may be due to the fact that there was an onion shortage; onions came in from India only on Day 5. There are loads of different kinds of salads, some bland European cheeses and diverse types of hummus. In addition, there is feta cheese, stuffed vine leaves, green and black olives, veg and non-veg samosas and spring rolls, koftas, and baba ghanoush or baingan bharta. Good cappuccinos and lattes. Flaky croissants and brioches, pastries and amazing Arabian/Persian/Yemeni sweets. A decadent baked (and often caramelised) bread pudding called Umm Ali is served at dinner. Obviously, the Qatari supermarkets are still well-stocked with FMCG. The Indian-origin Lulu supermarket chain has flown in a whole lot of perishable and non-perishable food items.

Strangely, no fresh fruit!

***

Gas prices have shot up.

I have given up watching the death and destruction on TV, and watch Looney Tunes, Anthony Bourdain, Fawlty Towers and Mr Bean instead. Priyam Paul, my editor at The Daily Star, has sent me some e-books which help to pass the time.

When I am not reading, or watching sitcoms, cartoons and travel and food documentaries, I reflect on what brought us to this war. I see the Persian Gulf from my room; it is still a brilliant blue. But it is also desolate since the Hormuz Strait was closed off. I see no cargo ships or container vessels; there are no cruise ships or tankers. For a maritime historian like me, this is not the Persian Gulf I know. After all, it has been a crossroads since recorded history! My India in the Indian Ocean World (2022) documents this history of two thousand years at the very least. Now, mobility is severely constrained.

Persian Gulf. Photo: Collected

We are living now in a world of fragmented geopolitics, of accelerated climate degradation, and of critical demographic shifts. The world is undergoing these changes along with increasingly disaffected groups of peoples, perhaps terrorists, some of them. We are seeing the rise of AI which, to my mind, is linked, along with the toxicity of social media, with the increasing authoritarianism that we see worldwide. It horrifies me when I see a young nation declare it will bring ‘civilisation’ to Iran. It disregards the fact that Iran-as-Persia predates Arab culture and is one of the world’s oldest culture areas. Not just the glory of Shi’ite Safavid Persia (1501–1736), which political theorists and analysts invoke when describing this civilisational space and whose heritage modern Iran draws on: think of the period from c. 550 BCE to 651 CE (Muslim conquest and start of Islamisation by the Rashidun Caliphate), when four mighty Persian empires ruled a large portion of the then-known world: Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sassanian. Persia challenged Egypt, Greece and Rome, and then it faced up to the Ottoman and Russian empires. This memory of resistance of 2500 years will not be easily erased.

However, the total disregard of international law and the collapse of the rules-based order will usher in a new regional order in West Asia. This will impact on the Gulf states. Once-biblical Lebanon is almost destroyed by a rampant Israel. Syria has closed its borders. As a rogue USA intimidates Persia and trains its eye on the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, it also destabilises Iraq. Iranian Kurds based in Iraq have been reactivated. How will this impact on the Turkish Kurds? Turkey, a NATO country, is already feeling threatened.

The relatively young post-WW1 statelets in the Gulf will lose out in the violent reshuffle in the greater region. The Dubai story was already over. And Oman had lost its sheen even earlier. Financial and service centres will shift eastward—to Singapore or perhaps to KL. As will global airline hubs. The Gulf states will see their importance in location, business and finance diminish. They will have to reconsider their dependence on the USA which has now become a double-edged sword. Iran will endure, but perhaps in a new form. But it will not be erased from the map of the world.

World.title: André Béteille: A sociologist Bangladesh should read
World.content:
My first encounter with the ideas of Professor André Béteille was in July 1966 in an introductory sociology course at the University of Dhaka (at that time in East Pakistan) through Professor Tom Bottomore’s book, Sociology: A Guide to Problems and Literature (1962). The emphasis on general theory of social stratification for an explanation of the Indian caste system found its empirical reflection, as Bottomore refers to, in the work of Béteille, especially in Caste, Class and Power: Changing Patterns of Stratification in a Tanjore Village (1965).

My second encounter with him was in the Fall of 1975 at Dalhousie University, Halifax where I was writing my Master’s thesis under Professor Bottomore, and he referred to read me Béteille’s “Closed and open social stratification” (1966). Reading Béteille after nine years under the Maple tree, I began to admire his empirical depth, comparative methodology, and theoretical clarity, which reshaped my understanding of social hierarchies in India.

In the Christmas of 1976, I had an occasion to share some of my understanding of Béteille’s work. At that time, I was at York University, Toronto where I was doing my PhD. Professor K. Ishwaran, one of our faculty members, who wrote Tradition and Economy in Village India (1966), invited me for Christmas dinner-- Turkey with cranberry sauce, cooked by his Dutch wife. There we talked about the contribution of both Béteille and his supervisor M. N. Srinivas towards understanding the impact of social change on Indian social stratification.

In order to realistically understand contemporary caste hierarchy, Béteille emphasised the “other factors such as class and power” that “have to be considered as independent variables” (1966). It appeared to me highly useful for comparative empirical research. It creates a distance from traditional essentialist and ideological perspective of inequality.

Borrowed from Max Weber, he focused on multidimensionality of stratification and examined how status, economic resources, and political control interact to shape multifarious social order. This was a tremendous contribution in the field of stratification studies. Though he focused on rural stratification, the model is also applicable to the study of urban social stratification.

It is puzzling that in Bangladesh universities, both sociology and anthropology disciplines overlooked and neglected the Weberian model of multidimensional stratification system: anthropology remained spell-bound under the dichotomous model of rural “ashraf-atraf”; and sociology was locked in the iron cage of simplistic Marxist model of “land ownership” under the name of peasant studies. In spite of teaching Weber’s “Class, Status, Party” (1922/1946) in the universities, there is a marked absence of the application of Weberian model in the study of rural and urban complex social hierarchy. Probably in Bangladesh, this shows the intellectual bankruptcy of these disciplines, which are suffering from morbidity.

In fact, in order to understand contemporary social change in Bangladesh, especially its regime of accumulation under crony capitalism, it is essential to understand the nexus between power and class. The determining power of traditional property ownership in the formation of classes and consequent class consciousness has diminished in Bangladesh.

The notion of political capitalism advanced by Max Weber is also useful in understanding Bangladesh social stratification, especially class formation. The party consciousness along with ruling party affiliation, may give legitimate or illegitimate access to economic resources, thereby determining class position in terms of life opportunities and life style. This in turn, heavily influence commodification of prestige and honour; and becomes marker of status.

André Beteille (1934 - 2026). Photo: Collected

The rural and urban dispossession, which is an integral part of neoliberal and crony capitalism’s regime of accumulation, is also the progenitor of emergent lumpen bourgeoisie, whose class position do not correspond with their demeaning status position. Again, the traditional status group in Bangladesh, as Béteille found in his Tanjore village study with respect to traditional caste, suffer from status dislocation, having less access to power and economic resources. The ontology of inequality and hierarchy can best be understood by the Weberian epistemology.

I think study of this process of social change, and its impact on inequality in Bangladesh, is vital towards understanding Bangladesh society. The internationally acclaimed Indian empirical model provided by Béteille can be one of the best guides to study the intersectionality of class, status and power in both urban and rural Bangladesh. It is unfortunate that social sciences in Bangladesh have neglected such a significant social dynamic that affects all our lives.

In March 1989, Professor Abhijit Dasgupta, a colleague of Professor Béteille, facilitated my direct meeting with him. Professor Dasgupta was kind enough to arrange a seminar talk by me in the sociology department of Delhi School of Economics. After the seminar, I paid a visit to Professor Béteille’s office room. He was very warm and hospitable to offer tea to me and my wife. He spoke in Bangla and affirmed his Bangali origin. I felt very comfortable to have a vibe of Bengal. I mentioned to him how I came to know of his work à la Bottomore and Ishwaran. I was so surprised to experience his stock of knowledge mediated by modesty and simplicity. The meeting with professor Béteille during the short-lived spring of Delhi was one of the most memorable events of my life. I wish his conceptual and methodological clarity inspire the young Bangladeshi sociologists to break the chain of ignorance, myopic framework, and the hegemony of intellectual infantilism.

A.I. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed is a professor in the Department of Sociology at the University of Dhaka.

World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: The war Putin wanted to keep away is coming home to Russia
World.content:
Olga was jolted awake by an explosion so powerful that her apartment building shuddered and the windows and furniture shook. Looking outside, she saw a plume of thick black smoke rising from a military equipment factory that had just been hit by a missile.

Residents panicked, said Olga, a 49-year-old choreographer. “We didn’t know whether we should run to a shelter,” she said. The strike on the plant left six people dead and another 26 injured, according to the local governor.

Olga doesn’t live in Kyiv, Kherson or any other Ukrainian city that’s been pounded for years by Russian President Vladimir Putin’s forces. This is Kirov, a Russian city about 800 kilometers northeast of Moscow known for its 16th century onion-domed monastery rather than being in a war zone.

World.title: Are Japan and the U.S. losing South Korea as an ally?
World.content:
The poor showing by U.S. President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the midterm elections has weakened his administration politically, raising questions about the future of American foreign policy and Washington’s commitment to longstanding alliances.

These uncertainties are particularly consequential in Northeast Asia, where strains in the U.S.-South Korea alliance threaten trilateral security cooperation with Japan.

Since South Korean President Lee Jae Myung took office after a snap election in June 2025, tensions in the alliance have grown, jeopardizing cooperation among Washington, Tokyo and Seoul as regional threats mount. Latent friction in the alliance stems from a steady accumulation of Seoul’s subtle pro-Beijing signals, perhaps due to its growing deference to Beijing’s preferences on intelligence and regional deterrence.

World.title: SoftBank logs $7 billion loss after U.S. data center costs swell
World.content:
SoftBank Group reported Tuesday its first net loss in almost two years after swallowing a $3.7 billion writedown over a U.S. data-center project amid rising fears around the sustainability of AI growth.

The Tokyo-based backer of OpenAI tumbled to a ¥1.12 trillion ($7.1 billion) loss in its fiscal second quarter around nonrefundable advance payments made to secure equipment and manufacturing capacity for its Ohio data-center campus. Analysts on average expected a profit of ¥129 billion.

Declines in the stock prices of chipmakers Arm Holdings and Intel, as well as South Korean e-commerce giant Coupang, further dragged down SoftBank’s bottom line. The Vision Fund segment, which oversees stakes in hundreds of tech startups, logged a loss of ¥81.6 billion, compared with market expectations for a profit.

SoftBank is increasingly seen as a proxy for sentiment toward OpenAI and the broader AI sector. Its shares have plunged more than 50% from their record high in June, hurt by fears over the debt it’s taken on to finance big AI bets and concerns that the Democratic sweep of U.S. midterm elections could stall many of founder Masayoshi Son’s projects.

Volatility remains high at SoftBank, which held a 13% stake in OpenAI at the beginning of October, with investors eager to gauge the risks and opportunities around its AI investments.

Last week, investors were weighing a valuation as low as $1.1 trillion for Anthropic, down from a previously touted figure of $2 trillion, people familiar with the matter said. OpenAI raised about $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, after initially seeking $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion value, Bloomberg News reported.

Founder Masayoshi Son’s reliance on debt markets to finance his expanding list of AI investments has made SoftBank’s bonds especially sensitive and lifting its credit default swaps hit their highest in years.

World.title: Japan to use COP31 to showcase environmental technologies
World.content:
Increasing the world’s electrification to 35% by 2035 is a key goal of COP31, the annual international climate change conference which began Monday in Antalya, Turkey.

While Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will not attend the conference, expected to draw 90,000 representatives from 200 countries and running until Nov. 20, Japan is using the event to showcase environmental technologies to help meet the electrification goal.

As COP31 host, Turkey is proposing a collective global goal to increase the share of final energy demand from electricity from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035.

The target is based on analysis from the International Energy Agency and the International Renewable Energy Agency and is designed to support implementation of the Paris Agreement and help keep the world on a pathway consistent with limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels.

The Environment Ministry’s COP31 Japan Pavilion features Japanese firms involved in providing a variety of advanced environmental technologies to increase electrification, including the use of perovskite solar cells.

Perovskite solar cells are light, flexible and can be installed in places where it’s difficult to put in more conventional solar cells.

The primary material for producing perovskite solar cells is iodine, and Japan has the second-largest share (about 30%) of its global production. Takaichi sees perovskite solar cells as a crucial part of Japan’s future energy policy.

“While conventional solar power generation is almost entirely dominated by China, I think the focus will shift to advanced technologies such as perovskite,” says Kenichiro Yamaguchi of the Mitsubishi Research Institute.

Other initiatives Japan is promoting at COP31 include energy conservation, carbon capture and storage, and waste reduction technologies.

Japan’s delegation is being led by Environment Minister Hiroyoshi Sasagawa, after Takaichi declined, for the second time, to attend the conference, citing a busy domestic schedule to attend the parliamentary debate over the tax cut bill.

This year marks the third year in a row a Japanese prime minister has been absent. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told reporters on Monday that only three prime ministers have attended the climate summits over the past 30 years.

Yamaguchi says that looking at past summits, it’s rare for the prime minister to participate. Normally, the head of the Japanese negotiating team is the environment minister. When the prime minister shows up, COP is then considered a forum for diplomacy that goes beyond climate change. That can mean talks end up deviating somewhat from individual business matters

“However, if the prime minister doesn’t participate, it may be difficult to make progress on major initiatives, such as economic cooperation that contributes to the dissemination of Japanese technology,” he said.

World.title: U.S. allies need a plan for a lame-duck Trump
World.content:
Conventional wisdom has it that after U.S. President Donald Trump suffered a stinging rebuke from American voters this month, losing both houses of Congress, he’s now all the more likely to lash out via foreign policy — the one area where his power remains undiluted.

That has Ukrainians fretting (and Russia’s state-controlled media speculating) that Trump could blame them for his defeat, decide that his legacy depends on forcing their capitulation to Moscow or both. Iranians worry he could try to “finish” them. Israelis are concerned he may follow the shifting tide of opinion against them. And if Cuba’s leaders didn’t already assume they’re on his menu, they now should.

Some of those fears may well materialize, but it’s far from clear how the least predictable U.S. president in memory will react. The one sure bet — as my Bloomberg Opinion colleague and Trump biographer Timothy O’Brien put it Thursday — is to expect volatility. Trump, he writes, has always tended “to double down when he fails, with little regard for consequences.”

World.title: Macron’s Angkor visit highlights France’s custodial role
World.content:
The newly restored West Mebon temple rises from a reservoir at Cambodia’s sprawling Angkor archaeological complex, the latest in a century of conservation projects led by former colonial power France.

French President Emmanuel Macron and Cambodian King Norodom Sihamoni will inaugurate the nearly 1,000-year-old temple on the sidelines of a summit of French-speaking nations in Phnom Penh on Nov. 15 and 16.

Conservationists have restored most of the original 16 towers and surrounding walls over the past 14 years, and put the finishing touches on a stone marker at the entrance last week.

World.content:
Sakana AI might go public next year and is considering a listing on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, Nasdaq or both for its initial public offering (IPO), media reports say.

According to Nikkei, which broke the news, the company’s market capitalization could exceed Mercari’s ¥680 billion ($4.3 billion) and set Sakana AI on track to become one of Japan’s most valuable startup listings. Goldman Sachs has been hired as an adviser, according to the report.

In an X post on Monday, Sakana AI said it has no near-term plans for an IPO.

“Our priority remains building a generational AI company that serves as Japan’s national AI champion,” the post read.

Reports of a Sakana AI IPO come as artificial intelligence companies globally face a broad range of challenges related to valuations, resistance to data centers and questions about the usefulness of the technology.

AI shares were particularly hard-hit after U.S. midterm elections on concerns that a Democratic Party-dominated House and Senate would lead to stricter AI regulations and slow data center construction.

The Nasdaq is down about 9% from its all-time high in part on AI’s retreat.

Sakana AI raised ¥32 billion ($200 million) in Series B funding from global sponsors including Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Google and Citi. Nvidia was a participant in an earlier Series A funding round.

Earlier this year, the company introduced Sakana Namazu, its first large language model (LLM), using Kimi 2.6, an open-weight model developed by China’s Moonshot AI.

In light of national security concerns related to overreliance on Chinese and U.S. models, Japan has made the development of its own LLMs a priority and has reportedly invested $6 billion in developing an AI via Noetra, a consortium that includes Sakana AI, SoftBank and Sony.

On Oct. 26, Sakana AI said that it was working to train its own LLM from scratch. Its planned Sakana Sawara series will include a large and a small model.

World.title: Japan to call for limiting children’s exposure to social media
World.content:
Upcoming government guidelines are expected to say that parents and other guardians should limit the exposure of young children to social media and other internet content, a draft showed Tuesday.

The draft, created by the Children and Families Agency, outlined key issues that need to be discussed to complete the guidelines for setting up an appropriate environment for children to use social media services and the internet.

During early childhood up to age 2, a critical period for the development of children’s minds and bodies, parents should select the content their children view and ensure they do not spend excessive time using digital services, the draft said.

In the draft, the agency divided children up to age 18 into six age groups and outlined precautions for each, saying that children’s interactions with social media and the online environments for them change with age.

The agency hopes that specific measures will be discussed at expert panel meetings and elsewhere to establish the guidelines to protect children from risks related to social media and other online services.

For children age zero to 2, the draft said that priority should be given to direct interactions with other people, stressing that parents should assess the purpose and necessity of their children’s use of social media and other digital services.

For those age 6 to 9, who begin using devices for educational purposes, the draft proposed providing more opportunities for them to think independently and make choices for themselves in a safe online environment.

For those age 13 to 15, who become more active in interactions on social media, the draft said that parents should respect children’s independence and privacy rather than trying to fully manage their online activities.

Schools should help children develop their judgment so that they can use social media appropriately, the draft said, calling on service providers to establish systems that children can use easily to seek advice and report problems.

World.title: Hong Kong’s Ocean Park urged to boost safety after second tower failure in 2 years
World.content:
Hong Kong’s Ocean Park has been urged to enhance its safety measures after an ageing observation tower broke down for the second time in two years, leaving 42 people stranded 70 metres above the ground.

Lawmakers called for changes on Tuesday, a day after the incident sent firefighters rushing to the scene and caused the ride to stop working for more than two hours.

While 40 customers and a staff member were able to make their own way to the ground through a safety passage inside the tower, one woman with mobility difficulties was only able to escape after a firefighter equipped with rope-rescue gear helped lower her to safety.

World.title: Nobel-winning UK scientist launches programme to develop hepatitis C vaccine in Hong Kong
World.content:
A British Nobel-winning virologist has launched a programme to develop the world’s first hepatitis C vaccine after joining a university in Hong Kong, tapping the city’s research funding, access to Chinese strains of the virus and partnerships with mainland drug makers.

Sir Michael Houghton, who won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the co-discovery of the hepatitis C virus, said he joined Baptist University after more than four decades in North America, as the United States and Europe had cut their science spending.

“President Trump and his ministers have really damaged the National Institutes of Health, and my research grant was cut. In Europe, economic problems because of inflation also mean less money goes to research,” said Houghton, who also leads the University of Alberta’s Li Ka Shing Applied Virology Institute in Canada.

World.title: WinterFest to spread across Hong Kong as ‘Symphony of Lights’ takes final bow
World.content:
Hong Kong’s annual WinterFest will expand beyond Central this year, reaching Tsim Sha Tsui and Causeway Bay with new attractions including steam trains and aurora light shows.

But the festival’s opening next Wednesday will also mark the final performance of “A Symphony of Lights,” the nightly Victoria Harbour show that has illuminated the city’s skyline for 22 years. It will be replaced by seasonal light shows.

The final performance, at 8pm, would include special pyrotechnic effects as a farewell, the Hong Kong Tourism Board said on Tuesday.

World.title: UK remains ‘much valued business partner’ to Hong Kong, John Lee says
World.content:
The United Kingdom remains a “much valued business partner” to Hong Kong, the city’s leader has said, while calling on British companies, investors and universities to explore opportunities in the Northern Metropolis.

Speaking at the annual summit of the British Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong on Tuesday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu also said the development of the university towns in the megaproject near the border with mainland China offered a timely opportunity for both sides to deepen collaboration in higher education.

“We have long invested in each other’s economies, and we continue to do so,” Lee said.

World.title: Richard Li’s FWD sets world record with sale of US$318m life insurance policy
World.content:
Richard Li’s FWD sets world record with sale of US$318m life insurance policy

Topping previous record by Manulife Singapore, sale highlights Hong Kong’s global status in wealth management, says broker Charles Monat

World.title: Minibus driver arrested in Hong Kong for alleged drug driving while carrying passengers
World.content:
A minibus driver has been arrested in Hong Kong on suspicion of driving under the influence of drugs while carrying passengers, after he tested positive for methamphetamine during a police interception.

Acting on intelligence, officers intercepted the minibus without incident on Tuesday and removed the seven passengers on board to safety, according to Senior inspector Pun Chun-ho of the Kowloon East task force’s enforcement and control division.

“Drug driving isn’t simply a rule violation, but a serious threat to the safety of passengers,” Pun warned.

World.title: Hong Kong civil servants to be given 12 hours of family care leave a year
World.content:
Hong Kong’s civil servants will be entitled to up to 12 hours of family care leave a year from January, with the government promising flexible, streamlined approval procedures as part of a “people-orientated” approach.

The Civil Service Bureau set out details of the initiative, first announced in September’s policy address, in a paper submitted to the Legislative Council’s public service panel on Tuesday.

Staff may use the leave to accompany family members to medical appointments, care for sick relatives, attend their children’s school activities or deal with household emergencies.

World.title: Paragliding association backs compulsory registration after self-taught pilot’s crash
World.content:
Hong Kong’s paragliding association has said it is open to compulsory registration amid mounting safety concerns after a self-taught pilot injured three hikers, while a sports expert has called for stricter regulation of the activity.

Simon Chan Siu-ming, executive secretary of the Hong Kong China Paragliding Association, said fellow enthusiasts had known about the pilot and his lack of proper training about nine months before Sunday’s accident and had urged him to seek professional instruction.

“Even if it becomes compulsory, we are very open to it, provided it brings positive changes for the sport and everyone’s safety,” Chan told a radio programme on Tuesday, referring to real-name registration.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019240/From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.title: From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019240/From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.content:
The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) closed in Shanghai on Tuesday after showcasing cutting-edge technologies in artificial intelligence, commercial aerospace, and innovative drugs.

The six-day event drew exhibitors from a record 162 countries, regions, and international organizations. A total of 4,142 overseas companies took part — also a record high — with more than 480 representative products making their global, Asian, or China debut.

U.S. wireless chipmaker Qualcomm exhibited the world’s first 6G terminal prototype — the first time the device has been shown publicly outside the lab. The prototype has been used in joint tests with China Mobile, China’s largest telecom operator, and Chinese telecom equipment manufacturer ZTE. The prototype will provide the foundation for 6G chips and support the technology’s commercial rollout.

The event featured an expanded medical devices and health care exhibition area, acting as the stage for the China debut of pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca’s new hypertension medication baxdrostat. The oral medication works by inhibiting the enzyme aldosterone synthase, which helps synthesize the blood pressure-regulating hormone aldosterone, and was approved in the U.S. in May.

German optical giant Zeiss also made its global debut of its new non-spherical lens PT Lunana, designed for myopia correction. Novartis, a Swiss multinational pharmaceutical company, showcased ianalumab, a drug used for treating the autoimmune illness Sjögren’s disease — also a China debut.

American electric vehicle company Tesla presented its Cybercab autonomous vehicle. Lacking a steering wheel or pedals, the vehicle relies on cameras and AI to drive. Hexagon — a global digital reality and metrology tech company — also displayed its industrial humanoid robot AEON.

Aerospace technology was also present, including the Zhuque-3 rocket developed by Chinese commercial aerospace company LandSpace. The rocket’s reusable booster, which uses liquid oxygen and methane as fuel, can land vertically, first achieved by the company in August.

Beyond showcasing new tech, the expo held its first exhibition area for 100 long-established, reputable international brands — from Canadian shoe companies to Spanish wineries — as well as hosted a trade and investment “matchmaking” conference, where companies and buyers met to sign cooperation agreements. The latter conference attracted more than 600 exhibitors and over 2,000 buyers from 59 countries and regions.

The deals reached at this year’s expo are projected to be worth a total of $85.45 billion over the coming year, up 2.3% from last year and a record high.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A view of the China International Import Expo in Shanghai, Nov. 6, 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019239/Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
World.title: Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019239/Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
World.content:
China has opened its first school dedicated to declining and obscure fields of study, with a focus on ancient and classical Chinese texts.

The School for Rare and Endangered Disciplines was inaugurated in Beijing on Nov. 6 under the University of Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (UCASS). At the opening, the university also announced the launch of a national alliance of more than 80 universities, museums, and cultural and research institutions to share resources, conduct collaborative research, and cultivate talent in related fields.

The school comes as the number of scholars studying ancient Chinese scripts dwindles. Nationwide, only about 500 people work in ancient Chinese writing studies, and of the roughly 4,500 known oracle bone characters — the oldest known fully developed form of Chinese writing and widely used for divination purposes during the Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) — nearly two-thirds remain undeciphered, underlining the need for further research.

The initiative also builds on previous attempts by UCASS to preserve such fields, such as establishing an institute for rare and endangered studies in 2024 to train future talent in fields such as bamboo and silk studies, which examines script on the two materials, as well as classical studies, Turkic studies, and Assyriology, or studies of the Ancient Near East.

Each student of the new school’s bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degree courses will be mentored by two members of the school’s more than 140 faculty members. UCASS has also built dedicated laboratories for the school’s use.

Students may pursue research in oracle bone studies, bamboo and silk studies, and classical studies. They may also train in over 10 ancient ethnic scripts, including Turkic, Tangut, Khitan, Jurchen, Manchu, Old Tibetan, Old Yi, Phags-pa, Naxi Dongba, and Zhuang.

“Ancient scripts like oracle bone script are on the verge of being lost, and some frontier history research relies on the survival of the country’s cultural roots and its long-term development,” Huang Dekuan, director of the Research and Conservation Center for Unearthed Texts at Tsinghua University, told state broadcaster CCTV.

Such disciplines are also hampered by scattered resources and research institutions working in isolation — key obstacles to research and transmission, according to CCTV.

China has called for increased focus on cultural heritage preservation in recent years. At an October press conference on cultural heritage protection, government officials called for advancing cultural heritage as a discipline, cultivating interdisciplinary talent in the field, and encouraging qualified universities to establish cultural heritage schools.

In a Nov. 7 commentary, domestic media outlet The Beijing News wrote that by emphasizing rare and endangered disciplines, the new school offers a lesson to other universities: schools should develop their own distinctive majors, resist the urge to offer only popular fields, and actively strengthen less mainstream majors.

“Only then can a university truly serve education,” it stated.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019245/Fallback to First Choice: Why Chinese Parents Are Rethinking Vocational Schools
World.title: Fallback to First Choice: Why Chinese Parents Are Rethinking Vocational Schools
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019245/Fallback to First Choice: Why Chinese Parents Are Rethinking Vocational Schools
World.content:
Coming from a Shanghai family with a strong academic background, Yang Fan had always felt studying at university was his destiny. The only problem was, he was flunking middle school.

“He’d make the same mistake with a character the entire semester. I just couldn’t get him to do it right,” says his mother, Zhao Xuan, who could only look on in frustration as Yang struggled with his homework night after night. “Given how much it was taking for him to get through middle school, I felt high school would crush him.”

Last summer, with the conventional academic pathway looking a bad fit for their 15-year-old son, Zhao and her husband began to consider China’s integrated secondary vocational-to-undergraduate articulation program. Launched as a 2014 pilot in Shanghai, the initiative sees students spend up to three years at a vocational school before transitioning to a partner university to complete a related four-year bachelor’s degree program.

Over the past 12 years, the number of participating educational institutions has rapidly expanded, now covering at least seven provincial regions, and applications have soared.

Shanghai alone has established 91 majors across 38 vocational schools and 18 universities, enrolling about 20,000 students and producing six cohorts of graduates. Planned enrollment this year was 2,756, up from just 120 in 2014 and a 17.5% increase from 2025.

Programs cover diverse fields including robotics, accounting, digital media arts, big data engineering, logistics, environmental design, hospitality management, cultural heritage restoration, smart manufacturing, performing arts, sound recording, information security, and materials science.

The trend reflects a sea change in attitudes toward vocational education in China. Technical skills training has long been stigmatized as “low status” and a “fallback option,” but as the country’s workforce undergoes a massive restructuring driven by an aging population, advancements in artificial intelligence, and an economic slowdown, more people feel it now makes students more employable compared to those with purely academic backgrounds.

In real terms, most students in the integrated program say their experiences are far less stressful than those of their peers at traditional Chinese high schools, and that they are encouraged to focus more on their personal strengths rather than sticking to a one-size-fits-all curriculum.

However, because most applicants are only in their mid-teens, it’s often parents who make the final decision, with research suggesting that more-passive children have only a vague idea of, or interest in, what might lie ahead.

The path less traveled

It was only when Zhao learned that the prestigious Shanghai Maritime University (SMU) would join the integrated secondary vocational-to-undergraduate articulation program in 2026 that she was sure the pathway was a “realistic match” for Yang.

Soon, Zhao and her husband, who holds a Ph.D., had researched the job prospects of various degree holders and consulted with their son, who was willing to give vocational school a try. For him, it was an opportunity to follow his growing interest in mechanics and spend time on activities he’d been forced to drop in middle school, such as table tennis and learning to play guitar.

In the 2026 zhongkao, the national high school entrance exam, Yang scored highly enough to earn a place this fall in the mechanical design, manufacturing, and automation major run jointly by Shanghai Harbour School and SMU.

With the increase in applications, programs have been setting higher admission thresholds. More than 80% increased their cut-off in 2026, and over half by 20 to 30 points. To secure a place in either of the two majors run in partnership with SMU, students must score at least 690 points out of a maximum 750.

In the final year of middle school, “we really pushed ourselves to the limit,” says Zhao, though she dismisses the idea that her son’s zhongkao score was a reflection of any academic acumen. “We got lucky. The exam was on the easy side.”

Kuang Ying, a professor specializing in vocational education at Shanghai’s East China Normal University, points out that students and parents today have far more information about the integrated program compared to when it started.

“People weren’t familiar with these programs, and many working-class families lacked the information they needed to make a reasoned decision back then,” she says.

Pan Yuxiao, who grew up in Shanghai’s northern Chongming District, was among the first students to enroll in the pilot in 2014. He’d wanted to continue his studies at a high school closer to the city center, but his zhongkao score was too low.

By chance, he came across a brochure about the integrated program. “There was hardly any information back then. The teachers didn’t know about it, and neither did the parents,” recalls Pan, who eventually enrolled in the mechanical engineering major offered by Shanghai Industrial Technology School and Shanghai Polytechnic University (SSPU).

Kuang believes that not only has awareness of such courses substantially improved since the inaugural cohort but parents’ priorities have also changed. “Now people are looking for a more certain future,” she explains. Families are no longer solely fixated on school rankings and prestige; they are taking a more honest look at their child’s academic standing relative to their peers and what they can realistically achieve. This allows them to make more informed, pragmatic choices tailored to a child’s abilities and circumstances, she adds.

The reason many have chosen the integrated program over a standard high school, then and now, is simple: It virtually guarantees a spot on a bachelor’s degree course. However, for some, mental health is another major factor.

Wu Yulu, a sophomore student at SSPU, scored 640 in the 2022 zhongkao, enough to get into a selective local high school in Shanghai. But she doubts she would ever have made it to college through the traditional route. “I just wouldn’t have had the stamina for it,” she says.

The pressure of middle school took its toll on Wu. In her first year, she would work on her homework late into the night and often woke up at her desk. When her grades began to drop, she took a leave of absence due to stress.

A 2022 report by the China Youth and Children Research Center based on interviews of 24,758 students in 10 provinces found that 23% of middle school students were at risk of depression, while 31% showed signs of anxiety.

When Wu returned to middle school the following fall, she had lots of material to catch up on but had learned to “let myself off the hook.” It was around then that she heard about the integrated vocational-to-undergraduate major in taxation that led to a bachelor’s from SSUP.

For Wu and her parents, it seemed a fitting path forward. “I wouldn’t have to wear myself out,” she says. As the program was still relatively unknown in 2022, she was one of only two students in her class who applied.

Same but different

As in Yang’s case, Jia Xinyi’s parents first suggested she join an integrated program, recommending she study early years education. This was 2017, and China had just relaxed its one-child policy. Her family predicted a baby boom and reasoned that Jia could land a stable job at a kindergarten, yet she had little interest in the subject.

When it came time to decide, Jia was torn. “No one could guarantee how things would turn out, but the integrated pathway offered a clearer route,” she says. She eventually settled on a major in materials science and engineering because a relative already worked in the field.

Once enrolled at Shanghai Material Engineering School, Jia found the daily schedule fairly typical: four morning classes, another four after lunch, and 30- to 90-minute study sessions in the evening. Chinese, mathematics, and English formed a core part of the curriculum for all three years, with students using standard textbooks. However, she feels the homework was far more manageable than at regular high schools.

Wu agrees. She says the learning atmosphere at her vocational school was relatively relaxed; she was no longer plagued by the workload-induced sleep deprivation she’d experienced in middle school.

However, on top of core academic subjects, vocational school students also take practical classes in their chosen field.

While preparing for a vocational qualification exam, Jia learned to conduct chemical analyses of construction materials, received skills training in cement production, and was given a factory tour. Pan says his teachers at Shanghai Industrial Technology School introduced him to 3D printing technologies and a five-axis machine center, an advanced cutting tool.

Professional skills competitions also offer a different dimension. Wu took the opportunity to enter contests in intelligent finance and taxation, and won awards for several videos she made after teaching herself how to use editing software. These achievements helped her come to terms with her tough middle school years and showed her that she could shine through her strengths.

In most provinces, students on the integrated pathway take a transition exam after three years.

Wu recalls that the test was undemanding. For the academic section, the pass mark was 180 points out of 300, while the only vocational requirement was that candidates reach 70% of the class average. “The pass rate was very high,” she notes, adding that only one student in her year had failed.

Parental guidance

Twelve years in, the integrated program is still a work in progress. Local education officials commonly visit participating schools to solicit student feedback on the teaching quality and the curriculum. Jia recalls that some of her classmates called for more class hours in physics and chemistry, as well as better-qualified teachers.

However, for her, the major challenge was what came next. While studying for her bachelor’s at the Shanghai Institute of Technology, Jia discovered that she needed to take the kaoyan, China’s national postgraduate entrance exam, to progress to one of the university’s master’s programs. To prepare, she had to start from scratch in several foundational academic subjects because her vocational school had devoted so little time to them. She believes this has since been addressed in training plans for subsequent cohorts.

Meanwhile, education experts are concerned by the fact that it’s typically parents pushing their children to choose the integrated program, rather than driven by personal interest.

According to an education industry magazine article written this June by a finance tutor at Shanghai Economic Management School, surveys show that roughly 80% of students on the integrated program had primarily followed their parents’ wishes in applying, “placing themselves in a passive stance” and leading to a “lack of initiative.”

Pan notes that several of his vocational school classmates had “no interest in their major and felt that their potential was being wasted.” Whenever Jia posted about her studies on social media, she also noticed that the vast majority of comments and questions were from parents.

Kuang believes few adolescents have the ability to think clearly about decisions with such far-reaching consequences. “Middle school students are often bewildered when it comes to making choices. Even high school graduates are,” she says, adding that China’s education system doesn’t provide children with enough formal career guidance or expose them to different professions early.

It’s been five years since Pan’s inaugural 40-strong cohort graduated from university. He estimates that only 25% to 33% of his classmates work in fields related to their majors. He initially found a job working with machinery after graduation but has since switched to the medical industry.

Jia is completing a postgraduate internship in environmental, health, and safety management, far removed from her academic focus of materials science. She believes it’s highly unlikely she’ll end up working in her field of study.

Switching track

As China’s real economy develops and the central government places greater emphasis on skilled professionals, Kuang says the integrated program’s growing popularity is inevitable. “Technical skills will become one of the major pathways to success,” she predicts.

Since 2014, the public has gained a better understanding of how the integrated program differs from conventional vocational education. Schools are committing quality resources and assigning their most capable teachers. “These positives give Chinese parents greater confidence in choosing this once-stigmatized pathway,” Kuang adds.

In Pan’s view, much of what students learn in high school is irrelevant to real life, while those who choose the integrated route are making a conscious decision to use their time and energy wisely.

Jia adds that parents are having to consider alternatives because the days when graduating from a prestigious university guaranteed a secure job are gone. However, she still worries that some see the integrated vocational route as a “back door” to a bachelor’s degree.

Yang started at Shanghai Harbour School this fall and hopes to take part in many extracurricular activities and competitions. On registration day, the incoming cohort was encouraged to pursue independent learning, which Zhao was glad to hear.

“We don’t want our child spending his time in a passive learning environment, simply being dragged along by others,” she says. “Choosing the integrated pathway doesn’t mean taking the easy way out. It means stepping onto a different track, one that still demands hard work but puts my son in the driver’s seat.”

(Due to privacy concerns, Yang Fan, Zhao Xuan, Pan Yuxiao, and Jia Xinyi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Chen Lei, Wang Zhaoxue, and Zhang Zhenyao.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.
