World.title: Lito Lapid worried Davao City accountant merely being used
World.content:
Senator-judge Lito Lapid. Photo from Sen. Lito Lapid office.

MANILA, Philippines — Senator-judge Lito Lapid has raised concerns about a Davao City accountant merely being used by different sectors, as she failed to answer several simple questions from the prosecution during Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.

At the tail end of the trial on Tuesday, Lapid asked Davao City Accountant Vingelin Bajan if she is being used, citing a supposed history with her previous accounting firm Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co. CPAs — as Bajan admitted that while she was a partner, she was not an active participant in the firm’s activities.

Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co. CPAs became a point of discussion as counsel for the prosecution Mae Divinagracia confronted Bajan with the accounting firm’s Article of Partnership which listed Bajan as a partner. According to Divinagracia, Bajan — who is testifying for the defense — used to be part of the accounting firm that audited companies linked to Duterte.

Article continues after this 

READ: Davao accountant was partner at firm that audited VP-linked companies

“Naaawa na po ako sa inyo eh, kaming dalawa ni Senator (Panfilo) Lacson. Gusto niyang magtanong (kaso) baka daw maiyak siya eh kapag nagtanong siya. Kasi sa haba-haba ng halos maghapon, ang mga tanong ng mga senator-judge, halos hindi niyo nasasagot,” Lapid said.

(I actually pity you, me and Senator (Panfilo) Lacson feel the same way. She wants to ask questions (but) he might tear up if he does. Because with the long hours we have dedicated this afternoon, you failed to answer almost all of the questions of senator-judges.)

“Eh nakikinig ang mga kababayan natin dito, ‘pag hindi kayo nakakasagot naiinis sila. Kami rin, sabi nga ni Senator Tulfo, Raffy, baka ma-contempt ka pa dito, lalo akong naaawa sa inyo. Ang iniisip namin, baka pumunta ka dito, nagagamit ka lang dahil kayo ang city accountant ng Davao na parang wala kayong alam,” he added.

READ: Barbers: VP shortchanged by her lawyers who fielded lying witnesses

Article continues after this 

(The people also listen to the trial, and if you fail to answer questions they are irritated. Us too, and Senator Tulfo, Raffy even said you might be cited for contempt, which will lead me to pity you more. We are thinking, you came here but you were being used because you are the city accountant Davao yet you seem to know nothing.)

Lapid then directly asked Bajan if she was being merely used, which the Davao City account denied.

Article continues after this 

“Sana kung ano, magsalita kayo ng totoo, ang hinahanap lang naman ng mga kasama ko rito ‘yong totoo lang. Kanina naiiyak kayo, lalo akong naaawa sa inyo. Sana hindi naman kayo nagagamit. Nagagamit ba kayo?” Lapid asked.

(I hope you speak the truth, because my colleagues here only want the truth. A while ago you nearly teared up, I pity you. I hope you are not being used. Are you being used by others?)

READ: Assessor quizzed: Why confirm property when VP’s SALN has no details?

“Hindi po […] Hindi po ako ginamit po your Honor,” Bajan said.

(No […] No I am not being used, your Honor.)

“Eh kasi ginagamit ‘yong pangalan niyo, wala naman kayong pakinabang. Ano ba ‘yon? Papayag ka bang gano’n, na gano’n na lang, na ginagamit ‘yong pangalan mo ng ibang firm na accountant, na hindi mo alam pati ‘yong ginagawa nilang mga audit o pati ‘yong mga kumpanya na sinasabi ng mga kasamahan kong senador dito na hindi niyo rin alam?” Lapid fired back.

(I say this because your name was used, but you did not have any benefit. What is that? Would you allow things to be that way, where your name is being used by other accounting firms while you do not know their activities or how they do audits, or their links to the companies that my colleagues mentioned earlier?)

Several of the questions raised by Divinagracia and senator-judges against Bajan resulted in her answering that she either does not know or she does not remember. This resulted in senator-judges, including Presiding Officer Francis Escudero, being frustrated with Bajan.

Divinagracia presented the accounting firm’s Articles of Partnership which was submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and showed that Bajan was a partner in 2003, or before she started being a job order worker for the city government of Davao.

Divinagracia presented another document, this time an amended Articles of Partnership where Bajan’s name was dropped. However, Bajan said she does not remember the said documents.

When Divinagracia failed to elicit an answer, Escudero stepped in, saying he finds it questionable that Bajan cannot remember the details of her work when certified public accountants are known to be very meticulous.

As Bajan remained unresponsive, Divinagracia then moved to a new point, asking her instead if she can recognize the original Articles of Partnership submitted to SEC by the accounting firm — including a portion that bore her signature.

As Bajan still failed to answer, Escudero pressed her for a response, asking why she is flipping through pages. Several senator-judges also questioned Bajan’s hesitation, like Senator-judge Francis Pangilinan wondering why she cannot answer whether the signature belongs to her.

Eventually, Bajan said it is her signature and her tax number, but she cannot remember when and if she signed it.

The prosecution panel has already called out the defense for bringing witnesses that seem to be doing more damage for the Vice President’s argument rather than to dismantle the allegations against her.

On Monday, prosecution spokesperson Robert Ace Barbers said Duterte is not getting enough for what she is paying her legal team if they will present evasive and lying witnesses like Davao City Assessor Engr. Jaime Adalin, whom he said tried to evade the prosecution’s questions.

Barbers’ comments came after Adalin was called out by counsel for the prosecution Benjamin Tolosa Jr., after the assessor concluded that the 379-square-meter parcel of land in Davao City’s Matina Crossing was the same as the property declared by the Duterte in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN).

The Matina Crossing lot is owned by Duterte’s husband, lawyer Manases Carpio. The defense claims that the lot is declared in Duterte’s SALN, but it was labeled as a residential lot in Barangay 74-A. Adalin, the defense’s first witness for the impeachment trial, explained that he used a property identification map to confirm that Matina Crossing property is the same as the lot in Barangay 74-A.

He also claimed that he counterchecked the Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT) and tax declarations of the Matina Crossing property, and it supposedly matched the Barangay 74-A lot’s assessed value of P82,046 and fair market value of P2,051,150.00.

However, Tolosa said it is impossible to confirm as there are other key details that cannot be seen in Duterte’s SALN.

Also, Tolosa noted that the acquisition cost of the two properties differed: the lot was supposedly bought by Carpio for P6 million while Duterte declared an acquisition cost of P10 million — leading the prosecution to believe that these are two different properties, and one of them was not declared by Duterte in her SALN.

World.title: Palace: Corruption issues affecting OVP employees’ mental health
World.content:
Presidential Communications Office (PCO) Undersecretary and Palace Press Officer Atty. Claire Castro addresses questions from the Malacañang Press Corps during a news conference. INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang on Tuesday raised corruption and excessive pressure as possible causes of the mental health concerns among employees of the Office of the Vice President (OVP).

During a meeting with Filipinos in Hong Kong, Vice President Sara Duterte said her office had launched a mental health program for employees affected by attacks from the Marcos administration.

READ: Palace to Sara Duterte: Show evidence behind safety, trust concerns

Article continues after this 

Reacting to this, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said the mental health concerns of OVP employees should not be downplayed or politicized, adding that their possible causes should be investigated.

“Hindi ito dapat maliitin, hindi ito dapat pinupulitika. So dapat mabigyan sila ng suporta, counseling; dapat malaman kung kailan ito nagsimula, kung ano ang pinanggagalingan nito,” she said at a briefing.

(This should not be downplayed or politicized. They should be given support and counseling, and we should determine when this started and what caused it.)

“Maaari bang ito ay dahil sa usaping kurapsiyon? Dahil ba may mga dapat na masiwalat na hindi nasiwalat? Mayroon bang mga tinatawag na excessive pressure?” she continued.

(Could this be due to corruption issues? Are there things that should have been exposed but were not? Is there what we call excessive pressure?)

Article continues after this 

Castro then enumerated government programs that OVP employees can access for mental health support, including the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation’s Outpatient Mental Health Benefit Package, the Department of Health’s Mental Health Program, and the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s “Tara, Usap!” initiative.

“At tandaan po natin, nagbibigay po ng free mental health services sa mga Pilipino ang National Center for Mental Health at nagbibigay din po ito ng outpatient psychiatric consultations, online consultations for eligible patients, 24/7 crisis support,” the Palace official said.

Article continues after this 

(Let us remember that the National Center for Mental Health offers free mental health services to Filipinos, including outpatient psychiatric consultations, online consultations for eligible patients, 24/7 crisis support.)

“So, kung anuman po ang nararamdaman ng mga empleyado ng Office of the Vice President, kailangan ninyo ng kausap, kailangan ninyong isiwalat ang nasa inyong dibdib para maiwasan ang bigat at masolusyunan ang anumang mental health issues, nandiyan po ang pamahalaan,” she continued.

(So, whatever the employees of the Office of the Vice President may be going through, if you need someone to talk to or someone you can confide in to help ease your burden and address any mental health concerns, the government is here to help.)

Castro also criticized Duterte’s remarks during her Hong Kong trip, where she urged the government to prepare the country’s food supply instead of advising Filipinos to prepare buckets in response to the looming El Niño.

“Ang maganda po kasi dito mas i-advise ninyo po ang Bise Presidente na magbasa po ng news, manood ng news mula sa mainstream media para malaman niya na ang kanyang ina-advise ay matagal na pong ginagawa ng gobyerno,” Castro said.

(It would be better to advise the Vice President to read the news and watch reports from mainstream media so she would know that the government has long been implementing the programs she is recommending.)

“Huwag lang po sanang manatili ang kaisipan sa balde kasi wala pong mararating kung balde lang hihinto ang kaisipan ng isang Bise Presidente,” she continued.

(Hopefully, the Vice President’s thinking will not remain limited to a bucket, because nothing will be achieved if her thinking stops at just a bucket.)

Castro further slammed Duterte’s comparison of the Philippines’ strength to China’s, saying the country’s strength was only as small as a pinky finger compared to China’s fist.

“Ang isang liderato, hindi dapat sumusuko. Ang sabi ng Pangulo, iisa lang ang bansa natin, iisang bansa ang dapat nating pinuprotektahan. Magkakaiba man ang opinion sa ibang bagay pero ang pagmamahal sa bansa ay hindi dapat nahahati-hati,” she said.

(Leadership should never give up. As the President has said, we have only one country, and it is the one country we must protect. We may have different opinions on other matters, but our love for the country should never be divided.)

“Kaya tandaan natin, baka marami nang Manchurian candidates ang nakapaligid sa ating bansa, mag-ingat po tayo,” Castro added.

World.title: Defense drops Matina Crossing barangay captain as witness
World.content:
The defense panel during Monday’s proceedings of the Vice President Sara Duterte impeachment trial. INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines – Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense panel on Tuesday withdrew as a witness Matina Crossing Barangay Capt. Cindy Colina.

Colina’s testimony was supposed to cover documents related to the official name of Brgy. Matina Crossing in Talomo, Davao City.

“We will no longer present the fifth witness in our list, Cindy Colina, the Punong Barangay of Matina Crossing… This is without prejudice to any subsequent motion that we will make on the court’s taking judicial notice of the geographical divisions with respect to the subject barangays,” lead defense counsel Atty. Sheila Sison told the court.

Article continues after this 

READ: Assessor quizzed: Why confirm property when VP’s SALN has no details?

To recall, a property owned by Duterte’s spouse, or Atty. Manases Carpio, was listed in the vice president’s statement of assets, liabilities, and net worth as located in Brgy. 74-A, but is Matina Crossing in its tax declaration.

This was among the properties the prosecution claimed Duterte wrongfully declared.

But the defense’s first witness, Davao City assessor Engr. Jaime Adalin, explained that 74-A and Matina Crossing are the same barangay. /mr

World.title: Myanmar Foreign Debt Falls to $10.8b but Experts Warn of Collapse
World.content:
Despite World Bank data showing Myanmar’s foreign debt fell to US$ 10.8 billion in 2025, experts warn loan repayments by the internationally isolated regime are fuelling economic collapse.

Myanmar’s external debt dropped from $13.5 billion in 2021 to $10.8 billion in 2025, according to the latest figures released by the World Bank on November 5. The report said public and public-guaranteed loans account for 95 percent ($10.3 billion) of the total debt which comes under three categories: multilateral, bilateral, and private creditors.

The World Bank and International Monetary Fund are Myanmar’s primary multilateral lenders, owed $3.8 billion, with Japan and China its largest bilateral creditors (owed over $1.5 billion).

As Myanmar’s top international donor, Japan funds special economic zones and large-scale infrastructure including railways and power grids. Japan remains Myanmar’s biggest creditor despite cancelling over 300 billion yen ($3 billion) in debt to facilitate financial reintegration in 2013 and then suspending new loans after the 2021 coup.

Meanwhile, Chinese loans have financed key infrastructure, energy, pipelines, and Belt and Road projects across Myanmar. Regular regime payments halved Chinese debt from $3 billion to around 1.5 billion between 2021 and 2025.

However, analysts warn that the heavy burden of foreign currency repayments amid an international aid freeze and deepening economic crisis are fuelling kyat depreciation and severe shortages.

“Having to make loan repayments during an economic crisis and foreign currency shortage has driven the country into trouble,” said a local economist, who requested anonymity for safety reasons.

“Repayments may reduce the debt, but there is no money left for imports — and no international aid to cover the outflows.”

He added that as a developing nation, Myanmar is dependent on international funding such as concessional loans and development grants to fund large-scale infrastructure.

Post-coup economic mismanagement compounded by foreign sanctions and an exodus of foreign investors have plunged Myanmar into severe economic crisis. At the same time, escalating armed conflict around key economic projects has stalled their development.

Against this backdrop, the regime’s Ministry of Finance and Revenue recently stated that the soaring 2025–26 budget deficit was driven by a drop in funding from its closest allies, China, India, and Russia, as key projects hit security snags. Speaking to lawmakers, deputy minister Kyaw Htin acknowledged that the expected foreign funding failed to materialize.

With access to international loans limited, the rubber-stamp parliament in October approved short-term export credit from Belarus, sparking widespread criticism that the high-interest loan repayments will only deepen hardships for the Myanmar public.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Plans April Vote in 55 Constituencies Despite Continued Clashes
World.content:
Myanmar’s regime plans to hold elections in 55 constituencies across 37 townships on April 4, 2027, including 12 townships where it has regained at least partial control from resistance forces in recent years. Voting was not held in those 12 townships during the regime’s general election in December 2025 and January 2026, which was widely dismissed as a sham.

In an announcement Thursday, the regime said it would hold voting in 34 Lower House constituencies, using the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system; five Upper House constituencies; and 16 regional/state parliament constituencies across the country.

The townships include Tonzang and Falam in northern Chin State and Tigyaing, Banmauk and Indaw in Sagaing Region, all recaptured by the regime this year, as well as Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region, which it recaptured in 2025.

Also included on the regime’s list of townships scheduled to vote in April are Sagaing’s Kawlin, which the Myanmar military recaptured in 2024, and the Sagaing resistance strongholds of Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo and Taze.

A military analyst pointed out that the regime only controls the towns in Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo, Taze, Tigyaing, Banmauk and especially Indaw.

“The regime wants to show it is able to control the whole country, and that its administration is operating,” said Zin Yaw, a military defector who has monitored Myanmar’s conflicts since defecting after the coup.

The absence from the list of southern Chin State towns that the regime has been trying to retake since May 2026, as well as Arakan Army-controlled towns in Rakhine State, amounts to an admission by the regime that it hasn’t been able to restore its authority in these areas, he said.

The regime announced Lower House elections in Myeik, Tanintharyi Region; Nyaunglebin, Pauk Khaung and Padaung in Bago Region; Chauk and Minbu in Magwe Region; Pyin Oo Lwin, Meiktila, Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; Kyaikmayaw in Mon State; Mayangone, Shwepyithar, Hlegu, Tamwe, Cocokyun and Hlaing Tharyar in Yangon Region; Kyaukme, Monghpyak, and Mong Pan in Shan State; Maubin in Ayeyarwady Region; and Zabuthiri, Dekkhinathiri and Ottarathiri in Naypyitaw.

The Upper House constituencies on the list are in Kachin State, Chin State, Magwe Region, Bago Region and Mandalay Region.

The list also includes state/regional parliament constituencies in Tonzang and Falam in Chin State; Tigyaing, Banmauk, Indaw, Kawlin, Pale, Yinmarbin, Taze and Shwebo in Sagaing Region; Zigon and Thegon in Bago Region; Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; and Yegyi in Ayeyarwady Region.

The Myanmar military recently suffered heavy losses to resistance ambushes in Indaw Township. Clashes continue there and in upper Sagaing.

Despite the ongoing armed conflicts in many areas, political parties cooperating with the regime’s electoral process said they are making preparations for the vote.

Saw Than Myint, joint secretary of the Shan and Ethnic Democratic Party (SNDP), which secured 37 seats in the regime-backed general election, said the party plans to compete in the upcoming by-election but is still discussing details.

People’s Pioneer Party (PPP) chair Saw Han Aye said the party hopes to field candidates in at least one-third of the 55 constituencies, as required under the Political Parties Registration Law for parties competing at the national level.

He acknowledged that security concerns remain in some areas, adding that participation would ultimately depend on individual candidates’ willingness.

The PPP was founded by Thet Thet Khine, a former regime minister who was barred in October 2025 from running in the general election on grounds of violating rules on personal debts.

The Irrawaddy contacted People’s Party chair Ko Ko Gyi, a former 88 Generation student protest leader, about the party’s plans but received no response.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s regime organized the nationwide election in three phases in December 2025 and January 2026, with voting in 263 out of 330 townships. Civilian leaders, including Aung San Suu Kyi, remained imprisoned, while major opposition parties had been dissolved.

With only nine parties participating at the national level, the election was dominated by the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and allied parties, allowing the USDP to secure a majority of the seats.

Since installing himself as president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic campaign in an effort to gain legitimacy for his regime, visiting China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia and India, while his military forces continue targeting civilians in attacks and atrocities. The absence of elections in the 55 constituencies has underlined his regime’s lack of legitimacy, observers say.

World.title: Over 2m Myanmar Migrants in Thailand Reject Regime’s Identity Document
World.content:
Over 2 million Myanmar migrant workers in Thailand have participated in a poll calling on the parallel National Unity Government (NUG) to issue identity documents amid a mass boycott of the regime’s new Certificate of Identity (CI) process.

The poll also aims to demonstrate to the Thai government that they recognize the NUG as their legitimate government, not the military regime.

Thailand hosts an estimated 4 million Myanmar workers, both documented and undocumented. Migrant worker groups estimate that at least 600,000 are required to apply for CIs in this round. However, most are staying away from the regime’s newly opened Thai CI centers in protest against new tax and remittance rules that critics condemn as extortion. To apply, workers must prove they have remitted 25 percent of their wages through official regime channels and paid 2 percent annual income tax. The vast majority are refusing, fearing payment would help fund the regime’s war on civilians while lending it political legitimacy.

Meanwhile, Thai opposition lawmakers and labor rights groups have urged the government to review or scrap the centers, branding them a threat to national security and sovereignty.

The workers themselves made their overwhelming opposition clear in a weeklong online poll launched Sunday by the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT). Many appealed to Thai authorities to grant them work and residency permits without the CI document.

The poll result reflected resounding support among migrant workers for an alternative identification process managed by the NUG, Khin Soe of the MMWRCCT told The Irrawaddy.

“The regime CI process is a trap to extract foreign currency and information for military conscription,” he said. “The workers know this, so they don’t want to apply.”

He said the poll result would be sent to the NUG’s Labour Department to push for worker ID issuance, while a separate workers’ online petition would be delivered to the Thai government.

“The Thai government may argue it has to cooperate with the regime on the CI process to ensure national security, but we are appealing to them on humanitarian grounds. If they need an alternative authority to issue identity documents, this poll shows that millions of workers want the NUG to do it. As guests living under Thai law, we are not making demands, we are simply presenting these results as a respectful request,” Khine Soe said.

Launched on October 18, the campaign and petition contain four requests, including the right to stay and work legally without a CI, and has drawn support from Thai labour rights groups and politicians.

Among them is MP Anuson Tamajai, a prominent economist who urged the government to review or cancel the CI centers, arguing their unchecked operations compromise national security and sovereignty.

Highlighting migrant workers’ indispensable role in Thailand’s economy, he also called for an investigation into whether demanding remittance and tax payments in exchange for ID certificates violates Thai law.

The Thailand Migration Reform group recently warned that allowing Naypyitaw to control migrant registration “undermines Thai sovereignty and fuels corruption.” It urged Thai authorities to revert to the Pink Card system for migrant workers.

On Friday, Thai Labor Minister Julapun Amornvivat told media after a meeting of the Foreign Workers Management Policy Committee that CIs are required by migrants’ countries of origin for identity verification, but the process operates entirely within Thai territory.

He said his ministry will send a formal letter to its regime counterpart expressing opposition to the mandatory remittance policy, arguing it undermines migrant worker rights and fails to align with international standards.

Dismissing the backlash, the cash-strapped regime has doubled down on its push to skim foreign currency from low-paid overseas workers. Newly appointed Labor Minister Maung Myint has threatened workers with legal action and a ban on returning home if they don’t make tax and remittance payments.

However, the boycott shows no sign of weakening, with only a trickle of applicants reported at the five CI centres across Thailand since they opened on October 14.

World.title: China Wields Carrot and Stick at Beijing Meet, Regime Seeks Elections in Shan, and More
World.content:
We’ll always hold your hand, Beijing promises Myanmar regime

“China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Myanmar investment minister Aung Kyaw Hoe on the sidelines of the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting on Tuesday.

The reassurance came as part of a carrot-and-stick package amid alarm in Beijing over recent meetings between U.S. and Myanmar officials that seemed to augur the start of re-engagement.

The U.S. has released an Integrated Country Strategy for its mission in Myanmar, which identifies goals for expanding Washington’s diplomatic, economic and humanitarian influence in the country. Besides singling out scam networks, it also sets goals for boosting American exports to the impoverished war-torn country and gain access to Myanmar’s “bountiful” rare earth resources—besides aiming to “counter China’s influence.”

Myanmar is China’s most important external source of rare earth minerals and a major global source of heavy rare earth elements, particularly dysprosium and terbium, which are essential for electric cars, wind turbines, advanced electronics and military technologies. But mines are concentrated in areas beyond the reach of the regime in Kachin and Shan states.

Online scam operations have become a major point of convergence and competition in the two superpowers’ approach toward Myanmar. During the meeting with Aung Kyaw Hoe, Wang urged his regime to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to the vast scam compounds that flourished there.

China grows impatient over stalled investment projects

But in the same meeting Wang applied plenty of stick, urging Myanmar’s regime to get a move on in realizing long-stalled projects that form part of the planned China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) that would provide Beijing with overland access to the Indian Ocean. Wang told Aung Kyaw Hoe the two sides must “coordinate development and security” so they can “steadily advance” key CMEC projects.

Wang’s message echoed remarks made by his President Xi Jinping during regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Beijing in June, when Xi also called for swift implementation of CMEC projects.

The corridor’s flagship schemes include the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port and special economic zone in Rakhine State and a planned railway linking Kyaukphyu with Yunnan via Mandalay and Muse. On China side, the railroad is already entering its final phase but on the Myanmar side fighting continues across many parts of the route.

Aung Kyaw Hoe promised the regime is doing all it can but, true to form, also used the occasion to beg for even more Chinese investment.

Border trade gates reopen as armed groups consolidate control

China has significantly eased restrictions on trade through several Myanmar border crossings controlled by Beijing-linked ethnic armed organizations, allowing fuel, medicines, construction materials and other previously banned goods to enter northern Shan and Kachin.

The move suggests China is adjusting its border policy to accommodate new realities on the ground, where it appears the military regime in Naypyitaw has permanently lost control. With Operation 1027, key border trade gates and routes in northern Shan fell into the hands of the ethnic Chinese Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), and its erstwhile partner in the Brotherhood Alliance, the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

Beijing initially closed the crossings to pressure them into making peace with the generals, but trade has long resumed and is now growing exponentially.

According to Chinese Customs at the Mengding crossing with MNDAA-controlled Chinshwehaw, the total value of trade there and at nearby Mangka eached 4.92 billion yuan in the first eight months of this year, up 49.3 percent on-year.

Customs figures also show increased trade through Namhkam crossing controlled by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army, as well as through the Kyin San Kyawt gate controlled jointly by the Brotherhood Alliance in Muse Township, which once accounted for some 70 percent of cross-border trade. The regime still controls a couple of crossings in Muse, where it bans the import of fuel from China.

In a move to prevent those groups from financing their armies through cargo taxation, the cash-strapped regime is now reduced to blocking routes south of Lashio, imposing a crackdown on what it calls “smuggled” goods—which in reality means roadside extortion.

Late last month, Min Aung Hlaing urged his ministers to intensify their crackdown on illegal trade and make sure that cross‑border commerce is conducted only through “legal” channels, i.e. those his regime controls. Myanmar’s consul general in Kunming met with the customs department director this week to discuss facilitating flows of “officially traded goods” between the neighbors and improving cooperation on customs procedures.

Naypyitaw seeks to roll out elections into Shan borderlands

Defence Minister Yar Pyae who also chairs the junta’s peace negotiation committee, this week visited areas held by China-linked ethnic armed groups with a view to rolling out the regime’s sham elections across their part of the country as well.

Yar Pyae went to Panghsang, the headquarters of United Wa State Army (UWSA), and Mongla, the fiefdom of the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA) near the Chinese border. The visit comes after Chinese Special Envoy to Myanmar Deng Xijun urged granting “high-level” autonomy to ethnic minorities.

Together with the MNDAA, they are widely regarded as being under heavy Chinese influence, with Chinese widely spoken and the yuan used as the major currency in their territories.

All three trace their origins to the 1989 mutiny that fractured the Communist Party of Burma. Most people in NDAA territory are ethnic Chinese with roots in Yunnan, but the Wa are a Mon‑Khmer-speaking people more closely related to the Palaung.

Both the UWSA and NDAA have long upheld ceasefires they signed with the military in 1989 in return for de-factor autonomy in their areas, sustained by cross‑border trade and Chinese investment.

In Mongla, Yar Pyae discussed holding the vote, which was omitted there when the regime orchestrated polls in the parts of Myanmar it controls in the winter of 2025-26 that led to military dictator Min Aung Hlaing declaring himself president. Naypyitaw is aiming for next April, regime media said. But none of the townships under the control of the UWSA or NDAA were included on the junta’s recently announced list of constituencies slated for catch-up and by-elections.

Historically, no national elections have been conducted either in Mongla or Panghsang, although voting has taken place in some townships of the constitutionally defined Wa Self-Administered Division where government administration was present. Formally, the UWSA is stuck at a stage of demanding official statehood, and the NDAA is demanding official autonomous status.

World.title: Arakan Army Faces Second Front at Bangladesh Border
World.content:
Amid intensified fighting as the Arakan Army (AA) closes in on the Arakan (Rakhine State) capital of Sittwe, a second front is heating up along the border with Bangladesh, where regime-aligned Rohingya armed groups are escalating conflict.

These attacks are not isolated border incidents. They reflect a history of cooperation between Myanmar’s military and Muslim armed organizations during the 2024 battles for Buthidaung and Maungdaw. For Bangladesh, they raise difficult questions about its security interests and the prospects of repatriating the hundreds of thousands of Rohingya refugees now within its borders. For the AA, they raise the question whether it can maintain stability across its home state.

A major concern is that armed networks established during the military regime’s territorial retreat are continuing to exert pressure on the AA while the main body of its forces confronts the regime elsewhere.

From cooperation to proxy warfare

During the 2024 Arakan offensive, the military suffered major territorial losses. Facing the AA’s advance, it cast around for additional manpower and local allies, and alighted on armed organizations that, ironically, were associated with a population it had systematically persecuted. One of them was the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA).

The International Crisis Group has documented the regime’s ammunition supplies to ARSA, along with recruitment arrangements that transferred Rohingya refugees to military facilities for training.

ARSA and another armed group, the Rohingya Solidarity Organization (RSO), received training, weapons and tactical support during the fighting while maintaining contacts with regime personnel after the AA captured Maungdaw in December 2024, according to the Transnational Institute.

Here was the military that was responsible for the 2017 atrocities that drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya into Bangladesh, brazenly cooperating with Rohingya armed organizations against the AA.

For the junta, however, the strategic advantages outweighed any qualms it might have had. Armed groups operating along the state’s northern frontier could challenge AA positions even after its own conventional military bases had fallen, and thereby divert precious resources from the AA’s other battlefronts.

As a bonus for a regime that has long sustained itself by divide-and-rule tactics, it risked deepening mistrust between the state’s Arakanese and Muslim communities.

Maungdaw remains a strategic front

Thus when the AA eventually captured Maungdaw, it transformed the military balance along the Bangladesh border but could not fully eliminate the armed groups operating through remote terrain and cross-border networks.

In September last year, ARSA fighters attacked an AA border security position near Inn Chaung village in northern Maungdaw. AA forces subsequently retook the position, while the attackers reportedly fled to Bangladesh.

Further clashes followed, and by late October this year, residents reported that ARSA was renewing recruitment, armed movements and attacks against AA outposts in northern and southern Maungdaw.

“ARSA activities have resurged in both northern and southern Maungdaw Township,” one resident told my news organization, Development Media Group.

With the AA confronting regime forces around Sittwe, repeated ARSA attacks could now force it to divert much-needed troops, intelligence resources and supplies to the border.

This would benefit Myanmar’s military even without direct command of these operations.

There is an important caveat. ARSA, RSO and a third militia active at the border, the Arakan Rohingya Army (ARA) have distinct leadership structures and interests. Their historical cooperation with the military regime does not mean that every recent attack was centrally coordinated.

Bangladesh’s border dilemma

A further complication lies in Bangladeshi involvement in these skirmishes. The AA accuses certain officers of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) of providing the Rohingya armed groups with logistical assistance, ammunition and intelligence, and allowing them to operate near border security positions.

The International Crisis Group, too, has documented the complicated relationships between these groups and elements of Bangladesh’s security establishment.

The allegations require credible investigation, but any such shenanigans must also be distinguished from official Bangladeshi government policy. Publicly, the BGB has denied supporting ARSA or the RSO.

Bangladesh faces legitimate challenges involving border security, with more than 1 million Rohingya refugees and the prospect of their eventual repatriation creating a massive headache for Dhaka.

But it will eventually have to confront the reality that the territory from which the refugees fled is now controlled by the AA, and that fundamentally changes the political realities.

Some Bangladeshi security personnel may still regard these avowedly Muslim armed organizations as potential leverage over the AA. But helping them with their cross-border attacks would now in fact undermine border stability and make peaceful repatriation more difficult.

In other words, Bangladesh’s security interests would be better served by stopping ARSA and co. from exploiting refugee communities, and instead maintaining effective communication with the AA authorities controlling the opposite side of the border.

Beyond armed groups and military control

The motivations behind Rohingya armed mobilization long predate any cooperation with Myanmar’s military.

Decades of discrimination, statelessness, displacement and uncertainty have created grievances that armed organizations can exploit. Refugees facing declining humanitarian assistance and limited opportunities are particularly vulnerable to recruitment and intimidation. But that cannot justify attacks on civilians, abductions or forced recruitment.

Nor should ARSA, RSO and ARA be treated as representative of Muslim communities as a whole. The Arakanese, Muslim and other communities in Maungdaw face threats from armed violence, disrupted livelihoods and insecurity. Abuses by all armed participants, including the AA, require impartial investigation and accountability.

The AA’s territorial gains have brought responsibilities extending beyond military security. Effective governance means it must protect civilians regardless of ethnicity or religion, address grievances and prevent communal tensions from escalating.

The Maungdaw conflict demonstrates that territorial control does not necessarily end a war.

Myanmar’s military has lost most of its positions in Arakan, yet its airpower, remaining military strongholds and historical relationships with armed groups continue to complicate the AA’s security calculations.

Preventing further escalation requires credible investigation of alleged weapons supplies and cross-border assistance, effective border management, protection of refugees from coercive recruitment, and sustained engagement between Bangladesh and the AA.

It also requires meaningful dialogue with Muslim civilian representatives and equal protection for all communities.

Unless the networks and grievances sustaining violence are addressed, no lasting peace can come to Arakan.

Aung Marm Oo is the editor-in-chief and executive director of Development Media Group, a news agency based in Arakan. He faces charges under Myanmar’s Unlawful Associations Act and has been in hiding since May 2019.

World.title: Hurry Up With Our Investment Projects, China tells Myanmar Regime
World.content:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has renewed Beijing’s call for the Myanmar regime to “steadily advance” key projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), which is designed to give Beijing direct access to Indian Ocean.

Wang made the remarks during a meeting on Tuesday with Myanmar Investment and Foreign Economic Relations Minister Aung Kyaw Hoe, who is in Beijing for the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.

A clearly exasperated Wang stressed the need for the two sides to “coordinate” development and security, as many parts of Myanmar are plagued by civil war, making it hard for the China-backed projects to proceed.

In turn, Wang promised Chinese support for the rebranded regime’s efforts to achieve international recognition. “China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” he said.

The remarks come as the U.S. shows signs of re-engaging with Naypyitaw in search of business.

Wang also called for stronger efforts to combat scams and online gambling. He urged Myanmar to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to online scam operations that flourished along the Thai-Myanmar border.

He urged Naypyitaw to do more to ensure the safety of Chinese nationals, organizations and projects operating in the country.

Aung Kyaw Hoe, for his part, promised that his regime does want to accelerate the CMEC projects and step up cooperation with China and regional countries in combating online scam operations. He duly thanked his hosts for supporting Myanmar in international forums, according to a statement from the Chinese Embassy.

When Myanmar’s putschist leader Min Aung Hlaing last visited Beijing in June after declaring himself president, Chinese President Xi Jinping also urged him to speed up the CMEC projects, a key component of Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

He too urged the regime to provide stronger security guarantees for Chinese personnel and investments in Myanmar, many of which are in areas now controlled by the resistance or ethnic armed organizations over which Beijing holds no sway.

The planned corridor includes several flagship projects, notably the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port in Rakhine State and a railway linking Kyaukphyu through Mandalay and Muse with China’s Yunnan Province.

The Kyaukphyu Special Economic Zone and deep-sea port project is particularly important for Beijing because it would provide China with direct access to the Indian Ocean while supporting economic development in Yunnan and other southwestern Chinese provinces.

But other than pay lip-service to the plans and hold out its hand for more investment, the Myanmar regime has done little to advance these projects, instead losing itself in dreams of reviving the long-mothballed Myitsone Dam Project in quite a different part of the country.

In its frustration, China has now reopened border crossings with areas controlled by ethnic armed organizations in northern Shan State to allow lucrative trade to resume, whether the regime likes it or not.

A China analyst told The Irrawaddy that Beijing “knows very well that Min Aung Hlaing’s stubbornness is holding everything up. The fighting is still going on, the peace talks haven’t delivered any results, there’s been no progress in northern Shan State, and the border crossings are still not operating normally.”

For the CMEC projects to move forward, Min Aung Hlaing “has to engage in talks with the ethnic armed groups first,” she added. “In that sense, I think China was quite deliberately sending that message.”

World.title: Kyat Slump Disrupts Thai Border Trade as Import Costs Rise
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of Myanmar’s currency has disrupted border trade with Thailand, prompting some traders and money changers along the border to suspend transactions as they struggle to cope with volatile exchange rates and mounting import costs.

The currency weakened to around 680 baht per 100,000 kyats this week, down from more than 700 baht in recent weeks. The currency also fell against the U.S. dollar, with the market exchange rate rising from just above 4,700 kyats per dollar at the end of October to more than 4,900 on Wednesday. The rate was just around 4,400 kyats in early October.

The latest slump is fueling concerns over another wave of inflation in a country heavily reliant on imports from Thailand. Myanmar imports a wide range of goods from its neighbor, including electrical appliances, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and foodstuffs, making fluctuations in the baht exchange rate significant for consumers.

Market insiders attributed the kyat’s latest decline to the regime’s plan to borrow 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to finance a budget shortfall for fiscal year 2026-27, which ends on March 31. The regime has already sold treasury bonds worth trillions of kyats, leading to speculation that it will simply print banknotes to cover the deficit.

They also pointed to Myanmar’s continued inclusion on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) blacklist, delays in export licensing and policy inconsistencies between ministries as factors undermining confidence in the market.

The swift depreciation of the kyat has left traders struggling to price goods and manage working capital.

“A gradual rise doesn’t create much difficulty. The problem is when rates surge rapidly,” a trader in Myawaddy told The Irrawaddy.

“If exchange rates rise further, we will need more capital to restock. Some traders have temporarily stopped trading and making payments, and are waiting to see where the market moves.”

The uncertainty has spread beyond traders. Some major money changers in Myawaddy and across the border in Thailand suspended transactions on Wednesday, opting to wait for the next day’s opening rates before resuming business, according to border exchange operators.

The volatility is not confined to the Thai border. Traders in Muse, on Shan State’s border with China, are facing similar difficulties as the kyat continues to weaken against the yuan, market sources said.

Traders warn that prolonged instability in foreign exchange markets could further squeeze trade. Importers say their profits are shrinking, but are reluctant to increase prices for fear that demand may decline further.

A trader in Myawaddy said transport costs remain a major contributor to rising prices, with expenses along trade routes increasing because of checkpoints and demands for unofficial payments.

“Price increases are caused more by transport costs than exchange rates,” he said. “Costs at checkpoints rise sharply whenever authorities announce crackdowns or tighter controls.”

Exporters also say the weaker kyat is raising shipping costs because freight charges, container fees and port services are paid in U.S. dollars. At the same time, they complain that mandatory foreign-exchange conversion rules prevent them from fully benefiting from higher market exchange rates.

Under existing regulations, exporters must convert 35 percent of their export earnings at the Central Bank’s official rate, creating a significant gap between official and market rates. The Central Bank’s official reference rate remains 2,100 kyats per dollar, while its market trading rate is about 3,660 kyats per dollar. The market rate was around 4,900 kyats on Thursday. Before the coup, the kyat traded at roughly 1,300-1,400 per U.S. dollar.

An exporter from Mon State explained that the depreciation of the kyat has sharply increased the capital required to buy export commodities such as corn and onions.

“Previously, we could buy a container of goods for 10 million kyats from local producers. Now it can require more than 15 million kyats,” he said.

Traders say prices of Thai imports, particularly electrical goods, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and food items, are already climbing as a result of the stronger baht and rising transportation costs.

World.title: Thai Foreign Minister to Visit Myanmar Ahead of ASEAN Summit
World.content:
BANGKOK—Thailand’s foreign minister said he will visit Myanmar on November 12, days before a regional summit where Bangkok will be pressing to normalize ties with the war-torn country.

Sihasak Phuangketkeow’s trip also comes during raised tensions along the countries’ shared border, where Bangkok said clashes between Myanmar’s military and ethnic rebels caused property damage and injured a Thai civilian in Thailand on Thursday.

His visit, announced late Tuesday, is scheduled shortly before a November 16-18 summit of leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila.

Myanmar’s leaders have not been invited to high-level ASEAN meetings since former general Min Aung Hlaing led a 2021 military coup that ousted democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war.

Sihasak told reporters in Beijing his government wants to “hear Myanmar’s latest position” ahead of the summit.

“De-escalation by all parties will help create a conducive atmosphere for essential dialogue and the peace process,” he said.

“If there is progress on these fronts, it will be a positive factor for ASEAN to consider at the leaders summit, as we decide how to move forward on the situation in Myanmar, including Myanmar’s participation in ASEAN meetings,” he added.

Sihasak, who last visited Myanmar in April, said he would meet his counterpart, Tin Maung Swe, on November 12, and a meeting with Min Aung Hlaing was “in the works”.

In July, Bangkok hosted a meeting between Tin Maung Swe and foreign ministers of several ASEAN member states, the first such gathering since the 2021 coup.

The following month Min Aung Hlaing met with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, with the two nations’ military chiefs holding talks two weeks after.

Min Aung Hlaing took over as civilian president in April following elections widely dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Since then he has been given a red-carpet welcome across the region, in India, China and several ASEAN nations.

Myanmar is expected to send a senior civil servant to the Manila summit.

Thailand has stepped up security on its western frontier following last week’s cross-border fire.

On Wednesday, Myanmar’s military blamed “terrorist insurgents”—the term it commonly uses to refer to ethnic-minority armed groups and pro-democracy forces—for wounding a Thai national, according to a statement in state media.

World.title: COP31: Transforming Kazakhstan’s Emissions Trading System Through Digitalization
World.content:
From Nov. 9 to 20, Antalya, Türkiye, is hosting the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31). Its main themes are climate finance, adaptation, the energy transition, reducing the energy intensity of buildings and reporting on commitments made.

Since the first days of its independence, Kazakhstan has been an active and responsible participant in global processes on sustainable development and climate change: it signed and ratified the Kyoto Protocol in 2009 and subsequently joined the Paris Agreement in 2016.

This was preceded by extensive expert and analytical work by the Ministry of Environmental Protection, renamed the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources in 2021, with support from the World Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the United Nations Development Program (UNDP), national experts and the National Chamber of Entrepreneurs of Kazakhstan.

Today, Kazakhstan positions itself as a leader in advancing the green energy transition not only in Central Asia but also across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Kazakhstan was the first country in the region to adopt a Strategy for Achieving Carbon Neutrality by 2060. This year, by Sept. 1 order of the Prime Minister, a Plan of Organizational Measures for implementing the Strategy was approved.

The plan will help integrate decarbonization principles into all areas of the national economy, including sectoral planning systems and the monitoring, reporting and accounting of greenhouse gas emissions on an innovative, digital basis.

The initiative of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to harness the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) is especially relevant to resetting the country’s national emissions trading system. Speaking at the BRICS+ summit on Sept. 13, he again underlined the role of AI in global development and noted that “Kazakhstan regards AI as a strategic priority and is ready to use its advanced computing infrastructure, as well as national and UN digital centers, to expand effective cooperation” for the country’s sustainable development.

COP31 experts note a revival of global carbon trading, particularly in the submission of projects to the voluntary carbon market, which undergo a multi-stage review by the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM). As regards the regulated greenhouse gas market – existing national emissions trading systems and their participation in global carbon trading – discussions continue on avoiding double counting and on building the necessary carbon infrastructure.

Among Asian countries, Kazakhstan was one of the first to launch an emissions trading system (KazETS). It covers 220 installations in the six basic sectors of the economy and is now undergoing a transformation through the development and introduction of auctioning and of production benchmarks drawing on EU and OECD experience. At the same time, full participation of Kazakh enterprises in global carbon trading and access to the carbon markets of other countries require, first and foremost: a gradual phase-out of free allowances; a higher price per tonne of greenhouse gases; the transfer of the existing MRV (monitoring, reporting and verification) system to a digital platform.

For Kazakh exporters, the absence of a modern, internationally recognised infrastructure for monitoring, reporting and verifying CO₂ emissions, and of verifiers accredited in line with international requirements, is currently a serious challenge. At the same time, the experience of leading carbon market players and platforms such as Sylvera, BeZero Carbon, Isometric and Calyx Global shows that AI makes it possible to assess the integrity and risks of carbon projects, to evaluate the carbon footprint and the contribution of enterprises and sectors to the Sustainable Development Goals, and to build digital solutions, including under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

At COP31, the National Pavilion of Kazakhstan will also present a number of digital solutions for resetting the national ETS and creating a regional digital climate hub with the support of the UNFCCC. We hope that this initiative, developed by experts of Astana Hub together with Green Academy, the University of Central Asia and the Kunayev Institute of Mining, with the support of the Swedish company Planboo and SagtaAI, will be supported by the delegations of the Central Asian countries and included in the outcome document of COP31.

The author is Professor Dr. Bakhyt Yessekina, a member of the Green Council under the President of Kazakhstan. Yessekina is the head of the Green Academy Scientific Research and Education Center.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Shaidorov Finishes Fifth at Cup of China, Overcomes Personal Barrier
World.content:
SHENZHEN – Kazakhstan’s Olympic figure skating champion Mikhail Shaidorov finished fifth at the ISU Grand Prix Cup of China on Nov. 8, scoring 263.49 points, nearly 57 points more than at his previous Grand Prix appearance in France. Speaking after the competition, Shaidorov said he had overcome a personal barrier despite missing the podium.

Japan’s Kao Miura claimed gold with 293.25 points, followed by Vladislav Dikidzhi with 282.44 and Evgeni Semenenko with 281.62. Japan’s Shun Sato placed fourth with 277.20 points.

Shaidorov entered the competition following a challenging Grand Prix de France in Angers, where he finished tenth with 206.55 points. After that event, he promised his supporters on Instagram that he would return stronger.

Asked in an interview with The Astana Times whether he had achieved the progress he was seeking, Shaidorov said the competition in Shenzhen marked an important step forward.

“If we look at my performance in France, practically nothing worked out there. But in Shenzhen, I fought until the very end and managed to overcome a certain barrier I had been facing. I’m very happy,” he said.

The Kazakh skater placed fifth in the short program on Nov. 6 with 94.87 points, improving his score from Angers by 14.62 points. His performance included a quadruple Lutz with a step-out, a triple Axel and a quadruple toe loop–triple toe loop combination.

In the free skate on Nov. 8, Shaidorov earned 168.62 points, placing sixth in the segment and fifth overall. His technical element score reached 88.71 points, compared with 58.84 in France.

The program featured a quadruple flip worth 14.14 points, although an underrotated quadruple Lutz and difficulties with other demanding elements affected his final score.

Asked what he considered his main achievement in Shenzhen and what he planned to work on next, Shaidorov placed particular emphasis on perseverance.

“I managed to fight against myself. That’s the most important thing, and I will continue doing that. As for the elements, they’ll work out sooner or later,” he said.

Shaidorov also spoke about what it means to represent Kazakhstan internationally and the support he receives from compatriots who travel abroad to attend his performances.

“It’s an incredible feeling that people travel from Kazakhstan to watch my performances. It’s very motivating because I think very few figure skaters receive this kind of support from their country,” he said.

He added that he hoped such support would inspire young Kazakh figure skaters to pursue their ambitions and compete at major international events.

Beyond the individual performances, international competitions such as the Cup of China also offer a broader opportunity for countries to connect with audiences across borders. According to Shaidorov, Kazakh supporters in the stands highlight the people-to-people dimension of sports diplomacy, extending national visibility beyond the sporting arena.

Although Shaidorov left Shenzhen without a medal, his improved result and comments reflected a clear step forward following his difficult performance in France.

World.title: Kazakhstan Presents Priorities for Europe-Asia Digital Corridor at Meeting in Chisinau
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan presented its priorities for strengthening digital connectivity between Europe and Asia at a high-level meeting organized by the European Commission and the government of Moldova in Chisinau on Nov. 9-10.

Kazakhstan’s Deputy Foreign Minister Arman Issetov took part in the Connectivity Platform Meeting – Digital, which brought together representatives of Central Asian, South Caucasus and Black Sea countries, Türkiye and the European Union, as well as international financial institutions and technology companies. The meeting focused on developing secure and sustainable digital connectivity between Europe and Asia.

Speaking at a ministerial panel session, Issetov highlighted Kazakhstan’s strategic role in advancing transport and digital connectivity across Eurasia.

He placed particular emphasis on the launch of the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic communication line between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan on Oct. 15. The project is expected to create new opportunities for an integrated digital corridor connecting Central Asia and Europe.

Issetov also highlighted prospects for expanding cooperation with the EU, including through the Global Gateway initiative and the Connectivity Platform, with a focus on developing digital infrastructure and implementing joint investment projects. He reaffirmed Kazakhstan’s readiness to further strengthen its technological partnership with the EU and advance regional digital connectivity.

World.title: Kazakhstan Highlights North Aral Sea Restoration at COP31 in Türkiye
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan presented its efforts to restore the North Aral Sea and rehabilitate ecosystems in the Aral Sea region during a panel session at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye.

The session on restoration of aquatic ecosystems was held at the Kazakhstan National Pavilion and featured Vice Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources Mansur Oshurbayev, reported the ministry’s press service.

Speaking at the event, Oshurbayev outlined the country’s measures to restore ecosystems in the Aral Sea region and help communities adapt to climate change.

“For Central Asia, climate change adaptation is first and foremost a matter of water. The history of the Aral Sea illustrates this better than anything else: when a water ecosystem is lost, the stability of the land, climate, human health and the economy of an entire region are also affected,” he said.

North Aral Sea shows signs of recovery

Oshurbayev highlighted the results of efforts to restore the North Aral Sea, noting that water management projects, including the construction of the Kokaral Dam with the participation of the World Bank, have helped preserve the northern part of the sea.

According to him, over recent years, the volume of water in the North Aral Sea has increased from 18.9 billion to more than 23 billion cubic metres. Kazakhstan is also carrying out large-scale afforestation efforts on the dried seabed to reduce the environmental impact of the Aral Sea disaster.

Between 2021 and 2025, forest reclamation activities covered more than 1.1 million hectares. Saxaul planting helps stabilize sandy soils and reduce the spread of salt and dust from the exposed seabed.

Regional cooperation and climate finance

Concluding his remarks, Oshurbayev stressed the importance of expanding international cooperation, attracting climate financing and developing joint scientific monitoring to support the restoration of aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems across Central Asia.

The panel provided an opportunity to present Kazakhstan’s experience in restoring the North Aral Sea and discuss broader approaches to water-related climate adaptation in the region.

Earlier, The Astana Times wrote that Kazakhstan is preparing to sign around 28 cooperation documents, including 19 memorandums of understanding with a preliminary package covering meteorology, energy transition, climate investment, clean technologies, environmental protection and healthcare.

World.title: Beyond Midterms: What America’s Political Shift Means for Central Asia
World.content:
The results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections in the United States have triggered a wave of political speculation in Washington. Discussions about a crisis within the Republican Party, the future of Donald Trump’s political movement, and the potential consequences for American foreign policy have quickly dominated political commentary. Yet much of what is now being described as an unexpected political earthquake was, in fact, widely anticipated.

The Democratic Party’s victory and its return to control of both chambers of Congress represent a significant setback for President Donald Trump. However, the outcome should be understood within the broader historical logic of American domestic politics rather than as an unprecedented transformation of the political system. The president’s party has historically tended to lose congressional seats during midterm elections, as voters use these contests to rebalance political power and express dissatisfaction with the administration.

In this respect, the 2026 results are not entirely surprising. Economic concerns, the rising cost of living, dissatisfaction with the administration, and the consequences of the war with Iran contributed to a broader electoral reaction against Republican leadership.

Washington’s domestic confrontation does not mean a foreign policy reversal

For international partners, the central question is whether the new congressional balance will fundamentally alter US foreign policy. The answer is more complicated than the immediate political headlines suggest.

Democrats will control both the House of Representatives and the Senate beginning in January 2027. This gives them important institutional instruments, including congressional oversight, control over appropriations, investigative hearings, and influence over legislation and senior appointments. The Trump administration will consequently face a more difficult political environment during its remaining two years.

However, the American political system does not give Congress exclusive authority over foreign policy. The president retains considerable constitutional and practical powers in international affairs, including the ability to conduct diplomacy, negotiate with foreign leaders, and direct many aspects of national security policy. Democrats will therefore have significant opportunities to constrain the administration, but they will not automatically be able to reverse its international strategy.

The most likely outcome is a period of increased political friction, institutional scrutiny, and uncertainty rather than an immediate transformation of America’s global priorities. The administration may find it harder to secure funding for certain initiatives and advance its legislative agenda. At the same time, Trump could increasingly rely on executive authority and seek foreign policy achievements to demonstrate leadership.

For Central Asia, this distinction is particularly important. Changes in the balance of power in Washington should not be interpreted as an automatic signal that American engagement with the region will either expand or contract.

Central Asia should look beyond party politics

Relations between the United States and Central Asia have developed over several administrations and increasingly acquired a strategic and economic dimension. The C5+1 framework, regional connectivity, critical minerals, energy security, trade diversification, and technological cooperation have become important elements of the relationship. These priorities are not exclusively associated with one political party.

Some of the most promising areas of cooperation with Central Asia are supported by broader American strategic interests. Competition with China, diversification of critical mineral supply chains, alternative trade routes, and stronger economic partnerships beyond traditional geopolitical centers are issues that extend across party lines.

For Washington, Central Asia is relevant not only because of its geographical position between Russia, China, and South Asia, but also because of its potential contribution to wider economic and strategic connectivity. Kazakhstan and its neighbors are seeking to diversify international partnerships, while the United States has an interest in ensuring that the region remains connected to global markets and does not become overly dependent on a single external power.

The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, commonly known as the Middle Corridor, illustrates this convergence of interests. Its strategic importance extends beyond transportation infrastructure. It concerns the resilience of international supply chains, access to European and Asian markets, and the diversification of trade routes across Eurasia. Growing discussions about connecting the Middle Corridor with the Three Seas Initiative and other European connectivity frameworks could create additional opportunities for US-European-Central Asian cooperation.

Critical minerals represent another important area. The United States is seeking to diversify access to strategic resources and reduce vulnerabilities in supply chains where China maintains a dominant position. Kazakhstan, with its mineral resources and potential for processing and industrial development, can become an important partner. However, realizing this potential requires long-term investment, predictable regulation, technological partnerships, and sustained political attention.

Technology is an equally important emerging dimension. Artificial intelligence, data centers, computing infrastructure, and digital connectivity are creating new opportunities for Central Asian states to position themselves within the global technological economy. As competition between the United States and China increasingly extends into technological standards, infrastructure, and access to computing capabilities, the region’s strategic choices will become more consequential.

These areas provide a practical foundation for bipartisan engagement. A Democratic-controlled Congress may approach certain aspects of international economic policy differently from the Republican majority, but the strategic rationale for strengthening American economic presence in Central Asia is unlikely to disappear.

What should Central Asia expect from Washington?

There are several developments that regional governments should monitor closely.

First, congressional scrutiny of the administration’s foreign policy could complicate initiatives requiring sustained funding or legislative approval. Programs related to development assistance, economic cooperation, and regional security may face greater political debate. This does not necessarily mean that they will be abandoned, but their implementation could become more dependent on congressional negotiations.

Second, US policy toward Russia and China will remain particularly relevant. Democrats may seek greater oversight of the administration’s approach to Moscow, including sanctions enforcement and the broader security implications of the war in Ukraine. At the same time, strategic competition with Beijing is likely to remain one of the few areas where a degree of bipartisan consensus survives. For Central Asian countries, this creates both opportunities and challenges: stronger American interest in regional connectivity may be accompanied by greater expectations concerning sanctions compliance, supply-chain transparency, and technological choices.

Third, the approaching 2028 presidential election will increasingly influence political debates in Washington. Potential presidential contenders will begin defining their positions, and foreign policy will become part of the broader competition over America’s international role. Central Asian governments should therefore avoid interpreting every political statement in Washington as a definitive indication of long-term policy.

The region’s response should remain pragmatic. Rather than aligning expectations with the political fortunes of individual American figures, Central Asian states should strengthen institutional relationships with Congress, the administration, think tanks, business associations, and state-level economic actors. Diversifying these relationships is the most reliable way to preserve continuity across political cycles.

From political uncertainty to strategic opportunity

The most important conclusion from the 2026 midterm elections is that the United States is entering another period of divided government. This will make domestic policymaking more complicated and may increase uncertainty in some areas of foreign policy. But it does not mean that America’s strategic interests in Central Asia are disappearing.

Periods of political transition can also create opportunities for countries capable of presenting clear and mutually beneficial proposals. Central Asia should use the coming period to strengthen its economic and strategic case in Washington: not simply as a region seeking greater American attention, but as a partner contributing to the resilience of global supply chains, energy security, critical mineral diversification, and Eurasian connectivity.

The United States will continue to debate its political direction, and the Republican Party will eventually have to define its post-Trump future. These developments deserve attention, but they should not distract regional policymakers from the longer-term strategic picture.

For Central Asia, the real question is not which party controls Congress. It is whether the region can translate its growing geopolitical and economic relevance into durable partnerships that survive changes in Washington. That is where the most consequential opportunities of the next two years will lie.

The author is Sapargali Shalgimbayev, the president of CFive Intellectual Platform (Astana, Kazakhstan).

The article is published as part of the partnership between The Astana Times and CFive platform.

World.title: Tokayev Highlights Kazakh Language’s Role in National Unity and Development
World.content:
ASTANA — President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev highlighted the importance of the Kazakh language as a factor of national unity, calling for stronger efforts to expand its use in education, culture and digital technologies, during the 10th congress of the International Kazakh Language Society on Nov. 10.

The congress is taking place ahead of the 35th anniversary of Kazakhstan’s independence. Tokayev described the occasion as a historic milestone, noting that the country had made significant progress in strengthening the country since gaining independence.

“We have established ourselves as a united nation, laid the foundations of our country and continued to strengthen them,” he said.

President Tokayev also cautioned against assuming that all challenges related to safeguarding independence had been resolved. Amid growing political, economic and ideological tensions worldwide, he said Kazakhstan’s response should be to strengthen unity and focus on shared national interests.

Kazakh language as a Constitutional priority

He said the new Constitution clearly defines the country’s historical roots, national identity and future direction, while firmly establishing the constitutional status of Kazakh as the state language.

“Therefore, treating the Kazakh language with respect is a civic and moral duty,” he said.

Tokayev stressed that the development of the Kazakh language is closely linked to the country’s broader economic and technological progress.

“If we become a strong, civilized state with a developed economy, leading innovations and technologies, and international recognition, the Kazakh language will also become a strong language,” he said. “As the country’s standing grows, so does the prestige of its state language. This is a fact.”

Kazakh-language education and cultural production expand

Tokayev also highlighted progress in education and cultural production. This year, 71% of children entering school were enrolled in Kazakh-language classes, while the number of Kazakh-language departments in colleges and universities has also increased.

He noted that more books, songs and films in Kazakh are reaching audiences. Of the more than 6,000 books published in Kazakhstan last year, 70% were in Kazakh. This year, 63 of the 71 films produced in the country were released in the state language.

“These figures show that there is strong demand for the Kazakh language among our people. This is a very encouraging development, and we must continue to strengthen this work,” Tokayev said.

Digital resources and AI

He added that the language’s future is not under threat and pointed to its growing presence on digital platforms and in advanced technologies. According to research conducted by OpenAI, Kazakh is among the languages whose use in artificial intelligence systems has expanded rapidly over the past three years.

At the same time, Tokayev identified the creation of a national digital database of Kazakh-language resources as a key priority.

“We often say that the Kazakh language has an exceptionally rich vocabulary. There is no doubt that this is true. Our literary and cultural heritage is also vast. However, it is difficult to say that much of this wealth has been fully and accurately transferred into digital systems,” he said.

Tokayev reiterated that promoting Kazakh should not come at the expense of other languages spoken in the country.

“Developing the Kazakh language does not mean hindering the development of other languages in our country. In other words, we must never pit our native language against other languages,” he said.

Tokayev warned against attempts to use language issues to provoke social tensions and conflict, saying those responsible should be held accountable under the principle of Law and Order.

World.title: Kazakhstan Advances Long-Term Development and Governance Framework for Alatau City
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is developing a long-term development plan and a special regulatory framework for Alatau City to lay the foundations for investment, business activity and urban governance, the Prime Minister’s press service reported on Nov. 9.

The Alatau City Council meeting, chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov, discussed the plan. Participants reviewed a draft 30-year development plan prepared with international consultants from Arup, a London-based multinational firm specializing in engineering and urban planning, based on an assessment of the territory, its economic and demographic potential, and the city’s spatial, transport and engineering infrastructure.

The plan aims to create a modern and sustainable city with an attractive investment environment, comfortable living conditions and predictable rules for businesses. It also addresses urban planning, environmental and territorial constraints, the integration of investment projects, and infrastructure needs in line with projected population and employment growth.

The council also reviewed two draft regulatory provisions intended to establish the legal framework for Alatau’s special legal regime. One sets common requirements for regulatory acts, including procedures for their preparation, adoption and implementation, as well as legal review, public consultations and publication in Kazakh, Russian and English.

The second document regulates the activities of legal entities operating as residents of Alatau under the special legal regime. It is intended to improve legal certainty, ensure regulatory transparency and create favorable conditions for business development and investment.

Participants also discussed establishing a Regulatory Commission, a collegial body within the city administration that will help develop Alatau’s regulatory framework. Candidates for independent membership include experts with international experience in law, investment, financial regulation, digital assets and urban planning.

The meeting also covered organizing specialized administrative bodies responsible for land management, urban planning, construction project support, digital asset development and providing services to residents and businesses through a one-stop-shop system.
