World.title: Kazakhstan tests Tumar 112 app to improve fire safety
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 10. Kazakhstan is piloting the digital fire prevention system Tumar 112 in its Abai Region as part of efforts to strengthen fire safety in residential areas, the press service of the country’s government reported.

According to the publication, the mobile application allows authorities to keep electronic records of residential inspections, document fire hazards using photographs and geolocation data, and build a unified database. Minister of Emergency Situations Murat Mukhanov presented the system at a government meeting.

The collected information is expected to help identify homes most vulnerable to fires, track the elimination of detected violations and provide emergency services with up-to-date information when responding to fire reports. Following the pilot project in Abai Region, the system is planned for further rollout across the country, the report says.

Alongside digital prevention measures, Kazakhstan is expanding its firefighting infrastructure and strengthening the resources of civil protection services. Nineteen fire stations have been built across the country this year, including seven universal facilities designed to accommodate both firefighting and medical services.

The country is also purchasing more than 160 fire engines, around 1,500 pieces of equipment and over 2,000 sets of protective clothing. Under the “Auyl Qutqarushylary” (Village Rescuers) programme, 312 firefighting points are currently operating and providing protection to 978 settlements.

The government is also increasing staffing levels in emergency response units, with 592 additional positions approved to strengthen their personnel capacity and readiness to respond to emergencies. During the heating season, particular attention is being paid to residential fire safety.

More than 93,000 homes belonging to socially vulnerable groups are included in the country's targeted fire prevention programme. Since August, authorities have cleaned 6,100 chimneys, repaired 3,100 stoves and 3,400 electrical systems, and installed more than 13,000 fire detectors.

A campaign titled “Check Your Parents' Home” has also been launched to identify and eliminate fire hazards in the homes of elderly people.

In North Kazakhstan Region, local authorities allocated 1.4 billion tenge ($3.1 million) from the regional budget in 2025 to strengthen the material and technical resources of civil protection services, with another 1.5 billion tenge ($3.4 million) earmarked for 2026. The funding has been used to purchase fire engines, all-terrain vehicles, boats, hovercraft, communication equipment, drones and thermal imaging cameras.

Under the Village Rescuers programme, eight firefighting points were established in the region in 2025 and another 14 opened this year. Seventeen additional points are planned by the end of 2026, which is expected to extend fire protection to 135 villages with a combined population of around 45,000.

The measures have helped reduce the number of fires in the region's residential sector by more than half. Since the start of the current heating season, 23 fires have been recorded, compared with 51 during the same period last year, with no deaths or injuries reported.

At the national level, the 2025-2026 heating season saw a 16% decrease in the number of fires compared with the previous season. The number of fatalities fell by 6.4%, while injuries declined by 26%.

More than 55% of fires during the heating season occur in residential buildings, primarily private houses. The main causes include violations of electrical appliance operating rules (39.2%), improper use of stove heating (29.6%) and careless handling of fire (11.5%).

World.title: Azerbaijani FM presents “Dostlug” Order to Serbian ambassador (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 10. Azerbaijan’s Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov has presented the “Dostlug” Order to Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Serbia Dragan Vladisavljević during a meeting in Baku, on November 10.

According to the Azerbaijani Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the parties discussed issues regarding the development of strategic partnership relations between Azerbaijan and Serbia and the expansion of bilateral cooperation.

At the beginning of the meeting, the "Dostlug" Order, awarded by the President of Azerbaijan to the ambassador in recognition of his contributions to the development of relations between the two countries, was presented to him, accompanied by a congratulatory message.

Expressing his deep gratitude for this high honor, Vladisavljević described it as a testament to the high value placed on Azerbaijan-Serbian relations.

During the meeting, satisfaction was expressed regarding the high level of relations between the two countries, which are based on friendship and mutual respect. Bayramov highlighted the role of political dialogue, reciprocal visits, and high-level contacts in the development of bilateral ties.

The parties noted the importance of mutual support for the norms and principles of international law, particularly regarding the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states.

Discussions also covered the expansion of economic and trade relations in recent years, the promotion of mutual investments, and the development of cooperation in sectors such as energy, transport and logistics, industry, agriculture, tourism, and the humanitarian sphere.

Furthermore, an exchange of views took place regarding cooperation within the framework of regional and international organizations, the alignment of positions on issues of mutual interest, and the continuation of mutual support.

During the meeting, the ambassador, who is concluding his diplomatic mission, was wished success in his future endeavors. Vladisavljević expressed his gratitude for the support and cooperation extended to him during his tenure in Azerbaijan and voiced his confidence that the friendly relations between Azerbaijan and Serbia would continue to develop.

World.title: Belarus, Turkmenistan hold political consultations on international legal cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 10. Belarus and Turkmenistan have reviewed the implementation of existing bilateral agreements and discussed the preparation of new international legal documents during consultations in Minsk, the press service of the Turkmen government reported.

According to the publication, the Belarusian delegation was headed by Andrei Popkov, Head of the Main Treaty and Legal Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, while the Turkmen delegation was led by Eziz Nazarov, Head of the Ministry's Treaty and Legal Department. Deputy Foreign Minister of Belarus Pavel Utyupin delivered the opening remarks at the meeting.

The consultations covered an inventory and reconciliation of international treaties and other legal documents currently in force between the two countries. The sides also examined practical aspects of implementing existing agreements and reviewed progress on draft bilateral documents.

Particular attention was paid to the safekeeping of original international treaties and current issues of international law.

Following the consultations, the heads of the two delegations signed a final protocol formalizing the agreements reached.

Notably, Turkmenistan and Belarus have maintained regular political and economic contacts, with the two sides describing each other as strategic partners. Economic cooperation has traditionally focused on industrial goods, machinery, agriculture, transport and infrastructure.

Earlier work of the Intergovernmental Turkmen-Belarusian Commission on Economic Cooperation identified mechanical engineering, agro-industry, construction, transport and communications among the areas with potential for expanded trade. Belarusian proposals included supplies of trucks, buses and agricultural machinery to Turkmenistan, while a Belarusian Machinery Service Center operates in Ashgabat.

The economic track remained on the agenda in 2026. During inter-ministerial consultations in Ashgabat in May, the sides reviewed bilateral trade and discussed ways to expand economic cooperation, including through the private sector. They also highlighted cooperation in education, science and culture.

World.title: Eleven unknown Australian soldiers killed in WWI formally identified
World.content:
Eleven Australian soldiers killed in World War I have been formally identified for the first time to ensure their service and sacrifice are recognised by future generations.

The men, long commemorated as unknown soldiers, were identified through extensive historical research, archaeological investigations, and DNA analysis.

Private Thomas Easton from Adamstown, NSW, was part of the Australian Imperial Force's 30th Battalion. (Supplied: Department of Defence)

The newly identified Australian soldiers are:

Private Roy Hawkins, 3rd Battalion AIF, of Armidale, New South Wales

Sergeant Charles Henry Nicholls, 46th Battalion AIF, of Ballarat, Victoria

Lieutenant Howard Victor Morey, 58th Battalion AIF, of Lilydale, Victoria.

Lieutenant John Maher Lyons MC, MM, MSM, 17th Battalion AIF, of Randwick, New South Wales

Lieutenant Andrew Anderson, 7th Australian Machine Gun Company AIF, of Bundaberg, Queensland

Second Lieutenant James Albert McMichael, 37th Battalion AIF, of Melbourne, Victoria

Private Thomas Easton, 30th Battalion AIF, of Adamstown, New South Wales

Corporal Harry Maitland Whiteoak, 2nd Australian Field Ambulance AIF, of Preston, Victoria

Private George Laban Lupson, 2nd Australian Field Ambulance AIF, of Fremantle, Western Australia

Private James Campbell, 2nd Australian Field Ambulance AIF, of Queenstown, Tasmania

Lance Corporal Alexander Joseph Jack, 2nd Australian Field Ambulance AIF, of Brunswick, Victoria

Lieutenant John Lyons MC, MM, MSM, from Randwick, New South Wales, was part of the Australian Imperial Force's 17th Battalion. (Supplied: Department of Defence)

Descendants of the identified soldiers, French authorities and independent researchers assisted Defence's Unrecovered War Casualties — Army (UWC-A) team, the Office of Australian War Graves and the Commonwealth War Graves Commission.

The federal government announced the identities for Remembrance Day, which this year marks 108 years since the Armistice was signed to end the conflict.

Name to be added to headstone 109 years after death

Among the 11 newly identified soldiers is Lieutenant Andrew Anderson, who was killed in action on September 20, 1917, during the Battle of Menin Road near Ypres, Belgium.

He was 23 years old.

Researchers say fellow soldiers buried Lieutenant Anderson on the battlefield near Westhoek, with an eyewitness account describing a roadside burial marked with a wooden cross.

In March 1919, an unknown soldier's remains were recovered from almost the same location and reinterred at Hooge Crater Cemetery.

Lieutenant Andrew Anderson from Bundaberg in Queensland was part of the Australian Imperial Force's 7th Machine Gun Company. (Supplied: Department of Defence)

The original grave registration record noted "Anderson on shirt", indicating that the soldier's clothing bore the name Anderson, but his identity was not established at the time.

More than a century later, an independent historical researcher identified the possible connection between that unknown soldier and Lieutenant Anderson.

In 2020, she submitted her findings to the Commonwealth War Graves Commission and the UWC-A team, who took up the investigation and established an evidentiary link between Lieutenant Anderson and the unknown Australian soldier.

Now, 109 years after his death, Lieutenant Anderson's headstone at Hooge Crater Cemetery can be replaced to commemorate him by name.

Lieutenant Howard Morey from Lilydale in Victoria was part of the Australian Imperial Force's 58th Battalion. (Supplied: Department of Defence)

'The ultimate expression of lest we forget'

Defence Minister Richard Marles said the identification was "deeply personal" for his family since Lieutenant Anderson was his great-uncle.

"Like so many Australian families, we've carried the story of a relative who served their country and never came home," Mr Marles said.

"For more than a century, Andrew Anderson's final resting place was unknown.

"To know where he now lies and to see him identified by name is profoundly meaningful for my family.

"His story is a reminder of the sacrifice made by a generation of Australians whose service continues to shape our nation. We are proud to remember that sacrifice this Remembrance Day."

Private James Campbell from Queenstown in Tasmania was part of the Australian Imperial Force's 2nd Australian Field Ambulance. (Supplied: Department of Defence)

Veterans' Affairs Minister Matt Keogh said it was through the dedication of military historians, archaeologists, researchers, forensic specialists, and the family members that the soldiers had now been identified.

"The identification of these soldiers who were killed in action across France and Belgium will provide long-awaited answers for families who have experienced generations of uncertainty," Mr Keogh said.

World.title: 'Please don't taser me': Canberra woman sues police over use of force
World.content:
Warning: This story contains footage that some readers may find distressing.

A woman who was tasered by police is suing seven ACT police officers over actions a magistrate has described as "unwarranted and exceedingly heavy-handed".

Officers were called to the Canberra suburb of Deakin in January after a report from a member of the public that a woman with a knife was yelling at passing cars and threatening to stab occupants driving past.

When they arrived, one officer aimed his taser at the woman and told her she was under arrest for having a knife in a public place.

"I haven't got a knife," she replied.

" I haven't done anything wrong bro, please don't taser me. "

Police body-worn camera footage obtained by the ABC shows the woman, who is Aboriginal and has an intellectual disability, being pulled to the ground and held face down by two male police officers.

The footage shows another officer triggering a taser on her bare back.

After that, police can be seen finding two pairs of scissors in her bag, one of which was broken.

A short time later, an officer threatens to "spray" the woman with capsicum spray if she "keeps trying to fight".

The body cam footage also shows handcuffs were placed around her wrists at her back, and she was moved headfirst onto the floor of the caged section of a police vehicle.

Special Magistrate Sean Richter watched the video footage during an ACT Magistrates Court sentencing hearing in September.

"I consider that the actions of the police in that matter were unwarranted and heavy-handed," he said.

" I find it amazing that in this day and age the police reacted in the way that they did. "

Special Magistrate Sean Richter described the actions of police as "unwarranted and heavy-handed". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The court heard the woman had lived with a mental impairment and neurocognitive disorder after receiving a traumatic brain injury in a car accident when she was 12.

"It's blatantly apparent to anyone that deals with this woman that she has a significant cognitive disorder and should be treated as such," Magistrate Richter said.

Magistrate Richter, a former member of the South Australian police force, described the actions of police as "incredibly heavy-handed" in circumstances where they were familiar with the woman's vulnerabilities.

"She's a woman who was putting up no resistance," he said.

" I sometimes wonder when we lost the ability to speak to people. "

The woman, known as Emma, was charged with five offences.

Her last name cannot be revealed because of legal reasons associated with an unrelated matter also before the courts.

The then-35-year-old, who was on bail at the time for other unrelated offences, spent a month remanded in custody at the Alexander Maconochie Centre.

By the time she was sentenced in September 2026, all but one charge — possessing a knife without a reasonable excuse — had been withdrawn.

She pleaded guilty to that offence and was convicted in September.

'The public needs to see'

The Aboriginal Legal Service (ALS), which represented Emma in her criminal case, said it was time police were accountable for their conduct.

Sharif Deen of the Aboriginal Legal Service called the footage "horrifying". (Supplied: Aboriginal Legal Service)

"This footage is horrifying, but it's something the public needs to see," ALS acting chief executive Sharif Deen said.

"Sadly, the Aboriginal Legal Service sees evidence of this every day.

" Independent police oversight is long overdue in the ACT. "

Lawsuit alleges misfeasance, assault and human rights breaches

A civil case filed on Emma's behalf accuses the Commonwealth and seven ACT Policing officers of assault and battery, breaching her human rights, and misfeasance in public office.

It alleges an officer made a series of misleading claims and omissions about the incident, which resulted in unsustainable charges being laid and the woman subsequently being refused bail.

It also claims the officers involved applied unlawful force during her arrest, and that they acted in a way that failed to consider and was incompatible with her human rights.

Police body worn camera footage shows the woman being pulled to the ground and held face down by two male police officers. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Lawyer Michael Lalor, who is representing Emma, said the case would have major legal significance.

"It raises questions in general about police use of force in relation to Aboriginal people, in relation to people with a disability — particularly the use of force with weapons," Mr Lalor said.

" It also raises questions about the standards which our community is prepared to accept in relation to policing. "

Mr Lalor is seeking damages for his client.

He said he was struck by his client's resilience.

"I think to anyone who's seen the footage, you could understand the effect it might have on someone," Mr Lalor said.

The defendants have not yet been required to file a defence.

ACT Policing said it noted comments made by the magistrate who sentenced Emma.

"As an associated civil claim is underway in relation to this matter, it would not be appropriate to provide further comment," a spokesperson said.

ACT Police Minister Marisa Paterson said she "shared the concerns of the community."

"ACT Policing plays a vital role in keeping our community safe, and I have confidence in the professionalism and commitment of its officers," she said in a statement.

Increasing use of tasers

The matter is among 29 civil proceedings on foot as of August 2026 that relate to ACT Policing action.

Eighteen of those include claims relating to unreasonable use of force by police.

ACT police officers are required to renew "use of force" qualifications annually.

They are also required to submit a "use of force" report when they use force that is not considered "routine".

ACT Policing has seen an increase in the use of tasers. (Getty Images: Sascha Schuermann)

In the last financial year, tasers were involved in 294 "use of force" reports — more than one in every five incidents.

That number has increased by 16 per cent since 2024-25.

Overall, the number of "use of force" reports submitted by ACT Policing rose from 1,175 to 1,387 in the 12 months to June 30, 2026.

World.title: Adelaide council backflips on fossil fuel ad ban amid Tour Down Under fears
World.content:
Adelaide City Council has backflipped on its ban of fossil fuel advertising in the city weeks after voting in favour.

On Tuesday Deputy Lord Mayor Carmel Noon put forward a special motion to revoke that ban "in its entirety". It passed eight votes to two.

"We should not make the decision first and find out the consequences afterwards," she said.

Speaking in support of the move to revoke the ban, Arman Abrahumzadeh said members would "deserve a spot in the national gymnastics team given the backflip that we've made".

The about-face followed a vote that narrowly passed two weeks ago in favour of banning oil, coal and gas companies from any advertising in council-owned public spaces, including on bus stops, banners and billboards as of July 2027.

The ban prompted backlash, including from the state government, due to concerns about how it might affect Australia's biggest cycling event, the Tour Down Under, whose main sponsor is gas giant Santos.

In feedback tabled alongside Cr Noon's motion, the council administration advised its support for rolling back the ban.

It said questions remained over the "legal validity" and "practical implementation issues" of the ban.

The Tour Down Under village has been a mainstay of the Adelaide CBD, but could be impacted by a ban on fossil fuel sponsorship. (ABC Radio Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Council to investigate implications of ban

Another motion also passed, calling on council administration to further investigate the implications of restricting fossil fuel s, and report back by May 2027.

But Lord Mayor Jane Lomax-Smith expressed concern that this new motion, which passed, six votes to four, could still impact the Tour.

"What worries me most, when there is a major event being planned, the details are designed to fit around the sponsors and by not having this report until May there will be a level of uncertainty of our capacity of having the event in our city," she said.

The council also asked the lord mayor to write to the state government over "growing community concern regarding the promotion of coal, oil and gas sponsorship on publicly owned assets within the City of Adelaide".

It will ask the government for "advice on how sponsorship and partnership arrangements are considered in the context of the South Australia [sic] Government’s Net Zero Strategy 2024–2030".

Jane Lomax-Smith remains concerned about the potential for a new motion to impact planning for the Tour Down Under. (ABC News)

Councillor Keiran Snape proposed the original ban and voted against its revocation on Tuesday.

"It's not ideal that the motion is being revoked, but the new motion coming in is an excellent compromise," he said.

"This council is firm on climate action and our community wants to see that happen as well."

Councillor Eleanor Freeman supported the original motion, but voted to rescind it on Tuesday.

"The intent two weeks ago was noble. Sometimes effect can outweigh intent. I feel there have been some undesired effects as a result of the [original] decision," she said.

"Tonight we looked to correct course and find a better way that's in partnership with the state government to investigate how we can have more climate action."

World.title: Trailblazing diabetes educator named 2027 NT Australian of the Year
World.content:
An educator and nurse credited with transforming diabetes care in Central Australia has been named the Northern Territory's 2027 Australian of the Year.

Helen Lamech has worked in the Northern Territory for more than 30 years, and has spent the past decade working to reduce diabetes rates in Central Australia and improve outcomes for people with the disease.

Helen Lamech has been named the NT's Australian of the Year for 2027. (ABC News: Xavier Martin )

She established Central Australia's first nurse-led diabetes clinic in Alice Springs, and regularly travels to remote NT communities, where diabetes affects up to two in five adults.

Ms Lamech estimates she has treated and helped educate more than 5,000 people in the NT and mentored more than 300 other health professionals, and says she likes to meet people wherever she can — in homes, schools, and parks — to chat about how to prevent and manage diabetes.

She said she hoped to use the award to take her diabetes advocacy to the national stage.

"We've got the worst diabetes rate in the world in Central Australia and I feel like we're not taking it seriously," she said.

"I am very passionate and I'm very blessed that I'm doing a job that I love and I get paid for it. I don't see it as a job."

Helen Lamech is "passionate" about her work as a diabetes educator in the Northern Territory. (Supplied: Helen Lamech)

Last night, Ms Lamech and four other Territorians were recognised at the 2027 NT Australian of the Year Awards ceremony in Darwin.

They will join the winners from all the states and territories at the national awards in Canberra on January 25 next year.

NT Senior Australian of the Year

During Cyclone Tracy, Pat King worked for three days straight as an ambulance volunteer — taking emergency calls, triaging survivors and helping families through the storm that flattened Darwin and left 66 people dead.

Fifty-two years years later, she's still serving the Top End community at the age of 74, with her efforts earning her the title of 2027 NT Senior Australian of the Year.

Today, Ms King offers confidential support to police officers as a volunteer chaplain with NT Police and the Australian Federal Police.

Pat King has been volunteering in the Top End since before Cyclone Tracy. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

She attributes her dedication to volunteering to her parents, who were missionaries and survived a World War II prisoner of war camp.

"Giving back to the community is part of what we do. It's how I was brought up," she said.

When asked whether she has plans to slow down, Ms King was quick to answer: "Good grief, no."

NT Young Australian of the Year

Katherine local Taitt Green is just 18, but he has already been involved in responses to fires, floods and cyclones as a volunteer with St John Ambulance, the NT Fire and Rescue Service and as an air force cadet.

Taitt Green says he enjoys helping others. (Supplied: Salty Dingo)

When a hay shed fire threatened large gas tanks in Katherine last year, Mr Green put his life on the line and risked an explosion to extinguish the blaze. During the floods in the town in March, he waded into chest-deep water to help a woman to safety.

"It all started at a young age for me," he said.

"My dad did the firies, SES and St John's. Once I turned 16 I joined up to better the community and help people.

"I guess I enjoy helping my community and serving others."

NT Local Heroes

Majors Niall and Michelle Gibson spend up to 100 hours in the air each year, visiting some of the most geographically isolated people in Australia as remote chaplains with the Salvation Army.

Each year they visit about 80 remote cattle stations, schools, police stations, health centres and outback towns, where connectivity is often limited.

Not only do the couple conduct weddings, funerals and christenings, they provide crisis support during events such as the Katherine floods early this year.

NT Administrator David Connolly presents Michelle and Niall Gibson with their award. (Supplied: Salty Dingo)

"All we do sometimes is just have a cup of tea with people, but it's so appreciated and it's great. We love all the people," Ms Gibson said.

"My word for the night is unbelievable ... the other people nominated are heroes of ours."

World.title: Khawaja denies starting 'witch hunt' over Sandpapergate claims
World.content:
Usman Khawaja has defended his version of events about the Australian Test team's 2018 ball-tampering saga in South Africa, after former teammate Mitchell Starc maintained the bowling group had no idea about 'Sandpapergate'.

During a wide-ranging interview on 7.30, Khawaja stuck to his guns on the issue once again splitting Australian cricket eight years after the infamous Test match in Cape Town when batsman Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball.

Khawaja also denied he intended to start a "witch hunt" or use the saga to sell copies of his newly released book, while conceding he was unsure if this would damage friendships he made throughout his career, especially with current Australian captain Pat Cummins.

"I'm not here to inflame the situation anymore," Khawaja told 7.30.

"I'm not here to go on a witch hunt.

"All I've ever wanted is for us to take accountability as a team and I don't think that's a lot to say.

"I'm not asking a lot from people and I say, 'we were a part of it, that was us'. Let's just take accountability.

"I was here to tell my truth, what I saw, what I felt, and to stick with those three guys that were made out to be the only people who have taken it [accountability]."

The three players Khawaja referred to were his childhood friend David Warner, then-Australian Test captain Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft.

Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith speak with umpires during the Test match. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman)

Smith and Warner, who was the vice-captain, were banned from cricket for 12 months and Bancroft received a nine-month ban.

Warner has since backed Khawaja's version of events "100 per cent", but on Tuesday afternoon Starc told Fox Cricket's season launch that he did not know a substance was taken onto the field to tamper with the ball.

In 2021, Starc joined fellow bowlers Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon in releasing a statement disputing any suggestion they had prior knowledge of ball tampering plans.

"I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but, from where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed, and my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021."

Cummins has not spoken publicly since the release of Khawaja's book titled Sabr: Finding my way in cricket and life.

Khawaja echoed comments made by former coach Darren Lehmann that ball tampering had been around a long time.

"If you read my book … the whole team was the architect," he said.

"Whether one person ball tampers or another.

"And when I say we were all the architects, I mean, we all need to take accountability as a team.

"I've been very clear not naming names."

He also denied his book was forcing anyone else to admit fault.

"I'm not forcing anyone to do anything," he told 7.30.

"Pat Cummins is a good friend of mine, Mitchell Starc, other players in the team, Shaun Marsh, Mitch Marsh; they're all very good friends of mine."

Khawaja 'not sure' friendship will survive this

Khawaja spoke to 7.30 about the special bond between him and Cummins, who he said had a "special place" in his heart.

Usman Khawaja and Pat Cummins were longtime teammates. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

"I always used to go off the field when they used to spray alcohol, and then Pat Cummins called me back; [that was] the first time in my life I felt really part of the Australian cricket team.

"That's why I've always had so much love for Patty.

" Even when I talk about it now, it's a very emotional time, a very emotional feeling for me. "

Asked if his book might damage that friendship, Khawaja said he didn't know.

"I'm not sure," Khawaja admitted.

"I've been friends with Pat a long time.

"I've given my reasons at the end of the day … I've always stood for my values and what I think is right … but I can't speak for Pat."

Not about selling books, says Khawaja

While Khawaja was also critical of Cricket Australia's investigation into the incident as being "rushed", he was asked about the timing of the revelations made in his book.

"A lot of people have put up a narrative that I'm somehow gaining from this, but at no stage was sandpaper ever discussed in 2023 when I signed my book deal," Khawaja said.

"My manager didn't even know about it until six months ago, neither did anyone really at Penguin.

"All they said to me was, write your story. Whether I wrote about sandpaper or not would not have made one bit of difference.

"When I gave it to them six months ago, they were shocked, because I don't really talk about this to anyone.

"I could have taken it out and they couldn't say a word, but I chose to put it in there."

Khawaja, the first Muslim to play cricket for Australia, wrote in the book about his role as a trailblazer for South Asian Australian cricketers.

At times during his career, the issue of racism was raised. Khawaja himself, in his book, says he felt that after Smith was banned, he was not made captain because of the colour of his skin.

Tim Paine became Test captain after Steve Smith was stood down. (AAP: Scott Barbour)

Rather than say being overlooked was racism, Khawaja told 7.30 it was simply how he felt at the time.

"There's no concrete evidence of that in terms of what I heard," Khawaja said.

"Whenever I talk about racism or anything along those lines, it's how I feel at the time, but yes that's how I felt.

"I caveat that at the same time with a year later, when Tim Paine was captain, I look back on it and I think, actually … Tim Paine was a great captain.

"At the time, I felt a bit aggrieved, but when I look back on it, I actually don't think it was the wrong decision."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: South32 refinery workers strike as $8b Alcoa takeover looms
World.content:
Maintenance staff at one of the world's biggest alumina refineries have gone on strike as they push for improved pay and conditions.

The industrial action by South32 staff at the Worsley Alumina facility, 200 kilometres south of Perth, comes ahead of a multi-billion-dollar takeover by US miner Alcoa.



Workers, alongside Electrical Trades Union (ETU) and Australian Manufacturing Workers Union (AMWU) representatives, formed a picket line along the refinery's entrance road on Tuesday morning.

More than 100 workers from the refinery are taking part in the industrial action. (Supplied: BHP)

In July Alcoa announced it would buy South32's major bauxite mine and alumina refinery as part of a deal worth more than $8 billion.

The strike marked the start of 48 hours of protected industrial action, coinciding with a planned shutdown at the main processing plant that refines raw bauxite into alumina at the site.

Union representatives are trying to finalise a renewed enterprise bargaining agreement before ownership changes hands in the first half of 2027.

Unions claim pay, condition gap

The dispute rests on what unions allege is a significant difference in working conditions between South32 staff and those doing similar work at Alcoa.

"What we're always open to do is negotiations," ETU WA secretary Adam Woodage said.

"However, we haven't heard from South32 since they had an overwhelming 'no' vote on their latest offer to this workforce."

Adam Woodage says South32 has been uncommunicative since the workers rejected its latest offer. (ABC South West WA: Kirsty Lichtenstein)

The union representatives also said the potential loss of discretionary bonuses after the Alcoa takeover could cost workers up to 10 per cent of their wages.

Workers on the picket line asked for their names to be withheld due to the potential workplace impact.

One employee of 15 years said the stoppage was ultimately about standing up for newer workers, who he said were receiving inferior pay and conditions despite performing identical work.

Another said conditions had been steadily whittled away since South32 was spun out of BHP in 2015.

Steve McCartney says the workers are facing the same challenges as most Australians. (ABC South West WA: Kirsty Lichtenstein)

AMWU WA secretary Steve McCartney said the decision to strike was not made lightly.

"They're like everyone else — they're trying to pay bills, they're trying to pay houses off, they're trying to get kids through school," he said.

"They deserve to be paid the same money, doing the same job at the same end of town."

A South32 spokesperson said the company continued to engage constructively with staff and noted a range of worker benefits beyond base pay.

The spokesperson said the existing "short-term benefit policy" would continue under Alcoa's ownership, which had been communicated to staff and unions.

"We want to find ways to address issues they may have while ensuring our operation remains sustainable," the spokesperson said.

"We have plans in place to support ongoing operations at Worsley Alumina during this time and do not expect any impact on our operations."

World.title: 22yo jockey dies from injuries sustained in race fall
World.content:
The family of young apprentice jockey Izzy Neale has confirmed she has died after suffering critical injuries from falling off her horse during a race in western NSW on the weekend.

In a statement posted on social media by Racing NSW, Izzy Neale's family said it was "with deep sadness and broken hearts that we announce the passing of our beloved Izzy".

They said she died "surrounded by her closest family and friends" and through organ donation "Izzy will give others the chance of life, bringing some comfort to family amid this devastating loss".

"Izzy rode horses before she could walk," the family's statement said. "Her love of horses was a lifelong passion that, more recently, had grown into a love of racing."

Izzy Neale's family said her organ donation would bring "some comfort" to her loved ones. (Supplied: Instagram )

The 22-year-old was riding in the Cotton Cup at Warren on Sunday when she suffered head injuries following a fall at the 400-metre mark during a 1,600m event.

She was treated onsite before being airlifted to Dubbo Hospital for further medical care, where she remained in a critical condition until her death.

Her horse, Marnoo, was euthanased after sustaining a near foreleg injury.

Tribute to medical staff

Her family said it was "deeply grateful for the love, kindness and support shown to Izzy and our family by her friends, the racing community and everyone who has been by our side during this heartbreaking time."

It also paid tribute to the medical staff who cared her "with such compassion" and the racing fraternity.

"We would like to thank Racing NSW and the NSW Jockeys Association for their care, compassion and support during this incredibly difficult time." they said .

"As we come to terms with our loss, we ask that our family's privacy be respected.

"Izzy was dearly loved and will forever be in our hearts."

World.title: Truck driver sentenced to community service over 2023 NT train derailment
World.content:
A Northern Territory truck driver who collided with a train at a railway crossing near Katherine has been sentenced to 150 hours of community service more than three years after the horror crash.

Christopher Berto pleaded guilty in the Darwin Local Court last month to two counts of careless driving causing serious harm over the collision that injured two train drivers in June 2023.

The 37-year-old Katherine man returned to court for sentencing today, supported by a large group of family members, and with a number of the victims' relatives also present.

Loading...

The court heard Berto was carrying 22 tonnes of gravel in a prime mover when the truck collided with the train, derailing several carriages.

Judge Steven Ledek said Berto failed to notice multiple warning signs indicating a train was approaching, including flashing lights, gongs and the train's horn, before attempting to brake 100 metres before reaching the crossing.

"It was at that point that he slammed on his brakes, having realised there was a train on the tracks and was coming through the crossing," he said.

In an apology letter tendered in court, Christopher Berto said there were "no words which could adequately express how sorry I am". (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

Judge Ledek said Berto was unable to stop the truck and instead accelerated through the crossing, crashing through the lowered boom gates and into the train.

"The impact was catastrophic," he said.

" The damage was carnage. "

The court heard one of the two injured men required surgery on his wrist as a result of the crash, while the other suffered ongoing back pain and was forced to give up his job as a train driver.

'No good reason' to miss warning signs

The judge said Berto had previously visited the crossing seven times on the morning of the accident.

"There is no good reason that a person could avoid all those alarms, gongs, signs and lights unless of course that person has become so familiar with the routine that they become less important and less instructive," he said.

In a letter of apology to the victims, which the judge read aloud in court, Berto said he held "deep regret" for his actions.

Steven Ledek described the damage caused by the crash as "carnage". (Supplied: NTPFES)

"There are no words which could adequately express how sorry I am for the pain, hardship and disruption I have caused," he wrote.

"I think often about what happened and the consequences you have had to endure because of these actions.

"I am truly remorseful knowing that both of you have had to live with the physical, emotional and financial consequences of this accident and it weighs heavily on me.

"While I cannot change what happened, I want you to know I accept responsibility and am genuinely sorry for the harm I have caused."

The train was derailed in the crash in the Katherine suburb of Cossack on June 14, 2023. (Supplied: Simone Siedel)

Prosecutor Rhiannon McGlinn previously told the court she would not ask for Berto, who had a spotless driving record and was not speeding at the time of the crash, to be disqualified from driving.

In sentencing Berto to a two-week intensive community corrections order today, Judge Ledek said a custodial sentence was warranted due to the seriousness of the crash.

But he said given his good character and the unlikelihood of him reoffending, it would be appropriate for him to serve his sentence in the community.

World.title: ‘My recollection hasn’t changed’: Starc rejects tampering claim as Khawaja dodges request to name players
World.content:
Updated SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘My recollection hasn’t changed’: Starc rejects tampering claim as Khawaja dodges request to name players Tom Decent, Scott Spits and Christy Doran Updated November 10, 2026 — 9:13pm ,first published 4:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Mitchell Starc has disputed Usman Khawaja’s explosive claim that every member of the Australian team knew about the ball-tampering plot during the infamous 2018 Test series against South Africa, declaring he has no intention of reading his former teammate’s book and suggesting their future relationship is now in Khawaja’s hands. Amid a series of disclosures in his autobiography, Sabr, which was released on Tuesday, Khawaja suggested the entire Australian team, including now captain Pat Cummins and other bowlers, knew about the plot to use sandpaper on the ball in the third Test in Cape Town eight years ago and that the tactic had also been deployed in the previous Test, in Gqeberha. Usman Khawaja has written about the sandpaper scandal in his new autobiography. Dan Peled But pressed on the ABC’s 7:30 on Tuesday night about whether specific players, including Cummins, were involved in conversations about ball tampering, Khawaja refused to answer. “I’m just not going to entertain that,” Khawaja said.



“And I say that for one reason – I wrote it [the details] in my book because it was a safe space for me to write. “It took a long time to, first, write the chapter .... and go over it and work out a way that it was as balanced as possible.” Asked specifically if Cummins had prior knowledge that sandpaper was being used to change the surface of the ball, Khawaja said: “I’m not going to answer that. I’ve written what I’ve written in my book. “I’ve come out and stood by those three guys [the suspended players David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft] and told my account of what I saw. “I’ve been very clear ... there are instances when I talk about ‘us’ and ‘them’, but I’ve been very clear in not naming names and staying out of it. I’m not going to start now.



“This has never been a witch hunt for me. “You’ve got to remember [that] Pat Cummins is a good friend of mine. Mitchell Starc, a lot of these guys [are and] other players in the team [are too]. “I’m not here to go on a witch hunt. All I’ve ever wanted is for us to take accountability as a team.” The latest sandpaper saga developments came as Starc’s wife and former Australian cricketer Alyssa Healy said she would have no problem sharing a commentary box with Khawaja and Warner this summer, despite describing the timing of the controversial book as “a little bit stinky”, while former England captain Michael Vaughan said he would have liked Khawaja to donate its profits to charity. Mitchell Starc said he “hadn’t paid much attention” to the claims made by Usman Khawaja in his autobiography. Janie Barrett



With Khawaja’s allegations – backed by Warner on Monday evening – threatening to overshadow the start of Australia’s home Test summer, Cricket Australia’s nightmare played out at a Kayo Sports launch in Sydney on Tuesday. Starc became the first member of Australia’s current Test team to face the media since Khawaja’s book reignited debate over who knew what during the ill-fated tour that culminated in Bancroft being caught concealing sandpaper down his trousers in Cape Town. The veteran fast bowler was polite but bristled visibly when asked questions about the scandal, with a Cricket Australia media manager attempting to move the press conference along to a different subject less than four minutes after it began. This time, the wounds of 2018 have been reopened not by the media but by two of Starc’s former Test teammates in Khawaja and Warner, with the latter saying everything in the book is “100 per cent” accurate. Mitchell Starc speaks to reporters at the Golden Sheaf Hotel on Tuesday afternoon. Janie Barrett



On 7:30, Khawaja was quizzed about whether he believed Cricket Australia perpetuated a “cover-up” to stop more players than the three affected from being banned. “I don’t feel like it was a thorough investigation,” Khawaja said. “Because I never got investigated – and I was sitting next to Cameron Bancroft the whole time. So it’s hard for me to say cover-up, but I will say it [the investigation] felt rushed.” As former Australian spinner Kerry O’Keeffe noted on Tuesday: “It’s the bubble around town. Who’s telling the truth? They could all be telling the truth.” Starc said he stood by a joint statement released in 2021 with fellow bowlers Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon denying they had any knowledge that sandpaper had been taken onto the field in Cape Town to tamper with the ball.



Sources close to the other three bowlers, speaking on the condition of anonymity, say they share Starc’s position and have no intention of backing away from their original statement. Cummins, the incumbent Test captain, is being encouraged to front the media this week and address allegations that he and others knew more than they have publicly acknowledged. “I thought we were here for the summer of cricket,” Starc said with a laugh. “I haven’t really paid much attention to it [the coverage of Khawaja’s claims]. Obviously, there are different opinions to about eight years ago. We were heavily drilled through the process at the time and since. I won’t speak on behalf of the bowlers, but where I stand, my opinion hasn’t changed. My recollection hasn’t changed from what we said in 2021.” Asked whether “everyone knew”, Starc responded: “It’s obviously in a book. That’s for someone to explain further. As far as our statement said [in 2021], we weren’t aware of it being taken on the field. That’s where I’ll leave it.” Asked whether he knew the ball was being tampered with in one way or another, Starc said: “We weren’t aware it was taken on the field to be tampered with. We saw it on the big screen [for the first time] in Cape Town. As far as the book’s concerned, I haven’t read it and probably won’t read it, so that’s for Usman to elaborate on.”



Starc also denied knowing that Bancroft or any other Australian player had used sandpaper during the second Test in Port Elizabeth, as alleged by Khawaja. “That’s the first I was aware of it [in Cape Town]. I’ll leave that for the said author to explain,” Starc said. Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins, Usman Khawaja and Josh Hazlewood. Getty Beyond the conflicting accounts of what unfolded in South Africa, Khawaja’s revelations appear to have strained relationships with some of his former teammates. Starc said he had not spoken to Khawaja “in the last day or two”, but when asked whether he would ever speak to him again, his response was telling.



“It’s up to him,” Starc said. One person who will have no choice but to work alongside Khawaja and Warner this summer is Healy, with all three part of the Kayo Sports and Fox Cricket commentary team. Alyssa Healy will share a commentary box with Usman Khawaja and David Warner this summer. Getty Images Speaking on the Keepin’ It Cricket podcast this week, Healy joked that she had been “scraping bits of Mitch off the bitumen after the bus just hit him over the last two days”. “The timing of it is a little bit stinky,” said the former Australian wicketkeeper. “I don’t like that. It’s coming off South Africa, which didn’t end well for the boys.”



But speaking on Tuesday, Healy dismissed suggestions there would be tension in the commentary box and said she had no intention of raising the controversy with either Khawaja or Warner, both long-time teammates of Starc. “I’m not one to sit there and worry about sitting next to anyone in the commentary box, regardless of who it is. We’re a team,” Healy said. Related Article Australian cricket Warner’s manager calls for honesty session after Cricket Australia refuses to re-open sandpaper investigation “From my perspective, it seems to be a little bit closer maybe for me than some of the other [commentators]. Most of the blokes back there just say, ‘Let’s move on and get back to the cricket’. But from my perspective, I’m completely comfortable with [working alongside them].” The controversy has generated so much attention since this masthead’s interview with Khawaja on Saturday that the retired opener admitted to Triple M on Tuesday even he had been surprised by the reaction. But Khawaja denied his revelations were motivated by money.



“The only gripe with me is that it’s come out in a book,” said Vaughan. “Obviously it’s a commercial game. Usman will say not, but I’d have loved for him to have announced that he’s bringing a book out and all the proceeds are going to charity.” With Australia preparing for the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on December 9, Starc made no secret of his frustration that the scandal had once again become a major talking point. “It’s definitely disappointing,” he said. “That’s what we’re talking about heading into what has already kicked off an exciting summer. Different people felt different ways about it at the time and throughout, and certainly through the last eight years. “I think not only the certain players, but certainly, there’s some staff members. ‘Boof’ [coach Darren Lehmann] for one has spoken a little bit as well. He’s not to be forgotten in all of that, too. I think Travis [Head] said it best the other day that the group has changed a lot. We certainly look forward to what’s coming up more so than what’s been gone.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

A crow that spent weeks perched atop a fluorescent light inside a Coles supermarket on Brisbane’s northside has finally left the store. A spokesman for Coles assured concerned customers that the bird was removed safely from the North Lakes store on Tuesday morning, after repeated failed attempts to catch it and coax it outside during its two-week ordeal. “We’re pleased to confirm the crow has been safely removed from our store, and we thank our customers and the community for their patience,” the spokesman said. The crow bides its time inside the North Lakes Coles last week. Julius Dennis However, he refused to reveal exactly how the crow was removed, or whether it made its own way to freedom.



The bird’s welfare generated concern among shoppers and hundreds of local Facebook users, who were initially outraged by rumours that Coles had contracted a third party to euthanise the bird. Coles denied that rumour last week. Many customers walked below the crow without even noticing it. Julius Dennis The crow appeared frazzled during its fortnight inside the store, perched on top of a ceiling light above the cosmetics aisle and leaving excrement on the floor below. The RSPCA visited the supermarket and was told food and water had been made available.



Few people were more relieved at the news of the bird’s new-found freedom on Tuesday than Melissa Webb, who works at a clothing store in the North Lakes shopping centre. Related Article Wildlife ‘I don’t understand’: Questions over plight of crow stuck in supermarket for 10 days Webb had been checking on the crow during her lunch break each day and advocating online for its rescue. But she remains worried about its welfare. “We’re pretty concerned that it will need some kind of care, or at least a good check over after this ordeal,” Webb said. “Hearing that it was just ‘removed’ is not good enough. I think Coles’ conduct around the entire situation has been really sad, especially considering how long the crow was in there, when we have local organisations who have done plenty of animal rescues in other stores and in other Westfields.”

World.title: ‘Definitely in the equation’: Kangaroos stars reveal contract stances
World.content:
SportNRLRugby League World Cup ‘Definitely in the equation’: Kangaroos stars reveal contract stances Nick Wright November 10, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Kangaroos winger Jack Bostock says he’s yet to decide his playing future, as Australian teammate Harry Grant shed light on the motives that would dictate his next move. The off-contract pair have thrown their focus on Australia’s Rugby League World Cup final clash against New Zealand at Suncorp Stadium on Sunday, before attention will turn to their future in the NRL. Bostock has been heavily linked to a shift away from the Dolphins to a host of New South Wales clubs – spearheaded by his junior outfit, the Dragons – while Grant is in the Gold Coast Titans’ sights. Harry Grant and Jack Bostock both insist their current NRL clubs are not out of the race for their signatures. Getty Bostock’s asking price has only risen since returning from a ruptured ACL in round nine, in a season that has included a Blues debut and seven tries in four World Cup appearances.



His form has tightened the retention battle of the Dolphins, who have re-signed Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow but are yet to secure the in-demand Herbie Farnworth, among other off-contract stars. Related Article Rugby League World Cup Walsh and Ponga’s first chapter was a battle for the ages. They are just beginning Bostock is adamant he has made no definitive call on where he will sign his next deal, while stressing the Redcliffe-based side remained well in the hunt for his services. “Apparently … I’m going to [every club], so I’m not too sure – maybe I’m going to play three or four games at each club in 2028,” he joked. “I’ve made it pretty clear the whole time my focus is on the World Cup, and then after the World Cup, contracts will be sorted. There’s a lot that goes into it, but it shouldn’t be too far after the World Cup [when I decide].



“I love it up here [in Queensland], so the Dolphins are still definitely in the equation. I’ve seen a lot of people jump to the conclusion when I said I was going to the open market, and they’ve pencilled that in as I’m leaving the Dolphins, but that’s definitely not the case.” Meanwhile, Grant’s decision not to take up a player option in his favour with the Melbourne Storm for 2028 has added his name to the free agency market. Loading The hooker is likely to command north of $1 million a season, regardless of whether he remains in Victoria or seeks a change of scenery, leading to suggestions a lifestyle shift could shape the avid surfer’s path. But Grant, who is yet to win a premiership, despite becoming a State of Origin and Test football mainstay, stressed ambition would ultimately be the most compelling factor in his decision.



“I’m committed to being the best version of myself as a rugby league player. A lot of talk has been around surfboards and surfing, but I think ultimately, I just want to get the best out of my career as a rugby league player. Related Article NRL 2026 Titans legend’s warning as Harry Grant poaching rumours swirl “I want to win, I want to compete, and ultimately, that will be where my heart lies.” When asked if there was a lure of returning to Queensland, Grant simply said: “I’m worried about footy, I’m worried about rugby league right now and the World Cup.” While the Storm have long been a powerhouse of the competition, their crash back to reality in 2026 has opened the door for similarly struggling clubs to prove they have compelling goals for Grant to consider.



Melbourne were forced to endure the shock of coach Craig Bellamy’s diagnosis with a neurodegenerative disorder and the loss of star edge forward Eli Katoa after suffering a brain bleed during last year’s Pacific Championships campaign with Tonga. The Titans, meanwhile, have wallowed in the NRL’s bottom four for the past five seasons but have the nucleus of a talented spine that Grant could inspire: halfback Zane Harrison, five-eighth Jayden Campbell, and fullback Keano Kini. Grant, however, said nothing had changed in Melbourne to suggest their best days were behind them as a club, and a departure was no fait accompli, given his tight relationship with chairman Matt Tripp, director of football Frank Ponissi, and Bellamy. “Nothing has changed, it’s been a learning process as a leader and as a player,” he said.



“Early on in the year, you understand how much winning games does mean to you and what it does take to win, and I think we had a different year and a different journey in that regard. “But that’s all behind us now, and when it comes time to knuckle down and get back to work, we’ll do that. There are a number of guys down there working at the moment, but my focus is on the World Cup and the opportunity we’ve got here.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Stressed and out of pocket: David Jones’ great-great-great grandson is owed money, too
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesDavid Jones collapse Stressed and out of pocket: David Jones’ great-great-great grandson is owed money, too Jessica Yun November 10, 2026 — 8:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Ben Nothling, entrepreneur and co-founder of footwear brand Holster, has his own fond memories of David Jones. His are a little closer to home. “Dad would always tell us stories,” Nothling said. “[Jones would] go over to the UK on buying trips, and bring back premium goods.” Ben Nothling, a sixth-generation descendant of the Welsh entrepreneur David Jones, owns a shoe business. Lauren Biggs photography Nothling’s father Martin was describing David Jones, the enterprising Welsh merchant who founded the eponymously named department store in 1838. It makes Ben a sixth-generation descendant, or the great-great-great grandson of Jones. When Nothling senior learned the once-iconic retailer had fallen, he was lost for words. “He actually couldn’t believe it,” said Nothling. “He’s really sad it’s all come to that. How did they collapse?”



Nothling’s shoe business is owed $130,000 by David Jones, and among hundreds if not thousands of suppliers caught in the fallout of David Jones’ spectacular collapse. A picture of Welsh entrepreneur David Jones, taken around 1860. Fairfax Media After studying business, Nothling founded the label with his wife Natalie Miller 25 years ago after visiting Bali and returning with a selection of shoes that he resold to enthusiastic demand. After the husband-and-wife duo turned their hand to designing their own (Natalie designs the prototypes), their vegan slides, sandals and sneakers now turn over about $10 million every year and are sold in 30 countries. Around 2010, Holster entered David Jones and never ran into any issues – until a few months ago, after David Jones started pushing out payment terms. Two shipments of shoes delivered to David Jones in June and July weren’t paid for, which was unusual.



“David Jones was a big account to us … We dealt with them for 15 years. They’d always paid us on time,” said Nothling. “They came back with a weird email saying, ‘We need to check. We’ll come back to you.’ Soon as they were overdue, we froze their account.” Another shipment prepared for delivery, worth $118,000, was put on ice. David Jones’ finance team sent through some payment dates, but those came and went. “Nothing came in. Suddenly, they collapsed,” said Nothling. “It’s a lot of money to lose. It makes you quite stressed and angry.” “We could’ve lost more than a quarter of a million [dollars] if we kept shipping stock.”





“You’re just upset about the way the company was run,” said Nothling. “Suppliers all got treated not in a good way. You feel sorry for the staff. It’s just a huge ripple effect.” David Jones’ collapse isn’t the first that Nothling has had to contend with this year. After returning from a holiday in Bali with his family earlier this year, he learned that home shopping network TVSN was shutting down. TVSN, which is having its own war with suppliers, owes him about $30,000. Other than a shelf of goods at Holster’s head office on Noosa Beach in Queensland, Nothling doesn’t operate any retail stores of his own, opting to grow the business through wholesale and online channels. He’s already run the numbers on a scenario where he doesn’t see any of the money back. Holster will survive, though cash flow will take a hit. “We can get through it, but retail’s not great,” said Nothling. “It would give you a bit of a kick.”



“You gotta be a smart operator here to make money in business.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

A new play about former prime minister John Howard’s gun reforms in the aftermath of the 1996 Port Arthur massacre will premiere in La Boite Theatre’s 2027 season. Brisbane’s 101-year-old theatre company will enlist Neil Armfield, one of Australia’s most distinguished directors, to stage the play, with revered actor Darren Gilshenan in the role of Australia’s 25th prime minister. The announcement of La Boite’s new season follows multiple redundancies at the company last month and the resignation of artistic director Courtney Stewart in May. A new artistic director is yet to be appointed, and the new season has been curated by a three-person guest panel chaired by former La Boite artistic director David Berthold.



Berthold said Calibre was one of the best new Australian plays he had read. It was written for La Boite by Brisbane playwright and composer Paul Hodge, whose works include shows about Bill Clinton and Joh Bjelke-Petersen. Related Article Exclusive

Immigration nation ‘One of the great Australian achievements’: Howard praises immigration “It tells a story that happened 30 years ago, but it’s a story that is still in our headlines,” Berthold said. Armfield, whose work includes landmark productions of Cloudstreet and The Secret River, said Calibre tackles an extraordinary moment in Australia’s recent history. “What’s fascinating is the collision of personalities, convictions and political pressures, and the sheer difficulty of achieving change when the stakes are so high,” Armfield said.



John Howard was only six weeks into his 11-year prime ministership when 35 people were killed by a gunman in Tasmania’s Port Arthur. Howard subsequently spearheaded major restrictions on gun ownership, which became one of his key political legacies. To write the play, Hodge interviewed the prime minister, former premiers, gun-control campaigners, gun-lobby representatives, and the families of victims. The massacre was previously the subject of a 2021 movie, Nitram. La Boite’s 2027 season consists of five shows, with two world premieres and two return seasons of proven musical successes.



In addition to Calibre, the company will premiere real estate drama Offset by Anchuli Felicia King. Lady Beatle, a rock cabaret featuring Naomi Price (Calamity Jane), was previously a hit for La Boite when it premiered there in 2016. La Boite productions are staged at its 400-seat theatre, The Roundhouse, on the QUT Kelvin Grove campus. La Boite Bigger and Blacker 2.0 revives the cabaret by Steven Oliver (ABC’s Black Comedy) and Michael Griffiths for NAIDOC Week. The Weekend is an adaptation of the novel by Charlotte Wood about three women reunited at the beach house of their recently deceased friend.



La Boite announced four redundancies last month citing rising costs, changing audience behaviours and increasing pressure on traditional funding models. Related Article Entertainment Artistic director quits 100-year-old theatre company It also announced the elevation of acting chief executive Ian Prowse to the role of executive director and co-chief executive in January 2027, while the company recruits its next artistic director/co-chief executive. Prowse told this masthead he brings 30 years of senior executive experience, three of them at La Boite, to his new role. “I understand the importance of balancing our artistic ambitions with commercial realities, supporting our people, and building a sustainable future for the company.”



Prowse said he expected the new artistic director to be appointed by the end of 2026. Tickets for the 2027 season are on sale now. Get alerts on significant breaking news as it happens.

World.title: ‘Forever in our hearts’: Apprentice jockey Izzy Neale dies after race fall
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing ‘Forever in our hearts’: Apprentice jockey Izzy Neale dies after race fall Craig Kerry Updated November 10, 2026 — 8:06pm ,first published November 9, 2026 — 9:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Apprentice jockey Izzy Neale has died at age 22 following a fall at Warren on Sunday. Neale had been in a critical condition since the shocking fall, which happened after the Kieren Hazelton-trained Marnoo faltered near the 400m mark of the Cotton Cup. Izzy Neale has died aged 22. Instagram Neale fell heavily and was unconscious when airlifted to Dubbo Hospital. Marnoo was euthanised after suffering a near foreleg injury. Neale’s family released a statement late on Tuesday saying she was “dearly loved and will forever be in our hearts”.



“It was with great sadness and broken hearts that we announce the passing of our beloved Izzy, surrounded by her closest family and friends,” it read. “Izzy rode horses before she could walk. Her love of horses was a lifelong passion that, more recently, had grown into a love of racing. View post on X “We are deeply grateful for the love, kindness and support shown to Izzy and our family by her friends, the racing community and everyone who has been by our side during this heartbreaking time.” The family thanked Racing NSW, the NSW Jockeys’ Association and medical staff for their support. They said Neale, through organ donation, will give others the chance of life and bring some comfort to them amid the devastating loss.



Neale, who hailed from Merriwa in the Upper Hunter, was working for Scone trainer Scott Singleton, and had 88 winners in a professional racing career that started in February 2024. “She was the nicest kid you would ever meet. We are heartbroken,” Singleton said. Neale also spent time under Randwick trainer John Thompson, who posted: “An absolute beacon of shining light. Always happy. Always smiling. Loved by everyone who met her. The world is poorer for the loss of a beautiful young lady. Heartbreaking.” Neale had ridden in Sydney 11 times and won a Highway Handicap on It’s A Tata for Brett Robb at Rosehill in July. Izzy Neale after winning on It’s A Tata at Rosehill in July. Getty Images



Racing NSW called off Monday’s meeting at Neale’s home track of Scone out of respect for the rider. That meeting will now be held on Wednesday. Diego Montes de Oca, who was riding Shadow Dane, was dislodged shortly after Neale’s fall and taken to hospital by ambulance. He sustained soft tissue injuries to his left foot and was discharged from hospital on Monday. The remaining race on Sunday’s program was abandoned. Neale’s death is the first of a jockey from a race fall in NSW since 2017 at Warialda, when Darren Jones succumbed to his injuries. Frenchwoman Marina Morel died after a trackwork fall at Gulgong in February 2022. In March 2024, Italian jockey Stefano Cherchi died from a race fall at Canberra. Mitchell Starc has disputed Usman Khawaja’s explosive claim that every member of the Australian team knew about the ball-tampering plot during the infamous 2018 Test series against South Africa, declaring he has no intention of reading his former teammate’s book and suggesting their future relationship is now in Khawaja’s hands. Amid a series of disclosures in his autobiography, Sabr, which was released on Tuesday, Khawaja suggested the entire Australian team, including now captain Pat Cummins and other bowlers, knew about the plot to use sandpaper on the ball in the third Test in Cape Town eight years ago and that the tactic had also been deployed in the previous Test, in Gqeberha. Usman Khawaja has written about the sandpaper scandal in his new autobiography. Dan Peled But pressed on the ABC’s 7:30 on Tuesday night about whether specific players, including Cummins, were involved in conversations about ball tampering, Khawaja refused to answer. “I’m just not going to entertain that,” Khawaja said.



“And I say that for one reason – I wrote it [the details] in my book because it was a safe space for me to write. “It took a long time to, first, write the chapter .... and go over it and work out a way that it was as balanced as possible.” Asked specifically if Cummins had prior knowledge that sandpaper was being used to change the surface of the ball, Khawaja said: “I’m not going to answer that. I’ve written what I’ve written in my book. “I’ve come out and stood by those three guys [the suspended players David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft] and told my account of what I saw. “I’ve been very clear ... there are instances when I talk about ‘us’ and ‘them’, but I’ve been very clear in not naming names and staying out of it. I’m not going to start now.



“This has never been a witch hunt for me. “You’ve got to remember [that] Pat Cummins is a good friend of mine. Mitchell Starc, a lot of these guys [are and] other players in the team [are too]. “I’m not here to go on a witch hunt. All I’ve ever wanted is for us to take accountability as a team.” The latest sandpaper saga developments came as Starc’s wife and former Australian cricketer Alyssa Healy said she would have no problem sharing a commentary box with Khawaja and Warner this summer, despite describing the timing of the controversial book as “a little bit stinky”, while former England captain Michael Vaughan said he would have liked Khawaja to donate its profits to charity. Mitchell Starc said he “hadn’t paid much attention” to the claims made by Usman Khawaja in his autobiography. Janie Barrett

This time, the wounds of 2018 have been reopened not by the media but by two of Starc’s former Test teammates in Khawaja and Warner, with the latter saying everything in the book is “100 per cent” accurate. Mitchell Starc speaks to reporters at the Golden Sheaf Hotel on Tuesday afternoon. Janie Barrett



On 7:30, Khawaja was quizzed about whether he believed Cricket Australia perpetuated a “cover-up” to stop more players than the three affected from being banned. “I don’t feel like it was a thorough investigation,” Khawaja said. “Because I never got investigated – and I was sitting next to Cameron Bancroft the whole time. So it’s hard for me to say cover-up, but I will say it [the investigation] felt rushed.” As former Australian spinner Kerry O’Keeffe noted on Tuesday: “It’s the bubble around town. Who’s telling the truth? They could all be telling the truth.” Starc said he stood by a joint statement released in 2021 with fellow bowlers Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon denying they had any knowledge that sandpaper had been taken onto the field in Cape Town to tamper with the ball.



Sources close to the other three bowlers, speaking on the condition of anonymity, say they share Starc’s position and have no intention of backing away from their original statement. Cummins, the incumbent Test captain, is being encouraged to front the media this week and address allegations that he and others knew more than they have publicly acknowledged. “I thought we were here for the summer of cricket,” Starc said with a laugh. “I haven’t really paid much attention to it [the coverage of Khawaja’s claims]. Obviously, there are different opinions to about eight years ago. We were heavily drilled through the process at the time and since. I won’t speak on behalf of the bowlers, but where I stand, my opinion hasn’t changed. My recollection hasn’t changed from what we said in 2021.” Asked whether “everyone knew”, Starc responded: “It’s obviously in a book. That’s for someone to explain further. As far as our statement said [in 2021], we weren’t aware of it being taken on the field. That’s where I’ll leave it.” Asked whether he knew the ball was being tampered with in one way or another, Starc said: “We weren’t aware it was taken on the field to be tampered with. We saw it on the big screen [for the first time] in Cape Town. As far as the book’s concerned, I haven’t read it and probably won’t read it, so that’s for Usman to elaborate on.”



Starc also denied knowing that Bancroft or any other Australian player had used sandpaper during the second Test in Port Elizabeth, as alleged by Khawaja. “That’s the first I was aware of it [in Cape Town]. I’ll leave that for the said author to explain,” Starc said. Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins, Usman Khawaja and Josh Hazlewood. Getty Beyond the conflicting accounts of what unfolded in South Africa, Khawaja’s revelations appear to have strained relationships with some of his former teammates. Starc said he had not spoken to Khawaja “in the last day or two”, but when asked whether he would ever speak to him again, his response was telling.



“It’s up to him,” Starc said. One person who will have no choice but to work alongside Khawaja and Warner this summer is Healy, with all three part of the Kayo Sports and Fox Cricket commentary team. Alyssa Healy will share a commentary box with Usman Khawaja and David Warner this summer. Getty Images Speaking on the Keepin’ It Cricket podcast this week, Healy joked that she had been “scraping bits of Mitch off the bitumen after the bus just hit him over the last two days”. “The timing of it is a little bit stinky,” said the former Australian wicketkeeper. “I don’t like that. It’s coming off South Africa, which didn’t end well for the boys.”



But speaking on Tuesday, Healy dismissed suggestions there would be tension in the commentary box and said she had no intention of raising the controversy with either Khawaja or Warner, both long-time teammates of Starc. “I’m not one to sit there and worry about sitting next to anyone in the commentary box, regardless of who it is. We’re a team,” Healy said. Related Article Australian cricket Warner’s manager calls for honesty session after Cricket Australia refuses to re-open sandpaper investigation “From my perspective, it seems to be a little bit closer maybe for me than some of the other [commentators]. Most of the blokes back there just say, ‘Let’s move on and get back to the cricket’. But from my perspective, I’m completely comfortable with [working alongside them].” The controversy has generated so much attention since this masthead’s interview with Khawaja on Saturday that the retired opener admitted to Triple M on Tuesday even he had been surprised by the reaction. But Khawaja denied his revelations were motivated by money.



“The only gripe with me is that it’s come out in a book,” said Vaughan. “Obviously it’s a commercial game. Usman will say not, but I’d have loved for him to have announced that he’s bringing a book out and all the proceeds are going to charity.” With Australia preparing for the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on December 9, Starc made no secret of his frustration that the scandal had once again become a major talking point. “It’s definitely disappointing,” he said. “That’s what we’re talking about heading into what has already kicked off an exciting summer. Different people felt different ways about it at the time and throughout, and certainly through the last eight years. “I think not only the certain players, but certainly, there’s some staff members. ‘Boof’ [coach Darren Lehmann] for one has spoken a little bit as well. He’s not to be forgotten in all of that, too. I think Travis [Head] said it best the other day that the group has changed a lot. We certainly look forward to what’s coming up more so than what’s been gone.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Down, down: Hapless Coles crow finally checks out after weeks-long ordeal
World.content:
NationalQueenslandWildlife Down, down: Hapless Coles crow finally checks out after weeks-long ordeal Marissa Calligeros and Julius Dennis November 10, 2026 — 9:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
