A crow that spent weeks perched atop a fluorescent light inside a Coles supermarket on Brisbane’s northside has finally left the store. A spokesman for Coles assured concerned customers that the bird was removed safely from the North Lakes store on Tuesday morning, after repeated failed attempts to catch it and coax it outside during its two-week ordeal. “We’re pleased to confirm the crow has been safely removed from our store, and we thank our customers and the community for their patience,” the spokesman said. The crow bides its time inside the North Lakes Coles last week. Julius Dennis However, he refused to reveal exactly how the crow was removed, or whether it made its own way to freedom.



The bird’s welfare generated concern among shoppers and hundreds of local Facebook users, who were initially outraged by rumours that Coles had contracted a third party to euthanise the bird. Coles denied that rumour last week. Many customers walked below the crow without even noticing it. Julius Dennis The crow appeared frazzled during its fortnight inside the store, perched on top of a ceiling light above the cosmetics aisle and leaving excrement on the floor below. The RSPCA visited the supermarket and was told food and water had been made available.



Few people were more relieved at the news of the bird’s new-found freedom on Tuesday than Melissa Webb, who works at a clothing store in the North Lakes shopping centre. Related Article Wildlife ‘I don’t understand’: Questions over plight of crow stuck in supermarket for 10 days Webb had been checking on the crow during her lunch break each day and advocating online for its rescue. But she remains worried about its welfare. “We’re pretty concerned that it will need some kind of care, or at least a good check over after this ordeal,” Webb said. “Hearing that it was just ‘removed’ is not good enough. I think Coles’ conduct around the entire situation has been really sad, especially considering how long the crow was in there, when we have local organisations who have done plenty of animal rescues in other stores and in other Westfields.”

World.title: ‘Definitely in the equation’: Kangaroos stars reveal contract stances
World.content:
SportNRLRugby League World Cup ‘Definitely in the equation’: Kangaroos stars reveal contract stances Nick Wright November 10, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Kangaroos winger Jack Bostock says he’s yet to decide his playing future, as Australian teammate Harry Grant shed light on the motives that would dictate his next move. The off-contract pair have thrown their focus on Australia’s Rugby League World Cup final clash against New Zealand at Suncorp Stadium on Sunday, before attention will turn to their future in the NRL. Bostock has been heavily linked to a shift away from the Dolphins to a host of New South Wales clubs – spearheaded by his junior outfit, the Dragons – while Grant is in the Gold Coast Titans’ sights. Harry Grant and Jack Bostock both insist their current NRL clubs are not out of the race for their signatures. Getty Bostock’s asking price has only risen since returning from a ruptured ACL in round nine, in a season that has included a Blues debut and seven tries in four World Cup appearances.



His form has tightened the retention battle of the Dolphins, who have re-signed Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow but are yet to secure the in-demand Herbie Farnworth, among other off-contract stars. Related Article Rugby League World Cup Walsh and Ponga’s first chapter was a battle for the ages. They are just beginning Bostock is adamant he has made no definitive call on where he will sign his next deal, while stressing the Redcliffe-based side remained well in the hunt for his services. “Apparently … I’m going to [every club], so I’m not too sure – maybe I’m going to play three or four games at each club in 2028,” he joked. “I’ve made it pretty clear the whole time my focus is on the World Cup, and then after the World Cup, contracts will be sorted. There’s a lot that goes into it, but it shouldn’t be too far after the World Cup [when I decide].



“I love it up here [in Queensland], so the Dolphins are still definitely in the equation. I’ve seen a lot of people jump to the conclusion when I said I was going to the open market, and they’ve pencilled that in as I’m leaving the Dolphins, but that’s definitely not the case.” Meanwhile, Grant’s decision not to take up a player option in his favour with the Melbourne Storm for 2028 has added his name to the free agency market. Loading The hooker is likely to command north of $1 million a season, regardless of whether he remains in Victoria or seeks a change of scenery, leading to suggestions a lifestyle shift could shape the avid surfer’s path. But Grant, who is yet to win a premiership, despite becoming a State of Origin and Test football mainstay, stressed ambition would ultimately be the most compelling factor in his decision.



“I’m committed to being the best version of myself as a rugby league player. A lot of talk has been around surfboards and surfing, but I think ultimately, I just want to get the best out of my career as a rugby league player. Related Article NRL 2026 Titans legend’s warning as Harry Grant poaching rumours swirl “I want to win, I want to compete, and ultimately, that will be where my heart lies.” When asked if there was a lure of returning to Queensland, Grant simply said: “I’m worried about footy, I’m worried about rugby league right now and the World Cup.” While the Storm have long been a powerhouse of the competition, their crash back to reality in 2026 has opened the door for similarly struggling clubs to prove they have compelling goals for Grant to consider.



Melbourne were forced to endure the shock of coach Craig Bellamy’s diagnosis with a neurodegenerative disorder and the loss of star edge forward Eli Katoa after suffering a brain bleed during last year’s Pacific Championships campaign with Tonga. The Titans, meanwhile, have wallowed in the NRL’s bottom four for the past five seasons but have the nucleus of a talented spine that Grant could inspire: halfback Zane Harrison, five-eighth Jayden Campbell, and fullback Keano Kini. Grant, however, said nothing had changed in Melbourne to suggest their best days were behind them as a club, and a departure was no fait accompli, given his tight relationship with chairman Matt Tripp, director of football Frank Ponissi, and Bellamy. “Nothing has changed, it’s been a learning process as a leader and as a player,” he said.



“Early on in the year, you understand how much winning games does mean to you and what it does take to win, and I think we had a different year and a different journey in that regard. “But that’s all behind us now, and when it comes time to knuckle down and get back to work, we’ll do that. There are a number of guys down there working at the moment, but my focus is on the World Cup and the opportunity we’ve got here.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

“As Arnotts market every variation of their Ginger Nut Biscuits as ‘the original one’ I had trouble obtaining the jaw breaking variety I was raised on in Sydney as a child,” informs Andrew McCarthy of Toormina. “The secret is in the bar code. “When Gregory Nell was talking about Ginger Nuts from Queensland, I thought he was referring to a certain political leader,” admits Peter Miniutti of Ashbury. “But then I remembered ginger is meant to be anti-inflammatory.”

“Thank you, Anne Shearman for reminding me of the David Jones catalogue (C8),” says Elizabeth Savage of Hughes (ACT). “As a child in Yeoval in the 1950s, it was a promise of a world beyond our local area, and a source of clothing. Unfortunately one year, two of us turned up at our Sunday School Anniversary in the same dress, both from the DJ’s catalogue!”

“We didn’t have a David Jones in Gosford and Mum would take me to F J Palmer and Sons to buy my Stamina clothes,” writes Allan Gibson of Cherrybrook. “And I remember the packs of Stamina cards in the packet in the top pocket. The cards featured Men of Stamina with 18 in each pack which featured an image of Pegasus.”

Tony Everett of Wareemba says that “recent discussion on the closing of DJ’s has recalled other long gone Sydney institutions. One was the Hotel Australia in Castlereagh Street. World.title: Stressed and out of pocket: David Jones’ great-great-great grandson is owed money, too
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesDavid Jones collapse Stressed and out of pocket: David Jones’ great-great-great grandson is owed money, too Jessica Yun November 10, 2026 — 8:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Ben Nothling, entrepreneur and co-founder of footwear brand Holster, has his own fond memories of David Jones. His are a little closer to home. “Dad would always tell us stories,” Nothling said. “[Jones would] go over to the UK on buying trips, and bring back premium goods.” Ben Nothling, a sixth-generation descendant of the Welsh entrepreneur David Jones, owns a shoe business. Lauren Biggs photography Nothling’s father Martin was describing David Jones, the enterprising Welsh merchant who founded the eponymously named department store in 1838. It makes Ben a sixth-generation descendant, or the great-great-great grandson of Jones. When Nothling senior learned the once-iconic retailer had fallen, he was lost for words. “He actually couldn’t believe it,” said Nothling. “He’s really sad it’s all come to that. How did they collapse?”



Nothling’s shoe business is owed $130,000 by David Jones, and among hundreds if not thousands of suppliers caught in the fallout of David Jones’ spectacular collapse. A picture of Welsh entrepreneur David Jones, taken around 1860. Fairfax Media After studying business, Nothling founded the label with his wife Natalie Miller 25 years ago after visiting Bali and returning with a selection of shoes that he resold to enthusiastic demand. After the husband-and-wife duo turned their hand to designing their own (Natalie designs the prototypes), their vegan slides, sandals and sneakers now turn over about $10 million every year and are sold in 30 countries. Around 2010, Holster entered David Jones and never ran into any issues – until a few months ago, after David Jones started pushing out payment terms. Two shipments of shoes delivered to David Jones in June and July weren’t paid for, which was unusual.



“David Jones was a big account to us … We dealt with them for 15 years. They’d always paid us on time,” said Nothling. “They came back with a weird email saying, ‘We need to check. We’ll come back to you.’ Soon as they were overdue, we froze their account.” Another shipment prepared for delivery, worth $118,000, was put on ice. David Jones’ finance team sent through some payment dates, but those came and went. “Nothing came in. Suddenly, they collapsed,” said Nothling. “It’s a lot of money to lose. It makes you quite stressed and angry.” “We could’ve lost more than a quarter of a million [dollars] if we kept shipping stock.”





“You’re just upset about the way the company was run,” said Nothling. “Suppliers all got treated not in a good way. You feel sorry for the staff. It’s just a huge ripple effect.” David Jones’ collapse isn’t the first that Nothling has had to contend with this year. After returning from a holiday in Bali with his family earlier this year, he learned that home shopping network TVSN was shutting down. TVSN, which is having its own war with suppliers, owes him about $30,000. Other than a shelf of goods at Holster’s head office on Noosa Beach in Queensland, Nothling doesn’t operate any retail stores of his own, opting to grow the business through wholesale and online channels. He’s already run the numbers on a scenario where he doesn’t see any of the money back. Holster will survive, though cash flow will take a hit. “We can get through it, but retail’s not great,” said Nothling. “It would give you a bit of a kick.”



“You gotta be a smart operator here to make money in business.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.content:
NationalQueenslandEntertainment Howard’s Port Arthur gun reforms to take centre stage in new Brisbane play Nick Dent November 10, 2026 — 8:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A new play about former prime minister John Howard’s gun reforms in the aftermath of the 1996 Port Arthur massacre will premiere in La Boite Theatre’s 2027 season. Brisbane’s 101-year-old theatre company will enlist Neil Armfield, one of Australia’s most distinguished directors, to stage the play, with revered actor Darren Gilshenan in the role of Australia’s 25th prime minister. The announcement of La Boite’s new season follows multiple redundancies at the company last month and the resignation of artistic director Courtney Stewart in May. A new artistic director is yet to be appointed, and the new season has been curated by a three-person guest panel chaired by former La Boite artistic director David Berthold.



Berthold said Calibre was one of the best new Australian plays he had read. It was written for La Boite by Brisbane playwright and composer Paul Hodge, whose works include shows about Bill Clinton and Joh Bjelke-Petersen. Related Article Exclusive

Immigration nation ‘One of the great Australian achievements’: Howard praises immigration “It tells a story that happened 30 years ago, but it’s a story that is still in our headlines,” Berthold said. Armfield, whose work includes landmark productions of Cloudstreet and The Secret River, said Calibre tackles an extraordinary moment in Australia’s recent history. “What’s fascinating is the collision of personalities, convictions and political pressures, and the sheer difficulty of achieving change when the stakes are so high,” Armfield said.



John Howard was only six weeks into his 11-year prime ministership when 35 people were killed by a gunman in Tasmania’s Port Arthur. Howard subsequently spearheaded major restrictions on gun ownership, which became one of his key political legacies. To write the play, Hodge interviewed the prime minister, former premiers, gun-control campaigners, gun-lobby representatives, and the families of victims. The massacre was previously the subject of a 2021 movie, Nitram. La Boite’s 2027 season consists of five shows, with two world premieres and two return seasons of proven musical successes.



In addition to Calibre, the company will premiere real estate drama Offset by Anchuli Felicia King. Lady Beatle, a rock cabaret featuring Naomi Price (Calamity Jane), was previously a hit for La Boite when it premiered there in 2016. La Boite productions are staged at its 400-seat theatre, The Roundhouse, on the QUT Kelvin Grove campus. La Boite Bigger and Blacker 2.0 revives the cabaret by Steven Oliver (ABC’s Black Comedy) and Michael Griffiths for NAIDOC Week. The Weekend is an adaptation of the novel by Charlotte Wood about three women reunited at the beach house of their recently deceased friend.



La Boite announced four redundancies last month citing rising costs, changing audience behaviours and increasing pressure on traditional funding models. Related Article Entertainment Artistic director quits 100-year-old theatre company It also announced the elevation of acting chief executive Ian Prowse to the role of executive director and co-chief executive in January 2027, while the company recruits its next artistic director/co-chief executive. Prowse told this masthead he brings 30 years of senior executive experience, three of them at La Boite, to his new role. “I understand the importance of balancing our artistic ambitions with commercial realities, supporting our people, and building a sustainable future for the company.”



Prowse said he expected the new artistic director to be appointed by the end of 2026. Tickets for the 2027 season are on sale now. Get alerts on significant breaking news as it happens.

World.title: ‘Forever in our hearts’: Apprentice jockey Izzy Neale dies after race fall
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing ‘Forever in our hearts’: Apprentice jockey Izzy Neale dies after race fall Craig Kerry Updated November 10, 2026 — 8:06pm ,first published November 9, 2026 — 9:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Apprentice jockey Izzy Neale has died at age 22 following a fall at Warren on Sunday. Neale had been in a critical condition since the shocking fall, which happened after the Kieren Hazelton-trained Marnoo faltered near the 400m mark of the Cotton Cup. Izzy Neale has died aged 22. Instagram Neale fell heavily and was unconscious when airlifted to Dubbo Hospital. Marnoo was euthanised after suffering a near foreleg injury. Neale’s family released a statement late on Tuesday saying she was “dearly loved and will forever be in our hearts”.



“It was with great sadness and broken hearts that we announce the passing of our beloved Izzy, surrounded by her closest family and friends,” it read. “Izzy rode horses before she could walk. Her love of horses was a lifelong passion that, more recently, had grown into a love of racing. View post on X “We are deeply grateful for the love, kindness and support shown to Izzy and our family by her friends, the racing community and everyone who has been by our side during this heartbreaking time.” The family thanked Racing NSW, the NSW Jockeys’ Association and medical staff for their support. They said Neale, through organ donation, will give others the chance of life and bring some comfort to them amid the devastating loss.



Neale, who hailed from Merriwa in the Upper Hunter, was working for Scone trainer Scott Singleton, and had 88 winners in a professional racing career that started in February 2024. “She was the nicest kid you would ever meet. We are heartbroken,” Singleton said. Neale also spent time under Randwick trainer John Thompson, who posted: “An absolute beacon of shining light. Always happy. Always smiling. Loved by everyone who met her. The world is poorer for the loss of a beautiful young lady. Heartbreaking.” Neale had ridden in Sydney 11 times and won a Highway Handicap on It’s A Tata for Brett Robb at Rosehill in July. Izzy Neale after winning on It’s A Tata at Rosehill in July. Getty Images



Racing NSW called off Monday’s meeting at Neale’s home track of Scone out of respect for the rider. That meeting will now be held on Wednesday. Diego Montes de Oca, who was riding Shadow Dane, was dislodged shortly after Neale’s fall and taken to hospital by ambulance. He sustained soft tissue injuries to his left foot and was discharged from hospital on Monday. The remaining race on Sunday’s program was abandoned. Neale’s death is the first of a jockey from a race fall in NSW since 2017 at Warialda, when Darren Jones succumbed to his injuries. Frenchwoman Marina Morel died after a trackwork fall at Gulgong in February 2022. In March 2024, Italian jockey Stefano Cherchi died from a race fall at Canberra. World.title: Inside the Wellington Town Hall after 13 years shut
World.content:
Audio player for " Wellington town hall redevelopment enters final phase " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/regions/2508279%2Finside-the-wellington-town-hall-after-13-years-shut

Wellington town hall redevelopment enters final phase Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

After 13 years boarded up and hundreds of millions of dollars in a budget blowout, the Wellington Town Hall upgrade has entered its final phase.

RNZ got a look inside the building on Tuesday, a redevelopment which advocates hope will leave the building's controversial legacy in the past, and become a gamechanger for cultural life in the city.

The building was sitting on its original unreinforced concrete piles on reclaimed coastal land when in 2013 it was deemed earthquake prone. The original budget for the project of about $43 million blew out several times at Wellington City Council to nearly $330m.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408162812112

The council said it was still doing final accounting, but programme manager for Te Ngākau, Farzad Zamani, said the final phase was looking as though it would come in $20m under the latest budget. He said the construction was extremely challenging.

"It's probably been one of the most complex strengthening projects in the history of New Zealand. So we had to lift the building up, base isolate the building which basically separated the building over-ground to the ground."

A stream was running underneath the building, and ground conditions were "terrible", Zamani said. Construction had to be balanced with keeping the Town Hall's top quality acoustics and retaining its heritage fabric.

The town hall has been boarded up for 13 years. RNZ / Mark Papalii

A modern entrance greets people as they walk through the doors - including light installations draping from the ceiling incorporating mana whenua and coastal design. The 121-year-old Adam Auditorium, with its famed acoustics and original 1906 organ, has been restored. Strengthening and restoration was designed by Athfield Architects and Archifact.

The town hall will also become home of the National Music Centre, a collaboration between Te Herenga Waka Victoria University of Wellington's school of music and the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra (NZSO).

Head of the music school, Professor Kim Cunio, said students will be able to practise and perform in the town hall with professional musicians, in new teaching and performance spaces.

Musicians in the new space. RNZ / Mark Papalii

He said Wellingtonians were right to scrutinise the "huge" cost of the project, adding that economic modelling showed there was a $3.2 return to every dollar of arts investment in New Zealand - and students in the inner-city would have flow-on effects.

"This is a really radical thing, what happens when you get hundreds of young people into a piece of civic infrastructure.

"Just imagine this building, everywhere you look there's someone practising and playing, so the building will just be alive with music all day."

Marc Feldman and Kim Cunio. RNZ / Mark Papalii

He said the venue could help build a future for young New Zealand musicians, who right now automatically look overseas for their careers.

"We have to offer actually something else, and I think culture is the thing that keeps young people in a town. Young people will get to make music, make art... but they'll also get to be a part of it."

Chief executive of the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra Marc Feldman said the acoustics in the town hall are phenomenal - and the music won't disappoint.

"It's sonically incredible whether you have a solo cello, or 150 musicians on stage, it is just phenomenal, you can hear everybody breathing or you're going to be able to hear the power of everything really up close - and the whole gamut of music is going to be here."

The council said it was still doing final accounting. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Feldman said the NZSO will be based at the site 135 days a year, and Wellingtonians can expect all types of sounds, from all types of genres.

Twenty-year-old trombonist Jakob Elijas, who's just completed three years of his music degree, said he wants the town hall to encourage other young musicians to study music.

"It's the difference between feeling inspired to make art and feeling uninspired. I think that your environment really shapes the music or art you create, in the sense that it gives you something bigger than yourself to look up to and be inspired by."

World.title: Punjabi community mourns three young people killed in Takinini BurgerFuel crash
World.content:
A Punjabi community leader has paid tribute to three young people killed in a Takanini crash on Sunday night.

The trio died after the car they were in lost control at a roundabout on Great South Road, came off the road and tore through an Auckland BurgerFuel restaurant.

Daljit Singh, spokesperson for the Supreme Sikh Society of New Zealand. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Posting on social media, president of the Central Sikh Association and Supreme Sikh Society Daljit Singh said they were "three young Indian Punjabis".

He added that it was "very sad news for the community", noting the crash happened on the night of Diwali.

"We cannot share their details or any information yet," Singh said.

"All three bodies will be sent to India as per the wishes of the family and we are in contact with the family members.

"On behalf of the community, our condolences are with family, friends at this sad time and the community will be asked for help as police investigations are completed."

Information about the trio would be shared once the police investigation was completed, he said.

Emergency services were called to the crash just after 10:15pm on Sunday night.

All three occupants were pronounced dead at the scene, police said. No one inside the building was injured.

World.title: Warning of possible floods amid severe thunderstorm alerts for North Island
World.content:
Severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours could hit much of the North Island, with multiple weather alerts in place.

MetService has issued an orange heavy rain warning for Bay of Plenty east of Whakatane, and the ranges of Tairawhiti north of Tokomaru Bay, until 10pm on Wednesday.

Thunderstorms and localised downpours are possible with rainfall intensities of 25mm-40mm an hour, meaning rivers may rise rapidly and there could be surface flooding and slips, the forecaster said.

Severe thunderstorm watches are in place across Auckland, Great Barrier Island, Coromandel Peninsula, Waikato and Bay of Plenty until 5am.

Heavy rain watches cover Auckland through to the central plateau, as well as the ranges of Westland District about and north of Mt Cook.

Driving conditions will be hazardous with surface flooding and poor visibility in heavy rain.

The forecasts follow heavy rain and storms in Auckland, and Canterbury on Friday and Saturday.

MetService meteorologist John Law said there were intense bursts of rainfall and flashes of lightning on Monday.

Most of the lightning struck off the coast of western Auckland and Waikato, with rain from Northland to Waitomo, he said.

Auckland, Great Barrier Island and Coromandel Peninsula are under severe thunderstorm watches until 2am on Wednesday, and Northland until 10pm.

MetService says people in these areas should be on the lookout for threatening weather conditions and monitor for possible severe thunderstorm warnings.

World.title: New Zealand gets another 'Fossil of the Day' award at COP31 climate conference
World.content:
New Zealand has continued its dubious run of 'Fossil of the Day' awards at the COP31 annual climate conference, winning on the opening day.

It's the fifth time in six years that New Zealand has received one of the awards, given out each day of the annual summit to countries seen to be backsliding on or blocking climate action.

Climate Action Network International (CAN), the NGO that hands out the awards, said New Zealand won for its "climate ambition" in dismantling its own climate commitments.

The citation includes the current shortfall to meeting New Zealand's Paris Agreement pledge, the formal complaint laid by a Dutch NGO over claims New Zealand has breached climate promises in its free trade agreement with the EU, and the government's decision to block legal action against climate polluters, including an existing court case.

New Zealand received the award last year for the government's decision to weaken the country's methane emissions target.

It was also given the award in 2021, 2022, and 2023.

"In just three years, [New Zealand's government] has gutted methane targets, let agricultural polluters off the hook and changed the law to shield corporations from climate litigation," CAN said.

The award was 'accepted' on behalf of New Zealand by one of CAN's New Zealand representatives, Bianca Ranson.

Ranson's father, Ngāpuhi climate activist Mike Smith, took the case against six major emitters that prompted the government's decision to block tort-based litigation over climate change.

"This government has placed the interests of corporate polluters and profit above its international climate commitments," Ranson said.

"These legal actions have profound implications for climate defenders and Indigenous peoples around the world, and we will continue to fight corporate polluters and negligent states."

WWF-New Zealand spokesperson Teall Crossen, who was attending COP31 at Antalya in Türkiye, said the award was embarrassing for a country that once positioned itself as a climate leader.

"As countries come together to try and find climate solutions, Aotearoa is standing out for all the wrong reasons with its appalling climate backsliding and continued reliance on fossil fuels."

It sent a message that "the world is watching", Crossen said.

"Whoever forms the next government needs to lift its game with a credible plan to phase out fossil fuels and make up the ground we've lost."

A spokesperson for caretaker climate minister Simon Watts said the minister was expecting "a constructive and positive COP31 and will be focused on opportunities to deepen climate change cooperation with key partners to support our transition to a climate resilient economy through innovation, technologies, and investment".

New Zealand would also be at the conference to "reinforce Pacific leadership on climate ambition and climate resilience, and to help secure international support for the region's priorities", the spokesperson said.

World.title: Ngāi Tūhoe mourns treasured son Tā Pou Temara
World.content:
Tears and tributes have flowed in Ruatāhuna as mourners from across the country gather to farewell Tā William Te Rangiua Pou Temara.

The celebrated academic, author, historian and teacher of Ngāi Tūhoe descent died on Sunday, surrounded by whānau.

He returned to Mataatua marae yesterday, to his hapū Te Urewera, where he will lie until Thursday.

Whitiaua Ropitini (Ngāi Tūhoe) told Pūkāea News Tā Pou was among the last of a generation raised by kuia and kaumātua, immersed in the tikanga and mātauranga of Te Urewera.

"I pakeke mai i te wā e tunu kai tonu ana ratou i runga i te ahi, e whai tonu ana. e hono tonu ana, e noho ki roto i te tūturutanga o taua ao. E whai tonu ana, e hono tonu ana te noho i roto i te tuturutanga o te taiao i te Urewera, i te tapu o Te Urewera i pakeke mai i roto i ngā tikanga. Koia tēnei reanga. kua tokoiti o te kainga, ka mutu pupuri ki ngā kōrero pupuri ki ngā mātauranga i kite rawa ia."

Ropitini said Tā Pou grew up when meals were still cooked over open fires. His knowledge came from living those traditions, making the preservation of what he shared all the more important as his generation dwindled.

Pūkāea News was at Mataatua marae as he was welcomed home for the final time.

Video player removed for printing https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ah6CX2RaOHA

Tā Pou Temara returns home to Mataatua Marae. Video / Pūkāea News

A man loved and mourned by many

Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po waiting to be welcomed onto Mataatua Marae. Pūkāea News

Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po led the first ope (group) onto Mataatua marae this morning it included a large contingent from Tainui, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Porou and Ngāti Awa.

Ngāti Awa also brought the kawe mate of Tā Hirini Moko Mead, another revered leader lost this year.

Rāhui Papa said the outpouring of grief reflected the standing of Tā Pou acknowledging specifically his enduring connection with Tainui and the Kiingitanga.

Kaihaka prepare to welcome manuhiri at Mataatua Marae in Ruatāhuna. Pūkāea News

Ko te amorangi ki mua, Ko te hāpai ō ki muri

As news of his death spread, Mataatua Marae and all marae across Ruatāhuna alongside whānau from across Te Rohe Pōtae o Tūhoe rallied to prepare Mataatua marae for his homecoming.

Te Kaahuirangi Te Rire told Pūkāea News the hāpai ō divided into groups to prepare for the influx of manuhiri.

Some organised the pōwhiri, others readied food and facilities, while others gathered meat and supplies.

Ruatāhuna ringawera hard at work preparing to host the masses. Pūkāea News

She said the many people working in front of and behind the pae reflected the love his people held for their kaumātua.

"Ahakoa te taumaha kei roto i a matou, ko te mea nui kei te oti nga mahi i runga i te aroha koira te mea nui kia matou kia kaua e pokea mātou I te taumaha pea..."

Despite their grief, she said, aroha remained at the heart of the work.
